While lawmakers negotiate and sometimes include various priorities, that is not the same as covertly inserting funds.

claim: "Forty percent of people in this country, illegally, are overstaying visas."
rationale: For the United States, multiple government and independent analyses in recent years have estimated that roughly four in ten unauthorized immigrants are visa overstays. That share depends on the year and methodology, so the statement is broadly accurate as a summary for U.S. estimates but would be misleading without specifying country and time period.

claim: "When people enter the service, there’s not a mental health evaluation."
rationale: The claim states categorically that no mental‑health evaluation occurs when people enter “the service.” In many common contexts (for example U.S. military entry and many government or clinical service intakes) applicants undergo medical entrance exams or intake screenings that include mental‑health questions, history review, or standardized screening instruments. Although a full psychiatric evaluation is not always performed for every entrant, the absolute statement that there is no mental‑health evaluation is inaccurate.

claim: "More than 27,000 Rhode Island jobs depend on trade with Canada."
rationale: I could not verify the specific figure of “more than 27,000” Rhode Island jobs tied to trade with Canada; official trade-job statistics are typically reported by year and by definition (direct vs. indirect) and available sources do not clearly support this precise number. Without a cited source or year the claim appears unsubstantiated and likely overstates what is reported in public trade-employment data.

claim: Says Barack Obama "put in place a board that can tell people ultimately what treatments they're going to receive."
rationale: This is inaccurate. The Affordable Care Act created bodies such as the Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) to recommend ways to curb Medicare cost growth and entities like PCORI for research, but the law explicitly did not give them authority to dictate individual patients' medical treatments or 'tell people what treatments they're going to receive.' Their roles were limited to policy recommendations and research, not direct clinical decision-making.

claim: Says in Chicago, "we take more guns off the streets than New York or L.A."
rationale: The blanket claim that Chicago removes more guns from the streets than New York City or Los Angeles is not supported by available law‑enforcement and public reporting: NYPD historically recovers more firearms annually than the Chicago Police Department, and LA data vary year to year. Without a specific timeframe or metric (seizures, recoveries, or arrests) the assertion as stated is misleading and likely false.

claim: "At my first ‘Let’s Get to Work Day’ … we sold out;" more than 240 dozen doughnuts by 8:30 a.m.
rationale: The claim gives a precise, high-volume sales figure (>240 dozen = >2,880 doughnuts) by 8:30 a.m. at a specific event, but I have no verifiable evidence in my knowledge base to confirm such a sale. Without contemporaneous receipts, organizer statements, or reliable reporting documenting that exact count and time, the claim remains unverified and should be treated as likely false.

claim: "California is 49th out of 50 in the United States in per capita housing units. Only Utah can lay claim to being lowest in per capita production."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate and imprecise. Rankings of housing units per capita vary by year and the metric (total units per resident vs. new units produced per year), and historically states such as New Jersey, New York, and Massachusetts have often ranked below California on units-per-person; Utah is not uniquely the lowest producer in every measure. The phrase “per capita production” is ambiguous and the claim presents a definitive ranking without a cited year or dataset.

claim: A second impeachment means Donald Trump loses his lifetime pension, travel allowance, Secret Service detail, and his ability to run for public office.
rationale: Impeachment by the House alone does not strip benefits or bar someone from future office — only a Senate conviction can remove from office and the Senate can also vote to disqualify from holding future federal office. Pensions, travel allowances and Secret Service protection are set by statute (e.g., the Former Presidents Act) and are not automatically revoked by impeachment or conviction; removing those benefits would generally require separate legislative or legal action.

claim: "Taxes for every New Yorker are lower today than when I started"
rationale: The claim is a universal statement that all New Yorkers pay lower taxes now than at an unspecified start date; that is almost certainly false. Tax burden depends on type (state income, local property, sales, federal), income, and locality, and many New Yorkers have seen higher property or local taxes or different state tax liabilities since the referenced start date. Even when some state tax rates or credits were changed, those changes did not uniformly reduce taxes for every single resident.

claim: Over the last 10 years, incomes for the top 1 percent "have grown." Meanwhile, the bottom half of the country, "they've seen their wages stagnate."
rationale: Broadly true: data from tax and household surveys over the past decade show that income gains have been concentrated at the very top, with the top 1% capturing a disproportionate share of national income growth. By contrast, median and lower-half wages and household incomes have grown little in real (inflation-adjusted) terms, so many in the bottom 50% experienced stagnation.

claim: "Actually, I won Wisconsin."
rationale: The sentence provides no speaker or timeframe, so as stated it is unverifiable and misleading. If intended to refer to the 2020 U.S. presidential election it is false—Joe Biden won Wisconsin; if intended to refer to 2016 it would be true that Donald Trump won Wisconsin. Because the claim lacks necessary context I rate the bare assertion false.

claim: "Japan drops vax rollout"
rationale: The statement that "Japan drops vax rollout" is false. Japan implemented and continued COVID-19 vaccination and booster campaigns and administered large numbers of doses; while there were temporary delays or isolated pauses (e.g., investigations or batch recalls), the country did not abandon its vaccination program. The claim omits timeframe and context, which would be necessary to assess specific temporary actions.

claim: Twenty-seven percent of Californians, almost 11 million, "were born in a foreign land."
rationale: U.S. Census Bureau/American Community Survey estimates put California's foreign-born share at roughly 27%, which corresponds to about 10.5–10.8 million people in recent ACS years — close to “almost 11 million.” The phrase “born in a foreign land” aligns with the Census definition of foreign‑born. Minor year-to-year changes can affect the exact count but the claim matches recent official estimates.

claim: "President Trump just saved Christmas for 13 million retirees."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: there is no documented, specific action by President Trump that unambiguously "saved Christmas" for exactly 13 million retirees. Major policy changes affecting millions (e.g., Social Security tax changes or benefit payments) would require legislation or clear executive action and public reporting, and no credible evidence ties a concrete policy to that precise claim or figure.

claim: "Congressman Cicilline, when he was the mayor of Providence, espoused a sanctuary city."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Mayor David Cicilline formally declared or publicly campaigned for Providence to be a designated "sanctuary city" while he was mayor (2003–2011). He did support immigrant-friendly policies and inclusion efforts, but that is different from officially espousing sanctuary-city status. Given the ambiguous use of "espoused" and lack of documentation of a formal sanctuary declaration under his administration, the claim is not supported.

claim: California’s shipping backlog is, in part, caused by a "California Truck Ban which says all trucks must be 2011 or newer and a law called AB 5 which prohibits Owner Operators."
rationale: The claim misstates both the truck rule and AB5’s effect. California and individual ports have adopted clean-truck/emissions rules that phase out older diesel rigs, but there is no single statewide “2011 or newer” truck ban that universally applies; model-year thresholds have varied by program and port. AB5 tightened independent‑contractor classification and initially affected some owner‑operators, but it did not outright prohibit owner‑operators and trucking received legal and legislative exemptions afterward. Major causes of port/backlog problems have been COVID demand surges, labor and chassis shortages, and terminal congestion rather than solely these laws.

claim: "Since 1970, the Clean Air Act has reduced toxic and health-threatening air pollution by 60 percent while our economy has grown more than 200 percent."
rationale: Government analyses (notably EPA summaries) report large declines in major air pollutants since the 1970 Clean Air Act amendments — commonly cited reductions are on the order of 60–70% for key pollutants — while U.S. real GDP has increased by more than 200% since 1970. The claim matches widely reported EPA statistics linking substantial emissions reductions with continued economic growth.

claim: Says he didn't cancel a political rally because after Sept. 11, "the New York Stock Exchange was open the following day."
rationale: The statement is incorrect. After the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks the New York Stock Exchange suspended trading and did not reopen the next day; the NYSE remained closed for the rest of that week and reopened on Sept. 17, 2001. Therefore saying it was "open the following day" misstates the historical fact.

claim: U.S. tariffs on China are "not hurting anybody" in the United States.
rationale: The claim is false. Tariffs are effectively taxes on imports and evidence from the U.S.–China tariff episode shows higher prices for U.S. consumers and firms that use Chinese inputs, supply‑chain disruption, and mixed labor effects (some protected producers gained but many downstream firms and consumers lost purchasing power). While some domestic industries saw benefits, the aggregate economic studies find measurable harm to U.S. consumers and industries rather than a situation where no one is hurt.

claim: "Trump's Cabinet is more white and more male than any first Cabinet since President Ronald Reagan’s."
rationale: Contemporary analyses at the time found that President Trump’s initial Cabinet appointments contained fewer women and fewer people of color than any incoming Cabinet since Ronald Reagan’s 1981 Cabinet. Compared with the first Cabinets of George H.W. Bush, Clinton, George W. Bush and Obama — each of which included larger shares of women and racial minorities — Trump’s initial roster was notably more white and male.

claim: Muslims "attempted to establish the first Islamic Sharia court inside the United States in the town of Irving, Texas."
rationale: This claim overstates and mischaracterizes events in Irving. Muslim community leaders discussed forming a private Islamic arbitration panel to mediate disputes, but it was not a government 'Sharia court' and any rulings would have depended on voluntary arbitration under Texas law. Similar faith-based arbitration (e.g., Jewish and Christian panels) and informal Islamic arbitration efforts elsewhere in the U.S. predate or parallel the Irving discussion, so it was not uniquely the "first."

claim: Says 25 percent of Austin's public school buildings are "underutilized."
rationale: The statement is unsupported as written because it gives a precise 25% figure without specifying the district, year, or how "underutilized" is defined. School building utilization rates vary by district (e.g., AISD versus charter schools) and change annually; I am not aware of a consistent, authoritative source that states exactly 25% of Austin public school buildings are underutilized. Without that context or a cited report, the claim cannot be verified and is likely misleading.

claim: "When you pull up to the gas pump to fill up your car, get your cell phone and search for Bluetooth devices. If a sequence of letters and numbers show up don’t pay at the pump. One of the pumps has a credit card skimmer inside of it. All of these skimmers run on bluetooth."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as an absolute statement. While some card skimmers use Bluetooth to transmit stolen data, many devices use other methods (e.g., internal "shimmers," devices that must be retrieved, cellular transmitters, or direct storage) and not all skimmers broadcast a detectable Bluetooth name. Seeing a Bluetooth device with alphanumeric characters near a pump is neither necessary nor sufficient proof of a skimmer.

claim: "An 8-year-old Ukrainian girl confronts a Russian soldier telling him to go back to his country."
rationale: There is no reliably sourced, independently verified evidence that a specific incident involving an 8‑year‑old Ukrainian girl confronting a Russian soldier and telling him to go back to his country occurred as claimed. While videos of children addressing soldiers circulated during the Russia–Ukraine war, many were misattributed, lacked corroborating metadata (date/place/identity), or were altered, so the specific claim is unproven and likely false as stated.

claim: Says Texas ranks 44th nationally in education funding per pupil.
rationale: Based on recent state-by-state per-pupil spending datasets (Census Bureau and compilations used by outlets like Education Week), Texas has ranked in the low 40s nationally for education spending per pupil; in several recent years it has been reported as 44th. Rankings vary by year and methodology, but stating Texas ranks 44th matches published figures for specific recent reporting periods.

claim: "Washington, D.C., now has greater population than Wyoming and Vermont, more active duty military than 29 states, more tax revenue than 29 states (and) a larger domestic product than 27 states."
rationale: The first part (D.C. has a larger population than Wyoming and Vermont) is correct based on recent Census counts. However the other comparisons are misleading or unsupported: the claim that D.C. has more active‑duty military than 29 states is unlikely (D.C. hosts relatively few resident active‑duty personnel), and comparisons of tax revenue and "domestic product" depend on year and accounting rules—while D.C.’s GDP and revenues exceed those of some small states, the specific counts (29 states for tax revenue, 27 for GDP) are not reliably supported without a precise year and metric.

claim: Under the 2017 tax law, "people who make under $75,000 will have their taxes raised in 2021 and every 2 years after that until 2027."
rationale: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act made most individual tax changes temporary and slated them to expire after 2025, which would revert many provisions in 2026 — not impose scheduled tax hikes in 2021 and every two years through 2027. The law does not include a provision that automatically raises taxes for people earning under $75,000 in 2021 and biennially thereafter; any future changes would require new legislation or different indexing rules.

claim: Says Gov. Greg Abbott offered the uncle of a Uvalde shooting victim money to say "we don’t need stronger gun laws."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Gov. Greg Abbott offered the uncle of a Uvalde victim money to say “we don’t need stronger gun laws.” Major news outlets and fact-checkers investigated related claims after the Uvalde shooting and found no documentation, recordings, or corroborating witnesses of such an offer, and Abbott’s office denied making any payment. The claim appears to be an unverified allegation without reliable sourcing.

claim: The fiscal cliff agreement was "the largest tax increase in history."
rationale: False. The 2012–2013 "fiscal cliff" compromise (mainly the American Taxpayer Relief Act) raised taxes on higher-income households and let a payroll-tax cut expire, but it did not amount to the largest tax increase in U.S. history. Historical episodes (e.g., wartime tax expansions in WWII and major budget acts in other decades) produced far larger revenue and rate changes than the fiscal-cliff measures.

claim: Obama would "experiment with socialism."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Barack Obama publicly said he would "experiment with socialism." His public statements and policy record show he described himself as operating within a mixed-market/capitalist framework and pursued market-oriented reforms (e.g., the Affordable Care Act, economic stimulus) that critics sometimes labeled "socialist," but he did not advocate experimenting with socialism as a stated policy goal.

claim: "The American people don't want us to raise taxes."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. Public opinion on taxes is mixed and context-dependent: many Americans oppose broad personal tax hikes but often support raising taxes on corporations or wealthy households or for popular purposes, so it is inaccurate to claim categorically that 'the American people' don't want any tax increases.

claim: "I helped win one of the biggest private lawsuits against Medicare fraud in history. The government declined to pursue the case, so my firm did, and we recovered $324 million for taxpayers."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific assertion that a private firm recovered exactly $324 million after the government declined to pursue that particular Medicare fraud case or that it ranks among the very largest private lawsuits in history. While qui tam relators and private firms have litigated False Claims Act cases and recovered substantial sums, most major Medicare fraud recoveries are documented in DOJ press releases and court records; this precise claim lacks corroboration in my available knowledge. Given the specificity (amount, government declination, and ranking) it should be confirmed with court or DOJ records.

claim: "I proudly voted for Hillary Clinton."
rationale: This is a personal claim about how an identified individual voted, and there is no verifiable evidence provided. Ballots are secret and without a public admission or corroborating record I cannot confirm the claim, so it must be treated as not proven.

claim: Says Barack Obama was silent on Iran "when the students took to the streets in Tehran and the people there protested, (and) the Green Revolution occurred."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate: during the 2009 Iranian Green Movement Barack Obama and his administration publicly commented on the protests, condemning violence and urging respect for peaceful assembly and free expression. Critics later argued his responses were measured or insufficiently forceful, but he was not silent at the time.

claim: Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas said: ‘Hey, all you wrinkly, white-aged has-beens: It’s time for you to die and let the next generation have your spot on the planet.’
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or reputable news report showing Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee uttered this quotation. The line appears to be an inflammatory social-media fabrication that has been widely circulated without verifiable sourcing. Established fact-checkers and searches of Congressional records do not corroborate the attribution.

claim: "The unemployment rate for folks who've never gone to college is almost double what it is for those who have."
rationale: U.S. labor‑market data consistently show substantially higher unemployment among workers without college experience than among those with college degrees; in many recent years the unemployment rate for people with no college has been roughly twice the rate for college graduates. The exact gap varies by year and by how ‘no college’ and ‘those who have’ are defined (some college vs. bachelor's degree), but describing it as “almost double” is a reasonable generalization for recent U.S. data.

claim: Says "(President) Reagan's second inaugural was moved inside the Capitol. It was. Because of a terrible snowstorm."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Ronald Reagan’s second-term public inauguration took place on Jan 21, 1985 (the 20th was a Sunday), and the public ceremony was held outdoors rather than being moved indoors due to a snowstorm. People sometimes conflate the private Sunday oath (a routine accommodation when Jan 20 falls on a Sunday) or bad weather at other inaugurations with being moved indoors for a storm, but the second inaugural was not relocated inside for weather.

claim: "Bill White used D.C. connections from his job in the Clinton administration to form a company that did business in the Middle East and defaulted on a $60 million loan."
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence that Bill White (the former Clinton administration official who later served as Houston mayor and ran for governor) formed a company using D.C. connections that did business in the Middle East and then defaulted on a $60 million loan. Major biographies and news coverage of his career do not report a $60 million loan default or such a Middle East business venture; the allegation appears to conflate or misattribute facts to someone with the same name. Given the lack of corroboration, the claim is not supported.

claim: If the General Assembly does not address the state's structural deficit, "more than 23,000 education professionals will be immediately yanked out of Pennsylvania schools."
rationale: The statement presents a specific immediate outcome as certain, but there is no automatic statewide mechanism that would instantly remove over 23,000 education professionals solely because the General Assembly doesn't 'address the structural deficit.' That figure appears to be a projection or worst‑case estimate offered by advocacy groups or some districts rather than a guaranteed, immediate statewide action; actual layoffs would depend on local district budgets, timing, and policy choices.

claim: Sherrod Brown "has been running for public office since Richard Nixon was president."
rationale: The claim implies Sherrod Brown began running for elected public office during Richard Nixon's presidency (1969–1974). Brown was born in 1952 and most standard biographical accounts place the start of his electoral career later; there is no clear evidence he launched public-office campaigns during Nixon’s term. Therefore the statement is likely inaccurate or overstated.

claim: Multnomah County has faced "11 straight years" of cuts
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as written: county budgets and expenditures typically fluctuate year-to-year and public records do not support a general, unqualified claim of 11 consecutive years of countywide cuts. Without a specified timeframe, budget category, or source, the claim reads like political rhetoric rather than a documented fact. To verify would require citing Multnomah County budget documents showing 11 straight annual reductions in the same budget measure.

claim: "McCain lobbied for (a) $10-million pork project honoring conservative justice."
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence that Senator John McCain lobbied for a specific $10 million earmark to honor a conservative justice. McCain was widely known for opposing pork-barrel earmarks and made few such requests, and major media reporting of earmark controversies does not support this specific claim. Without a named justice, bill, locality, or precise time, the claim appears unsubstantiated and likely conflates or misattributes actions by another politician or project.

claim: "David McCormick paid for attacks on Donald Trump."
rationale: There is no clear, publicly documented evidence that David McCormick personally funded campaign attacks specifically targeting Donald Trump. While McCormick has spent personal funds in his own political races and opponents or allied groups sometimes run anti-Trump ads, reliable reporting or FEC records linking McCormick directly to payments for attacks on Trump are lacking. Without specific, verifiable evidence tying him to payments for anti‑Trump ads or opposition research, the claim is unproven and treated as false.

claim: "We have developed a wind industry (in Washington state) from zero to $6 billion in 12 years."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false because it provides no source and is ambiguous about what the $6 billion represents (investment, annual revenue, lifetime project value, etc.). Washington State had some wind activity before the 12-year window and publicly available summaries of wind-sector growth do not clearly document a discrete increase from zero to $6 billion in a 12-year span.

claim: "We’re already bombing seven countries."
rationale: The claim is too vague to be judged true as stated because it does not define who “we” are or when. If “we” means the United States during parts of the 2010s, US airstrikes/drone strikes were carried out in about seven countries (commonly cited: Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, Libya, Pakistan, Yemen, Somalia), so the phrasing can be misleading absent a timeframe and definition of “bombing.”

claim: Stay-at-home orders "actually are the law of these states."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad statement. While many U.S. stay‑at‑home directives were issued as executive or public‑health orders that carried legal force in specific states, their legal status varied by state and over time (some were advisory, some had enforceable penalties, and some faced legal challenges). Saying they “actually are the law of these states” without specifying which states or the legal basis misrepresents that variation.

claim: "Gas prices have never been higher, and Exxon Mobil's profits have never been higher."
rationale: The two-part claim mixes contexts. While U.S. retail gasoline prices reached record nominal highs in 2022, gasoline prices have been higher in inflation-adjusted terms in past decades, so the absolute statement “have never been higher” is misleading. Exxon Mobil did report its largest-ever annual profit in 2022 (around $55 billion), so the second half can be true for that year, but the combined blanket claim as stated is false without a timeframe or price-adjustment clarification.

claim: Says professional football coach Rex Ryan "won championships in New York. The AFC, I think, twice."
rationale: Rex Ryan’s New York Jets did reach the AFC Championship Game twice (after the 2009 and 2010 seasons) but lost both games, so he did not “win” the AFC championship twice. He did win the AFC East division once (2009), but he never won two AFC conference titles as head coach in New York.

claim: Under Rick Scott, there has been a "historic $20 billion in funds for education."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Florida’s education appropriations reached roughly $20 billion per year during Rick Scott’s tenure and he often touted ‘record’ education funding, there is no clear evidence he produced a $20 billion net increase in education funding; the phrase is ambiguous about whether it means a cumulative increase or total annual funding. Without a specific timeframe or whether the figure denotes new money versus total allocation, the statement as presented is not supported.

claim: "In sanctuary cities, local officials order police to release dangerous criminal aliens to prey upon the public instead of handing them over to ICE to be safely removed."
rationale: The claim is a broad and misleading generalization. Sanctuary policies typically restrict certain forms of cooperation with federal immigration detainers absent a warrant or probable cause, but they do not direct police to deliberately release ‘dangerous’ criminals to harm the public; many jurisdictions expressly retain exceptions for violent offenders and transfer people when there are criminal charges or warrants. Isolated cases of released noncitizens later committing crimes have occurred, but they do not demonstrate a systematic policy to intentionally let dangerous individuals prey on the public.

claim: "Calling for the assassination of the president is a federal crime."
rationale: Federal law makes it a crime to threaten or solicit the killing of the President (for example 18 U.S.C. § 871 and solicitation statutes), so calling for the President's assassination can be prosecuted as a federal offense. However, whether a particular statement is criminal depends on context and legal tests for threats, solicitation, and First Amendment limits on incitement.

claim: Says Bill Clinton opposes President Barack Obama's plan to raise taxes on wealthy Americans.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Bill Clinton publicly opposed President Obama’s general proposals to raise taxes on high-income Americans; as a former president Clinton has historically supported higher tax rates on the wealthy and campaigned with Obama on fiscal measures. The claim is presented without context or a specific policy and conflicts with Clinton’s known public positions favoring letting top-end tax cuts expire or raising revenue for deficit reduction. Because the assertion is broad and unsupported, it is classified as false.

claim: Says a military Humvee labeled "COVID-19 quarantine team" was on Interstate 696 in Michigan.
rationale: Multiple independent fact-checks and statements from Michigan authorities found the image was miscaptioned or altered and there is no evidence a military Humvee labeled "COVID-19 quarantine team" was operating on I‑696. Law enforcement and the National Guard denied any such marked quarantine teams on that highway, and image analysis showed the signage was not authentic.

claim: Photo shows Joe Biden "doesn’t wear a mask on a plane."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because no specific photo, date, or context is provided. President Biden has been photographed both wearing and briefly not wearing a mask in transit (e.g., moments of eating or after policy changes), so a generic claim that a photo shows he "doesn't wear a mask on a plane" is misleading without the image and context.

claim: "The states that have raised the minimum wage (this year) have had faster job growth than the states that haven’t raised the minimum wage."
rationale: The claim is an unqualified generalization and cannot be treated as fact without specifying the year, which states, the size/timing of increases, and controlling for other factors. Empirical evidence on state-level minimum wage increases is mixed: short-term job growth comparisons often reflect differences in underlying economic conditions, industry mix, and timing rather than a uniform effect of raises. Therefore the blanket statement that states that raised the minimum wage "this year" have had faster job growth than those that haven’t is not reliably supported.

claim: A congressional laundry closed due to the partial government shutdown.
rationale: There is no evidence that a distinct 'congressional laundry' was closed as a result of a partial federal government shutdown. Most widely reported shutdown impacts affected executive-branch services and agencies; the legislative branch is funded differently and routine accounts for Congress and its offices generally continued to operate. News coverage of shutdown effects does not corroborate the specific claim.

claim: Mental health provisions related to mass shootings "got over 90 votes in the Senate."
rationale: There is no clear instance of a major federal mental‑health provision tied to mass shootings receiving over 90 votes in the U.S. Senate. For example, the major recent bipartisan bill addressing gun violence and some mental‑health measures (the 2022 Bipartisan Safer Communities Act) passed the Senate 64–34; other related measures typically had much narrower margins or failed.

claim: The Southern strategy is a "myth" that "never happened."
rationale: The claim that the Southern Strategy is a "myth" that "never happened" is false. Political scientists and historians have documented a decades-long Republican effort to win white Southern voters after the civil rights era through coded racial appeals and policy positions, with primary-source evidence (campaign memos, speeches, Nixon tapes) and clear electoral realignment patterns supporting this. While scholars debate the relative weight and intent of different actors, the broad phenomenon is well-established.

claim: "Here are the facts: there is no massive wave of migrants pouring into California. Overall immigrant apprehensions on the border last year were as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years (and 85 percent of the apprehensions occurred outside of California)."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate because recent U.S. border enforcement data show encounters/apprehensions in the last few years were at multi-decade highs, not as low as in nearly 50 years. While it is true that a large majority of southern border encounters occur outside California (California accounts for a relatively small share of total apprehensions), the statement that overall apprehensions last year were very low is contradicted by official CBP encounter trends showing elevated totals.

claim: "There are places in America that are among the most dangerous in the world. You go to places like Oakland. Or Ferguson. The crime numbers are worse. Seriously."
rationale: The claim overstates the comparison. While some U.S. cities and neighborhoods (including parts of Oakland and, at times, Ferguson) have high violent-crime rates relative to other U.S. places, they are far below the homicide and violent-crime rates seen in the world’s most dangerous cities (many of which are in Central and South America and have per‑capita homicide rates several times higher). Using standard per‑100,000 population homicide and violent‑crime metrics, Oakland and Ferguson do not rank among the very highest globally.

claim: Says "there have been some job gains in the McMansion State since Mr. Christie took office, but they have lagged gains both in the nation as a whole and in New York and Connecticut, the obvious points of comparison."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not uniformly true across plausible time windows. While New Jersey’s job growth under Gov. Christie (he took office in January 2010) did lag the national rate and New York in many post‑recession years, Connecticut’s performance relative to New Jersey varied by year and by whether one measures absolute jobs or percentage growth; Connecticut did not consistently outpace New Jersey for the entire Christie tenure. Because the statement asserts a general lag against all three comparators without specifying timeframe or metric, it overstates and is therefore false as a general claim.

claim: Says Chris Christie was "behind" in the polls against Jon Corzine during the 2009 governor's race.
rationale: This is misleading. In the 2009 New Jersey governor's race, Chris Christie led or was tied with Jon Corzine in most major polls after the Republican primary and went on to win the election; while a few isolated early polls may have briefly shown Corzine marginally ahead, it is inaccurate to assert generally that Christie was behind in the polls. Thus the blanket claim that he was behind is false or at best misleading without a specific time frame.

claim: Scott Maddox is a "lobbyist."
rationale: Scott Maddox is primarily known as the former mayor of Tallahassee and a Florida political figure who was later indicted and convicted in a corruption/bribery case; he is not generally identified as a professional lobbyist. Public reporting and records characterize him as a politician and defendant rather than as a lobbyist.

claim: "The Nevada Gaming Commission did not find Trump ‘trustworthy’ enough for a gaming license."
rationale: The widely reported finding that Trump was not "trustworthy" or "suitable" was issued by the Nevada Gaming Control Board (the investigative body), which recommended he be declared unsuitable; reports often conflate that action with the Nevada Gaming Commission. The Commission is a separate adjudicatory body and the distinction between the two entities is important for accuracy.

claim: President Barack Obama’s health care reform "slashed $500 billion from Medicare."
rationale: The statement is misleading. The Affordable Care Act included provisions that reduced projected Medicare spending by roughly $500 billion over about a decade (per CBO/CMS estimates), but that was achieved mainly by lowering future provider and Medicare Advantage payments and other savings—not by immediate cuts to traditional Medicare benefits for current enrollees. Calling it a $500 billion "slash" to Medicare implies direct benefit cuts, which overstates what the law did.

claim: Gov. Rick Scott's sale of the state planes was "not proper."
rationale: The statement asserts an improper sale as a factual claim of wrongdoing, but available public records do not show an authoritative finding that the sale itself was illegal or improper. Governor Scott did sell state aircraft early in his term and faced criticism for later use of private charters, but state reviews and reporting focused on optics and policy choices rather than a conclusive official determination that the sale was 'not proper.'

claim: A Muslim immigrant in Michigan can list his second, third or fourth wives as "extended family" and qualify for welfare.
rationale: U.S. law does not recognize polygamous marriages, and state/federal benefit programs require truthful reporting of household composition and legal relationships. Welfare eligibility in Michigan (SNAP, TANF, Medicaid) is based on who lives together and their legal/immigration status, and misrepresenting multiple spouses as 'extended family' to obtain benefits would be fraud and is not an approved way to qualify. Routine program rules and verification prevent automatic acceptance of multiple 'wives' as extended family for benefits.

claim: Justice Antonin Scalia agreed for the Supreme Court to hear a case about whether Barack Obama is eligible to be President.
rationale: False. The Supreme Court never granted review of a case determining Barack Obama’s presidential eligibility and denied or dismissed the various "birther" petitions; there is no public record that Scalia secured the four votes needed to take such a case. Individual justices cannot unilaterally "agree for the Court to hear" a case — four justices must vote for certiorari — and no evidence shows Scalia voted to grant cert on an eligibility challenge.

claim: Video shows Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer laughing at Novak Djokovic after he was stuck in an Australian airport.
rationale: The claim is false: Djokovic's high-profile Australian airport detention (January 2022) involved immigration processing and restricted access, and major reports indicate Federer was not present in Australia to be part of such an encounter. Viral clips circulating with that caption were misattributed or taken from other events/angles or edited; they do not show Federer and Nadal laughing at Djokovic during his airport detention.

claim: Says former NBA player Rick Fox was also on board with Kobe Bryant
rationale: False — Rick Fox was not among the people on the helicopter that crashed with Kobe Bryant on January 26, 2020. Contemporary news reports and official passenger lists identified Kobe Bryant, his daughter Gianna and seven others (plus the pilot), and did not include Rick Fox.

claim: "A [bank] surveillance camera capturing a criminal’s face and other identifiable traits would certainly discourage robbery attempts and serve as a deterrent to robbers."
rationale: The claim's use of 'certainly' is unsupported. Empirical studies and meta-analyses show CCTV can reduce some types of property crime in particular settings, but its deterrent effect on robberies and violent, motivated offenders is mixed and far from guaranteed; offenders can use masks, alternative entry points, or avoid visible cameras. Cameras are more reliably useful for post‑crime identification and prosecution than as a universal preventive measure.

claim: The seven nations identified in Donald Trump's travel ban were "identified by the Obama administration as the seven most dangerous countries in the world in regard to harboring terrorists."
rationale: There is no record that the Obama administration formally designated those seven countries as “the seven most dangerous countries in the world in regard to harboring terrorists.” The seven countries in Trump’s initial travel ban (Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Yemen) overlap with various U.S. designations and conflict-zone assessments (e.g., Iran and formerly Sudan on the State Sponsors of Terrorism list; others had active terrorist groups), but Obama did not issue a single ranking naming them as the seven most dangerous for harboring terrorists.

claim: The novel coronavirus was "man-made."
rationale: Genomic analyses by multiple independent groups found features of SARS‑CoV‑2 that are consistent with natural evolution and lack signatures typical of purposeful genetic engineering. The virus is closely related to coronaviruses found in bats and other wildlife, and the scientific consensus (including public health agencies and virologists) is that a zoonotic spillover is the most likely origin; there is no credible evidence that it was deliberately man‑made.

claim: Says Texas economy is about 30 percent larger than Australia’s.
rationale: Recent nominal-GDP comparisons show Texas's economy is in the roughly $2.0–2.5 trillion range while Australia’s national nominal GDP has been roughly $1.5–1.9 trillion in recent years, which makes Texas about 20–40% larger and consistent with an "about 30% larger" statement. The exact percentage varies by year and whether one uses nominal USD or PPP-adjusted figures, but the general magnitude claimed is accurate for recent data.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "wants higher standards for toy guns than real guns."
rationale: There is no credible record of Bernie Sanders saying he wants higher standards for toy guns than for real guns; this reads like a mischaracterization or satirical distortion. Sanders' documented gun-policy statements focus on regulating real firearms (background checks, assault-weapons restrictions), not prioritizing toy-gun standards over real guns.

claim: John McCain's tax plan will give no reduction "for 100-million American families."
rationale: The statement overstates and mischaracterizes McCain's plan. Analyses of McCain's 2008 tax proposals showed cuts were concentrated among higher-income households but did not result in zero reductions for as many as 100 million families; the U.S. had roughly 110–120 million households then, and independent tax-analyses found benefits distributed across income groups. Thus the literal claim that 100 million families would receive no reduction is not supported.

claim: "Tennessee just banned Plan B and made it a crime punishable by a $50,000 fine to order it."
rationale: This claim is not true as stated. As of the latest reliable reports, Tennessee has not enacted a statewide ban on Plan B (levonorgestrel emergency contraception) nor passed a law imposing a $50,000 criminal fine for ordering it; Plan B is widely available over-the-counter and the cited penalty figure appears to come from misreported or conflated proposals aimed at abortion drugs rather than an enacted ban on emergency contraception.

claim: Pennsylvania rejected 372,000 mail-in ballots
rationale: This is false. Pennsylvania did not reject 372,000 mail‑in ballots; official state reporting and post‑election summaries show rejected mail/absentee ballots in the low tens of thousands for recent elections, far below 372,000. The larger number appears to be a conflation or misinterpretation of other totals (such as total mailed or returned ballots) rather than actual rejections.

claim: "The Texas unemployment rate is now the lowest it’s been in 40 years & Texas led the nation last month in new job creation."
rationale: The claim bundles two time-sensitive assertions without a date; I could not verify that, at the unspecified “now,” Texas’ unemployment rate was the lowest in 40 years. State unemployment levels and monthly job gains are reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics and vary month-to-month — Texas has had very low unemployment recently and has led the nation in job gains in some months, but the blanket, undated statement is not verifiable and likely inaccurate as written.

claim: Photos show "Ukrainian Christians pray outdoors, in the snow, for their country in this phase of war danger."
rationale: The claim points to unspecified photos and so cannot be independently verified from the information given. Although there are documented instances of Ukrainians praying in public during the war, without the original images, timestamps, and location metadata the assertion that these particular photos show Ukrainian Christians praying outdoors in the snow for their country is unconfirmed. Given the lack of provenance, the claim is treated as unproven.

claim: "Fifteen years ago, you couldn't even get a pizza delivered in that neighborhood."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim about a specific neighborhood and time but provides no location or evidence, so it cannot be established as true. Major pizza chains and local delivery services have operated in most urban and suburban neighborhoods for decades, making the blanket claim that delivery was impossible fifteen years ago implausible without supporting local data. Therefore the claim is likely false as stated.

claim: Says Rep. Justin Amash "votes more with the Democrats than with the Republicans."
rationale: False. Over the course of his House tenure Amash was a Republican until mid‑2019 and, by aggregate roll‑call similarity metrics and public analyses, generally voted more often with House Republicans than with Democrats. He did break with Republicans on notable issues (e.g., impeachment and some civil‑liberties votes) and aligned with Democrats at times, but those exceptions do not make his overall voting record one of greater alignment with Democrats.

claim: "Seventy percent of all Texans are overweight or obese."
rationale: The statement as written — that 70% of all Texans are overweight or obese — is misleading. State and national health surveys show adult overweight-plus-obesity estimates can be near 65–75% in some years, but prevalence varies by age group, data source and year, and children have substantially lower rates, so the blanket claim about "all Texans" is not reliably true. Precise estimates require specifying adults vs. all ages and a time period.

claim: The Republican replacement for Obamacare does not give massive tax cuts to wealthy Americans.
rationale: This is false for the main Republican repeal proposals (e.g., the 2017 AHCA/BCRA). Those plans repealed several ACA tax provisions (such as the net investment income tax and the 0.9% Medicare surtax and removed the individual mandate penalty) and replaced progressive subsidies with less-progressive credits, producing net revenue losses and estimates showing the largest tax gains flowed to higher-income households. Nonpartisan analyses concluded the tax changes disproportionately benefited wealthy Americans rather than eliminating large benefits to them.

claim: "President Obama's suggested reduction in spending for next year: $0."
rationale: The claim is false because President Obama’s budget proposals consistently contained specific proposed spending changes rather than a blanket $0 reduction for “next year.” Presidential budgets and accompanying documents lay out dollar amounts of increases and cuts for particular programs and often proposed net savings or increases depending on the year and baseline, so an assertion of a $0 suggested reduction is unsupported without a specific year or source.

claim: A video shows Kim Jong Un calling Joe Biden a "thug," a "coward," and "mentally unstable" in a speech.
rationale: The circulating clip was a manipulated/edited video: the English insults were not part of the original North Korean speech. Independent fact‑checks and linguistic comparisons showed the audio/subtitles were fabricated; official North Korean outlets did criticize U.S. policy but did not use those explicit English insults toward President Biden in the authentic speech.

claim: U.S. Senate candidate Todd Akin was "partly right" that a woman's body has a way of shutting down so that a pregnancy doesn't occur if she's raped.
rationale: This is false. Medical experts and empirical research show there is no physiological mechanism that reliably "shuts down" pregnancy after rape; pregnancies do and do commonly result from sexual assault. While extreme stress can sometimes affect ovulation timing, that does not prevent fertilization or implantation in a consistent way and cannot be relied on as a protective mechanism.

claim: Under the Iran nuclear deal, "we give them $150 billion, we get nothing."
rationale: This statement is inaccurate. The often-cited “$150 billion” refers to estimates of Iranian assets frozen abroad and projected future oil revenue, not a single lump-sum payment by the United States, and much of those funds were illiquid or encumbered. The JCPOA imposed significant, verifiable limits on Iran’s enrichment, stockpile and centrifuge activities and established IAEA inspections and monitoring — so it was not the case that the negotiators “got nothing.”

claim: "One third of our age group (Millennials) have moved back in with their parents."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not generally supported as a universal fact. Available U.S. and international data show sizable variation by country, cohort definition, and year — some studies show increases in young adults living with parents (especially during the COVID-19 pandemic), but many pre-pandemic estimates for Millennials do not show that one-third have 'moved back in.' Because the claim gives no timeframe or place, the blanket one-third figure is not verifiable.

claim: Thanks to the Trans-Pacific Partnership, "Vietnam is drafting and presenting unprecedented labor reforms, changing their Constitution to recognize worker organizations in Vietnam for the first time."
rationale: While the Trans-Pacific Partnership negotiations did pressure Vietnam to commit to labor-law changes and to draft reforms, Vietnam has not actually amended its constitution to legally recognize independent worker organizations for the first time. In practice Vietnam's legal framework continues to give primacy to the state-affiliated Vietnam General Confederation of Labour and independent unions remain effectively barred; promised constitutional and law changes have been limited and incomplete.

claim: In Iraq, "violence is down to an all-time low" since the start of the war.
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as written. Violence in Iraq has fluctuated since 2003 with major spikes (notably the 2006–07 sectarian war and the 2014–17 ISIS conflict); while violence has been lower than those peaks in some recent years, it is not unambiguously at an all-time low since the start of the war and depends on which metric and period are used.

claim: "Our university campuses by federal law do not check the immigration status of their students just as our public schools don’t."
rationale: The claim is false. There is no federal law that broadly prohibits colleges and universities from asking about or verifying students' immigration status; higher education institutions routinely collect status information for residency, tuition classification, visas, and financial aid. By contrast, K–12 public schools are constrained by the Supreme Court's Plyler v. Doe (1982) ruling, which bars states from denying access to public elementary and secondary education to undocumented children — there is no equivalent federal bar for higher education.

claim: U.S. Rep. Jim Langevin didn't want a border fence to block illegal immigration "because he is afraid that someone will get hurt trying to go around the fence."
rationale: There is no reliable record or reputable reporting that Rep. Jim Langevin uttered the quoted line about being afraid someone would get hurt trying to go around a border fence; the claim appears to be a fabricated or misattributed quote. Langevin's public record shows he has supported border security measures while also emphasizing humanitarian concerns, but not this specific wording or assertion.

claim: Says "Bush Jr. handed Obama a $1.4 trillion deficit" and Obama "reduced Bush Jr.’s deficit to just $492 billion."
rationale: The claim mixes up years and attribution. The roughly $1.4 trillion shortfall refers to the FY2009 deficit (driven by the financial crisis and policies enacted during the 2008–09 transition), not a deficit that President Bush “handed” to Obama as a single end-of-term number; the FY2008 deficit under Bush was about $459 billion. Deficits did fall from the post-crisis peak during Obama’s presidency (falling into the mid‑$400 billions by the mid‑2010s), but the statement’s phrasing and exact numbers are misleading and incorrect in attribution and timing.

claim: Says a crisis actor played the parts of a shooting victim and the mothers of shooting victims in Las Vegas, Orlando and Thousand Oaks.
rationale: This claim is a circulated conspiracy theory that has been repeatedly debunked: there is no credible evidence that a single “crisis actor” played victims or mothers in the Las Vegas (2017), Orlando (2016) and Thousand Oaks (2018) shootings. Independent reporting, victim identifications, family statements, official records and fact-checkers corroborate that the people portrayed were actual victims or relatives, not paid actors. The pattern of reuse of similar-looking images and social media misattribution explains how the false claim spread.

claim: "The Doherty Campaign, unlike the Cicilline Campaign, is funded mostly by individual donors -- not the big PACs that Cicilline relies on."
rationale: I cannot confirm the categorical claim as stated. U.S. House campaigns typically receive a mix of individual contributions and PAC money and public FEC/OpenSecrets data are needed for a given candidate and cycle; without specifying which 'Doherty' and which election year the statement overgeneralizes. While Cicilline has taken PAC contributions as an incumbent, it is inaccurate to assert Doherty is funded 'mostly' by individuals and Cicilline relies on 'big PACs' without examining specific campaign filings.

claim: "If you’re a low-wage worker and you’re single and don’t have children, we’re literally taxing you into poverty."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. In the U.S., many low-wage single childless workers owe little or no federal income tax because of the standard deduction, though they do pay payroll and sales taxes which reduce take-home pay; those taxes can worsen hardship but are not universally the sole reason people fall below the poverty line. Some very low pre-tax earners could be pushed below the poverty threshold after taxes, but the blanket statement that single, childless low-wage workers are "literally taxed into poverty" is inaccurate without specific income, tax, and benefit details.

claim: By allowing brewpubs to sell beer, Georgia could become like Mexico with only a couple of manufacturers controlling all aspects of market.
rationale: The claim is speculative and contradicted by how brewpubs operate: brewpubs are typically small, local producers and allowing on-site or retail sales generally increases local competition and consumer choice rather than concentrating production. Mexico’s beer market concentration (historically dominated by two large brewers) resulted from long-term corporate consolidation and distribution structures, not from laws allowing brewpub sales. There is no evidence that permitting brewpub retail sales in Georgia would create a market dominated by only a couple manufacturers controlling all aspects of the market.

claim: "By the way, I'm not raising tolls 50 percent....Jon Corzine did."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Jon Corzine implemented a blanket 50% increase in tolls statewide. Corzine's administration proposed and enacted some toll and fee increases and faced criticism over transportation funding, but reported toll hikes under his tenure were smaller or specific to particular facilities rather than a one-time 50% across-the-board raise.

claim: "This is the slowest job recovery since Hoover."
rationale: The statement is misleading and lacks context. Analyses of U.S. payroll and employment recoveries show the post‑2007–09 job recovery was the slowest in the post‑World War II era, but invoking Hoover (the 1930s Great Depression) is inaccurate and conflates different data series and measures; the Great Depression-era contraction and recovery were far deeper and longer. Therefore the blanket claim as stated is not supported.

claim: Says Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio "had it set so that the winner takes everything, because they wanted to make sure that I didn't get anything" in the Florida primary.
rationale: False. Florida’s Republican delegate rules in 2016 allowed winner-take-all for contests on or after March 15, and the state party’s rules (not two individual candidates) governed how delegates were awarded. There is no evidence that Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio personally “set” the allocation to deny any particular candidate delegates or that they controlled the party rulemaking to that end.

claim: Ninety-six percent of failing schools are spending above $8,400, the average annual per student expenditure, and 26 percent spend considerably more than that.
rationale: The claim gives precise percentages but provides no source or timeframe, and those exact figures are not supported by known national education spending data. U.S. per‑pupil spending has varied by year and state (and in recent decades has generally exceeded $8,400), but available federal datasets do not substantiate that 96% of 'failing' schools spend above $8,400 or that 26% spend 'considerably more.' Without a clear definition of 'failing' and a citation, the specific percentages are not verifiable and are likely incorrect.

claim: "Rick Scott's even saying he wants more offshore drilling."
rationale: Sen. Rick Scott has publicly advocated expanding domestic oil and gas production and explicitly supported increased offshore drilling in statements and policy proposals. Multiple public remarks and his votes and press releases in the past several years have called for opening more federal offshore areas to energy development.

claim: "The child tax credit, if we don't do it, there will be no tax relief for working families. How much tax relief working families get under tax reform is entirely dependent on whether or not we put in place an increase to the child tax credit."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because tax relief for working families can come from many provisions besides an increased child tax credit (CTC). Rate changes, a higher standard deduction, expansions of the Earned Income Tax Credit, targeted credits or payroll tax changes can all provide relief; conversely a CTC increase alone does not guarantee overall net relief for every working family. Therefore relief is not "entirely dependent" on a CTC increase.

claim: "[The] unemployment rate in the Philadelphia metro area is now at its lowest level ever recorded."
rationale: The statement is unsupported as a general claim because it provides no date and historical Bureau of Labor Statistics metro-area series show earlier periods (notably pre‑pandemic 2019) with similarly low or lower unemployment for the Philadelphia metropolitan area. Without a specific time reference or clarification of which unemployment series (seasonally adjusted, not seasonally adjusted, or a specific sub‑MSA) it is not accurate to assert it is the lowest ever recorded.

claim: Says "I have been through the gauntlet, when we had riots in that Capitol."
rationale: The statement cannot be confirmed as true given the information provided: it lacks the identity of the speaker, the date, and which 'Capitol' riot is being referenced. Without specific, independently verifiable evidence (news reports, official records, or contemporaneous documentation) tying that person to being physically present and having 'been through the gauntlet' at a particular Capitol riot, the claim is not verifiable and is treated as false.

claim: Says Jason Carter has "gotten David Axelrod to come down and be his campaign advisor."
rationale: There is no reliable public evidence that David Axelrod formally joined Jason Carter’s campaign as his campaign advisor. While Axelrod has advised prominent Democrats, contemporary news coverage and campaign materials from Carter’s run do not document Axelrod taking on that role, so the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: St. Pete Beach's local version of Amendment 4 resulted in "seemingly endless lawsuits (that) decimated the city's legal budget and forced the city to raise the property tax rate."
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated evidence that St. Pete Beach’s local ‘Amendment 4’ produced “seemingly endless” lawsuits that literally decimated the city’s legal budget and directly forced a property tax rate increase. While the city has faced litigation over local measures at times, municipal budgets and millage rates are influenced by many factors and I found no reliable documentation showing lawsuits from a single local amendment caused the described fiscal collapse and mandated a tax hike. The claim appears exaggerated and lacking supporting public audit or news evidence tying causation so strongly.

claim: Says Alaska Sen. Mark Begich "is on record supporting a carbon tax, even pushing Harry Reid to make it a priority."
rationale: There is not a clear public record that Senator Mark Begich explicitly supported a standalone carbon tax or publicly pushed Majority Leader Harry Reid to prioritize one. Begich has at times expressed support for market-based approaches to climate (and earlier showed openness to cap-and-trade), but he largely avoided endorsing a labeled "carbon tax" and there is no well-documented instance of him urging Reid to make a carbon tax a priority.

claim: Says crime is ‘rising’ in Manchester and has gone up 19 percent under Mayor Ted Gatsas.
rationale: This claim is false as stated. Public crime data for Manchester, New Hampshire over the years Ted Gatsas served as mayor do not show a clear, across-the-board 19% increase in crime; reported trends were mixed with some categories and short periods up and others down. The statement appears to cherry-pick a percentage without specifying the exact timeframe, crime categories, or baseline used.

claim: "Florida is one of only three states that require licenses for commercial interior designers."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate or at least misleading. State regulation of interior designers varies (licensure, registration, title-protection) and the count of states that require licensure for commercial interior designers is not strictly limited to three; numbers also change over time and depend on whether one counts title acts versus practice licensure and whether 'commercial' is singled out. Thus the definitive statement 'one of only three states' is incorrect without a specific definition and date.

claim: Says Gov Tony Evers’ administration deemed dentists non-essential
rationale: False. Governor Evers’ administration did require postponement of non‑urgent/elective dental procedures during the early COVID‑19 response, but it did not formally label dentists as universally “non‑essential” and emergency/urgent dental care was still permitted. The action was a temporary public‑health restriction on elective services rather than an across‑the‑board designation of the profession as non‑essential.

claim: "The average American is working through the month of May just to pay off the government."
rationale: The claim overstates and is misleading. Independent measures of the combined federal, state, and local tax burden (commonly summarized as “Tax Freedom Day”) typically place the average American’s tax burden in April in recent years, not working through the entire month of May just to pay taxes. The statement also conflates paying annual taxes with "paying off the government" (which could imply paying the national debt), making it inaccurate as phrased.

claim: Says he would be first CPA to serve as Texas comptroller.
rationale: The statement that he would be the first CPA to serve as Texas comptroller is almost certainly incorrect because the office has a long history and past holders have included people with accounting credentials. Saying one person would be the first CPA ignores that previous officeholders have had professional accounting backgrounds. Without naming the person or time frame, the novelty claim is implausible on its face.

claim: "Drunk" Nancy Pelosi "was removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Speaker Nancy Pelosi was intoxicated and removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans. Congressional proceedings and press coverage do not record any incident in which Pelosi was forcibly removed for drunkenness or for using profanity toward members; viral clips making that claim have been debunked or taken out of context. Removal of a member from the floor is a formal, recorded action and would have been widely reported if it had occurred.

claim: As first lady, Clinton would travel to places that were "too small, too poor or too dangerous" for the president.
rationale: Hillary Clinton as First Lady made numerous overseas trips to countries that were small, poor or in unstable conditions (for example her 1996 visit to Bosnia/Tuzla). She and her campaign repeatedly characterized those trips with language like “too small, too poor or too dangerous” to emphasize she visited places presidents typically did not. The statement accurately summarizes her record and her own phrasing about those visits.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's Iran nuclear deal "lined the pockets of the world's number one state sponsor of terrorism with your money."
rationale: The claim is misleading and inaccurate. The 2015 Iran nuclear agreement (JCPOA) eased sanctions and led to the release/unfreezing of Iranian assets and restored oil revenues, but it did not involve a direct payment of U.S. taxpayer money to Iran; moreover the deal was negotiated by the Obama administration and multilateral partners (Clinton was not the lead negotiator). Calling Iran the “world’s number one state sponsor of terrorism” is a political judgment rather than a verifiable factual outcome of the deal.

claim: "Suez Canal blocked by huge container ship named Evergreen. Evergreen shipping is most likely a cover for human and sex trafficking" by Hillary Clinton.
rationale: While it is true the Suez Canal was blocked in March 2021 by the container ship Ever Given operated by Evergreen Marine, there is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton said Evergreen is likely a cover for human and sex trafficking. The trafficking assertion is an unfounded conspiracy with no substantiation in reputable reporting or public records, and fact-checkers have not found Clinton making such a claim. Therefore the combined statement is false and appears to be a misattribution paired with a baseless allegation.

claim: "The Katy Freeway, or Interstate 10 west of Houston, is the widest freeway in the world, with up to 26 lanes, including frontage road lanes."
rationale: The Katy Freeway (I-10 west of Houston) was expanded and in its widest segment contains as many as 26 marked lanes when main lanes, managed lanes and parallel frontage roads are all counted. It is commonly described in engineering and news accounts as the widest freeway in the world, though that designation depends on how one counts lanes and auxiliary roads.

claim: The Banking Committee voted a 1,336-page bill "out of committee in 21 minutes with no amendments, with the understanding that before the bill came to the floor, we would reach this bipartisan agreement."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim as stated and it reads like a precise, contested quote lacking context (which committee, date, or bill number). Congressional committee records and press accounts typically document markups and amendments; a 1,336‑page bill cleared in exactly 21 minutes with no amendments is implausible without corroborating public records. Given the absence of clear, attributable evidence for those exact details, the claim is treated as false pending a supporting source.

claim: Opening the schools "is a local determination, but it’s not a state determination."
rationale: The statement presents school reopening as solely a local determination and not a state determination, which is inaccurate as a general claim. Authority over school openings varies by jurisdiction, and in many U.S. states governors, state education agencies, or state public health authorities have legal power or used emergency orders to require or restrict school openings. While local school districts often make operational decisions, they frequently operate under state laws, regulations, or pandemic directives that can control reopening.

claim: The proposed Gogebic mine in northern Wisconsin "could be extended as long as 21 miles."
rationale: I cannot find authoritative support that the Gogebic mine as proposed would be able to be expanded to a continuous 21-mile mining operation. Public filings and environmental reviews around the Gogebic Taconite proposal describe a more limited project footprint and discuss a mineral belt/corridor and possible future exploration, but not a definitive plan to extend active mining 21 miles. Claim appears to conflate speculative exploration corridor language or hypothetical future expansions with the actual proposed mine boundaries.

claim: "If we pass immigration reform, it will make wages go up on average $250 for the average household."
rationale: This is a precise, quantitative causal claim that lacks general empirical support because effects of “immigration reform” vary greatly by the specific policies, timing, and modeling assumptions. Economists do not have a single consensus estimate that passing unspecified immigration reform would raise average household wages by exactly $250; studies typically show small and often distributional effects that depend on legalization, labor-market composition, and time horizon. Because the claim states a definitive dollar amount without those qualifications, it is not supported as a fact.

claim: "Never in American history has so much been spent at one time. Never in American history will so many taxes be raised and so much borrowing be needed to pay for this reckless spending."
rationale: The absolute claim is incorrect: U.S. history includes episodes of equal or larger fiscal mobilization, borrowing, and tax increases—most notably the Civil War and World War II, when federal spending and debt rose to historically high levels relative to the economy. Major 20th-century programs (New Deal/WWII, Great Society) and other crises have required large tax changes and borrowing, so saying "never" is false without additional qualifiers.

claim: Says Ayn Rand said, "The question isn’t who is going to let me; it’s who is going to stop me."
rationale: The line is widely attributed to Ayn Rand in popular quote collections, but researchers have not found a verifiable primary source in her published works or recorded interviews supporting the attribution. That pattern indicates the statement is likely a misattribution or paraphrase rather than a documented Rand quotation.

claim: A DeKalb sewer project "will create up to 4,000 direct jobs per year at peak production, many of which will be set aside exclusively for DeKalb residents."
rationale: There is no independent, verifiable evidence that a DeKalb sewer project will create 4,000 direct jobs per year at peak; large infrastructure estimates are often presented as total 'job‑years' or peak construction positions far lower than 4,000/year. Claims that positions will be "set aside exclusively" for county residents are usually overstated—local hire goals or preferences may exist, but absolute exclusivity is typically constrained by procurement, labor law, and contractor labor needs.

claim: Every former North Carolina governor opposes "constitutional amendments Raleigh lawmakers put on the ballot this fall."
rationale: The claim that every former North Carolina governor opposes the amendments is demonstrably too broad. Former governors span multiple parties and public records and news coverage show some former governors opposed the measures while others either supported them or did not take a public position, so unanimity is unsupported.

claim: "Since 1961 … our private economy has produced 66 million private-sector jobs. So what's the jobs score? Republicans 24 million, Democrats 42 (million)."
rationale: The headline numbers are misleading: total private‑sector job gains and the split by party depend on the exact start/end months and the method of attributing job changes to presidents. BLS payroll series and contemporary fact-checks show different totals and party splits when consistent months are used, so the quoted “66 million; Republicans 24m, Democrats 42m” is not a robust, verifiable figure. The statement cherry‑picks a methodology and presentation that overstates certainty about party attribution.

claim: "More Americans receive food aid than work in (the) private sector."
rationale: This is false based on typical counts: private‑sector employment in the U.S. is on the order of well over 100 million people, while the largest single food‑assistance program (SNAP) serves roughly 40–45 million monthly and other programs (school meals, WIC, food banks) overlap and do not sum to more than private‑sector employment. Even allowing for all forms of food aid combined, unique recipients are far fewer than the total number of private‑sector workers.

claim: Says protesters at the Wisconsin state Capitol on the night the state Senate passed collective bargaining changes damaged the windshield of his car.
rationale: There is no contemporaneous, independently verified reporting or police documentation that links Capitol protesters the night the state Senate moved on collective bargaining to damaging a specific individual's car windshield. Claims like this circulated anecdotally during the 2011 Wisconsin protests but were not substantiated by reliable sources and were disputed. Given the lack of evidence tying protesters to the damage, the claim is not supported.

claim: "7 out of 10 Oregon families living in poverty have at least one parent who works."
rationale: The precise statement is not verifiable as written. Public data commonly report that a large share of children in poverty live in families with at least one worker (often cited as about 7 in 10 nationally), but that statistic refers to children and varies by state and year; the specific claim that 7 out of 10 Oregon families in poverty have a working parent is unsupported without a cited year or source and may conflate measures. Because state-level rates and definitions (families vs. children, timeframe for “works”) differ, the claim is misleading as stated.

claim: Says Texas schools have had "massive increases" in class sizes with Rick Perry as governor.
rationale: The claim is an exaggeration. State and federal data over Rick Perry’s tenure (2000–2015) show only modest, uneven changes in average class sizes and pupil–teacher ratios in Texas rather than a uniform, statewide “massive” increase — some grades saw small increases at times (notably after mid‑2010s budget pressures) while early‑grade class‑size caps and local district staffing decisions limited large statewide jumps. The statement therefore overstates and mischaracterizes the actual trend.

claim: "There are no provisions in here that substantially affect or advantage the big Wall Street bankers."
rationale: The statement is a universal negative about an unspecified text and therefore implausible without seeing the document. In practice, many legislative or policy texts include tax, regulatory, compliance, or funding provisions that can materially affect large Wall Street banks, so claiming there are ‘no provisions’ that substantially advantage them is unlikely to be true. Proving a complete absence would require exhaustive review of the exact text, which is not provided here.

claim: Republicans extended unemployment insurance under President Bush "when he asked to extend unemployment insurance."
rationale: The claim is too broad and lacks context; there is no clear, single event showing Republicans uniformly extended unemployment insurance simply “when [President] Bush asked.” While Congress (including some Republicans) has approved unemployment benefit extensions during both Bush administrations in various instances, extensions were often bipartisan or driven by congressional action rather than a unilateral Republican response to a presidential request. The statement as phrased is misleading without specifying which Bush, what time period, or which legislative action is meant.

claim: Says Steve Spinnett has court judgments against him for trespass and harassment.
rationale: I cannot verify that Steve Spinnett has court judgments for trespass and harassment based on available public information. The claim provides no jurisdiction, dates, or case numbers, and there are no widely reported news items or accessible court records linking that exact name to such judgments. Without corroborating legal documents or credible reporting, the assertion is unverified and therefore judged false.

claim: "South Korea sprays rioters with dye so they can be identified & arrested later."
rationale: South Korean riot police have used colored dye in water cannons and spray during demonstrations to mark protesters so they can be identified later. Multiple media and watchdog reports document this tactic in past large protests, though it is not necessarily used at every event and practices vary by situation and unit.

claim: Gov. Scott Walker received a $7,300 pay raise.
rationale: The claim is false as stated. There is no clear, reliable record that Governor Scott Walker received a one‑time $7,300 pay raise; gubernatorial pay in Wisconsin is set by statute and any adjustments have been public and do not match this specific lump‑sum figure. Without a date or additional context the statement is misleading.

claim: Says there are half as many students in one Georgia technical college than there were two years ago.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which Georgia technical college or which two-year period are meant, and no supporting enrollment data is provided. While a 50% drop in enrollment over two years is possible in extreme cases, such a large change is uncommon and would require authoritative college or system enrollment reports to confirm. Absent that evidence, the statement should be treated as false.

claim: Says Luke Messer and Todd Rokita "voted to fast-track Obama’s trade deals."
