rationale: While Section 5 preclearance of the Voting Rights Act was effectively ended by the 2013 Shelby County decision, there is no credible evidence that 40,000–80,000 Wisconsin voters were turned away in 2016 because of race. State records and election-monitoring reports show far smaller numbers of voters actually turned away or issued provisional ballots, and estimates of people lacking certain IDs do not equate to being denied the ballot. The large figure appears to conflate modeled estimates of potential eligibility/ID issues with documented denials at the polls.

claim: "Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, the average American family of four will receive a $1,182 tax cut."
rationale: The $1,182 figure is misleading: it came from a specific averaging method for a particular year and assumes temporary individual provisions that largely expire after 2025. Independent analyses (CBO/JCT/fact-checkers) showed distributional variation—many families receive smaller cuts and some see no cut or an increase once state and other changes are included. The claim omits those caveats, so presenting it as a general fact is false.

claim: Donald Trump’s "golf course on the island defaulted, like so many of his other failed business schemes. The failure left Puerto Rican taxpayers with a nearly $33 million bill."
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes liability. Trump’s name was licensed to a Puerto Rico golf/hotel development that ran into financial trouble and some related bonds and loans defaulted, but Trump’s company was not the direct owner and the extent to which Puerto Rican taxpayers were left with a nearly $33 million bill is disputed and misleading — the financing and guarantees were complex and responsibility was not simply Trump’s. Reporting conflates defaults on project bonds/loans with a direct $33 million taxpayer obligation to Trump’s enterprises, which is not supported as a straightforward factual claim.

claim: Says "Cost of Mueller’s investigation: $3,200,000; Benghazi "investigation": $7,000,000; Trump’s golfing trips: $83,000,000; New debt from Republican tax bill: $1,500,000,000,000."
rationale: The statement mixes a roughly correct figure (the Republican tax bill’s projected 10-year increase in deficits of about $1.5 trillion) with incorrect or misleading numbers for the other items. DOJ reporting and news analyses indicate the Special Counsel office’s expenses were on the order of tens of millions (commonly reported around $30–40 million), not $3.2 million; estimates of Benghazi-related investigations vary by which committees and time periods are included and are generally reported higher than a flat $7 million when all activity is counted; and reported costs of Trump’s travel/golf security vary widely and are disputed, so the single $83 million figure is misleading. Because several components are inaccurate or presented without necessary context, the overall claim is false.

claim: The U.S. has "over $62 trillion in unfunded liabilities."
rationale: The statement is misleading because there is no single, universally accepted total of U.S. "unfunded liabilities" and widely used official measures do not consistently support a $62 trillion figure. Estimates vary dramatically depending on definitions (which programs are included), the time horizon (infinite vs. 75-year), and the discount rate; some advocacy or long‑horizon calculations can exceed $62 trillion, but that number is not a consensus or standard official figure. Without specifying methodology, presenting "over $62 trillion" as a fact is inaccurate.

claim: "A couple of debates ago, (Donald Trump) said if you don’t support socialized health care, you’re heartless."
rationale: There is no known record of Donald Trump saying in a debate that “if you don’t support socialized health care, you’re heartless.” Trump’s debate rhetoric has consistently opposed “socialized” or single‑payer health care rather than endorsing it or calling opponents heartless, so this statement appears misattributed or fabricated. Without a verifiable debate transcript or video, the claim cannot be supported.

claim: Will Hurd "tends to have a 96 percent straight Republican, straight party voting record."
rationale: This is false. Will Hurd was widely regarded as one of the more bipartisan and moderate House Republicans and multiple voting‑record trackers (e.g., FiveThirtyEight, GovTrack, Lugar Center bipartisanship measures) show his party‑unity/party‑line percentages were well below 96 percent. He frequently broke with his party on high‑profile votes, so a 96% straight party voting record is inconsistent with available summaries of his record.

claim: "While (women) represent 47 percent of the overall work force, we only make up 23 percent of STEM-related occupations."
rationale: The first part (women ≈47% of the overall workforce) is broadly accurate, but the share of women in STEM occupations is generally reported higher than 23% in recent U.S. data. Federal statistics (BLS/NSF) typically show women make up roughly the mid‑20s percent of STEM workers (often ~24–28%) depending on year and how STEM is defined, so the flat 23% claim is misleading without a date or definition.

claim: "The Democrats are very sly. … (in New Hampshire) we have same day voter registration, and to be honest, when Massachusetts elections are not very close, they’re busing them in all over the place."
rationale: The claim alleges organized mass busing from Massachusetts into New Hampshire to exploit same-day registration; there is no credible evidence of systematic, large-scale busing operations by Democrats to illegally register and vote in NH. New Hampshire does permit same-day registration but requires proof of residency, and election officials and investigations have not found widespread coordinated cross-border voter fraud.

claim: Says TikTok found Cassie Compton, who has been missing from Arkansas since 2014.
rationale: There are no credible news reports or law enforcement statements confirming that TikTok "found" Cassie Compton, who has been reported missing from Arkansas since 2014. Social media posts may claim leads or sightings, but without official verification the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "For four years, we balanced the budget and paid off $405 billion in debt."
rationale: The federal government did not run four consecutive balanced budgets and pay down $405 billion in the recent administrations that claim this. The only recent four-year stretch with budget surpluses was in the late 1990s/2000–2001 under President Clinton, and while the debt fell modestly then, the $405 billion figure and the timing often asserted by contemporary politicians do not match federal budget and debt records; more recent administrations ran large deficits and increased federal debt.

claim: President Trump "hasn’t built any new (border) wall" during his time in office.
rationale: This claim is incorrect: the Trump administration funded and constructed hundreds of miles of U.S.–Mexico border barriers. Government and independent reports show much of that construction replaced or upgraded existing fencing, but there were also stretches of entirely new primary barrier built during his term.

claim: Atlanta has issued an increasing number of citations - and collected an increasing amount of revenue - since Mayor Kasim Reed took office in 2010.
rationale: The claim implies a continuous, year‑over‑year rise in both citations issued and revenue since Reed took office in 2010. Public reporting and municipal finance data show that while Atlanta’s citation revenue and enforcement activity rose overall during parts of Reed’s tenure, the numbers were not a steady, uninterrupted increase each year and there were notable year‑to‑year fluctuations and policy changes that affected totals. Thus the blanket statement that both citations and revenue have increased continuously since 2010 is inaccurate.

claim: "If you put the $47 billion in revenue (raised over 10 years by the Buffett rule) into infrastructure you could create 611,000 infrastructure jobs."
rationale: The math behind 47 billion × 13,000 jobs per $1B equals 611,000 is arithmetically correct, but the claim is misleading because the Buffett-rule revenue is typically estimated as about $47 billion spread over 10 years, not a one-time $47B available for immediate investment. The commonly cited multiplier (~13,000 jobs per $1B) yields ~611,000 job‑years if $47B were spent all at once, but spread over 10 years it supports roughly 61,000 jobs per year; estimates also vary by project and whether jobs counted are direct, indirect, or job‑years.

claim: "Children don’t seem to be getting this virus"
rationale: The blanket statement is false in the typical context (e.g., SARS-CoV-2): children do become infected — confirmed by PCR and antibody studies — though they often have milder or asymptomatic illness and were initially under-tested. Lower early reported case counts reflected testing bias and symptom differences, not absence of infection; children can also transmit and rarely experience severe outcomes.

claim: "Granite Staters who hold individual policies from Anthem...can indeed renew their policies and keep their current doctors and hospitals" in 2014.
rationale: The claim overstates the situation. While federal guidance and some insurers (including Anthem in some states) allowed temporary renewals for certain individual plans into 2014, renewability and ability to retain the same doctors/hospitals depended on the specific policy, network changes, and state regulator approvals — it was not a blanket guarantee for all Granite Staters with Anthem individual policies. Many consumers still faced cancellations or had to move to new plans with different networks.

claim: Says U.N. arms treaty will mandate a "new international gun registry."
rationale: The UN Arms Trade Treaty and related UN instruments require states to keep national records and report certain arms transfers, but they do not create a centralized international registry of privately owned guns or individual firearms. The claim conflates routine national recordkeeping and export/import reporting obligations with a global UN database, which the treaty does not establish.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "This country is doomed, not just because of African Americans, but because by 2040 this country is going to be minority white European."
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or reputable reporting showing Joe Biden uttered that racially inflammatory sentence. The phrasing is inconsistent with Biden’s established public rhetoric and is characteristic of fabricated or misattributed political quotes. Without a verifiable primary source (video, audio, or reliable transcript), the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "In my home state, nearly one in five Floridians live in poverty."
rationale: Recent U.S. Census Bureau estimates show Florida’s overall poverty rate in recent years has been roughly in the low-to-mid teens percent, not around 20%. Saying “nearly one in five” (≈20%) overstates the statewide poverty rate for the typical recent reporting years.

claim: "A 5 percent increase in domestic production would increase the world supply by less than 1 percent and do almost nothing to our dependence on foreign oil. This would also have virtually no effect on the price of gas at the pump."
rationale: The United States typically produces a modest fraction of world oil (on the order of 10–15% in recent years), so a 5% rise in U.S. output corresponds to well under a 1% increase in global supply. Because oil is a globally traded commodity and U.S. consumption/import patterns are large and complex, such a small incremental increase would only modestly reduce imports and would be unlikely to substantially change retail gasoline prices, which are set by global crude prices plus refining, distribution and tax costs. The claim’s qualitative conclusion — that a 5% domestic production boost would have negligible global-supply, import-dependence, and pump-price effects — is therefore supported by these magnitudes.

claim: Says 2010 video clip showing coffins in a field proves "COVID was planned."
rationale: A 2010 video predates the emergence of SARS‑CoV‑2 by nearly a decade, so footage of coffins filmed then cannot by itself prove a pandemic was planned. Coffins in a field can result from many unrelated events (disasters, drills, funerals) and reusing old/unverified footage is a common misinformation tactic that does not demonstrate intent or foreknowledge.

claim: "Border agents discover body of 6-year-old girl: 'She was raped By 30 men'."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or law-enforcement confirmation that border agents discovered the body of a 6-year-old girl raped by 30 men; such an extreme, widely consequential crime would have been documented in mainstream news and official statements. The claim mirrors a pattern of sensational viral posts that have been debunked by fact-checkers and lacks verifiable details (time, place, agency).

claim: "Under ‘Trumpcare,’" domestic violence and sexual assault "could be considered pre-existing conditions."
rationale: Republican repeal-and-replace proposals commonly called “Trumpcare” (e.g., AHCA/BCRA/Graham–Cassidy) included waiver authority and provisions that would let states and insurers limit or charge more for coverage based on prior health conditions. Injuries and diagnosable mental-health conditions stemming from domestic violence or sexual assault are health conditions and therefore could have been treated as pre-existing under those relaxed rules, so the statement that they “could be considered pre-existing conditions” is accurate.

claim: "8% of the votes cast" in Michigan’s Aug. 4 primary, 864 mailed ballots, came from dead voters. "NOTHING TO SEE HERE!!!"
rationale: The claim is false. The 864 mailed ballots referenced are a tiny fraction of the ballots cast in Michigan’s Aug. 4 primary (well over one million ballots), not 8% (which would be tens of thousands). State election officials and subsequent fact-checking found many of those records were clerical matches, duplicates, or otherwise not evidence of widespread votes cast by deceased people, and they were not sufficient to alter results.

claim: "Moderna has been pulled in Iceland and pulled for everyone under age 30 in Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark due to heart issues."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Nordic health authorities did issue age- and sex-specific restrictions preferring Pfizer over Moderna (Spikevax) at times because of a small increased risk of myocarditis in younger people, but the policies varied by country and were not a uniform, blanket “pull for everyone under age 30” across Finland, Sweden, Norway and Denmark. Iceland did not implement a permanent nationwide withdrawal of Moderna for all ages; guidance and age/sex cutoffs differed and changed over time.

claim: "This administration is slashing the Navy to pay for more Obamacare."
rationale: There is no evidence the administration directly 'slashed the Navy' in order to fund expanded Obamacare. Defense funding comes through separate appropriations and observed reductions in Navy programs were tied to overall budget caps/sequestration and congressional choices, not a direct transfer to pay for the Affordable Care Act.

claim: "There's only four senators senior to me ... there's still 44 older than me."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify the speaker or the date, and it mixes two distinct measures (seniority by service and chronological age). Both the number of senators senior in service and the number older in age change over time, so without a named senator and timestamp the statement cannot be confirmed. Because of this missing context I classify it as false as presented.

claim: Says Joe Biden wants to "defund the police."
rationale: This is false: Joe Biden has publicly and repeatedly said he does not support 'defunding the police.' His campaign and policy proposals have emphasized police reform, community policing investments, and targeted federal support rather than eliminating police budgets, and he criticized the 'defund' slogan during the 2020 campaign.

claim: "Right now, in every major poll, national poll and statewide poll done in the last month, six weeks, we are defeating Trump, often by big numbers and always at a larger margin than Secretary Clinton is."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that every major national and statewide poll in the past month/six weeks shows 'we' beating Trump by large margins and always by more than Clinton; that is contradicted by available public polls, which show varying leaders and margins across different pollsters and states. Polling results differ by methodology and timing, and several reputable polls during comparable recent periods showed ties, narrow margins, or Trump leads in some states. Therefore the universal and comparative parts of the claim are not supported.

claim: The U.S. military "is in 130 countries. We have 900 bases around the world."
rationale: The counts in the claim are not supported as a definitive factual statement. Official and widely cited counts vary by definition, but DoD and independent analyses typically report U.S. military presence and permanent installations in far fewer than 130 countries, and the often-cited figure of ~800–900 “bases” depends on a very broad definition that includes many small sites, leases, and host-nation facilities. Because the numbers depend heavily on how one defines “in” a country and what counts as a “base,” the claim as a precise factual claim is misleading.

claim: "To children and the vast majority of young and middle-aged adults and the vast majority of teachers, (the coronavirus) poses virtually zero threat."
rationale: The claim is false because while children and many young adults have lower average risk of severe acute COVID-19 than older adults, their risk is not "virtually zero": measurable numbers of children and younger adults have been hospitalized, have died, and can suffer post‑infectious complications (e.g., MIS‑C, long COVID). Likewise, many teachers are older or have comorbidities and studies have documented infections and outbreaks linked to schools, so the statement overstates safety and ignores transmission risks to others.

claim: Says Georgia ranks "near the bottom in per capita transportation spending."
rationale: The claim is too broad and lacks a time frame or definition of “per capita transportation spending.” Depending on the year and whether one counts state-only versus state+local or capital versus operating outlays, Georgia has at times been below the national average but is not consistently ranked “near the bottom.” Without a specific metric and year, the statement is not reliably supported.

claim: Says Connie Mack "failed to pay his child support."
rationale: There are no widely reported or documented court judgments showing that former Congressman/Senator Connie Mack (III or IV) 'failed to pay his child support.' Major public records and media coverage of these politicians do not include a verified child-support default, so the claim appears unsubstantiated or conflated with another individual.

claim: Says Obama administration delay of health care law's employer mandate affects about 1 percent of the American workforce.
rationale: The employer mandate applies to firms with 50+ full-time equivalent employees and the announced delay mainly affected employers in the 50–99 employee range; those firms employ well more than 1% of the U.S. workforce. Contemporary analyses and labor‐force size distributions showed the number of workers employed by such firms was several percentage points of total employment, so saying the delay affected only about 1% is misleading and likely incorrect.

claim: A video shows Joe Biden lost and confused on stage.
rationale: A short or edited clip cannot reliably demonstrate that Biden was 'lost and confused'—such behavior can result from camera framing, pauses while locating notes or teleprompters, or selective editing. Without the full uncut video, event context, and independent verification, the claim is not supported and is likely misleading.

claim: Says Bubba Watson wrote a viral Facebook post about Black Lives Matter.
rationale: There is no well-documented record that golfer Bubba Watson authored a widely shared/viral Facebook post about Black Lives Matter. The claim appears to conflate Bubba Watson with Darrell “Bubba” Wallace, the NASCAR driver who has publicly supported Black Lives Matter and been the subject of viral social-media items. Without a specific post or credible sourcing, the attribution to Watson is incorrect.

claim: "Prison phone companies charge as much as $25 for a 15-minute call."
rationale: This is accurate in the sense that multiple regulatory reviews and news investigations have documented per‑minute prison phone rates that translated into roughly $20–$25 (and in some cases higher) for a 15‑minute call, particularly in certain jails and contracts prior to rate caps and renegotiations. Reforms and FCC rate caps have lowered many of those charges, but historically and in some locations companies did charge that much.

claim: Says Jeff Foxworthy wrote a ‘fence test’ for Republicans and Democrats.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that comedian Jeff Foxworthy authored a political “fence test” for Republicans and Democrats. Foxworthy is known for comedic “You might be a redneck…” routines, and political “tests” dividing parties have circulated online as memes often misattributed to public figures. Absent a verifiable primary source attributing such a partisan test to him, the claim is not supported.

claim: Huckabee "was one of the highest taxing governors that we had in this country and rivaling Bill Clinton in terms of the Cato ratings."
rationale: The statement overstates and mischaracterizes Cato Institute evaluations. Cato’s fiscal report cards score governors on tax and spending performance and generally showed Huckabee as having a mixed fiscal record (some tax increases and some cuts), but he was not widely identified as one of the nation’s highest‑taxing governors nor clearly “rivaling” Bill Clinton on Cato’s ratings. Without a specific year or metric the claim is misleading.

claim: Judithanne McLauchlan "was part of a group that supports imposing a state income tax on Floridians."
rationale: I found no credible public reporting or biographical information through mid-2024 that identifies Judithanne McLauchlan as a member of a group advocating imposition of a Florida state income tax. Without verifiable sourcing tying her to such an advocacy organization, the claim appears unsupported and likely false.

claim: "North Korea is telling its people that their men’s national team is in the World Cup final."
rationale: There is no evidence that North Korean state media has told citizens the men’s national team is in a World Cup final, and historically the DPRK men’s team has never reached a World Cup final (their best modern result was the 1966 quarterfinals). Contemporary reporting and historical records do not support the claim, so it appears to be false or a misrepresentation.

claim: In the 1970s, "the swine flu broke out . . . under another Democrat, President Jimmy Carter."
rationale: The major 1976 "swine flu" event (an H1N1 cluster at Fort Dix and a nationwide vaccination campaign) occurred during President Gerald Ford's administration. While an H1N1 virus reappeared in 1977 during Jimmy Carter's presidency, that 1977 event is generally described as the "Russian flu" and not the 1976 swine-flu outbreak referenced in the claim.

claim: "The Florida Legislature has not filed a lawsuit to fight Amendments 5 and 6."
rationale: I cannot confirm that the Florida Legislature has definitively not filed a lawsuit over “Amendments 5 and 6.” As of my June 2024 knowledge cutoff there were no clear reports showing the Legislature itself initiating such a suit, but absence of evidence is not proof. Because I lack up-to-date verification and the claim is absolute, I rate it as likely false pending current records.

claim: "Dems have removed any mention of ‘God’ from their Platform."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad blanket statement and is false. U.S. Democratic Party platforms have historically included references to God and faith, and recent years did not amount to a wholesale removal of all mentions — while 2020 saw the Biden campaign and DNC emphasize priorities over a traditional long platform, that is not equivalent to an across‑the‑board deletion of any reference to God. The statement lacks a specific year or document and mischaracterizes the party’s records.

claim: "Las Vegas shooting witnesses report multiple gunmen dressed as security guards."
rationale: In the immediate aftermath of the 2017 Las Vegas mass shooting multiple attendees told reporters and police they heard fire from different directions and some described seeing men in security-type or tactical clothing, leading to reports of multiple gunmen disguised as security. However, extensive investigations by Las Vegas police and the FBI later found no credible evidence of additional shooters and concluded the attack was carried out by a lone gunman. The claim as written — that witnesses reported multiple gunmen dressed as security guards — describes those initial witness reports, not the verified outcome.

claim: The newly drawn congressional district map in Arkansas "keeps communities together."
rationale: The claim is vague and contested; independent observers and opponents have said Arkansas’s new congressional map splits municipalities, counties and communities of interest rather than preserving them. Without specifying which communities are meant, the general statement that the map “keeps communities together” is not supported and is contradicted by public criticism that the lines were drawn for partisan advantage.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to replace" Obamacare "with a single-payer system."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Donald Trump said he wants to replace Obamacare with a single-payer system. Throughout his campaigns and presidency he consistently advocated repealing and replacing the Affordable Care Act with market-based alternatives (tax credits, interstate competition, and private insurance), and he criticized single-payer proposals promoted by Democrats. The claim appears to misattribute or misinterpret his positions.

claim: Says Arizona congressional candidate Christine Jones "called Hillary Clinton ‘a capable and respected leader,’ and an ‘effective’ secretary of state. ... Hillary Clinton effective? Christine Jones thinks so."
rationale: I find no reliable record or contemporaneous reporting showing Arizona Republican candidate Christine Jones publicly described Hillary Clinton as “a capable and respected leader” and an “effective” secretary of state. Given Jones's party affiliation and public statements during her campaigns, such praise would be atypical and would likely have been noted by local and national outlets if made. Without a verifiable primary source for the quote, the claim appears to be a misattribution or unsupported.

claim: Says Barack Obama said that "ordinary men and women are too small-minded to govern their own affairs" and that individuals should "surrender their rights to an all-powerful sovereign."
rationale: There is no credible record of Barack Obama saying those lines; the phrasing is inconsistent with his documented speeches and public remarks and no reputable news or archival sources attribute that language to him. The quotation appears to be a fabricated or misattributed attack often circulated in political rhetoric rather than a verified Obama statement.

claim: "Obama’s daughters caught on camera burning US flag at DC protest."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Malia or Sasha Obama were filmed burning a U.S. flag at a Washington DC protest. Major news outlets and fact-checkers have debunked viral posts that misidentify protestors, and the footage cited in those claims shows different, unverified individuals. The claim appears to be based on miscaptioned or doctored social media content rather than verified reporting.

claim: Chris Christie "cut equal pay for women, calling it 'senseless bureaucracy.' "
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Chris Christie abolished legal equal-pay protections for women or explicitly 'cut equal pay for women.' While Christie pursued budget cuts that trimmed or reorganized certain state programs and sometimes disparaged regulations as 'senseless bureaucracy,' that is not the same as eliminating equal-pay laws or broadly removing pay protections for women. The claim conflates program funding/administration moves and a critical phrase with an outright repeal of equal-pay rights, which is unsupported.

claim: Mitt Romney previously believed "that abortion should be safe and legal in this country." Now he is "prolife."
rationale: Mitt Romney publicly identified as pro‑choice in the 1990s, including statements such as “abortion should be safe and legal in this country.” Over the 2000s he reversed that stance and by his 2008/2012 presidential campaigns he described himself as pro‑life. The claim summarizes a documented change in his public position on abortion.

claim: Says he "will protect your guaranteed benefits" in Medicare while "Mitt Romney would take away Medicare as guaranteed benefits."
rationale: The claim as stated is misleading. Romney's 2012 proposal would have replaced Medicare for future beneficiaries with a premium-support (voucher-like) system that would not guarantee traditional defined benefits, but his campaign maintained that current seniors' benefits would be protected. Saying Romney would outright 'take away' guaranteed Medicare benefits without specifying timing or which beneficiaries overstates and mischaracterizes his plan.

claim: Says he authored legislation "to guarantee coverage to people with pre-existing conditions -- no matter what happens to Obamacare."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who “he” is or which specific bill is meant, and many politicians have claimed to sponsor protections for people with pre-existing conditions while proposing bills that differed substantially in scope. Without a named sponsor and bill text, I cannot confirm authorship or whether the legislation would in fact guarantee coverage regardless of the ACA’s fate. Because of that missing context the claim as stated is classified as false/unverified.

claim: "There is a growing body of evidence that radiation in excess of what the government says are the minimum amounts you should be exposed to are actually good for you and reduce cases of cancer."
rationale: The mainstream scientific consensus and major health agencies do not accept that exposures above recommended limits reduce cancer; claims of beneficial low‑dose 'radiation hormesis' come from limited, inconsistent, and often methodologically weak studies and have not overturned precautionary guidelines. Dose limits are set to minimize risk because available epidemiological and mechanistic data do not demonstrate a net protective effect of higher radiation exposure.

claim: "Eighty percent of the net new jobs created in the state of Texas since 2009 went to the foreign-born."
rationale: This claim is not supported by available labor-force data. BLS payroll counts and Census/ACS household employment data show the foreign‑born share of employment in Texas in the 2010s was in the mid‑teens to low‑20s, and independent fact‑checks have tracked the 80% figure as a substantial overstatement — native‑born workers accounted for a large share of net job gains. Therefore the claim that 80% of net new Texas jobs since 2009 went to the foreign‑born is false.

claim: A Colgate toothpaste is subject to "recall."
rationale: The claim is unspecified (no product variant, lot, jurisdiction, or timeframe) and cannot be verified as stated. There is no clear evidence of a currently active, widely announced recall of a Colgate toothpaste; while Colgate items have had occasional recalls in the past, the blanket present-tense assertion is unsupported.

claim: Says as secretary of state she was reserving judgment about the Trans-Pacific Partnership and "hoped it would be the gold standard."
rationale: This accurately describes public remarks made by Hillary Clinton while she was U.S. secretary of state. In news reports and transcripts from 2012 she said she was keeping an open mind / reserving judgment about the Trans-Pacific Partnership and expressed that she hoped it would become the “gold standard” for trade agreements.

claim: Says the D.C. city council passed a law banning lethal rat trapping.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that the D.C. Council enacted an outright ban on lethal rat trapping. Council activity in recent years has focused on regulations encouraging integrated pest management and restricting certain inhumane devices (e.g., glue traps or certain rodenticides), but not a blanket prohibition on killing rats by trapping. The claim overstates or misrepresents typical local ordinances.

claim: "While the initial increase in oil prices resulted in a near instantaneous increase in gas prices for consumers, the subsequent decrease in crude oil prices has failed to meaningfully provide relief for Georgia's families at the pump."
rationale: The claim is presented without a defined timeframe or quantitative benchmark for “meaningfully,” making it unverifiable as stated. Gasoline retail prices do often rise quickly when crude spikes and can fall more slowly, but the extent to which price declines failed to relieve Georgia families varies by period, local taxes, refinery/distribution margins and retail competition. Without specifying dates and data, the blanket assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says Miami-Dade Mayor Carlos Gimenez "approved a 67% pay raise for himself and increased his own pension. He makes $250,000 a year, more than almost every big-city Mayor in the country. He also kept his taxpayer-funded Mercedes-Benz after slashing $400 million in government jobs and spending."
rationale: The claim mixes true facts with exaggeration and misleading context. Gimenez’s Miami‑Dade mayoral pay has been around $240–$250K (so the $250K figure is basically correct), but there was not an uncontested unilateral 67% self‑pay raise — salary adjustments are set by the county and the 67% figure inflates cumulative/relative changes and is misleading. Allegations that he ‘increased his own pension,’ ‘kept a taxpayer‑funded Mercedes‑Benz,’ and ‘slashed $400 million in government jobs and spending’ conflate different budget actions, public vehicle use rules, and disputed cut figures; those elements are exaggerated or lack direct causal linkage to a single self‑approval act.

claim: "97 percent of the work that Planned Parenthood does is about mammograms and preventative health."
rationale: The claim is false. Planned Parenthood clinics generally do not perform mammograms (they refer patients for mammography) and the oft-cited “97%” number is a misleading way of counting discrete services (tests, screenings, contraception refills) rather than the share of the organization's work, revenue, patients, or staff time. Fact-checks have noted that counting every test or supply as a separate service inflates the preventive-services percentage and does not support the claim as stated.

claim: Georgia is the second-fastest growing state for international tourists.
rationale: The claim is presented without a timeframe or source and cannot be verified as a general statement. State-by-state rankings of international visitor growth change year to year and by metric (percent growth vs absolute increase); while Georgia (U.S. state) has seen strong increases in some years, it is not consistently the "second-fastest" growing state across datasets. Without a specific year and data source the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: The ACLU didn't call for an investigation (of the Newark police department), they called for an immediate federal monitor.
rationale: This claim presents an either/or that is not supported by public record: the ACLU (particularly the ACLU of New Jersey and related civil‑rights groups) publicly urged a Department of Justice pattern‑or‑practice investigation into the Newark Police Department and also pressed for federal oversight/monitoring as a remedial step. In other words, they called for investigation and for federal monitoring as part of the response, not exclusively one or the other.

claim: "Trump’s tax reform plan was nothing more than a middle-class tax increase."
rationale: This claim is incorrect as stated: the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act delivered immediate tax reductions for many middle-income households (through lower individual rates, a doubled standard deduction, and an expanded child tax credit) while also providing large benefits to corporations and high-income taxpayers. However, many individual provisions are temporary and some middle-class taxpayers—especially in high-tax states or after expirations—saw smaller cuts or increases, so it is not accurate to say the plan was “nothing more than a middle-class tax increase.”

claim: "Last year, we were in the range of 850,000 and that was the most in five years. … We are letting more people become citizens than has happened in years."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated and appears misleading. Public immigration/naturalization statistics from U.S. government sources show annual naturalization counts fluctuate and do not clearly support an assertion that 'last year' ~850,000 was uniquely "the most in five years" without a specified country and year, so the statement as presented is inaccurate or unsupported.

claim: Dr. Anthony "Fauci told us there’s nothing to worry about. That’s his quote, ‘There’s nothing to worry about.’"
rationale: This is a misleading paraphrase rather than a documented direct quote. Public records of Dr. Fauci’s remarks in early 2020 show he said the immediate risk to the U.S. general public was low at certain points and advised against routine mask use early on, but he did not have a well-documented, on-the-record quote phrased exactly as “There’s nothing to worry about.” His statements emphasized monitoring and evolving risk, not an absolute ‘nothing to worry about’ assurance.

claim: "Currently, 23 percent of our military's infrastructure is graded as 'poor' while 9 percent is 'failing.'"
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because it gives no source, timeframe, or which nation's military and which infrastructure subset are meant. While defense reports (particularly U.S. Department of Defense installation condition reports) do use categories like “poor” and “failing” and have at times reported roughly similar percentages for specific years or asset classes, the exact claim “currently, 23% poor and 9% failing” cannot be confirmed and is likely misleading without a cited report and date.

claim: "Fluoride in the water, that was originally done by the Nazis!"
rationale: This claim is false. Community water fluoridation grew out of early 20th-century dental public‑health research in the United States (notably work by H. Trendley Dean) and was first implemented on a city scale in Grand Rapids, Michigan in 1945; there is no credible historical evidence that the Nazi regime originated municipal water fluoridation. Although Nazis committed many crimes and unethical medical experiments, that history does not support the specific assertion that they invented or initiated public water fluoridation.

claim: As the number of vaccines administered to children has increased in the United States, so has the autism rate.
rationale: Historically, both the number of recommended childhood vaccine doses in the U.S. and reported autism prevalence have risen over recent decades, so the correlation statement is factually correct. However, extensive epidemiological research finds no causal link between vaccines (including MMR or thimerosal) and autism; increases in diagnosed autism are largely attributed to changes in diagnostic criteria, awareness, and screening.

claim: Says Loretta Lynch was part of "a stunning collection of calls to violence and murder from the intolerant, unhinged leftists in the Democrat party."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or public record that Loretta Lynch called for violence or murder; as U.S. Attorney General she publicly condemned violence and there are no documented speeches or recordings showing her making such calls. The phrase appears to be a rhetorical smear grouping her with extremist statements rather than a factual report of her actions or words.

claim: "The state is set to recapture an additional $500 million in Robin Hood payments from taxpayers and not one penny of it will go to public education in Texas."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. 'Robin Hood' recapture payments are part of Texas school finance law and are generally used in the state’s foundation school program to fund public education by redistributing tax wealth from property‑rich to property‑poor districts; while specific budget proposals have at times shifted how recapture interacts with tax relief, it is incorrect to assert the state will recapture $500 million and that none of it will go to public education without citing a specific enacted law that diverts all such funds. The exact $500 million figure and the absolute statement 'not one penny' are not supported by standard practice or available summaries of recent enacted budgets as of mid‑2024.

claim: The United States "spends more on potato chips than we do on ALL energy R&D."
rationale: This is incorrect. Annual U.S. retail spending on potato chips is on the order of a few to low‑teens billions of dollars, but federal energy R&D budgets alone and the combined public-plus-private energy R&D spending are substantially larger (tens of billions annually when DOE, other agencies, and corporate energy R&D are included). Even comparing just federal energy R&D, DOE and related program budgets are comparable to or exceed potato‑chip consumer spending, so the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: The state crime lab under Attorney General Josh Kaul "is testing significantly less items than former AG Brad Schimel and is still taking longer to test many categories of key items in comparison to Schimel, including DNA."
rationale: I cannot verify the blanket statement that Kaul’s crime lab is testing “significantly less” and universally taking longer than under Schimel. Public data and reporting from the period show mixed results depending on the category, time window, and counting methods (some categories improved while others experienced delays), and pandemic-related staffing and operational changes affected throughput. Because the claim asserts a broad, comparative pattern without specifying a timeframe or metrics, it overstates what can be reliably supported.

claim: Says "$57,000 is the mean [income] in our state" for a family.
rationale: The claim cannot be confirmed as stated because no state, year, or source is specified; state average family incomes vary substantially and change over time. Official statistics frequently report median household income rather than a mean family income, so $57,000 might be true for some specific state/year but is not verifiable from the provided statement.

claim: Says the Clintons "burst through their own self-pronounced guidelines" by accepting foreign donations. "There is a clip of Bill Clinton saying we're not going to take foreign donations."
rationale: Public reporting shows the Clinton Foundation accepted donations from foreign governments and foreign entities while Hillary Clinton served as Secretary of State, and Bill Clinton has been recorded saying the Foundation would not take foreign government donations. The claim conflates those two facts: there is a clip of Bill Clinton stating they would not take foreign donations, and the Foundation nonetheless received donations from foreign sources at times that overlap with Hillary Clinton’s government service. Context and timing affect the interpretation of any guideline violations, but the basic elements of the claim are supported by public records and media reporting.

claim: "Private prison systems are calculating how many new beds (they will need) based on the ... number of third graders."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that private prison companies explicitly calculate future bed needs solely or directly from counts of third graders. While educational outcomes such as third‑grade reading levels are correlated with later incarceration risk and researchers sometimes use them as predictors, private prison capacity planning is based on demographic, crime, sentencing and policy projections rather than a simple headcount of third graders. The claim overstates a specific, documented practice by private prison systems.

claim: "The total (state) payroll has gone down. The total amount of the number of workers in the state has gone down. I like the fact that the bulk of that is just by retirements."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it fails to specify which state or timeframe and provides no supporting data. State payroll and employee headcounts vary by jurisdiction and period; some states have seen declines while others have not, and separations can be due to retirements, layoffs, resignations, or hiring freezes. Without citing specific state payroll/headcount reports and separation reason breakdowns, the assertion that totals have gone down and that the bulk is from retirements is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Before the pandemic, just over 40,000 were on continuing UI claims. Now, there are well over 100,000 on state or federal UI benefits."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it gives no jurisdiction or dates; nationally, continuing (insured) unemployment claims before the pandemic numbered in the millions, not ~40,000. While some individual states or localities might have had ~40,000 continuing claims pre‑pandemic and later exceeded 100,000 across state+federal programs, the statement as written is ambiguous and therefore misleading. Without a specified state and time reference the numeric comparison cannot be confirmed.

claim: Video shows man trying to "fill entire pickup bed with fuel amidst last month’s fuel shortage."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified from the statement alone and is unsubstantiated without the original video, date, and location. Social media clips are frequently miscaptioned or taken out of context, and transporting large volumes of loose fuel in an open pickup bed is hazardous and uncommon, making the specific narrative unlikely without corroborating evidence.

claim: "America has been vaccinating cattle for coronavirus for years, yet the news tells you it’s new and gunna kill you all so go buy mask."
rationale: While coronaviruses infect many animals and vaccines for certain animal coronaviruses (e.g., bovine coronavirus) have existed, those are different viruses from the novel human SARS‑CoV‑2 that emerged in 2019. There is no evidence that America has been vaccinating cattle against SARS‑CoV‑2 for years, and public health warnings about a new human coronavirus and mask guidance reflect the novel virus's human health risk, not a secret cattle vaccination program. The claim conflates distinct animal vaccines with the new human pandemic virus and misrepresents public health messaging.

claim: "The ‘tax plan’ rolled out by @realDonaldTrump would have cut his taxes by $30 million in 2005 (the only year we have returns for)."
rationale: The $30 million reduction is not a uniquely established fact but an estimate that depends on modelling choices. While some media analyses applying Trump’s 2016 proposal to his publicly released 2005 return produced a roughly $30–31M estimate, other plausible assumptions about treatment of capital gains, pass‑through income, deductions and the AMT produce different results, so the claim presented as an absolute fact is unsupported.

claim: Housing prices dropped for the 30 months prior to Barack Obama taking office, "and they have stabilized, they've been about flat since the president came in."
rationale: The claim mixes a partly true statement with a false one. U.S. house prices broadly peaked in mid-2006 and were falling through 2007–2008 (so a multi-year decline into Jan 2009 is accurate), but prices did not remain "about flat" after Obama took office — major indices continued to fall into 2009–2012 before bottoming and recovering. Therefore the overall claim is misleading/false.

claim: "U.S. police killed more people in just one month than the U.K.’s did in over a century."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad and misleading claim. U.S. law‑enforcement kills on the order of hundreds to around a thousand people a year (roughly dozens to a low hundreds per month), while fatal shootings or police‑caused deaths in the U.K. are comparatively rare; however, whether one U.S. month exceeds a U.K. century depends on exact definitions (which part of the U.K., which years, shootings only or all police‑related deaths). Without a clear timeframe and definition the absolute claim cannot be supported as stated.

claim: When Sara Gideon "knew the truth about" sexual allegations against a state lawmaker, "she could have called for an immediate investigation, but didn’t…Gideon knew for months, using her power to cover up."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and official records do not show credible evidence that Speaker Sara Gideon ‘knew the truth’ about sexual allegations and used her authority to cover them up. Allegations appear to stem from partisan attack claims and there is no documentation or verified witness testimony demonstrating she blocked or knowingly delayed an investigation. Legislative complaints were handled through standard procedures and no public record substantiates the specific charge that she deliberately concealed misconduct for months.

claim: "As governor, Kasich delivered the largest tax cut in the nation."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. While Governor Kasich signed significant tax reforms in Ohio, independent analyses (including tax-policy groups and fact-checkers) found those changes were not the largest tax cut in the nation — comparisons vary by metric (dollars, percent of state revenue, per-capita, or rate change) and other states enacted larger or more aggressive cuts. The statement omits timeframe and measurement, which changes the result.

claim: "As we watch the news from Colorado with horror and sympathy for the families, we should remember that each day more than 80 Americans are killed by gunfire, unnecessary tragedies."
rationale: This is accurate for recent years: U.S. vital statistics report roughly 40,000–50,000 firearm deaths per year, which translates to well over 80 deaths per day on average. Those totals include suicides, homicides, accidental shootings, and legal intervention. Annual totals vary year to year, but the multi‑year averages support the claim.

claim: "The majority of minimum wage workers...are mothers."
rationale: Available U.S. labor statistics and analyses do not support that over half of minimum-wage workers are mothers. A substantial share of minimum-wage workers are teenagers and young adults without children, and most datasets show parents (and specifically mothers) make up well under 50% of workers at or near the minimum. Percentages vary by year and definition, but the claim that a majority are mothers is not supported by typical national data.

claim: "Richard Nixon was the last president to be impeached."
rationale: Richard Nixon was not impeached by the full House; he resigned in August 1974 after the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment but before a House vote. Subsequent presidents have been impeached by the House—most notably Bill Clinton in 1998 and Donald Trump (most recently in January 2021)—so Nixon is not the last president to have been impeached.

claim: The Central Falls fire department is "one of the lowest, if not the lowest, paid fire departments in the state and entire region."
rationale: This is an unverified, broad comparative claim. While Central Falls is a small, fiscally constrained city and its public wages have sometimes trailed larger municipalities, establishing it as “one of the lowest, if not the lowest” in the state and an entire multi-state region requires up-to-date, position-specific salary data and clear regional boundaries; that evidence is not provided. The statement is therefore likely an overgeneralization and cannot be accepted as factual without detailed payroll comparisons.

claim: "President Obama himself attempted to filibuster Justice Alito, who now sits on the Supreme Court."
rationale: Barack Obama did not personally mount a filibuster against Samuel Alito. Alito was nominated by President George W. Bush and confirmed by the Senate in early 2006; while some Senate Democrats opposed or considered a filibuster, Obama did not lead or conduct one (he voted against the nomination and spoke in opposition).

claim: "Obama’s Private ‘security’ Company Sets Up Massive Camps Outside 3 Major Cities."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Barack Obama owns or operates a private security company that has established 'massive camps' outside three major cities. Post-presidency, Obama’s known ventures are the Obama Foundation and production company Higher Ground, and former presidents’ security is provided by the U.S. Secret Service. Media reporting and official records do not support the existence of such camps linked to Obama.

claim: "There was never a single shred of evidence presented to anyone" that the attacks in Benghazi, Libya, were "spontaneous, and in fact, the CIA themselves understood that early on."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate: early public and internal materials did include references to a spontaneous protest tied to an anti‑Islam video, and the CIA’s initial talking points and some analysts considered protest-related explanations in the days after the attack. Subsequent intelligence and congressional reviews concluded the assault was a planned terrorist attack, and assessments within the intelligence community evolved and were not uniform from the outset, so it’s false to say there was “never a single shred of evidence” or that the CIA uniformly understood the non‑spontaneous nature immediately.

claim: "In the last year, Wisconsin ranked third in Midwest job growth."
rationale: I cannot confirm the claim because I lack up-to-date employment data beyond my 2024 cutoff and the statement is ambiguous about the exact 12‑month period and data source. Job‑growth rankings change by source (BLS payrolls vs. household survey), by whether they measure percent change or absolute jobs added, and by the specific time window, so without a cited dataset the claim is not verifiable. Given the uncertainty I mark it false pending a precise timeframe and source.

claim: A monthly "police and fire protection fee" on all Wisconsin phone bills does nothing to support police and fire.
rationale: The claim is overly broad and inaccurate: Wisconsin municipalities are authorized to assess a police and fire protection fee and many jurisdictions have collected and used such fees to reimburse local governments for emergency services. While there have been disputes and occasional audits or legal challenges about how some collections were handled, the fee itself is intended and often used to support police and fire budgets rather than doing “nothing.”

claim: "McCain opposes repeal of the death tax."
rationale: The claim is false. John McCain historically supported rolling back or repealing the federal estate ("death") tax—especially relief for small businesses and family farms—and included estate-tax reductions in his 2008 tax proposals rather than opposing repeal. He was not broadly opposed to eliminating the estate tax.

claim: Bill Nelson’s vote for the Affordable Care Act "cuts $500 billion from Medicare to pay for new government programs."
rationale: The ACA did include roughly $500 billion in reductions to projected Medicare spending over a decade, but those were primarily cuts to provider and Medicare Advantage payments and reductions in payment growth, not direct benefit cuts for current beneficiaries. Those savings were counted among the law’s offsets to help finance coverage expansions and reduce the deficit, so framing the vote as simply "cutting $500 billion from Medicare to pay for new government programs" is misleading. The claim conflates projected Medicare spending reductions with taking benefits away from Medicare enrollees and misstates the purpose of the savings.

claim: Says Thom Tillis "refuses to say what we should do to combat ISIS."
rationale: The claim asserts that Thom Tillis refuses to say what should be done to combat ISIS, but public record shows he has repeatedly articulated policy positions — supporting U.S. airstrikes, partnering with local forces, and measures to deny safe havens and funding to ISIS. While he may have declined to outline detailed operational plans in some interviews or debates, that is not equivalent to a blanket refusal to state how to combat ISIS. Without a specific time or quote, the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "We had the highest number of (military) sexual assaults ever reported in the last year" and "we had the lowest conviction rate and the lowest prosecution rate."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated because it lacks a defined population and timeframe and cannot be confirmed as stated. Public military sexual-assault data (e.g., annual DoD reports for the U.S.) show year-to-year variation with recent increases in reports but do not clearly support a blanket statement that the most recent year was the highest ever while also having the lowest prosecution and conviction rates; those rates fluctuate and depend on definitions and reporting mechanisms. Without specifying which military and which year, the assertion is not verifiable and is likely incorrect as a categorical claim.

claim: Says Barack Obama "founded ISIS. I would say the co-founder would be crooked Hillary Clinton."
rationale: The claim is false. ISIS traces its roots to al-Qaeda in Iraq and jihadist networks that emerged after the 2003 Iraq war and the Syrian civil war, with leaders such as Abu Musab al-Zarqawi and later Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi; there is no credible evidence that Barack Obama or Hillary Clinton 'founded' the group. While some U.S. policies (and the 2003 invasion) are widely cited as contributing to the conditions that allowed ISIS to grow, that is different from directly founding the organization.

claim: "Ten years ago, John McCain offered a bill that said he would ban a candidate from paying registered lobbyists."
rationale: There is no clear record that John McCain introduced a bill specifically “banning a candidate from paying registered lobbyists.” McCain did champion campaign‑finance and lobbying reforms (e.g., McCain‑Feingold and later lobbying reform efforts) that restricted gifts, disclosure, and influence, but the claim’s precise prohibition and timing are not supported by evidence. The statement appears to conflate general anti‑lobbyist reform positions with a specific statutory ban he did not propose.

claim: Says "Rob Portman voted for the bipartisan bill to affirm climate change is real, humans significantly contribute to it and it needs to be addressed."
rationale: The claim is likely false as stated because there is no clear public record of Senator Rob Portman voting for a distinct, high‑profile bipartisan bill whose purpose was simply to affirm that climate change is real, human‑caused, and must be addressed. Portman has supported some environment‑related measures but generally opposed major climate legislation, and the claim provides no bill name or date to verify a specific affirmative bipartisan vote. Without a named measure, the assertion cannot be substantiated.

claim: The Keystone XL pipeline "would have produced 830,000 barrels of oil per day, more than enough to offset what we import from Russia."
rationale: The claim mixes a correct capacity figure with incorrect implications: Keystone XL's advertised capacity was about 830,000 barrels per day, but a pipeline transports oil — it does not 'produce' it. Whether that volume could 'offset' Russian imports is misleading because U.S. imports from Russia have varied by year and were often lower than 830,000 bpd, and pipeline deliveries of Canadian heavy crude would not automatically replace Russian shipments due to market routing, refinery needs, and potential for exports. Thus the statement as given is misleading and inaccurate.

claim: "#GradInsurance debacle is a DIRECT result of #ObamaCare. #MIZZOU has to break the law to do the right thing."
rationale: The statement that a “GradInsurance debacle” is a DIRECT result of the Affordable Care Act and that MIZZOU must break the law is unsupported. While the ACA changed reporting and coverage rules that prompted institutions to revise plans, disputes over graduate student insurance typically involve multiple factors (budget, contract language, student classification, state rules) and do not automatically force an institution to violate law. The claim conflates causal attribution and legal necessity without evidence.

claim: "Hillary Clinton invented ISIS with her stupid policies. She is responsible for ISIS."
rationale: This claim is false. ISIS developed from al‑Qaeda in Iraq and the consequences of the 2003 US invasion, regional sectarian conflict, and the Syrian civil war; while US policies and interventions (and some actions supported by Hillary Clinton as Secretary of State) affected regional instability, there is no evidence that Clinton 'invented' or directly created ISIS. Responsibility for ISIS is complex and shared among many state and nonstate actors and conditions.

claim: "Fifty percent of the Ottawa police force have all turned in their resignation."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official statements indicating that half of the Ottawa Police Service submitted resignations. A loss of 50% of sworn officers would be a major, widely reported event; public records and media coverage around the period in question instead describe staffing pressures, retirements, or leaves, not a mass resignation of half the force. The claim appears to conflate staffing issues or isolated departures with a widespread mass resignation.

claim: "Even Fairfax County doesn’t pay the kind of (school administration) salaries that Richmond is paying right now."
rationale: I cannot verify the blanket claim and it is likely false as stated: Fairfax County Public Schools is a very large, well-funded district that routinely pays competitive administrative salaries, and whether Richmond pays more depends on specific positions and timing. Without a named job title, salary figures, and date, the comparison cannot be supported as a general statement that Richmond pays higher admin salaries 'right now.'

claim: Says the Congressional Budget Office "is expecting a protracted economic malaise for at least the next decade under current policies."
rationale: This is not an accurate characterization or direct quote from the Congressional Budget Office. CBO projections (e.g., the Budget and Economic Outlook reports) forecast modest real GDP growth and rising deficits and debt under current law, but they do not state the U.S. will experience a “protracted economic malaise for at least the next decade.” The claim therefore misstates CBO language and tone.

claim: "Thirty-four of the last 44 (debt ceiling increases) have been for less than a year. So, this notion that short-term is somehow the exception, it's actually the rule."
rationale: The statement is misleading because whether an increase is “for less than a year” depends on how you count distinct actions (temporary increases, short-term ‘patches’, or multi-year suspensions). Independent fact-checkers and historical tallies of U.S. debt-limit actions show different counts depending on definitions, and there is not clear support for the precise claim that 34 of the last 44 were under one year. Without a consistent definition and dataset the numeric assertion is not reliably true.

claim: At the State of the Union address, Democrats, "even on positive news … were like death and un-American. Un-American. Somebody said, ‘treasonous.’ I mean, yeah, I guess, why not? Can we call that treason? Why not?"
rationale: There is no reliable record that this exact sequence of lines was spoken 'at the State of the Union address' by a stated speaker. The wording appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution of post‑address comments (often by or about President Trump) rather than something actually said during the formal State of the Union speech itself. Without a clear, attributable source tied to the address, the claim as stated is inaccurate.

claim: Biden was responsible for "ending genocide in Bosnia."
rationale: This overstates Joe Biden's role. As a U.S. senator in the 1990s Biden advocated lifting the arms embargo on Bosnian Muslims and supported intervention, but the end of the Bosnian war and the stop to mass killings resulted from NATO air campaigns and diplomacy (notably the Clinton administration and negotiator Richard Holbrooke) and a multinational effort culminating in the 1995 Dayton Accords. Biden was a participant and advocate, not the sole or primary person 'responsible' for ending the genocide.

claim: In 2013, under a Democratic Senate, "a majority of the Senate voted in favor of" gun-related legislation sponsored by Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley and Ted Cruz, "but the Democrats filibustered it."
rationale: This reverses who blocked gun measures in 2013. The well-known Senate vote that year (the Manchin–Toomey background‑check amendment) did receive a Senate majority but failed to reach the 60‑vote cloture threshold and was blocked by Republicans, not Democrats. There is no clear instance in 2013 where a GOP‑sponsored gun measure had majority support and was filibustered by Democrats.

claim: "Hollywood celebs: We will go on ‘total strike’ if Trump does not resign."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hollywood celebrities collectively declared a contingent “total strike” demanding President Trump resign. While individual celebrities frequently make political statements and unions (like SAG‑AFTRA) have organized industry strikes on labor issues, a mass political strike tied to a president’s resignation was not reported by mainstream media or by organized industry bodies. The claim appears to be a fabricated or sensational social‑media claim rather than a documented coordinated action.

claim: Says when Rhode Island Lottery was proposed, "state residents were enticed to vote for it with the promise that the money would be used for education."
rationale: When Rhode Island voters authorized a state lottery in the early 1970s the proposal was explicitly pitched as a way to raise revenue for public purposes, most prominently education. Campaign materials and the ballot/legislative framing emphasized that lottery proceeds would be used to support schools, which was a common selling point for state lotteries at that time.

claim: For African-Americans between the ages of 17 and 20, "the real unemployment rate … is 51 percent."
rationale: The 51% figure is not supported by official labor statistics for African-Americans aged around 17–20. BLS data show much lower unemployment rates for Black teens (commonly reported for ages 16–19) — typically in the 20–40% range depending on year — and even broader measures that add discouraged or marginally attached workers do not reliably produce a 51% "real" unemployment for a 17–20 age group. Fact-checkers have flagged similar 51% claims as misleading because they rely on nonstandard definitions and cherry‑picked age ranges.

claim: "The Pentagon itself says that we could eliminate 20 percent of U.S. bases."
rationale: There is no known authoritative Pentagon statement that explicitly says “we could eliminate 20 percent of U.S. bases.” Pentagon officials and outside analysts have at times discussed base reductions and studies have modeled various cut levels, but I could not find a direct Pentagon claim quantifying a 20% eliminable share. Without a specific citation or context (domestic vs. overseas, timeframe), the blanket quote is unsupported.

claim: Says Rob Portman "said the auto rescue was a lousy deal for Ohio."
rationale: I could not find authoritative evidence that Rob Portman used the exact words "the auto rescue was a lousy deal for Ohio." While Portman publicly criticized aspects of the 2008–09 auto rescue and argued it had downsides for Ohio taxpayers and manufacturers, attribution of that precise quoted phrase appears unsupported and is likely a paraphrase rather than a direct quote.

claim: "We haven't had any legislation which took away one gun in the past 20 years from anybody in this country--not one."
rationale: This claim is false. Over the past 20 years multiple laws have authorized removal of firearms from specific individuals — for example domestic-violence restraining-order statutes, laws requiring surrender after felony convictions or certain mental-health adjudications, and state “red flag”/extreme risk protection orders (many enacted since 2014–2018) have resulted in guns being seized or surrendered. Therefore it is incorrect to say no legislation has led to the removal of a single gun in that period.

claim: "There are 3.6 million jobs sitting vacant, in part because there aren’t enough qualified applicants to fill them."
rationale: The statement is misleading: the raw figure “3.6 million jobs sitting vacant” does not match U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics job-openings totals for most recent periods (these have been substantially different depending on the month/year), and the causal claim is oversimplified. While employers report skill gaps for some roles, surveys and BLS analysis show multiple drivers of vacancies — wages/benefits, working conditions, childcare/transportation and pandemic-related factors — not solely a shortage of qualified applicants.

claim: "Whales live as long at SeaWorld" as they do in the wild.
rationale: The broad claim is incorrect: for species kept at SeaWorld (notably orcas and belugas), peer-reviewed analyses and population data have generally found captive individuals have shorter average lifespans than their wild counterparts, although a few captive animals have lived long lives. SeaWorld's own historical records and independent scientific studies showed higher early mortality and reduced median life expectancy in captivity, even if husbandry has improved over time.

claim: The president's health care proposals will cause "most Americans to have their premiums increased, not decreased, and hundreds of millions of people lose their current insurance coverage."
rationale: Independent, authoritative analyses of major presidential proposals to change U.S. health policy (for example CBO analyses of repeal/replacement proposals) have projected coverage changes measured in the tens of millions, not “hundreds of millions,” and premium effects vary by age, income, and state rather than causing higher premiums for most Americans. The claim therefore overstates both the number losing coverage and the breadth of premium increases and is not supported by the available evidence.

claim: "President Obama has increased the federal workforce 192,000 individuals -- about 10 percent since he’s taken office -- while we’ve lost 2 million jobs."
rationale: This statement is misleading. The cited ~192,000 increase largely reflected temporary Census hires and other definitional inclusions (and often includes Postal Service employees); when temporary census workers are excluded, the federal civilian workforce was roughly flat or slightly lower early in Obama’s term. The “2 million jobs lost” phrase is vague about timeframe and mixes aggregate private-sector job losses during the recession with federal staffing counts, so the comparison is apples-to-oranges.

claim: Says the percentage of officers the Chicago Police Board fired after hearing their cases or who chose to resign prior to a board hearing roughly doubled during her tenure.
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not supported by clear public data: available records from the Chicago Police Board and reporting show year-to-year variation in firings and pre-hearing resignations rather than a consistent, roughly twofold increase attributable to a single official’s tenure. Without a specified timeframe and baseline, the claim’s ‘roughly doubled’ characterization cannot be verified and appears to overstate trends.

claim: Says the "only valid reason to oppose voter ID is that you plan to cheat," and "every Democrat in Congress opposes voter ID."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate on both counts. Opposition to voter ID is commonly based on documented concerns about disproportionate disenfranchisement, administrative barriers, and the scarcity of in‑person voter fraud — not only an intent to cheat. Likewise, it is false that every Democrat in Congress uniformly opposes all voter ID proposals; some Democrats have supported versions with accommodations (free IDs, same‑day registration, or other safeguards) or bipartisan compromises.

claim: "Last year," Obama "administration officials released into our neighborhoods more than 36,000 criminal immigrants who had nearly 88,000 convictions. The crimes included hundreds of convictions for murder, rape and kidnapping and thousands of drug-related crimes."
rationale: The numbers are a misleading aggregation of ICE data and do not support the claim as stated. The ~36,000 figure comes from multi‑year ICE reporting about aliens with prior convictions or pending charges who were recorded as released from ICE custody, but many releases were due to court orders, local prosecutors, transfers or deportations rather than a policy of deliberately releasing dangerous individuals into communities; the nearly 88,000 figure counts prior convictions and outstanding charges (often multiple per person) and includes many nonviolent offenses. While some released individuals had serious convictions, the claim’s wording overstates causation and omits key context about how and why releases occurred.

claim: An email from Hillary Clinton to Donna Brazile Oct.17th, 2016 stated: "If that f-----’ bastard wins, we’re all going to hang from nooses! You better fix this s---!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence in the published Clinton email releases or widely reported Wikileaks material that Hillary Clinton wrote this violent, profane sentence to Donna Brazile on Oct 17, 2016. Such an incendiary quote would have been prominently reported and archived; searches of the released correspondence and mainstream reporting do not corroborate it. The phrasing and context match patterns of fabricated viral quotes rather than authenticated emails.

claim: "Over 40 percent of small and mid-size banks that loan money to small businesses have been wiped out since Dodd-Frank has passed."
rationale: This is not supported by available banking data: since Dodd‑Frank (2010) only a few hundred banks failed during the post‑crisis period, far fewer than 40% of the nation’s small and mid‑size banks. The overall decline in the number of community and regional banks over recent decades is largely driven by mergers and consolidation rather than a 40% ‘wipe‑out’ attributable to Dodd‑Frank. Attributing such a large percentage of closures specifically to Dodd‑Frank is not supported by evidence.

claim: Says he "is the reason we do not pay a toll every time we pass over the bridge at MoPac and William Cannon."
rationale: The statement attributes sole credit to a single unnamed person for preventing tolls at the MoPac/William Cannon bridge. Decisions about tolling are made by state transportation agencies, regional toll authorities, and sometimes the legislature or courts, not unilaterally by one individual, and there’s no clear evidence that one person alone is responsible for the absence of a toll there. Without identifying the person or providing supporting evidence, the causal claim is unsupported and therefore false.

claim: "We sell 40 percent of our guns without a background check."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous (unspecified “we”) and there is no reliable, general evidence that 40% of all gun sales occur without background checks. Federal law requires licensed dealers to run checks and most retail sales go through such dealers; estimates of private-party/no-check sales vary widely by state, time period and methodology and do not support a single nationwide 40% figure.

claim: The IRS is "going to be in charge of our health care."
rationale: This claim is misleading. The IRS enforces tax law and administers tax-related provisions of health legislation (for example calculating and delivering premium tax credits, processing information returns and collecting tax penalties), but it does not operate health care systems, make medical decisions, or run Medicare/Medicaid programs — those functions are carried out by HHS/CMS and state agencies and by health care providers.

claim: "Fifty seats have already changed hands from the Republicans to the Democrats since Donald Trump was elected."
rationale: The statement is false as presented and is misleading because it does not specify which offices are meant. Verifiable federal results do not support a 50-seat flip from Republicans to Democrats since 2016: Democrats reclaimed the U.S. House in 2018 with roughly a 40-seat net gain, and there was not a comparable 50-seat switch in the Senate or governorships. Without a clear definition of “seats” and cutoff date the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccine is the "deadliest vaccine ever made."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that COVID-19 vaccines are the "deadliest vaccine ever made." Large clinical trials and extensive post‑authorization safety monitoring across billions of doses have shown serious adverse events and deaths causally linked to the vaccines are extremely rare, and overall benefit–risk assessments find vaccines prevent far more deaths from COVID-19 than they cause. Claims that it is the deadliest rely on misinterpreting raw passive-reporting counts (e.g., VAERS) or conflating coincidental deaths with vaccine-caused deaths.

claim: In the 100 days since its passage, the economic stimulus has "saved or created nearly 150,000 jobs."
rationale: The claim is unsupported as presented because it lacks crucial context (which stimulus, which 100‑day window) and there is no independent payroll data showing a discrete +150,000 jobs attributable within a 100‑day period. Government statements about jobs “saved or created” are often projected or program‑level counts (contracts/grants) rather than measured changes in employment, so the plain claim is not verifiable as a factual statement. Without a clear source, the figure should not be taken as established fact.
