claim: Says Republican U.S. Rep. Bob Dold "continues to side with his Republican leadership and the NRA in blocking consideration of a bill that would keep firearms out of the hands of people on the terrorist watch list."
rationale: The claim asserts a continuing, explicit alignment by Rep. Bob Dold with House leadership and the NRA to block consideration of a specific ‘‘terrorist watch list’’ firearms bill, but it provides no specific vote or time period and there is not clear public evidence that Dold repeatedly led or publicly coordinated with the NRA to block such a bill. Dold’s record on guns was mixed—he sometimes supported limited background-check measures and at other times voted with his party on procedural matters—so the broad, ongoing charge that he ‘‘continues to side’’ with leadership and the NRA in blocking consideration is unsubstantiated without a specific vote or timeline.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's "campaign hasn't been clear about when she wiped her server of her work emails."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and public records showed inconsistent statements from Clinton campaign lawyers and spokespeople about the timing of when emails on her private server were deleted, and investigators later documented deletion activity and confusion about dates. Because multiple sources noted conflicting timelines and the campaign did not provide a single clear, consistent date in early disclosures, the characterization that the campaign "hasn't been clear" is accurate.

claim: "If we use (Tax Increment Financing) funding, that's going to take funds from the general fund for Pinellas County, as it will take funds from the general fund for the city of St. Pete."
rationale: Tax Increment Financing (TIF) redirects the incremental increase in property tax revenue within a redevelopment area to the TIF/CRA rather than to general funds of participating taxing authorities. That commonly reduces a municipality’s general fund receipts when the city is the TIF sponsor, so the city impact is accurate; however the county’s general fund is affected only if the county’s share of the increment is included or the county agrees to participate. The claim asserts an automatic county general-fund loss, which is not universally true without local agreement or statutory requirement.

claim: "New Jersey's governor cut $1.6 billion from public education while handing out $2.1 billion in corporate tax breaks, more than the entire previous decade."
rationale: The claim mixes figures and timeframes in a way that independent reporting and fact‑checks do not support. New Jersey did see reductions in state school aid under Governor Christie and the state has granted sizeable business tax incentives, but the specific pairing — a $1.6 billion cut to public education concurrent with $2.1 billion in corporate tax breaks that exceed the entire previous decade — is not supported by authoritative budget records or contemporary fact‑checks; the numbers are aggregated differently across years and programs and are therefore misleading.

claim: "Wind powers nearly 13 million homes across the country."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as a stable fact because it provides no country or timeframe and resembles an industry “equivalent homes” estimate that changes year to year. Claims that wind "powers X homes" are calculated by dividing annual wind generation by average household electricity use and can be presented differently by different sources, so the flat assertion that wind currently powers nearly 13 million homes is misleading without context. Because of that ambiguity and variability I rate the claim as false in its presented form.

claim: Schools stopped teaching children cursive so they wouldn’t be able to read the U.S. Constitution and other historical documents.
rationale: This claim is false. Declines in cursive instruction stemmed from curricular changes (e.g., emphasis on keyboarding, Common Core priorities, and limited classroom time), not a coordinated effort to prevent reading historical documents. Many schools and states still teach or have reinstated cursive, and the Constitution and other documents are widely available in printed and transcribed forms. There is no credible evidence of an organized policy to stop teaching cursive for that purpose.

claim: "Joe, I keep hearing you every morning talking about the biggest tax increase in history, but you don't mention it's also the biggest tax cut in history.''
rationale: The statement asserts the same tax action is both the largest tax increase and the largest tax cut, which is logically inconsistent without additional qualifiers. There is no widely accepted evidence that a single policy simultaneously constituted both the biggest increase and the biggest cut in history; such claims depend on specific metrics, time periods, and whether one measures revenue, rates, or particular tax categories. As presented, the claim is misleading and unsupported.

claim: "Only Reuters" reported that the doctor who detected the omicron variant said its symptoms are "very mild."
rationale: This is false. Multiple major news organizations reported the South African doctor’s comments about Omicron being mild (many quoting or paraphrasing her), not just Reuters. Outlets such as the BBC, CNN, The Guardian and others ran stories repeating her characterization or similar descriptions.

claim: "You couldn’t buy a cannon when, in fact, the Second Amendment passed."
rationale: The claim is false as stated. In the late 18th century cannons and other artillery were manufactured and sold to militias, privateers, merchants and wealthy individuals, and state militias commonly had artillery pieces; while ordinary citizens rarely owned them due to cost and practical restrictions, private purchase was possible. Thus it is incorrect to say one categorically "couldn't buy a cannon" when the Second Amendment was adopted.

claim: "Child support card" in Delaware "controls what mothers can and cannot buy with child support money."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. Child support payments are private funds and, in most jurisdictions including Delaware, are not delivered on a state-controlled card that restricts specific purchases; purchase restrictions are a feature of public assistance EBT/TANF or SNAP benefits, not child support. A child-support debit/prepaid card (if used) generally functions like a normal bank/debit card and does not legally prevent mothers from buying particular items.

claim: "There aren't too many people outside protesting" his speech at the Phoenix Convention Center.
rationale: The claim is unverified and subjective: it asserts there "aren't too many people" protesting but gives no date, speaker identity, or objective measure. Protest attendance at events like speeches at the Phoenix Convention Center varies and is reported with photos and counts; without contemporaneous evidence the statement cannot be confirmed. Because of missing specifics, I treat the claim as unsupported and therefore not factual.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court decided in 1982 that non-citizen children must get free K-12 education.
rationale: The U.S. Supreme Court in Plyler v. Doe (1982) held that states cannot deny free public K–12 education to children based on their immigration status. The Court found that undocumented children are protected by the Equal Protection Clause and struck down a Texas law that barred them from public schools.

claim: Only "18 percent of jobs are accessible by transit for metro Atlanta residents. 33 percent for those living in the city."
rationale: The claim is presented without a source or definition of key terms (time threshold, year, or which boundaries count as 'metro' vs 'city'), and accessibility percentages vary by dataset and methodology. Some studies produce figures in the same range (single‑digit-to‑30 percent) depending on the travel‑time cutoff and year, but the precise statement as quoted cannot be confirmed as a general, sourced fact and is therefore misleading without context.

claim: Florida retirees and families "lost tens of thousands of dollars" in deposits on failed Trump condo projects, but he "pocketed their money and walked away."
rationale: It is true that some buyers of failed Trump-branded condo projects (including in Florida and elsewhere) lost deposits that were often tens of thousands of dollars when developers defaulted or projects stalled. However, reporting and court records indicate many of these projects were developed by third parties or went through bankruptcies and there is no clear evidence that Donald Trump personally "pocketed" buyers' deposits and walked away; his role was frequently as a licensor of the Trump name rather than the primary developer. The claim therefore overstates the proven facts about who kept the money.

claim: "They delayed my swearing-in here in Massachusetts for a couple weeks so they could ram (the health care law) through."
rationale: There is no evidence that Massachusetts or Senate officials intentionally delayed a swearing‑in to allow passage of the federal health‑care law. The timing of swearing‑ins after special elections is governed by state certification and Senate scheduling; contemporaneous reporting about the 2010 Massachusetts special election (Scott Brown) shows routine certification and a swearing‑in shortly after the election rather than a deliberate hold to "ram" legislation through. Assertions that officials delayed a swearing‑in for that purpose are not supported by the available record.

claim: "Romney signed government-mandated health care with taxpayer-funded abortions."
rationale: Romney’s 2006 Massachusetts health reform did institute an individual mandate for insurance coverage, but it did not create a blanket requirement that taxpayers fund abortions. Federal restrictions (the Hyde Amendment) and state funding rules govern abortion payments, and the reform law did not itself mandate taxpayer-funded abortion coverage. The claim conflates the mandate with an untrue automatic provision of taxpayer-funded abortions.

claim: Facebook video shows "counting Biden’s votes at 2 a.m."
rationale: There is insufficient information to confirm that the Facebook video actually shows ballots being counted for Biden at 2 a.m.; the claim asserts a specific provenance and time that cannot be verified from the statement alone. Social media videos are frequently reposted, miscaptioned, or lack reliable timestamps, so without the original file, metadata, or independent fact‑checking the claim is unproven and likely misleading.

claim: "The president gave the (auto) companies to the UAW."
rationale: This is false as stated. In the 2009–2010 auto industry rescues the federal government took temporary equity stakes and negotiated with the UAW, and the UAW’s retiree health trust (VEBA) received stock and concessions, but the companies were not handed over to the UAW and remained under company/government control during restructuring and later private ownership.

claim: "Violent crime is now going down for the first time in a long while."
rationale: The statement is too broad and not reliably true as written. Violent-crime trends vary by country, state and city and depend on the exact timeframe and data source; while some U.S. jurisdictions and recent months have shown declines after pandemic-era peaks, others remain elevated and national time series are mixed. Saying it is "now going down for the first time in a long while" overgeneralizes and cannot be confirmed without specifying place and period.

claim: "During his 18-year Senate career, (Russ Feingold) supported judges who voted to deny your individual Second Amendment right. … (He) promises to protect those rights, but that's not what his record shows."
rationale: The statement makes a broad claim without naming specific judges or votes; while Feingold was a senator from 1993–2011, judicial doctrine on the Second Amendment shifted over that period (notably with the Supreme Court's 2008 Heller decision). There is no clear, documented pattern showing Feingold systematically “supported judges who voted to deny” an individual Second Amendment right, and the assertion overgeneralizes and lacks specific corroborating confirmation-vote examples.

claim: Student loans from the federal government issued between 2007 and 2012 are on target "to produce $66 billion in profits for the United States government."
rationale: The statement is misleading. The frequently-cited "$66 billion" comes from federal budget accounting conventions for a particular set of student loans and reflects a projected cash-flow surplus under official federal scoring, but that result depends on the accounting method and specific cohort definitions. Using fair‑value accounting or different time windows and risk adjustments produces a very different (often negative) result, so the plain claim as stated is not reliably true without context.

claim: "Both China and Japan have surpassed us, with Japanese cars now getting an average of 45 miles to the gallon."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: Japanese cars do not average 45 miles per gallon across the board. Official fuel-economy data and common conversions show typical new-car averages in Japan (depending on test cycle) are considerably lower than 45 mpg, and China’s fleet efficiency has improved but is not clearly above U.S. levels in comparable metrics. The statement also conflates countries and lacks a clear metric/timeframe.

claim: Says Oregon canned blueberries will be cheaper in South Korea thanks to a trade agreement.
rationale: There is no clear evidence of a new trade deal that specifically lowers South Korea’s import cost for Oregon canned blueberries. The U.S.–Korea Free Trade Agreement has been in place since 2012 and tariff treatment of processed fruit is product-specific; prices in market also depend on exchange rates, shipping, and distribution margins. Absent a named, recent agreement or tariff schedule change explicitly covering canned blueberries from Oregon, the claim is unsupported.

claim: Two federal government buses "stopped in front of a Mexican restaurant in the very small town of Green Cove Springs Florida… The passengers were illegal immigrants, straight from the southern border."
rationale: There is no credible, corroborated reporting or official confirmation that two federal government buses carrying migrants directly from the southern border stopped in Green Cove Springs, Florida. Claims like this have not been verified by local authorities or mainstream news and migration transports are often organized by state/local agencies or private contractors rather than ‘federal government buses’ originating at the border.

claim: Imitation dairy products often differ nutritionally from those they mimic, and labeling them "milk" or "cheese" or "yogurt" is "against the law."
rationale: The first part is accurate—plant-based and other imitation dairy products frequently have different nutrient profiles than the animal-derived products they mimic. The second part, however, is false as a blanket statement: whether labeling a product "milk," "cheese," or "yogurt" is illegal depends on jurisdiction and specific regulations, and such labeling (often with qualifiers like "almond milk") is commonly permitted in many places. Thus the absolute claim that such labeling is "against the law" is incorrect.

claim: Dollar General "added 2,500 stores and 20,000 jobs" during his four-year tenure as CEO.
rationale: The claim is imprecise and does not match public company reporting for a specific four‑year CEO term. Dollar General did expand substantially in recent years, but the phrase “added 2,500 stores and 20,000 jobs” ascribed to a single four‑year CEO tenure is not supported by consistent figures in company annual reports or widely cited press summaries and appears to conflate or misattribute totals. Without a precise named CEO and exact four‑year window, the stated numbers are unreliable.

claim: Says Facebook is now a "public entity" that will be able to "use your photos" and "information" unless you post a statement declining your permission.
rationale: This is false. Facebook is a private company (albeit publicly traded) and it does not automatically gain new rights to use your photos and data simply because you fail to post a disclaimer. Use of user content is governed by Facebook’s Terms of Service, privacy settings, and applicable law, and a unilateral status update cannot override those agreements or legal frameworks.

claim: "Individuals with mental illnesses die an average of 25 years earlier than those without a mental illness."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. Research shows people with severe mental disorders (e.g., schizophrenia, bipolar disorder) have a substantial mortality gap—commonly reported around 10–20 years earlier—while some specific studies report gaps approaching 25 years for particular diagnoses or subgroups; it is not the average for all individuals with any mental illness.

claim: Says 100,000 are on waiting list to attend Texas charter schools.
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and cannot be verified as a definitive fact without a date or source. While charter advocates and some news stories have at times cited figures near 100,000 for Texas charter waitlists, statewide totals vary by year and by how waitlists are counted (duplicates, multiple schools, and different reporting methods). Because the claim is presented as an absolute current fact but lacks sourcing and the number is inconsistent across reports, I rate it as false/unsupported as stated.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson wants to put 100,000 troops, including 25,000 Americans, "into the area where ISIS is."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Sen. Ron Johnson explicitly called for deploying 25,000 American troops as part of a 100,000‑troop force 'into the area where ISIS is.' Public statements and reporting on Johnson show he advocated stronger action and training/arming regional forces, but did not endorse sending that specific number of U.S. combat troops. The claim appears to misstate or inflate his comments.

claim: There are nanoparticles in the COVID-19 vaccine that will help people "locate you" via 5G networks.
rationale: This claim is false. COVID-19 vaccines do not contain metal, RFID, GPS, or other active tracking nanoparticles; authorized mRNA vaccines use lipid nanoparticles to carry mRNA, which are non‑metallic and not capable of emitting or receiving radio signals. Locating a person via 5G would require an active powered transmitter or large detectable hardware and there is no credible evidence from manufacturers, regulators, or independent tests supporting such tracking capabilities in vaccines.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccines "were released to the public after only two months of testing in healthy humans."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. Large COVID-19 vaccine trials began months before public rollout (e.g., Phase 1/2/3 trials for Pfizer–BioNTech and Moderna started in spring–summer 2020) and tens of thousands of participants were enrolled in Phase 3 trials before Emergency Use Authorizations in December 2020. The confusion likely stems from regulators noting a median of roughly two months of follow-up after the second dose at the time of EUA, but that is not the same as only two months of testing in humans.

claim: Quotes Gene Hackman as saying that Trump could "easily turn out to be one of the best presidents that America has ever seen."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that actor Gene Hackman publicly praised Donald Trump with that quote; such a striking endorsement would have been widely reported but does not appear in reliable news, interviews, or obituaries. Hackman largely avoided public political commentary in later years, and the attribution appears to be a misquote or a piece of satire or misinformation.

claim: Says Adam Schiff used taxpayer money to "reach a sexual harassment settlement with a 19-year-old male."
rationale: There is no credible public record or reliable reporting showing Rep. Adam Schiff used taxpayer funds to settle a sexual harassment claim with a 19-year-old male. Fact-checking outlets and House disclosure records reviewed through mid-2024 do not corroborate the allegation, and Schiff’s office has denied such payments. Given lack of documented settlement or official payment record, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "If the Republicans were the majority, (Rep. Barton) would have actually the gavel and the chairmanship."
rationale: The claim presents a categorical conditional that Rep. Barton would definitively hold the gavel and chairmanship if Republicans were the majority. While the majority party does control committee chairs and a ranking member often becomes chair after a power flip, chair assignments are determined by party caucus rules, elections, seniority and other political considerations, so it is not guaranteed. Therefore the absolute claim is false as stated.

claim: "60 percent of the jobs lost in the 2008 recession were living-wage jobs. Of the jobs we’ve gotten back, only 40 percent are living-wage."
rationale: The statement conflates an ambiguous term ('living-wage') with commonly cited figures about 'middle- and high-wage' job shares. Analysts (e.g., EPI/Brookings) reported that roughly 60% of jobs lost in the Great Recession were middle- or high-wage and that only about 40% of jobs regained in some recovery windows were middle- or high-wage, but those figures depend on the exact timeframe and wage-category definitions, so the claim as worded is misleading and unverified.

claim: Malia Obama was "among 10 arrested in racist Antifa attack," and the cop who arrested her was "found dead under suspicious circumstances."
rationale: There are no credible news reports, police records, or reputable fact-checks showing Malia Obama was among ten arrested in a racist Antifa attack, nor that an arresting officer was later found dead under suspicious circumstances. The story matches a pattern of fabricated viral claims and conflations rather than documented events involving President Obama's daughter.

claim: Says Gen. David H. Berger, commandant of the U.S. Marine Corps., refused Nancy Pelosi’s request to use the Marines for inauguration security, telling her "we don’t work for you."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Gen. David H. Berger told Speaker Nancy Pelosi “we don’t work for you” while refusing a request to use Marines for inauguration security. The quote and scenario circulated on social media and were debunked by multiple fact‑checks; it appears to be a misattribution or fabrication. The Commandant’s public statements and news coverage do not support this exchange.

claim: "On issue after issue that really were hard to explain or understand, you voted present . . . And anytime anyone raises that, there's always some kind of explanation."
rationale: The claim makes a factual assertion about a pattern of voting (“on issue after issue … you voted present”) and consistently offered explanations, but no specific person, timeframe, or supporting voting record is provided to verify this pattern. Without identifiable context and documentary evidence (roll-call votes, transcripts, or public statements), the pattern cannot be confirmed. Therefore I judge the claim false as stated due to lack of verifiable data.

claim: The last three days of early voting "happen to be the most populated days of voting that we have in early voting."
rationale: The statement is presented as a universal fact but early voting patterns vary widely by jurisdiction and election. While many places do see heavy turnout on final days (and some weekends), data from different states and elections show peak early voting can occur on weekends, single high-turnout days, or scattered days rather than always the last three days.

claim: "150,000 (oil spill) claims have been filed by Floridians, but only 40 percent of them have been paid."
rationale: The precise claim (150,000 Florida claims and only 40% paid) is not supported by consistent public records. Reporting on Deepwater Horizon claims shows varying totals by state and by program (Gulf Coast Claims Facility vs. later BP settlement) and payment rates changed over time; many claims initially denied were later paid, so a blanket figure like this is misleading.

claim: Facebook users can avoid "problems with your Facebook going against community standards" by changing your settings.
rationale: Facebook’s community standards apply to content regardless of a user’s privacy or audience settings; changing settings can limit who sees your posts but does not exempt content from removal or enforcement. While privacy or audience controls may reduce visibility and thus the chance of reports, they do not guarantee avoidance of policy violations or account penalties.

claim: "There was no violence on the Senate side, in terms of the chamber."
rationale: The claim is incorrect for the most commonly referenced event (the January 6, 2021 Capitol breach): rioters entered and occupied the Senate chamber area, sat on the dais, and there were physical confrontations and assaults on officers protecting the Senate. Multiple arrests and reports document force used by rioters on the Senate side as well as damage and disruption inside the chamber. Therefore it is inaccurate to say there was no violence in or around the Senate chamber.

claim: Says abortion is "the leading cause of death for black Americans and kills as many as 1,000 black children every day."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. Federal vital statistics list heart disease and cancer as the top causes of death for Black Americans, and routine death tallies do not classify abortions as a leading cause; moreover, dividing recent U.S. abortion totals by days and the approximate share among Black women yields a much lower figure than 1,000 Black abortions per day. The statement conflates different definitions (fetal terminations vs. civilian deaths) and overstates recent abortion counts.

claim: Says that as president, Barack Obama has not gone to the Texas-Mexico border
rationale: This claim is false. As president, Barack Obama did visit the U.S.-Mexico border in Texas during his time in office — most notably a 2014 trip to the Rio Grande Valley/McAllen area to review Border Patrol operations and the surge of unaccompanied migrant children.

claim: H&M advertised a sweatshirt that said, "Koolest Kid in the Klan."
rationale: This is false. There are no reliable reports or H&M product records showing a sweatshirt with the phrase "Koolest Kid in the Klan"; the well-documented H&M controversy involved a children's sweatshirt reading "Coolest Monkey in the Jungle," and images claiming the Klan phrase have been shown to be doctored or fabricated. The claim appears to be a viral falsehood rather than a real H&M advertisement.

claim: A video shows Joe Biden speaking slowly and slurring on the Fourth of July.
rationale: The claim as stated is not verifiable from the information given: no specific video, source, or year is provided. Many short clips of President Biden speaking slowly or slurring have circulated online and some have been misdated or edited, so absent an original authenticated source tying the footage to a particular Fourth of July it cannot be confirmed. Because of that uncertainty I classify the claim as false as presented.

claim: The media "never show crowds."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that is contradicted by routine news and entertainment coverage: television and online outlets commonly show crowd shots at protests, rallies, sporting events, concerts, parades, and public ceremonies. While individual outlets or segments may choose not to show crowds or may selectively frame them, that does not support the blanket assertion that media 'never' show crowds.

claim: Republicans included "the Akin amendment in the Republican Party platform, which bans abortion, even for rape victims."
rationale: There is no evidence the national Republican Party adopted an "Akin amendment" that explicitly bans abortion even in cases of rape. Todd Akin’s controversial comments were personal and drew attention, but the GOP platform did not formally codify an amendment named after him that removes rape exceptions; state platforms vary and individuals proposed different measures, but the claim as stated is inaccurate.

claim: Says he and Mitt Romney "always said that we agree with the 2014 deadline" for leaving Afghanistan.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Mitt Romney consistently said he agreed with a hard 2014 U.S. withdrawal deadline. During the 2012 campaign Romney repeatedly criticized setting fixed timetables for withdrawal and declined to commit to a specific rigid deadline, even though NATO/ISAF plans aimed to transition combat operations by the end of 2014. Therefore the statement that 'he and Mitt Romney always said that we agree with the 2014 deadline' is not supported.

claim: The CDC "adjusted the US Covid deaths from 153,504 to 9,210."
rationale: This is a misrepresentation. The CDC did not retroactively reduce the U.S. cumulative COVID-19 death total from ~153,504 to 9,210; the much smaller number cited relates to a specific subset or timeframe (for example a particular week or deaths where COVID-19 was listed under a specific cause category) and not a revision of the overall death toll. Multiple fact-checkers and CDC documentation show the numbers refer to different categories of death counts, not a downward adjustment of the total deaths.

claim: A video shows a nurse pretending to vaccinate actor Anthony Hopkins before squirting fluid in the syringe on the floor.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or reliable verification that a video shows a nurse pretending to vaccinate Anthony Hopkins and then squirting fluid on the floor; reputable news outlets and fact-checkers did not corroborate that claim. Many viral clips are misattributed or edited, and vaccinators sometimes expel small amounts of fluid or air which can be misinterpreted as 'squirting.' Because the claim rests on an unverified interpretation of a video, it is assessed as false.

claim: "The administration raises revenue for nationalized health care through a series of new taxes, including a light switch tax that would cost every American household $3,128 a year."
rationale: This specific claim is false. No credible administration proposal or enacted law includes a literal “light switch tax,” and independent budget analyses and fact-checkers found no credible estimate that Americans would pay $3,128 per household annually from such a levy; revenue plans for expanded public health programs typically rely on payroll, income, corporate, prescription-drug, or insurance-related measures and produce much smaller per-household effects. The “light switch” figure appears to be a fabricated or grossly misleading characterization of proposed revenue changes.

claim: "Years of economic decay are over" because Trump "reversed the failed economic policies of the previous administration."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the U.S. was not in "years of economic decay" before Trump—GDP and employment were generally improving—and while Trump-era policies (tax cuts, deregulation) coincided with some short‑term growth, they also increased deficits and had mixed effects. Furthermore, attributing an end to broad economic decline solely to policy reversal is a strong causal claim not supported by the overall evidence, especially given the 2020 pandemic recession. Thus the assertion that "years of economic decay are over" because Trump reversed prior policies is unsupported.

claim: "Austin is the largest city in the U.S. or Texas with no geographic representation" on its city council.
rationale: Austin's City Council currently includes ten single-member district seats plus a mayor elected at-large (the so-called 10‑1 system), so it does have geographic representation. The claim likely conflates current practice with an older at-large arrangement or lacks a specified timeframe, but as stated it is incorrect.

claim: "According to (Barack) Obama’s newest unconstitutionally enacted law, health care professionals are now required to violate HIPAA privacy laws and submit medical data to the government," which is "then used as justification for gun confiscation."
rationale: The claim is false. There is no Obama-era (or subsequent) federal law that requires health care professionals to violate HIPAA and turn over patients' medical records en masse to the government to justify gun confiscation. HIPAA generally prohibits unauthorized disclosure of protected health information, and while it permits limited disclosures (e.g., for public health, mandatory reporting, or court orders), those are narrow exceptions and do not equate to a blanket requirement to surrender medical data for firearm seizures.

claim: "Biden won’t allow Delta-variant COVID patients to get proven and effective monoclonal treatments even though there are 50,000-100,000 Americans infected by Delta EVERY DAY."
rationale: The claim is false because the Biden administration has not barred monoclonal antibody treatments; federal agencies (FDA/HHS) have adjusted emergency use authorizations and distribution based on evidence of which specific monoclonal products remain effective against particular variants. Some monoclonal antibodies with reduced activity against certain variants were limited or revoked for safety/effectiveness reasons, while others (for example casirivimab/imdevimab/REGEN‑COV) retained authorization and continued to be distributed. The stated daily infection figure (50,000–100,000 Delta infections every day) is imprecise and varies by date and surveillance method.

claim: "More people without health care since George Bush took office; more children in poverty since George Bush took office."
rationale: Contemporary U.S. government data show the number of people without health insurance and the number of children in poverty rose during George W. Bush’s time in office (early 2000s through 2007–2008). Census and health-insurance surveys documented increases in the uninsured population and in child poverty counts compared with the period just before he took office.

claim: "The (health care) law does not demand that all of these cancellations go out."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act set minimum coverage standards for plans sold after 2014 but did not literally require insurers to cancel every existing policy. Many of the cancellation notices resulted from insurer business decisions, state regulatory actions, or loss of ‘grandfathered’ status after plan changes rather than an across‑the‑board statutory mandate; HHS later issued limited flexibility to allow some renewals.

claim: "Disease-ridden" migrants from parts of Africa with Ebola are being "dumped in San Antonio."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that migrants infected with Ebola are being intentionally "dumped" in San Antonio. U.S. public-health authorities (CDC/local health departments) and major news outlets have not reported Ebola cases tied to migrant arrivals there, and routine border/public-health screening would identify and prompt response to Ebola infections. While migrants have been transported between U.S. cities, that does not substantiate the claim of deliberate dumping of Ebola-infected people.

claim: Says Bill Gates said, "We need to develop a digital certificate that shows who has received all the vaccinations. Only those with all the required vaccinations may travel, visit churches, participate in sports and music events, get a job, etc."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Bill Gates ever said the quoted sentence. Gates has discussed developing digital records or ‘certificates’ to show vaccination or test status in the context of COVID-19, but he did not advocate the specific laundry-list of bans (travel, churches, sports, jobs) in that phrasing and major fact-checkers have found the quote to be fabricated or misattributed. The claim appears to conflate or invent language not present in his public statements.

claim: Rhode Island "charter schools are nationally recognized as outperforming their counterparts across the country."
rationale: The claim overstates the evidence. National studies and summaries of charter-school performance (e.g., large-scale CREDO analyses and other evaluations) show mixed results that vary widely by state and by individual school; Rhode Island is not broadly cited as a national exemplar whose charter schools uniformly outperform traditional public schools across the country. While some individual Rhode Island charter schools may perform well or have received awards, there is no consensus national recognition that Rhode Island charters as a group outperform their counterparts nationwide.

claim: "The price of soybeans has fallen 50% since 5 years before the election. A big reason is bad (terrible) trade deals with other countries."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which election and five-year window and thus cannot be verified as stated. While soybean prices have fallen at times and U.S.-China trade tensions (tariffs/retaliation) contributed to weaker U.S. soybean demand around 2018–19, prices are driven by multiple factors (global supply, yields, weather, currency, biofuel demand) and a 50% fall attributed mainly to “bad trade deals” is unsupported without a specified timeframe and causal analysis.

claim: Says "we had to cut 13 billion dollars in state spending over two years."
rationale: The statement lacks essential context (which state and which two-year period), so it cannot be verified as written. State budget cuts of $13 billion over two years could be true for some large states or for aggregated categories, but without a named jurisdiction and timeframe the claim is unsubstantiated. Because verification requires specific budget documents or official statements, the claim as presented is not verifiable.

claim: "Leonardo DiCaprio explains why he’s moving to Casselberry, Florida."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or confirmation that Leonardo DiCaprio is moving to Casselberry, Florida, nor that he has publicly explained such a move. Major entertainment and news outlets have not reported any verified relocation plans to that small Florida city, and the claim appears to be clickbait or misinformation. Given DiCaprio’s well-documented residences and high public profile, such a move would be widely covered if true.

claim: Wisconsin has "the fastest-shrinking middle class in the country."
rationale: The claim is too definitive and not supported by consistent data: rankings of which state has the fastest-shrinking middle class vary by data source, timeframe, and definition of “middle class.” Fact-checkers and analyses of Census/Pew/Brookings measures have found Wisconsin among states with declines in middle-income share in some periods but not universally the fastest. Because different metrics produce different leaders, the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "Just passed into law today: You cannot go 5 miles over speed limit" in North Carolina.
rationale: There is no evidence that North Carolina's legislature just passed a law specifically making it illegal to drive 5 mph over the posted limit; traffic laws already prohibit exceeding posted limits and enforcement discretion or local rules vary, but no statewide change 'passed today' to single out +5 mph has been reported. Claims like this have appeared as social posts and are not supported by official NC General Assembly or DMV announcements.

claim: Says "Joe Biden is absolutely on board with defunding the police."
rationale: Joe Biden has repeatedly said he does not support “defunding the police” and his campaign and administration proposals have focused on police reform, accountability, and targeted investments in community violence prevention rather than wholesale defunding. Public statements and policy positions from Biden and his team contradict the claim that he is "absolutely on board" with defunding law enforcement.

claim: Says Jacob Blake "declared he had a gun in the car and was going to go get it" and was "brandishing" a knife
rationale: Contemporaneous body‑camera and bystander video, plus official investigative summaries and multiple fact‑checks, do not show Jacob Blake declaring he had a gun in the car or saying he would go get one, nor do they show him brandishing a knife at officers. What is visible is Blake moving around and leaning into the SUV before being shot; a small folding knife was reportedly recovered later, but there is no reliable evidence he announced a gun or brandished a knife at officers in the footage or audio.

claim: Says of El Paso that some years, "in a city of almost 700,000, we had five murders the entire year. Our average over the last 10 years is 18 (murders per year). We exceeded that average just on one day" after a gunman opened fire at a Walmart in the city.
rationale: The statement bundles several specific numeric claims that cannot be fully verified here. While the El Paso Walmart shooter in August 2019 killed 22 people (which would exceed an 18-per-year average), I cannot confirm from available internal knowledge that El Paso ‘‘some years’’ had only five murders or that the exact 10-year average was 18 murders per year. Because key numeric components (the ‘‘five murders’’ year and the precise 10-year average) are not independently corroborated in my knowledge, the composite claim is judged false as stated.

claim: "More than 32,000 Americans lose their lives to gun violence each year."
rationale: This is accurate: U.S. vital statistics from the CDC/NCHS report annual firearm deaths well above 32,000 in recent years (roughly 40,000–50,000 per year). Those totals include suicides, homicides, unintentional and other firearm-related deaths, so the claim's threshold is comfortably exceeded.

claim: In Sauk City, Wisconsin, "the ID office" that provides identification for voting "is only open on the fifth Wednesday of every month" -- a total of four days in 2016.
rationale: This specific claim is unsupported and implausible: municipal and state offices that issue identification (DMV branches or city clerk offices) normally maintain regular posted hours rather than opening only on the rare "fifth Wednesday" of a month. While 2016 did contain only a small number of fifth-Wednesday dates, there is no reliable evidence that Sauk City limited ID issuance to those four days. The statement appears to conflate an exceptional schedule or isolated reporting with an ongoing policy.

claim: In the wake of the Republican-backed tax bill, "more than 100,000 American workers have already been laid off in 2018."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Republican-backed 2017 tax law directly caused more than 100,000 American workers to be laid off in 2018. While a number of companies announced workforce reductions in 2018, fact-checkers and employment data show those cuts were largely due to restructurings, mergers, automation or other business reasons, and the total layoffs cannot be reliably attributed to the tax bill.

claim: Says the USMCA is the "biggest trade deal ever made."
rationale: The claim is false. The USMCA is an update to NAFTA among three countries and is large, but it is not the largest trade deal ever — multilateral arrangements like the EU single market and WTO commitments (and other large regional blocs) encompass more members and far greater trade volume. Saying it is the "biggest trade deal ever made" is an overstatement without a specific metric.

claim: "Military arrests former President George W. Bush."
rationale: There is no credible evidence, reporting, or official statement that the U.S. military has arrested former President George W. Bush. An apprehension of a former president by the military would be extraordinary, widely reported, and inconsistent with U.S. legal norms governing civilian arrests. Therefore the claim is false.

claim: "Barack Obama had 150 days in the U.S. Senate where he was able to vote quite often 'present.' "
rationale: The statement is inaccurate and mixes terms (days vs. votes). Official Senate roll-call records and contemporary fact-checking show Obama cast far fewer than 150 "present" votes during his 2005–2008 Senate tenure, so he did not have 150 days in which he repeatedly voted "present." The claim therefore overstates and mischaracterizes the voting record.

claim: "Congress files charges against Nancy Pelosi."
rationale: This is false. Congress does not 'file charges' in the criminal sense — prosecutors (federal or state) bring criminal charges — and Congress has not brought any articles of impeachment or similar formal charges against Nancy Pelosi. Members of Congress can be investigated or expelled by their chamber, but no such expulsion or impeachment of Pelosi has occurred.

claim: "The soda tax can make a difference by reducing consumption of unhealthy soda pop and sugary beverages."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and real-world implementations show that excise taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages reduce purchases and consumption; examples include evaluations of Mexico's national tax, municipal US taxes (e.g., Berkeley, CA), and the UK's Soft Drinks Industry Levy which also prompted reformulation. While effect sizes vary with tax level and local context, the preponderance of evidence supports that a soda tax can decrease consumption of unhealthy sugary drinks.

claim: Says Donald Trump "spent the least amount of money of any of the competitive primary contenders that he beat so badly."
rationale: The claim is not supported by campaign finance records and reporting from the competitive Republican primary contests (notably 2016). Multiple major rivals (e.g., Jeb Bush, Marco Rubio, Ted Cruz) spent equal or substantially more than Trump, and some lower-spending candidates were not considered among the main competitive contenders—so Trump was not uniquely the lowest spender among the competitive opponents he defeated. Because the statement lacks a clear election cycle or definition of “competitive,” it is misleading as stated.

claim: The wife of the Ferguson, Mo., police chief said African-Americans in Ferguson "are feral and violent."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the wife of the Ferguson police chief publicly declared African-Americans in Ferguson "are feral and violent." Major news organizations and independent fact-checkers traced the allegation to unverified or misattributed social-media posts and found no authenticated source for the quote.

claim: "Pope Francis says covid vaccine will now be required to enter heaven."
rationale: This claim is false. Pope Francis has encouraged COVID vaccination as an act of charity and a public-health responsibility, but he has not said vaccines are required to enter heaven or made any doctrinal pronouncement linking vaccination to salvation. No Vatican or papal statement supports the asserted requirement.

claim: "An estimated 8 million children worldwide live in orphanages or residential institutions. Shockingly, 80 percent of these children are not orphans."
rationale: The rough estimate of about 8 million children in residential care has been widely quoted (e.g., past UNICEF/advocacy estimates), but the blanket claim that 80% of those children are not orphans overgeneralizes and is not robustly supported by global, up-to-date data. Studies and NGO reports from some countries show high proportions of children in institutions having living parents, but proportions vary greatly by country and the 80% figure is based on selective samples and advocacy summaries rather than a definitive global census. Because definitions and data collection differ, the 80% claim is unreliable as a universal global fact.

claim: "There's only three countries in the entire world where there's no paid vacation by law, we happen to be one of them."
rationale: The United States does not guarantee paid vacation at the federal level, but the claim that only three countries worldwide lack any statutory paid annual leave is not reliably supported. International data and reporting vary over time and by definition (some lists cite Liberia and Papua New Guinea, others include different small states or territories), so the precise count is uncertain and likely not exactly three.

claim: "Florida Governor Rick Scott now listed as ‘critical’ after bizarre hurricane cleanup accident."
rationale: This claim is false. Rick Scott is not the current Florida governor (he served as Florida’s governor from 2011–2019 and later served as a U.S. senator), and there are no credible news reports showing he was listed as 'critical' after a hurricane-cleanup accident. The story appears to be a misattribution or fabrication rather than a verified medical report from reliable outlets.

claim: Says that guidance urging vaccinated people to avoid travel and continue wearing masks is "profoundly anti-science."
rationale: Characterizing guidance that advises vaccinated people to limit travel and keep wearing masks as 'profoundly anti-science' is inaccurate. Such guidance is typically grounded in epidemiological evidence about breakthrough infections, variant transmissibility, and the precautionary principle while data are evolving, so it reflects a science-based, risk-reduction approach rather than an anti-scientific stance.

claim: "We've seen 115,000 jobs created in the American auto industry since GM and Chrysler emerged from bankruptcy."
rationale: Contemporary BLS employment data and independent fact-checks found that motor-vehicle and parts manufacturing employment rose by roughly 115,000 jobs after GM and Chrysler emerged from bankruptcy in mid-2009. Fact-checkers used BLS series for motor vehicles and parts to arrive at a figure consistent with the claimed 115,000 jobs over that recovery period.

claim: "Sotomayor has had her rulings thrown out by the court a troubling four times."
rationale: The statement is unsupported and ambiguous. It does not specify which court or time period, and public reporting does not establish a clear, indisputable count of exactly four Sotomayor rulings being "thrown out." While some of her appellate opinions have been reversed over the years, the exact number depends on definitions and timeframe, so the claim as stated is misleading.

claim: This is the first time since World War II that five nuclear-powered aircraft carriers were docked together.
rationale: The claim is incorrect or misleading. Nuclear-powered carriers did not exist during World War II (the first, USS Enterprise CVN-65, entered service in 1961), so saying “since World War II” is anachronistic, and there have been occasions since the 1960s when multiple nuclear-powered carriers were in the same port or docked at the same time. The phrasing is ambiguous and the specific assertion that this is the first such occurrence is not supported by historical fleet movements.

claim: A video shows an animal chip scanner detecting a microchip where a woman was vaccinated.
rationale: There is no evidence that human vaccines contain microchips, and vaccine ingredient lists do not include any tracking chips. Animal microchip scanners detect RFID transponders or can register metal or electronic interference (for example from needles, syringe components, or external metal), so a beeping scanner during or after an injection is plausibly explained by such artifacts rather than an implanted chip. Multiple fact-checks and basic knowledge of how RFID readers work support this.

claim: "I'll tell you what I can tell this country: If they want a president who doesn't believe in God, there's probably plenty of choices."
rationale: The sentence is an opinionated, speculative claim and not a verifiable fact. There is no evidence that there are "probably plenty" of viable U.S. presidential choices who openly do not believe in God; historically major-party nominees have almost always professed religious belief, and the number of credible nonbelieving candidates is small and context-dependent. Because the claim is vague and unverifiable, it cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: Says President Donald Trump "put out a $297 million contract to a vendor to show him how to hire Border Patrol. So, the first payment they made was $14.8 million. You know how many Border Patrol they hired with $14.8 million? Two."
rationale: I find no reliable evidence that President Trump personally issued a $297 million contract to a vendor to “show him how to hire Border Patrol,” nor that a first payment of $14.8 million produced only two hires. Federal hiring and procurement for DHS/CBP are handled through established contracting processes with multiple awards and oversight, and contemporary reporting does not corroborate the specific dollar amounts and outcome claimed. The statement appears to conflate or misrepresent contract purpose, parties, and hiring results.

claim: "Paul Ryan has blocked all action to strengthen our gun laws."
rationale: The claim is overbroad and inaccurate. As House Speaker Paul Ryan had influence over which bills reached the floor and opposed many Democratic gun‑control proposals, but he did not unilaterally block “all” efforts to strengthen gun laws — some measures were considered or passed in Congress and state legislatures pursued reforms. The absolute wording makes the statement false.

claim: "I remember landing under sniper fire."
rationale: This is a first-person memory claim with no supporting details (who said it, when, where, witnesses or records), so it cannot be independently verified. In the absence of corroborating evidence I treat the statement as unproven and thus classify it as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "24 of every 100 kids in school today speak Spanish."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous (no country, age range, or definition of “speak Spanish”) and is not supported as a universal fact. U.S. education and census data show the share of school‑age children who speak Spanish (or speak Spanish at home) varies by year and state and is not uniformly 24 per 100; estimates commonly differ from that precise figure. Therefore presenting a single flat rate of 24/100 as a general truth is misleading.

claim: North Carolina is home to "two rivers of the top five most polluted rivers" in the U.S.
rationale: There is no authoritative, widely used national ranking that places two North Carolina rivers among the top five most polluted in the United States. Major national lists and EPA/advocacy summaries of the most polluted U.S. rivers typically feature rivers such as the Ohio, Mississippi, Anacostia, Hudson and Arkansas, while North Carolina rivers are cited for local or regional pollution problems but not commonly two entries in a national top five. Without a specific source or metric the claim is not supported.

claim: "Marjorie Taylor Greene just scrubbed her Twitter feed of all things Gaetz."
rationale: I cannot verify the claim as stated and have no contemporaneous evidence that Greene removed all references to Matt Gaetz from her Twitter account. Social media posts and deletions are time-sensitive and would require screenshots, archives, or reputable reporting to confirm; absent that, the claim is unverified. Because I lack corroborating sources, I treat the assertion as false until substantiated.

claim: "The only time government employment has gone down during a recession has been under me."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: government employment has fallen during other recessions besides the one under the unspecified speaker. For example, during the 2007–2009 Great Recession state and local government payrolls declined substantially, and earlier downturns (early 2000s) also saw government employment drops, so it is not true that this occurred only under the claimant.

claim: "95 percent of the income gains in the last few years have gone to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The statement is misleading because whether the top 1% received 95% of recent income gains depends on the exact country, income measure, and time window; no authoritative source supports that precise figure generically for "the last few years." Empirical studies (e.g., work by Saez, Zucman, and Piketty) show that in some narrow post-recession windows a very large share of gains went to the top 1%, but the share varies substantially across periods and definitions and is not universally 95% for a recent multi‑year span.

claim: Says he predicts the weather better than Punxsutawney Phil.
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable because it does not identify who “he” is or provide any source showing the person said they predict the weather better than Punxsutawney Phil. Without a named individual, quote, or context, there is no evidence to confirm the assertion. If a specific person and source are provided, the statement could be checked for accuracy.

claim: "Black and Latino people in NYC are arrested at TEN times the rate of white people for virtually the same rate of marijuana usage."
rationale: The claim overstates and mischaracterizes the empirical record. While multiple analyses and NYC data have shown large racial disparities in marijuana possession arrests (Black New Yorkers have in some years been arrested many times more often than whites despite similar usage rates), combining Black and Latino people and asserting a uniform “TEN times” multiplier is not supported across available years and datasets. The general point (disparate arrests despite similar usage) is true, but the specific numeric phrasing is inaccurate or misleading.

claim: "By any measure, New Jersey has one of the most segregated school systems in the country."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim (“by any measure”) that overreaches. New Jersey is frequently ranked among the most racially and economically segregated states by several common metrics (e.g., exposure/isolation indices, dissimilarity, and district-level segregation), but rankings vary by the specific measure, years analyzed, and whether one looks within-district vs. between-district segregation. Because not every conceivable metric or dataset places New Jersey at the very top, the blanket wording is inaccurate.

claim: Says Dr. Robert Gallo, the man who helped discover the HIV virus, confessed he was "forced" to "create the HIV virus as a secret weapon to wipe out the African race."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or record that Dr. Robert Gallo ever confessed to being "forced" to create HIV as a weapon; this claim is a baseless conspiracy theory. Gallo is a prominent virologist involved in early HIV research, but the scientific consensus is that HIV arose from zoonotic transmission (SIV to humans), not laboratory creation or a targeted weapon. Assertions of a confession appear only on fringe/hoax sources and contradict public statements and historical records.

claim: "Gov. (Rick) Perry helped balance his budget with about $6 billion worth of federal help, which he happily took, and then started blaming the members of Congress who had offered that help."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and fact-checks show that Perry's administration accepted roughly $5–7 billion in federal stimulus and Medicaid matching funds that were used to help cover Texas budget shortfalls. After taking those funds, Perry publicly criticized Washington and some members of Congress for federal policies and spending, creating the appearance he accepted federal help while blaming federal lawmakers.

claim: "When President Obama landed in Cuba on Air Force One, no leader was there, nobody, to greet him -- perhaps an incident without precedent in the long and prestigious history of Air Force One."
rationale: Contemporaneous news reports and official accounts say President Obama was met at José Martí International Airport by Cuban officials including Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez; President Raúl Castro did not meet him on the tarmac but hosted later formal meetings and ceremonies. The claim that "no leader was there, nobody" and that this was without precedent is inaccurate and ignores standard diplomatic practice where heads of state do not always personally meet visiting leaders at the plane.

claim: "The difference between what I support and what you support, Vice President Biden, is that you require them to opt in (to a Medicare public option), and I would not require them to opt in. … They would automatically be enrolled. That’s a big difference. … Are you forgetting what you said two minutes ago?"
rationale: The statement accurately characterizes the policy difference: Joe Biden’s public-option/buy-in proposals during the 2019–2020 Democratic primary were voluntary choices people would have to elect (opt in), while advocates of single-payer/’Medicare for All’ described universal coverage where people would be automatically covered. Thus saying Biden “requires them to opt in” versus an automatic enrollment proposal is a correct contrast.

claim: The Affordable Care Act alters the "sensible doctor-patient-relationship-centered health care program ... we see today."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act introduced major insurance, payment, and delivery changes (e.g., insurance market rules, Medicaid expansion, essential health benefits, value‑based payment models and accountable care organizations) that altered incentives, administrative rules, and care delivery. Those changes have affected how clinicians make decisions, document care, and interact with insurers and patients, thereby changing aspects of the traditional doctor–patient relationship. The degree and direction of change vary by setting, but the statement that the ACA alters that relationship is supportable.

claim: "Of the top five cities for staged automobile accidents, three are in Florida. … We rank No. 1 in the country in staged auto accidents."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific, current ranking of cities and a No. 1 status for staged auto accidents, but there is no single, consistent national dataset or authoritative annual ranking that supports that exact claim. While Florida has frequently been identified by insurers and law‑enforcement reports as having a high incidence of staged/induced accidents, city‑level rankings vary by source and year, so the precise ‘‘top five with three in Florida’’ and ‘‘No. 1’’ claims are unsubstantiated as a definitive fact.

claim: Says Rick Scott "cut Medicaid" so people can't "get Obamacare."
rationale: This is misleading. As Florida governor Rick Scott rejected the ACA’s Medicaid expansion and sought budget reductions/changes in state Medicaid programs, but stating he “cut Medicaid so people can't get Obamacare” overstates causation and intent and conflates Medicaid cuts with blocking all ACA coverage. The state refusal to expand Medicaid limited eligibility for ACA-era Medicaid coverage, but does not cleanly equate to a purposeful cut to prevent people from enrolling in “Obamacare.”

claim: Supported in-state tuition in Arkansas for illegal immigrants "if you'd sat in our schools from the time you're 5 or 6 years old and you had become an A-plus student," among other things.
rationale: The claim presents a specific quoted statement and a position (supporting in-state tuition in Arkansas for undocumented immigrants) but provides no speaker, date, or verifiable source. There is no reliable record of that exact quote or a documented, attributed public statement matching those words; without attribution it cannot be confirmed as factual.

claim: Says the FDA said that Pfizer "falsely misled" the agency about the safety of the COVID-19 vaccines and that the shots are killing more people than they save.
rationale: This claim is false. The FDA has not issued a public finding that Pfizer "falsely misled" the agency about vaccine safety, nor has any credible regulatory or scientific body concluded that COVID-19 vaccines are killing more people than they save. On the contrary, large-scale clinical trials, real-world effectiveness studies, and regulatory safety reviews show the authorized COVID-19 vaccines substantially reduced hospitalizations and deaths, while identified serious adverse events are rare.

claim: "More than one in five of veterans aged 20 to 24 can’t find a job to support their family or to ease the transition to civilian life."
rationale: I cannot verify the claim as stated. Official labor statistics (BLS) track unemployment for young veterans and while their unemployment has at times been elevated, recent BLS unemployment rates for veterans aged 20–24 have not consistently exceeded 20%, and the claim also mixes a subjective inability to 'support their family or ease the transition' with a concrete unemployment rate. Without a specific source or timeframe, the statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Only in the Third World do you see this habitual use of prosecutions of former leaders."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. Prosecutions of former leaders are not limited to the so-called "Third World": developed democracies have prosecuted or charged ex-leaders as well (for example, South Korea prosecuted multiple former presidents, Italy repeatedly prosecuted Silvio Berlusconi, France charged Nicolas Sarkozy, and Spain pursued legal cases over Catalan leaders). Thus it is false to assert such prosecutions occur only in poorer countries.

claim: Under Gov. Tom Corbett, "Pennsylvania ranks 49th in job creation."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it gives no timeframe or data source and is not supported by standard labor statistics for Corbett's term. Bureau of Labor Statistics and contemporary fact-checks show Pennsylvania did not rank 49th in overall job creation across Governor Corbett’s full term; rankings vary by metric and period but Pennsylvania typically ranked substantially higher than 49th. Without a specific metric (percent change, absolute jobs, private vs. total employment) and dates, the claim as stated is false.

claim: "Biden says he doesn’t need voters to get elected."
rationale: There is no credible record of President Biden saying he “doesn’t need voters to get elected.” Public speeches, interviews, and official transcripts do not contain such a statement and it contradicts the political reality that elected officials rely on votes. The claim appears to be a misquote, paraphrase, or fabricated statement rather than an accurate quotation.

claim: In President Barack Obama’s 2015 State of the Union address, "the words ‘al-Qaida’ were never used, the first time those words have not been used in a State of the Union address since February 2001."
rationale: The official transcript of President Obama’s January 2015 State of the Union does not include the words “al-Qaida.” Contemporary fact-checking noted that every State of the Union address between George W. Bush’s February 2001 speech and 2015 had used the term at least once, making 2015 the first omission since February 2001.

claim: Says last year "13 million (health insurance) rebates went out, in all 50 states. Another 8.5 (million) rebates are being sent out this summer, averaging around 100 bucks each."
rationale: The specific totals and average in the claim cannot be confirmed and do not match the way CMS publishes annual Medical Loss Ratio (MLR) rebate data. CMS releases year-by-year rebate totals and average payouts that vary; the claim omits the year and appears to mix figures in a way not supported by publicly reported MLR numbers.

claim: Jim Renacci "voted repeatedly to end Medicare."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Jim Renacci voted for Republican budgets and proposals that sought to restructure Medicare (for example toward premium‑support or block‑grant models) and supported GOP health-care measures, but he did not cast votes that literally ‘‘ended’’ Medicare as an existing program. Saying he "voted repeatedly to end Medicare" overstates those votes and omits important context about the policy changes those measures proposed.

claim: "Statistics show one male cat can father 420,000 kittens in five years."
rationale: The 420,000 figure is a viral, misleading extrapolation that assumes an unrealistically large and continuously available pool of fertile female cats and uninterrupted impregnation. In reality queens have limited reproductive rates (gestation ~63 days, typically 2–4 litters/year with ~3–5 kittens per litter) and social/territorial and ecological limits make siring hundreds of thousands of kittens by one male in five years implausible.

claim: A photo shows ex-Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin wearing a "Make Whites Great Again Hat."
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and image-forensics analysis found the circulated photo was digitally altered to add the slogan; the original widely published photograph of Derek Chauvin does not show him wearing a hat reading “Make Whites Great Again.” The claim therefore misrepresents the authentic image.

claim: "Studies have shown that voter fraud is non-existent in Texas."
rationale: While multiple academic and government studies find voter fraud in Texas to be extremely rare, it is not literally non-existent; there are documented and prosecuted instances (e.g., absentee ballot and registration fraud) over the years. Therefore the absolute claim that studies show fraud is non-existent is inaccurate.

claim: Says Democratic opponents Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith support sanctuary policies.
rationale: The claim presents as if both Democrats unequivocally support "sanctuary policies," but public record shows Cal Cunningham has repeatedly said he does not support sanctuary cities, and Erica Smith’s positions emphasize immigrant protections and limits on cooperation with federal immigration enforcement rather than an explicit blanket endorsement of formal "sanctuary" policies. Because the term "sanctuary policies" is often used loosely, asserting both candidates unequivocally support them is misleading.

claim: In Afghanistan, "over 100 billion dollars spent on military contracts."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about timeframe and who awarded the contracts, and there is no clear evidence that military contracts solely for Afghanistan exceeded $100 billion. Public accounting typically reports larger totals for overall U.S. war costs (which include operations, reconstruction, and veterans’ care) and often combines Iraq and Afghanistan when discussing contract totals; the subset labeled strictly as Afghanistan military contracts is generally reported as lower. Because definitions and periods vary, the assertion as stated is not reliably supported.

claim: It’s warmer on Mars than it is in parts of the United States and Canada during the polar vortex.
rationale: Mars surface temperatures vary widely (roughly −125°C at winter poles up to about +20°C in equatorial daytime), so many Martian locations and times are warmer than the extreme cold reached in parts of the United States and Canada during strong polar vortex events. Polar vortices can drive ground temperatures well below −40°C to −50°C in affected regions, colder than typical mid-latitude or equatorial Martian daytime temperatures, so the comparison can be true for those specific cold Earth locations and times.

claim: "Under (Obamacare), you can’t reward a person for better behavior. You can’t have incentives to be healthier."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. The Affordable Care Act does not ban incentives for healthier behavior; it creates rules for employer and insurer wellness programs and allows financial incentives or premium differentials within limits (for example, final federal rules have permitted incentives up to a percentage of total plan cost and higher allowances for tobacco cessation programs). The law also imposes nondiscrimination, privacy, and program-design requirements rather than a blanket prohibition on rewards for healthy behavior.

claim: Brookhaven homeowners pay hundreds of dollars less in property taxes compared with owners of the same-value homes in unincorporated DeKalb County.
rationale: The claim is misleading as a blanket statement. In Georgia homeowners pay county and school taxes plus any municipal (city) millage, so Brookhaven residents generally pay DeKalb County and school taxes plus a Brookhaven city tax; whether they pay "hundreds less" than identical homes in unincorporated DeKalb depends on specific millage rates, exemptions, and special districts. In many cases Brookhaven homeowners pay equal or higher total taxes, so asserting a general savings is not supported without year- and property-specific data.

claim: Say North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper was arrested for driving while intoxicated in Stanly County.
rationale: There are no credible news reports or public records indicating North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper was arrested for driving while intoxicated in Stanly County; such an event involving a sitting governor would have been widely covered. The claim appears to be a false or mistaken attribution, possibly confusing someone else with the same name.

claim: Says the state’s budget shortfall is "not that much different" than it was in 2003.
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable and unlikely to be accurate because it gives no state, year of the current shortfall, or whether figures are nominal or inflation-adjusted. State budget gaps vary widely over time and must be normalized for inflation, population, and accounting changes; comparing an unspecified current shortfall to 2003 without those details is not supportable.

claim: "Workers in the United States are making less than they were almost 20 years ago, and yet they are working harder."
rationale: The statement bundles two broad claims that aren’t supported for the overall U.S. workforce. Over the last ~20 years median and average wages adjusted for inflation have been roughly flat to modestly up (not generally lower), and official series for usual weekly hours or annual hours per worker show little net increase—hours have been mostly stable or slightly down for many groups. While some low‑paid groups saw real declines and many workers report greater intensity or insecurity, the blanket claim about all U.S. workers is inaccurate.

claim: "I cut spending while serving in the state Legislature"
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who “I” is, which state legislature, or the time period, and no supporting evidence is provided. Determining whether someone actually cut spending requires examining their voting record, sponsored bills, and enacted budgets, so under this uncertainty the claim is treated as false.

claim: "The Clintons' foundation took millions from foreign governments" including United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.
rationale: Publicly disclosed donor lists and tax filings for the Clinton Foundation and related entities show it accepted donations from foreign governments and state-controlled entities, and reporting by multiple news organizations documents multi-million-dollar contributions from countries including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. While exact totals and timing vary by report and whether contributions were to the foundation or affiliated entities, the core claim that the foundation took millions from those foreign governments is supported by the record.

claim: Says the Obama administration purged "training courses and information about Islamism, jihad, Sharia, and the Muslim Brotherhood."
rationale: This is false as stated. There were documented instances in the mid-2010s where particular federal training materials and guidance were revised to avoid certain language about Islam or extremism, but credible reviews and fact-checking found no evidence of an administration-wide purge of all training courses and information on Islamism, jihad, Sharia, and the Muslim Brotherhood.

claim: "President Obama has the most border patrols and border security deployed at the border of any previous president."
rationale: Public staffing and deployment records show that under President Obama the Border Patrol and CBP workforce reached historically high levels (Border Patrol agents exceeded 20,000) and the administration authorized multiple border support deployments (including National Guard and DHS surge personnel). Compared with previous administrations, these totals and deployments were larger, so the broad claim is accurate. However the statement is imprecise about which specific personnel or timing is meant.

claim: "The Cleveland police has issued a stand down order to officers."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence or widely reported official announcement that the Cleveland Division of Police issued a blanket 'stand down' order. Such orders are uncommon and would almost certainly be documented in news reports or official city/police statements, which are not present in known records up to mid‑2024. Absent a specific date, source, or corroboration, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Missouri has one of the highest rates of uninsured children in the country."
rationale: Missouri's rate of uninsured children is generally near the national average and not typically listed among the states with the very highest child uninsured rates. National survey analyses (e.g., American Community Survey and KFF summaries) consistently identify states such as Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, and Florida as having higher child uninsured rates than Missouri.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to keep big government in charge" of federally-owned land.
rationale: This claim is contradicted by Donald Trump’s stated policy positions and actions, which generally sought to reduce federal control of public lands—favoring transfers to states, increased resource development, and shrinking or reversing national monument designations. Saying he “wants to keep big government in charge” of federally-owned land mischaracterizes his public record and proposals to devolve or open up federal lands rather than expand federal management.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s "Make America Great Again" hats were made in China.
rationale: Multiple reputable news outlets and fact-checkers found that a large share of the early 'Make America Great Again' hats sold by Donald Trump's campaign were manufactured in China. While some later production was shifted to other countries and occasional U.S. runs occurred, the general claim that MAGA hats were made in China is accurate for the campaign's early merchandise.

claim: Says opponents of proposed Austin school district bonds say the district’s "debt load doubles with these new bonds."
rationale: Local reporting and campaign materials around the Austin school district bond proposals show opponents repeatedly asserted that the district’s debt would roughly double if the new bonds passed. The claim refers to opponents’ message (what they said), not to an independent calculation of debt impact, which is why it is verifiable as a statement made by opponents rather than as an outcome guarantee.

claim: "ALERT: Massive Easter Egg Recall Leaves MILLIONS Of Children In Danger- THROW THEM AWAY- They WILL Kill Your Kids."
rationale: The claim is sensational and gives no specific manufacturer, product name, date, or authoritative source.
