While Missouri (and some Missouri cities like St. Louis) has had higher violent‑crime and homicide rates than the national average, crime trends vary by offense and year; national crime did not uniformly decline across all categories and time periods, and Missouri’s trends have fluctuated rather than consistently diverging from the national picture. The blanket statement that ‘overall crime throughout the country is going down but not here in Missouri’ is therefore not supported as a general fact.

claim: "U.S. comedian Kevin Hart in critical condition after gory car crash."
rationale: This is false. While Kevin Hart was involved in a serious rollover car crash in September 2019 and suffered back injuries that required surgery, contemporary news reports described him as conscious, talking and not in critical condition; he subsequently recovered. There are no credible reports saying he was in critical condition after a 'gory' crash.

claim: "ISIS is in 32 countries."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as a precise, current fact. Open-source reporting and government assessments identify ISIS central nodes in Iraq and Syria and a number of affiliated or inspired groups across a dozen to perhaps two dozen countries at various times, but reputable sources do not support a definitive count of 32 countries without more context. The claim omits timeframe and a definition of what counts as “in” (direct control, active fighters, affiliate groups, or mere claims).

claim: There "are 500 registered Republicans moving" to Texas "every day."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that 500 people who were already registered Republicans in other states relocate to Texas and re-register there every single day. Voter registration and migration data do not track prior-party registration in a way that supports that precise daily figure, and similar claims have been traced to misinterpretations or cherry-picked timeframes.

claim: "I have always been focused on reining in the deficit."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement — that the speaker has "always" been focused on reining in the deficit — which is not verifiable without a continuous, comprehensive record demonstrating consistent prioritization of deficit reduction. In practice, public officials' budgets and votes often include tradeoffs (tax cuts, spending increases, emergency measures) that have at times increased deficits, so without a specific, documented lifelong record the claim is not supported.

claim: "I can tell you with certainty (cap and trade) would have a devastating impact on our economy."
rationale: The statement asserts an absolute, certain outcome that cap-and-trade would be 'devastating' to the economy; that is an opinionated prediction, not an empirically proven fact. Experience with implemented cap-and-trade systems (e.g., EU ETS, RGGI, California) and numerous economic models generally show modest macroeconomic costs or manageable sectoral adjustments rather than universally devastating impacts, and outcomes depend strongly on policy design and mitigation measures.

claim: Nevada Republicans "didn’t do one single thing to cut spending" in 2015.
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement and is not consistent with the 2015 Nevada budget process. Republican actors — including the Republican governor and GOP legislators — proposed spending-reduction amendments, used vetoes and pursued cost-saving measures during the 2015 session and budget negotiations, so it is incorrect to say they did “nothing” to cut spending. Saying they “didn’t do one single thing” overstates and ignores those efforts.

claim: The poorest counties in the U.S. are in Appalachia and "happen to be more than 90 percent white."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate and misleading. While some of the poorest counties are in Appalachia, many of the very poorest U.S. counties (by median household income or poverty rate) are in the Mississippi Delta, the Black Belt, and on Native American reservations, and those counties are not predominantly white; racial composition of the poorest counties varies widely.

claim: Says Connie Mack "is protecting Chevron oil from a multi-billion dollar lawsuit over pollution of rivers and rainforests."
rationale: There is no clear, credible public record that a person named Connie Mack personally acted to shield Chevron from the Ecuador multi‑billion dollar pollution judgment. Chevron did face a long, well‑publicized lawsuit over oil contamination in Ecuador, and some U.S. politicians and firms have supported Chevron in various ways, but I could not find documented evidence that Connie Mack took specific official steps to ‘protect’ Chevron from that lawsuit as claimed. The statement appears to conflate general corporate advocacy with a specific actionable intervention by Connie Mack.

claim: Says an arts tax would provide "funding for certified arts and music teachers for every elementary school serving Portland residents."
rationale: This claim overstates what an arts tax can guarantee. Local tax measures typically authorize funding for arts education but do not legally guarantee that every elementary school will receive a certified arts or music teacher; staffing placements are determined by school districts, available funding, and implementation rules. Therefore saying the tax would provide certified teachers for every elementary school serving Portland residents is misleading without the specific ballot language and enforcement mechanism.

claim: Says he did not tell former President Barack Obama "don’t go" after Osama bin Laden
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and lacks a clear subject or source; there is no verifiable public record that a named official said they did not tell President Obama “don’t go” regarding the bin Laden operation. Major accounts and memoirs about the 2011 raid document deliberations among US leaders and military planners but do not record a widely reported exchange phrased that way. Because the statement as presented cannot be substantiated and the speaker is unspecified, I judge the claim false pending a clear sourcing.

claim: "We’re 49th in the United States in new businesses created."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it does not specify which state, which time period, or which metric of 'new businesses created' is being used. Authoritative sources (Census Business Formation Statistics, BLS/BEA datasets) show rankings vary by year and by whether you count absolute filings, employer startups, or per-capita rates, so the blanket claim is unsupported without more context and is likely incorrect.

claim: According to a national survey, transit "ridership" among people age 16 to 34 increased 40 percent between 2001 and 2009.
rationale: I cannot confirm a national survey that shows a 40% increase in transit "ridership" for ages 16–34 between 2001 and 2009. Publicly cited sources from that period (e.g., analyses of the National Household Travel Survey) report mixed changes depending on the metric used (trips per person, share of travel, or absolute riders) and often show smaller or more nuanced shifts rather than a uniform 40% rise nationwide. The claim appears to conflate different measures or to overstate findings from selective analyses or local markets.

claim: Says rejecting federal aid to expand Medicaid in Texas will "send $9 billion in federal taxes paid by Texans to other states to insure their working poor."
rationale: The claim frames federal taxes paid by Texans as directly "sent" to other states and asserts a specific $9 billion figure without specifying a time period or methodology. In reality federal tax revenue is pooled and federal Medicaid matching payments are allocated based on states' enrollment and eligibility choices; if Texas declines expansion, it forgoes federal matching funds that could have been spent in Texas, and some federal dollars will fund expansion in other states — but the exact amount depends on modeling assumptions and timeframe. Because the statement is phrased as a direct transfer of Texans' taxes and cites a precise number without context, it is misleading.

claim: "Barack Hussein Obama will … force doctors to assist homosexuals in buying surrogate babies."
rationale: There is no evidence that President Obama proposed or implemented any federal policy that would force doctors to assist same-sex couples in "buying surrogate babies." Surrogacy arrangements are governed largely by state law and private contracts, and medical professionals have legal and conscience protections; the Obama administration expanded LGBT nondiscrimination protections but did not mandate physicians to facilitate surrogacy transactions. The claim appears to be a baseless, sensationalized misrepresentation of policy positions.

claim: Says Barack Obama "robbed Medicare (of) $716 billion to pay for ... Obamacare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act was projected by the Congressional Budget Office and Medicare actuaries to reduce Medicare spending by about $716 billion over roughly the 2010–2019 decade, but those were spending reductions and payment restructurings (for example cuts to Medicare Advantage overpayments and provider payment adjustments), not a literal one-time seizure of $716 billion from Medicare to pay for the law. Describing it as Obama having "robbed Medicare" is misleading because the actions were budgetary savings and payment policy changes rather than a direct transfer of trust-fund dollars to finance coverage.

claim: Under the GOP tax law, "if you live in Hinsdale, Illinois … you are now being double-taxed to the tune of $35,000."
rationale: The 2017 GOP tax law capped the state-and-local-tax (SALT) deduction at $10,000, which can raise federal tax bills for high-tax-area, high-income households in places like Hinsdale, but it does not literally impose a universal “double tax” of $35,000 on all Hinsdale residents. Any $35,000 impact would be an estimate that applies only to certain high‑income, high‑property‑tax filers and depends on income, filing status, and specific tax payments, so the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: "US Capitol raided 2/2/21."
rationale: There was no large-scale raid of the U.S. Capitol on February 2, 2021. The widely reported violent breach occurred on January 6, 2021 during the Electoral College certification; credible sources and official records do not report a comparable raid on 2/2/21.

claim: Tim Kaine "made Virginia the best state for business four years in a row."
rationale: The claim combines two assertions — that Virginia was the #1 state for business for four consecutive years and that Tim Kaine "made" that happen. Public rankings of "best state for business" come from different outlets (CNBC, Forbes) with varying results and methodologies, and records do not clearly support an uncontested four-year consecutive #1 under Kaine nor a direct causal claim that he alone "made" it so. Without specifying the ranking source and years, the assertion is not verifiable as stated and overstates causal responsibility.

claim: "Johns Hopkins University confirms: You can be vaccinated with a PCR test, even without knowing"
rationale: The claim is false. PCR diagnostic tests use swabs and laboratory reagents to detect viral genetic material and do not contain or deliver vaccines or immunizing agents, and there is no credible record of Johns Hopkins confirming such a claim. Assertions that tests can 'vaccinate' people have been repeatedly debunked as misinformation.

claim: Says the Multnomah County Library system "is the second busiest in the nation."
rationale: The claim is misleading as stated: Multnomah County Library is not the second-busiest library system in the United States by overall measures such as total circulation or visits. Rankings vary by metric (total circulation, circulation per capita, visits) and by year, and larger systems (e.g., New York, Los Angeles, Chicago) outrank Multnomah by absolute totals. Without a specific metric and year, the blanket assertion is unsupported.

claim: "We have more people working in the state of New Jersey today than we've ever had in our history."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as stated because it lacks a clear time reference and metric (jobs located in NJ vs. residents employed). Official measures (BLS nonfarm payrolls, household employment, and state labor reports) have different historical peaks and have only in recent years recovered to or past some prior highs; without specifying which series and what date “today” means, the blanket statement cannot be confirmed. Given the ambiguity and shifting monthly data, I judge the claim unreliable as presented.

claim: "They’re going to be giving these people who come across the border, giving them smartphones."
rationale: The claim asserts a general program of giving smartphones to people who cross the border, but there is no evidence of a federal policy that hands out smartphones to migrants. Reporting and fact-checks show occasional instances where NGOs or local groups provide donated phones or SIM cards, and migrants may already possess phones, but not a government-run blanket distribution of smartphones as implied. The statement is therefore misleading and unsupported as a general claim.

claim: Since he and Scott Walker took office in 2011, "60,000 new jobs have been created in this state -- 40,000 of them were created in Madison and the Madison area."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. Official labor data (BLS and Wisconsin workforce reports) show Wisconsin added substantially more than 60,000 jobs in the years after 2011, and the Madison metropolitan area did not account for two‑thirds of the state’s net job gains. The numbers cited (60,000 statewide, 40,000 in Madison) do not match published payroll/employment series for the period starting in 2011.

claim: "In Ohio, we invested in our children, raising school funding by 5.5 percent in the last budget."
rationale: The claim is too specific to be verified as stated: Ohio budget increases for K–12 vary by biennial budget and by which measure is used (total appropriations, per-pupil funding, or base funding). Public budgets in recent years did increase K–12 funding in different amounts, but I cannot confirm that the most recent enacted state budget raised school funding by exactly 5.5% across the commonly reported metrics. Because the statement lacks a specific budget year and funding metric, it cannot be confirmed as fact.

claim: Says the National Labor Relations Board told Boeing that it "can't build a factory in a non-union state."
rationale: This wording misstates the NLRB's action and authority. The NLRB alleged Boeing committed unfair labor practices by shifting work to a nonunion facility and sought remedies (including orders affecting transfers and hiring), but it did not issue a blanket prohibition saying Boeing "can't build a factory in a non-union state." The agency enforces labor law and can seek remedies through administrative proceedings, not an absolute ban on building facilities.

claim: A man arrested by Lubbock, Texas, police for a gun threat said "his accomplices will be going to different Wal-Mart stores and shooting."
rationale: I cannot corroborate this precise quoted threat from any reliable reporting I recall about a Lubbock arrest; major news coverage of similar incidents typically quotes exact threats and notes accomplices if alleged. Without an identifiable source, the specific claim that the man said his accomplices would go to different Walmart stores and shoot appears unverified and likely incorrect as stated.

claim: "mRNA Vaccines Show No Mortality Benefit - Danish Study"
rationale: The claim is misleading. While a specific Danish analysis may have reported no statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality in a particular population, timeframe, or analytic setup, a large body of randomized trials and real-world studies show mRNA COVID-19 vaccines substantially reduce COVID-19–related deaths. The Danish finding (if it exists) is context-dependent and does not support the blanket statement that mRNA vaccines show no mortality benefit.

claim: "There are 300,000 babies born deformed every year in this country because of women who are alcoholics while they're carrying those children to term."
rationale: The numeric claim is not supported by public health data. CDC and other health authorities estimate fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) at roughly 0.2–1.5 per 1,000 live births and fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD) estimates vary but do not reliably support 300,000 attributable "deformed" births per year in a country with ~3–4 million annual births. The statement also conflates alcoholism with any prenatal alcohol exposure and uses the vague term "deformed," overstating both cause and scale.

claim: Says Sara Gideon "voted to defund" the Freeport police "and gave the money to a nonprofit she helped run."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Independent fact-checks and contemporaneous reporting show there was no vote to dismantle or defund the Freeport police department; the disputed town council action involved reallocation or withholding of a small line-item or grant, not eliminating the police force. Likewise, Gideon did not unilaterally "give" police funds to a nonprofit she ran — the municipal budget process and any grants involve votes and administrative actions, and the characterization overstates her role and intent.

claim: Says that in New Mexico, "illegals are issued emergency welfare EBT cards with $1k a month +$200 for each child, for at least 5+ years until they see a judge."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate and misleading. Federal SNAP/EBT rules require qualifying immigration status and do not authorize routine issuance of EBT benefits to undocumented migrants; New Mexico has not had a documented statewide policy of giving undocumented people $1,000/month plus $200 per child on EBT for years while they await a court date. While states or localities may provide limited emergency shelter or services to migrants and immigration court waits can be lengthy, that is not the same as the described ongoing EBT payment program.

claim: "Our conservative Georgia values are under attack" ... (People) are "calling for the removal of George Washington and Thomas Jefferson statues."
rationale: The claim mixes a subjective opinion (“our conservative Georgia values are under attack”) with an empirical assertion. The opinion cannot be verified; there is no clear, documented evidence of organized calls in Georgia specifically to remove statues of George Washington and Thomas Jefferson. Public debates over monuments in recent years have primarily targeted Confederate-era statues rather than Washington or Jefferson in Georgia.

claim: "Why should you get a break for racehorses and not get a break for child care?"
rationale: The claim as phrased is misleading and lacks context: it asserts that people receive a governmental “break” for racehorses but not for child care, which is not generally true. In many jurisdictions there are explicit tax credits, subsidies, or employer‑provided benefits for child care (e.g., child tax credits, dependent care FSAs, subsidized childcare programs), while any tax treatment of racehorse expenses is specific and limited and varies by law. Without a specific country and law, the broad comparative claim is false or unsupported.

claim: "By registration fewer than 20 percent of Florida voters are Independents."
rationale: This is false. Florida’s “No Party Affiliation” (often reported as independents) reached about 20% by 2020 and has generally been at or above the low-to-mid 20 percent range in subsequent statewide registration tallies, so fewer than 20% is not an accurate characterization of recent registration data. The claim omits a timeframe and thus conflicts with available registration totals from 2020–2024.

claim: "You take Pulse nightclub. If you had one person in that room that could carry a gun and knew how to use it, it wouldn’t have happened, or certainly to the extent that it did."
rationale: The statement is a categorical counterfactual that cannot be established as fact. Empirical evidence about armed bystanders stopping mass shooters is mixed and highly context-dependent, and in many real incidents outcomes hinge on timing, surprise, training, and situational chaos; an armed person in the room might have prevented some harm but also could have failed or increased danger through crossfire. Because it asserts a definitive outcome for a complex, uncertain scenario, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "It has been estimated that only 12% of workers in businesses that are likely to stay open during this crisis are receiving paid sick leave benefits as a result of the second coronavirus relief package."
rationale: The specific 12% figure is not a well-supported, widely accepted estimate and appears to conflate different measures (eligibility, take-up, and types of businesses). The Families First Coronavirus Response Act (the primary early paid‑leave statute) covered many employees of small and mid‑sized employers while excluding others (e.g., certain health‑care workers and some small businesses), and published analyses produced a range of higher coverage estimates rather than a single 12% number. Without a clear source and with ambiguity about “businesses likely to stay open,” the claim overstates certainty and misstates the consensus estimate.

claim: John McCain "began his career in Washington as a lobbyist when he was appointed in 1976 as the Navy's liaison to the United States Senate."
rationale: This is false: in the mid-1970s McCain served as a Navy officer assigned as the Navy’s liaison to the U.S. Senate, but that was an official military posting representing the Navy, not a private-sector lobbying job. Describing that assignment as beginning his Washington career “as a lobbyist” mischaracterizes the role and McCain’s position at the time.

claim: Says Chris Christie "vetoed equal pay for women 3 times. He only let the bill pass once it became a damaging campaign issue."
rationale: The claim that Christie vetoed equal-pay legislation three times and only let it pass once it became a damaging campaign issue overstates and simplifies the record. Public reporting and New Jersey legislative records show Christie opposed or vetoed certain pay-equity measures at points, but there is not clear evidence of three distinct vetoes of the same equal-pay bill and the timeline and reasons are more complex than the claim asserts. The assertion that he only allowed passage due solely to campaign damage is a causal claim that is not directly supported by legislative records or contemporaneous statements.

claim: "Six justices" on the U.S. Supreme Court have been "confirmed in presidential election years since 1912."
rationale: True. Six justices since 1912 were confirmed in presidential election years: Louis Brandeis (1916), Benjamin Cardozo (1932), William Brennan (1956), William Rehnquist (1972), Anthony Kennedy (1988), and Amy Coney Barrett (2020). Each of those confirmations occurred in years when a U.S. presidential election took place.

claim: "To this day, (the Cuban government) is a regime that provides safe harbor to terrorists and fugitives."
rationale: Cuba has in fact granted asylum and long-term refuge to individuals wanted by the United States and designated by U.S. authorities as terrorists or fugitives — the most prominent example being Assata Shakur, who has lived in Cuba since the 1980s and remains there. Historically Havana has sheltered other political fugitives and hosted guerrilla delegations, even while sometimes cooperating in peace talks or returning some individuals, so the general characterization that the regime provides safe harbor to certain fugitives is supported.

claim: The United States is "the oldest democracy" in the world.
rationale: The claim is false as stated. The U.S. federal system dates to the late 18th century, but other polities have older continuously operating democratic or representative institutions — for example Iceland's Althing (founded in 930) and San Marino's long-standing republican institutions. The U.S. does hold the world's oldest written national constitution still in continuous use (1787), which often causes the confusion.

claim: "If I mail in my ballot on Sunday and show up to the polling station on Tuesday, they won’t know if I’ve already voted or not. That, my friends, is a serious concern for all of us."
rationale: False. In most jurisdictions mail-in/absentee ballots are tracked and the voter’s record is updated when a mailed ballot is issued and/or received, and poll workers check those records at in-person polling places to prevent a second regular ballot being cast. If a voter shows up after already mailing a ballot they are typically offered a provisional or spoiled/replacement process and duplicate votes are not counted. While processing times and exact procedures vary, systems are designed to detect and prevent double voting.

claim: "Mike Trainor...still owes $250,000 to the state."
rationale: I could not verify that any individual named Mike Trainor currently owes $250,000 to a state; reputable news coverage and public records through mid-2024 do not substantiate that specific claim. The statement is vague about which Mike Trainor, which state, and the time period, so it cannot be confirmed and appears unsupported by available information.

claim: "Obamacare … means that for up to 20 million Americans, they will lose the insurance they currently have, the insurance that they like and they want to keep."
rationale: The claim that 'up to 20 million' Americans will lose the insurance they currently have is misleading and not supported by mainstream estimates. Independent analyses and government estimates showed that only a minority of people—primarily in the individual/non‑group market—faced plan cancellations because of ACA conformity rules, and many employer plans were unaffected or people were eligible for replacement coverage or subsidies; the widely cited cancellation totals were far smaller than 20 million. The phrase 'the insurance that they like and want to keep' is subjective and not verifiable for a population-level numeric prediction.

claim: "Mitt Romney has been asked to lead Health and Human Services in Biden administration."
rationale: This claim is false. There are no credible reports that President-elect Biden or his team asked Senator Mitt Romney to lead Health and Human Services; Biden nominated Xavier Becerra as HHS Secretary, who was later confirmed. Romney remained a sitting Republican senator and was not tapped for that cabinet post.

claim: Says the KKK marched in Mebane, N.C., after Trump’s victory
rationale: There is no reliable contemporaneous reporting or documentation that a Ku Klux Klan march occurred in Mebane, North Carolina, after the 2016 presidential election. Viral claims and images circulating online were not substantiated by local news, law enforcement, or established fact-checkers and appear to be misattributed or misdated.

claim: 52 jobs have been saved or created in Florida's 34th Congressional District.
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific claim that exactly 52 jobs were saved or created in Florida's 34th Congressional District. There is no widely available authoritative reporting or public data that corroborates this precise number, and the statement lacks crucial context (timeframe, program, or source) needed to verify it.

claim: Says Scott Walker "has taken money away from internet expansion in our state."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated — it does not name a state, program, time period, or what spending was allegedly removed. Scott Walker was Governor of Wisconsin and his budgets and vetoes altered many line items over time; some proposals increased broadband grants while other budget changes reduced or reprioritized funds, so there is no clear, single factual basis to assert he broadly “took money away from internet expansion in our state.” Without specifics this generic claim is not supported.

claim: Forty percent of gross domestic product "is state, local, or federal money."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and therefore misleading. While total government receipts or total government spending (federal + state + local) can approach or exceed roughly 35–45% of U.S. GDP in certain years (notably during COVID-era stimulus), it is not a stable, universally true fact that exactly 40% of GDP “is state, local, or federal money” — the percentage varies by year and by whether one counts spending, revenues, or transfer payments.

claim: Says "in Oregon only 41 percent of adults have ever been tested" for HIV.
rationale: I cannot confirm that exactly 41% of Oregon adults have ever been tested for HIV. State-level estimates from CDC/BRFSS and other surveys vary by year and by the age range reported, and no single authoritative recent source universally reports a 41% figure for Oregon. Because the claim lacks a cited year or data source it is unverified and likely misleading as presented.

claim: Says Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie made a late-night visit to Kinko’s to forge President Barack Obama’s birth certificate two days before Obama unveiled it to the media.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hawaii Gov. Neil Abercrombie ever visited a Kinko’s to forge President Obama’s birth certificate. The allegation is a baseless conspiracy theory; contemporaneous news accounts and fact-checkers reported that Abercrombie had said he had seen Hawaii birth records in state files, not that he forged any documents, and no proof of a Kinko’s visit or forgery has ever been produced.

claim: Says she introduced a ban on "dirty dancing."
rationale: The statement is vague and provides no subject or context, and there is no evidence of any legislator having introduced a law explicitly banning a category called “dirty dancing.” While some localities regulate public decency or dance venues, claims framed as a specific ban on “dirty dancing” are typically rhetorical or mischaracterizations rather than literal legislation. Given the lack of corroborating evidence, the claim is assessed as false.

claim: Says the Vatican confirmed that Pope Francis and two aides tested positive for coronavirus.
rationale: False. The Vatican did confirm that two people in its service tested positive for coronavirus, but Vatican spokespeople repeatedly said Pope Francis did not test positive (reports indicated he tested negative and showed no symptoms). Multiple news outlets and Vatican statements debunked claims that the Pope himself had COVID-19.

claim: Quotes show Joseph Stalin and Joe Biden expressed similar views about counting votes.
rationale: The alleged similarity is misleading: the Stalin line attributed to him (e.g., “Those who cast the votes decide nothing. Those who count the votes decide everything.”) implies that counting is how outcomes are controlled, whereas Joe Biden’s public statements (especially during vote‑counting disputes) have urged that all ballots be counted to reflect voters’ will. Those are opposing positions, not similar ones.

claim: Says state Senate President Stephen "Sweeney gave us the nation's highest income tax rates, driving out jobs."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. New Jersey under Senate President Stephen Sweeney did not enact the nation's highest state income tax rates (states such as California and New York have had higher top marginal rates), and asserting that Sweeney alone "gave" those rates and directly "drove out jobs" is a causal claim not supported by clear evidence. Job losses and relocations are driven by many factors beyond a single legislator's actions or a single tax measure.

claim: "With her solution, terrorists can still today — and by the way ISIS knows it, they have been advertising it — buy guns online and at gun shows in the United States of America."
rationale: Under U.S. federal law licensed dealers must run background checks, but private sales (including many gun-show transactions and sales arranged online through classifieds) are not federally subject to universal checks in many states, which creates a pathway for prohibited actors to obtain weapons. Open-source reporting and counterterrorism analyses have documented that ISIS propaganda has encouraged sympathizers to acquire weapons locally and exploit legal loopholes, so the broad claim is accurate though specifics vary by state and circumstance.

claim: "We've seen local union after local union rush to their school boards, their city councils, their technical school boards and rush through contracts in the past two weeks that had no contributions to the pension and no contribution to health care."
rationale: The claim is a broad, time‑limited assertion about many local unions across different boards that cannot be verified from available public information and appears to be a sweeping generalization. While individual contracts that reduce or exclude employer contributions to pensions or health care can occur, there is no documented evidence showing a widespread, multi‑jurisdictional rush over a specific two‑week period as described.

claim: The "Back the Blue" Act that Gov. Kim Reynolds signs means you can't wear the American flag. "So throw out those towels and swimsuits ... or you’re a criminal!"
rationale: The claim is false. Iowa’s “Back the Blue” law signed by Gov. Kim Reynolds increases penalties for assaulting or interfering with law enforcement and includes provisions against concealing identity to avoid arrest in the context of riots or violent protests, but it does not prohibit wearing the American flag or flag-patterned towels/swimsuits. The viral wording misrepresents provisions about concealment and criminal conduct as a blanket ban on flag apparel.

claim: "We’re second only to Boston in college students per capita."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it omits which city/area and which year or data source is meant; many U.S. college towns (e.g., Cambridge MA, Ann Arbor, Ithaca, Madison, Berkeley, Boulder, College Station) often rank at or above Boston on students-per-capita depending on boundaries and enrollment definitions. Because the statement is ambiguous and likely incorrect for many plausible referents, it cannot be accepted as fact. To verify would require specifying the city, year, and whether city limits or metro area and which student populations are counted.

claim: "There is nothing in the current state public records law that prohibits sensitive or confidential business information from being just that, confidential."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated because most U.S. state public records (open records) laws include explicit exemptions or procedures allowing agencies to withhold trade secrets, proprietary commercial information, or other confidential business data. Many statutes and court decisions require agencies to protect legitimately confidential business information or allow withholding when disclosure would cause competitive harm, so it is not true that state law universally contains nothing prohibiting confidentiality.

claim: "This is the same (farm) bill we voted on a few weeks ago, with the exception of one or two sentences."
rationale: There is insufficient specific evidence to support the blanket claim and, absent a direct bill identifier and date, it is unlikely to be literally true. Legislative practice normally results in multiple amendments and textual changes between versions, and assertions that only "one or two sentences" were changed are verifiable only by a line-by-line comparison of numbered bill versions, which has not been provided. Therefore the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: "The permission to engage was given before the word RPG was ever used."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and lacks any context (which incident, who authorized engagement, and when the term "RPG" was spoken), so it cannot be verified as true. Without contemporaneous records (radio logs, video timestamps, or official after-action reports) the sequence of authorization versus the utterance of the word cannot be established, so I treat the unreferenced claim as not factual.

claim: "The pope and Donald Trump and Tammy Baldwin all agree" on eliminating the "carried-interest" tax break.
rationale: Sen. Tammy Baldwin has publicly supported legislation to end the carried-interest tax preference, and Donald Trump has at times said he would close or curb the carried-interest loophole. However, Pope Francis has criticized tax avoidance and financial speculation broadly but has not issued a specific policy call to eliminate the carried-interest tax break, so the claim that all three explicitly "agree" on eliminating it overstates the pope's position.

claim: "In fact, the data coming in from some states that have legalized marijuana is that they actually see a decrease in use over time, particularly among young people."
rationale: Multiple state-level surveillance reports and national surveys have found that adolescent marijuana use has not risen and in some legalized states has declined over time, particularly among younger teens. While findings vary by state and time period, the empirical trend described — decreases in youth use in some legalized states — is supported by existing data.

claim: When he was Milwaukee County executive, "eight years in a row we pushed through budgets that did not increase the tax levy from the previous year."
rationale: Public budget records and contemporary reporting indicate Milwaukee County’s property tax levy did increase in at least one year during Scott Walker’s tenure as county executive, so the statement that there were eight consecutive budgets without any levy increase is inaccurate. The claim also appears to conflate the tax levy (the dollar amount the county collects) with taxpayers’ bills or with levy limits and accounting maneuvers that can mask real tax changes.

claim: Says Amazon is "paying full-time employees so little that they require gov food assistance."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes: while reporting has shown that some Amazon employees (including full‑time warehouse workers) have enrolled in government food assistance programs, it is not true that Amazon universally pays full‑time employees so little that they require such aid. Amazon implemented a $15/hour minimum in 2018 and many full‑time roles include benefits and higher pay, so SNAP usage among employees is limited to a subset rather than universal.

claim: Says Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "didn't change his position" on a two-state solution.
rationale: Netanyahu has publicly shifted his stance over time. He endorsed a conditional two-state framework in his 2009 Bar-Ilan speech (accepting a demilitarized Palestinian state under strict conditions) but later, notably during the 2015 campaign and in subsequent years, publicly rejected the creation of a Palestinian state or emphasized conditions that amount to opposition. Those changes show his position has not been constant.

claim: Claims the U.S. military is using "polymer drone flies" that look and act like a large fly.
rationale: There is no credible public evidence that the U.S. military is currently deploying operational "polymer drone flies" that look and act like large flies. While government labs and universities have developed insect-scale flying prototypes and worked on cyborg insects and micro-air-vehicles, these remain research prototypes with severe capability and endurance limits and are not known to be field-deployed as described.

claim: Low gas prices in Russia, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia show that Joe Biden’s decision to cancel the Keystone Pipeline project is to blame for U.S. prices.
rationale: False. Low pump prices in Russia, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia largely reflect those countries' abundant domestic production and government-set subsidies or low taxes, not U.S. pipeline policy. U.S. gasoline prices are driven mainly by global crude prices, refining capacity, taxes and regional supply/demand, so cancelling Keystone XL alone cannot explain U.S. price levels.

claim: Says there is a "traditional 60-vote threshold for confirming Supreme Court nominees."
rationale: There is no formal or constitutional 60-vote requirement to confirm Supreme Court nominees. Historically the Senate often required 60 votes to invoke cloture and end a filibuster on nominations, which became a common Senate practice for controversial nominees, but confirmations themselves are by simple majority and the Senate changed its cloture rules for Supreme Court nominees in 2017. Saying there is a "traditional 60-vote threshold" is misleading because it conflates a filibuster/cloture practice with a formal confirmation rule.

claim: Sarah Palin endorsed a Wasilla policy that charged sexual assault victims for their "rape kits."
rationale: Contemporaneous news reports and later fact-checks found no evidence that Mayor Sarah Palin endorsed or implemented a Wasilla city policy requiring sexual assault victims to pay for forensic 'rape kits.' Billing for forensic exams, when it occurred, was handled by medical providers or insurers, not by a city policy enacted by Palin. The claim conflates hospital billing practices with a municipal directive.

claim: In the U.S. Constitution, "there’s a little section in there that talks about life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness."
rationale: The phrase "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness" appears in the Declaration of Independence (Thomas Jefferson's 1776 text), not in the U.S. Constitution. The Constitution does protect "life" and "liberty" through due-process clauses (e.g., Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments) but does not contain the specific wording about the "pursuit of happiness."

claim: Photos show celebrities reacting to Will Smith slapping Chris Rock.
rationale: Multiple reputable news organizations and photographers captured and published photos from the 2022 Academy Awards showing audience members — including well-known celebrities — with visible reactions immediately after Will Smith slapped Chris Rock. While some circulated images were later miscaptioned or taken from different moments, genuine photos and video frames of celebrity reactions do exist.

claim: Says the word newspaper stands for "north, east, west, south, past and present event report."
rationale: This is a folk etymology/backronym. The English word 'newspaper' derives from 'news' (new information) + 'paper' and dates to early modern English usage; it was not formed as an acronym for compass points and time.

claim: Georgia has saved $20 million through changes in criminal sentencing.
rationale: The claim lacks a cited source or timeframe and I could not confirm a definitive, verifiable figure that Georgia has saved exactly $20 million from criminal sentencing changes. Georgia did enact sentencing and criminal-justice reforms in the 2010s that advocates say produced savings, but reported amounts and periods vary across studies and government reports and do not consistently show a standalone $20 million figure. Without a specific source or period, the precise $20 million claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "When I was born, defense spending was 60 percent of the budget. It's now 17 percent."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it omits which “budget” is meant. Defense has at times been ~60% of U.S. discretionary spending in mid‑20th century accounts, but it was not 60% of the total federal budget except in wartime peaks; today defense is about 15–20% of total federal outlays (and roughly 40–50% of discretionary spending). Without specifying discretionary vs. total budget and a birth year, the flat “60% then → 17% now” statement is inaccurate.

claim: The mobilization of the military in response to the storms in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands "is the largest ever mobilization of our military in a naval and marine operation" and an Air Force carrier there "was the first-ever as well."
rationale: The claim is false. Historical disaster responses (for example Hurricane Katrina in 2005 and international responses such as the Haiti 2010 relief) involved equal or larger military and naval/marine deployments by various measures, so the Puerto Rico/USVI response was not uniquely the largest ever. The wording about an "Air Force carrier" is also incorrect: aircraft carriers are Navy vessels and the Air Force does not operate carriers, so calling any Air Force carrier "first-ever" is factually wrong.

claim: The DeWine campaign is "receiving money from so many more people. (Cordray's) money is coming almost exclusively from the party, labor unions, and special counsel that he has given business to."
rationale: The statement overstates and mischaracterizes campaign finance patterns. Public campaign finance records and reporting show both DeWine and Cordray received money from a mix of individual donors, party committees, PACs, and interest groups; Cordray was not funded “almost exclusively” by the party, labor unions, and special counsel. Without a specific time frame or citation, the claim appears to be a partisan exaggeration rather than an accurate summary of filings.

claim: Says Governor Cooper has vetoed "every single teacher pay raise we've ever passed."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and false. Governor Cooper did veto some budget bills that included teacher raises, but he also signed multiple budgets and measures that implemented teacher pay increases, so he did not veto "every single" teacher pay raise passed.

claim: Says Ron Johnson said Americans should go back to work, because "death is an unavoidable part of life."
rationale: Sen. Ron Johnson publicly urged reopening during the early COVID-19 pandemic and was reported saying that death is an unavoidable part of life as part of his argument that Americans should return to work. Multiple contemporaneous news reports and televised interviews quoted him making this point in the context of lifting lockdowns.

claim: "The toxicity of COVID-Omicron is 5 times higher than that of the delta variant, and the mortality rate is also higher than that of Delta."
rationale: Available epidemiological and clinical data indicate Omicron (initial lineages) caused, on average, less severe disease and lower rates of hospitalization and death than the Delta variant, not five times higher toxicity or mortality. While Omicron is more transmissible, multiple studies and public-health reports found reduced intrinsic severity after accounting for immunity, so the claim contradicts the prevailing evidence.

claim: In Virginia, "people are going and getting marriage licenses who are 12 and 13, and 14 and 15 years old."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Virginia currently issues routine marriage licenses to 12–15 year olds. Virginia law requires parental consent and judicial approval for minors and recent state reforms have tightened age-related safeguards; reports of marriages that young in Virginia are extremely rare and would be exceptional cases rather than a general practice. The claim as stated implies routine issuance to pre-teens, which is not supported by available legal rules or reporting.

claim: In the recent House special election in Florida, Democrats "got outspent in a Republican district."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated — it names only “the recent House special election in Florida” without specifying which district or date. Special-election spending varies by race; in some Florida special elections Republicans outspent Democrats, while in others Democrats raised and spent heavily. Without identifying the specific contest and reviewing campaign finance and outside spending reports, the blanket assertion cannot be confirmed and is therefore judged false as presented.

claim: "McCain opposes a woman's right to choose."
rationale: John McCain consistently identified as pro‑life and supported laws and votes that restricted abortion access (e.g., supporting the Hyde Amendment and bills limiting abortion). While he allowed certain exceptions (such as rape, incest or to save the mother's life), his legislative record and public statements opposed the broad 'right to choose' as framed by abortion-rights advocates and Roe-era protections.

claim: "Ohio student suspended for staying in class during National Walkout Day"
rationale: I could not find corroborating credible reports that an Ohio student was suspended merely for remaining in class during National Walkout Day. Major contemporary coverage documented students being disciplined for participating in walkouts in 2018, not for staying in class; absent specific identifying details or reliable local reports, the claim appears unverified and likely false.

claim: "Court orders Obama to pay $400 million in restitution."
rationale: This is false. There is no record or credible reporting of any court ordering former President Barack Obama to pay $400 million in restitution, and such a judgment would have been widely reported and documented. The claim appears to be a rumor or misattribution.

claim: "Eighty percent of the antibiotics in this country are fed to livestock."
rationale: When the claim is understood as the commonly cited U.S. statistic, it is true that most antibiotics sold by weight have historically gone to food animals — commonly reported in the 70–80% range. However the exact percentage varies by year, the classes counted (all antibiotics vs. ‘medically important’ only), and whether sales or doses are measured.

claim: The Obama administration "was successful in rushing a massive spending bill through Congress in just two days — after which it sat on the president's desk for three days, while he was away on vacation."
rationale: The claim is vague and no well-documented instance matches that description. Major Obama-era spending bills (e.g., the 2009 stimulus, 2010 appropriations) went through longer congressional processes and there is no clear record of a massive spending bill being passed in just two days and then left unsigned on the president’s desk for three days while he was on vacation. Without a specific bill or date the assertion appears to conflate or misstate events.

claim: "We’re losing almost 6,000 state jobs."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and provides no timeframe, jurisdiction, or source; as stated it cannot be verified. Whether nearly 6,000 state jobs are being lost depends on the specific state and period and should be supported by official payroll or budget layoff data. Without that context the assertion is not demonstrably true.

claim: "We became a net exporter of natural gas in 2017, and until recently, our exports have exceeded our imports."
rationale: The first clause is true — according to U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) data the United States became a net exporter of natural gas in 2017 when exports (pipeline + LNG) exceeded imports. The second clause as worded is misleading: exports have generally continued to exceed imports in the subsequent years rather than having only done so “until recently,” so implying that the U.S. recently reverted to net importer status is incorrect without a specific time frame or metric.

claim: "Barack Hussein Obama will ... force local authorities to allow Occupy protesters to live in parks."
rationale: The President does not have authority to unilaterally compel state or local governments to permit encampments in municipal parks, and there is no evidence the Obama administration forced localities to allow Occupy protesters to live in parks. While the federal government can issue guidance or enforce federal civil-rights laws in some cases, land-use and park policing are primarily local responsibilities and the administration did not mandate local governments to permit encampments during the Occupy movement. The claim therefore misstates both legal authority and historical fact.

claim: The oil industry has "9,000 permits to drill now. They could be drilling right now, yesterday, last week, last year."
rationale: The statement that the oil industry currently has 9,000 ready-to-use drilling permits is misleading. Publicly available federal and state permitting data do not support a blanket, current figure of 9,000 immediately actionable permits, and many so-called "permits" are applications pending review or are subject to additional approvals, leases, logistical constraints, and market decisions that prevent immediate drilling. The claim conflates different permit types and jurisdictions and ignores operational and economic constraints on turning a permit into a rig on location.

claim: "27 U.S. Air Force pilots resign over COVID-19 vaccination mandate."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that exactly 27 U.S. Air Force pilots resigned specifically over the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. Reporting and official DoD statements documented a small number of separations, retirements, or administrative actions across active-duty, Reserve, and National Guard personnel, but fact-checkers and military sources did not corroborate a precise count of 27 pilot resignations attributable solely to the mandate.

claim: Says Jeb Bush tweeted "Ok boomer" at Donald Trump.
rationale: There is no credible record that Jeb Bush tweeted “Ok boomer” at Donald Trump. Such a notable, unusual exchange would have been widely reported and preserved in media and tweet archives, and Jeb Bush’s known Twitter history does not include that phrase directed at Trump. It’s more likely a fake/impersonation or misattribution if such a post circulated.

claim: "Clinton's former pastor convicted of child molestation."
rationale: The claim is vague and not supported by credible reporting: there is no well-documented or widely reported case of a pastor specifically identified as “Clinton’s former pastor” being convicted of child molestation. Major news outlets and public records up through mid-2024 do not record a conviction that matches this phrasing, and the statement appears to conflate or misattribute allegations about unrelated religious figures. Without a named individual or reliable source, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The only time over the last 25 years when the state’s unemployment rate exceeded the U.S. average was when (Mary) Burke was commerce secretary."
rationale: This claim is unlikely to be true. Mary Burke served as Wisconsin’s commerce secretary roughly 2009–2011, but state and national unemployment rates have crossed many times over multi-decade spans; BLS state series show other periods in the last 25 years when a state’s unemployment exceeded the U.S. average. The statement is also ambiguous about which state and exact 25‑year window, so its exclusivity claim is not supported without specific BLS time-series evidence.

claim: "I do provide universal health care."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as written because the subject "I" is unspecified; universal health care refers to health coverage for all residents without undue financial hardship and requires evidence of law, policy, or coverage statistics. Without a named actor (country, government, or individual) and supporting data, the statement cannot be confirmed and should be treated as false.

claim: Says "Monica Lewinsky Found Dead" in a burglary.
rationale: This claim is false. There have been no credible news reports or official statements that Monica Lewinsky was found dead in a burglary; she has been publicly active in recent years. The story matches patterns of viral hoaxes about public figures rather than verified reporting.

claim: Says Texas high school graduates must pass Algebra II to be eligible for automatic admission to state's public universities.
rationale: This is not universally true. Texas' automatic-admission system (the “top 10%” rule) primarily grants eligibility based on class rank rather than a single course; while older recommended-diploma curricula did include Algebra II, automatic-admit rules do not universally require passing Algebra II. Individual universities or specific degree programs may still require Algebra II or equivalent, and state graduation rules have changed (House Bill 5), creating alternative diploma paths.

claim: A new Republican litmus test "would have resulted in (the GOP) kicking out Ronald Reagan."
rationale: The claim is a speculative counterfactual without evidence; Ronald Reagan is widely regarded as a defining GOP figure and there is no documented party action or credible analysis showing a contemporaneous ‘‘new litmus test’’ would have led to his expulsion. While Reagan held some positions (e.g., support for immigration amnesty in 1986, willingness to compromise with Democrats) that differ from positions of certain modern Republican factions, that does not demonstrate the party would have formally ‘‘kicked him out.’’

claim: "Illegal immigration and the crime rate are as low as they’ve been in decades."
rationale: The claim conflates two separate metrics and is not supported by recent trends. Unauthorized border encounters and estimated illegal/undocumented crossings rose sharply in 2021–2023 (record high monthly/annual encounters), and the unauthorized immigrant population is not at decades-long lows. Meanwhile U.S. violent and property crime rates fell from 1990s peaks but experienced notable increases around 2020–2021 and have not uniformly returned to decades-low levels across all categories and locales.

claim: "Last year, there were an additional 81,000 pages of government regulations. If you stack that up, it would be a three-story building."
rationale: Federal regulations are typically published in the Federal Register and recent years have seen on the order of ~80,000 pages added; using standard office paper thickness (≈0.1 mm per sheet), 81,000 pages would stack to roughly 8.2 meters (≈27 feet), which is reasonably described as about a three‑story building (depending on story height). The phrasing is an approximate visualization rather than a precise engineering claim.

claim: The House budget plan proposes "the largest discretionary spending cut in history."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it’s vague about the time window and metric (nominal dollars, percent of GDP, or 10-year total). While recent House Republican budgets have proposed substantial discretionary reductions, historical actions such as the 2011 Budget Control Act (sequestration) and other past budget proposals and enactments produced equal or larger discretionary reductions by several measures. Without a clear baseline and time frame, the claim that it is "the largest in history" is unsupported.

claim: Benzene has "never been proven to be harmful."
rationale: This claim is false. Benzene is a well-established human carcinogen and hematotoxicant with extensive epidemiological, clinical, and laboratory evidence linking occupational and chronic exposures to leukemia, aplastic anemia, and other blood disorders. International and national health agencies classify benzene as carcinogenic and regulate exposure limits accordingly.

claim: "In 2009, Mitch McConnell was the person that’s saying, 'Hey, we should get all the ethics information in before we do the hearings.' "
rationale: There is no well-documented attribution of that specific quote to Mitch McConnell in 2009. Contemporary news coverage and searchable public records from 2009 do not show McConnell making that exact statement, and the phrasing appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution rather than a verifiable direct quote. Because the claim names a specific person and year but lacks corroborating sourcing, it is assessed as false pending evidence to the contrary.

claim: Says a photo shows Adam Schiff and Jeffrey Epstein.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporary reporting that Adam Schiff was photographed with Jeffrey Epstein. Epstein’s known social and photographic connections have been documented by major news outlets and public records, and Schiff’s name does not appear among verified associates; viral images claiming such a pairing have been debunked or shown to be misidentifications or manipulations.

claim: Says Rick Scott "thinks employers should be able to deny women coverage for birth control."
rationale: Rick Scott has repeatedly opposed the Affordable Care Act contraceptive mandate and supported religious/conscience exemptions that allow employers to opt out of covering birth control. His public statements and policy positions as governor and senator-backed measures align with the view that employers should be permitted to decline contraceptive coverage for employees.

claim: The federal tax code has "loopholes that are giving incentives for companies that are shipping jobs overseas."
rationale: The claim is factually supported: U.S. federal tax rules have long included provisions (for example, deferral of U.S. tax on active foreign earnings, transfer-pricing rules, and opportunities for corporate inversions) that can lower or postpone tax on income earned abroad and thereby create financial incentives to locate jobs or activities overseas. Although the 2017 tax reform (TCJA) changed many rules and reduced some incentives, tax coding historically and currently influences offshoring decisions.

claim: Says Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones told players: "Stand for the Anthem or you’re off team."
rationale: This claim accurately summarizes Jerry Jones’s publicly stated position from July 2017 when he told Cowboys players he expected them to stand for the national anthem and said he would bench or not want players who refused to stand. The wording in the claim is a paraphrase of his remarks rather than an exact verbatim quote, but it captures his stated intent to remove/bench players who didn’t stand.

claim: About 750,000 people die in China each year from auto emissions.
rationale: This number is much higher than mainstream estimates. Global Burden of Disease/WHO estimates attribute around one to 1.4 million deaths in China annually to ambient air pollution from all sources, while peer-reviewed studies that apportion deaths specifically to vehicle (road-transport) emissions generally find far fewer deaths—typically on the order of tens to a few hundred thousand, not ~750,000. The claim therefore overstates the deaths attributable solely to auto emissions.

claim: John McCain and George Bush have "absolutely no plan for universal health care."
rationale: Neither John McCain (notably during the 2008 campaign) nor President George W. Bush proposed comprehensive plans to establish universal health care; both favored market-based reforms (e.g., health savings accounts, tax credits, Medicare Part D) and opposed government-run universal coverage. Thus the claim that they had 'absolutely no plan for universal health care' is accurate in the sense that they did not advance policies to achieve universal coverage.

claim: "One hundred and ninety-four countries signed the Paris Agreement to control greenhouse gases. Our own voluntary agreement to accomplish the same goal — the Under2  MOU — has 165 signatories, representing a billion people."
rationale: The statement mixes a slightly incorrect figure with a broadly correct one. The Paris Agreement was signed by almost all countries (about 195 parties) and counts vary with timing and whether the EU is counted, so the precise number '194' is not robust. The Under2 MOU having roughly 165 subnational signatories representing on the order of one billion people is broadly accurate, but the mismatch and time-sensitive nature of these counts make the overall claim misleading.

claim: "Hillary replaces Kamala Harris."
rationale: There is no evidence that Hillary Clinton has replaced Vice President Kamala Harris. As of mid-2024 Hillary Clinton held no federal office and no nomination or congressional confirmation occurred to install her as vice president; under the 25th Amendment a replacement requires presidential nomination and confirmation by both Houses of Congress. Therefore the claim is false.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "was literally present when we pressed the reset button with Russia just a few months after Russia had invaded Georgia."
rationale: Hillary Clinton, as Secretary of State in early 2009, physically presented the symbolic “reset” button to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov at a meeting in March 2009. That gesture occurred several months after Russia’s August 2008 invasion of Georgia, so saying she was “literally present” for the reset soon after the invasion is accurate.

claim: "I have more military experience than anybody who’s arrived behind that desk since George H.W. Bush."
rationale: The speaker (commonly attributed to Donald Trump) has no documented military service, while presidents since George H.W. Bush include George W. Bush, who served in the Texas Air National Guard. Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden also have no active military service, but because at least one post‑Bush president has documented military service, the blanket claim that the speaker has more military experience than anyone arriving behind that desk since H.W. Bush is false.

claim: Says presidential candidate Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said, "Social Security must (be) expanded to illegal immigration, it’s their right."
rationale: There is no credible record or reliable reporting of Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand saying the quoted line that Social Security “must be expanded to illegal immigration, it’s their right.” Gillibrand has supported immigration reform and pathways to citizenship and discussed expanding benefits in some contexts, but the exact quote appears to be a mischaracterization or fabrication and would also require congressional law changes to take effect.

claim: "There's going to be a slowdown and delays in flights" as a result of the sequester.
rationale: The automatic budget cuts known as the sequester have historically forced reductions in FAA staffing and operations (including planned furloughs of air-traffic controllers and reduced air-traffic management capacity). Those cuts reduce throughput at busy airports and increase the likelihood of slower operations and flight delays, especially at peak times. The exact magnitude and timing depend on how cuts are implemented and on local traffic conditions.

claim: Republican candidate for Georgia governor "dabbled" in birther conspiracy theories.
rationale: The claim is vague and lacks a named candidate or timeframe; there is no clear, widely documented evidence that a recent Republican nominee for Georgia governor explicitly promoted or repeatedly advanced birther conspiracy theories. While some national Republicans have entertained or amplified birther ideas in the past, that behavior is not established for a Georgia gubernatorial candidate without a specific person and citation. Because the statement is unspecific and unsubstantiated as given, it is assessed as false.

claim: "Pfizer CEO has not yet had vaccine."
rationale: The claim is false as stated. Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla publicly announced and documented receiving a COVID-19 vaccine in January 2021 (and subsequently received follow-up doses), and this was widely reported in news coverage and his own public statements.

claim: Says Missouri Democratic Senate candidate Jason Kander is "attending fancy dinners all over the country."
rationale: The claim is vague and unverified: while political candidates commonly attend fundraising dinners, there is no documented evidence that Jason Kander was specifically "attending fancy dinners all over the country." Kander ran a Senate campaign primarily focused on Missouri and while he likely participated in some out-of-state fundraising, describing it as traveling to fancy dinners nationwide overstates known facts.

claim: "One in 19 Americans today get SSDI or SSI. That's one in 19 Americans (who) are disabled."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate in both parts. Current Social Security program totals and unique-recipient estimates do not support exactly 1-in-19 Americans, and equating receipt of SSDI/SSI with being disabled is wrong because SSI can be paid to aged/blind persons and some SSDI/SSI payments go to non-disabled dependents, while many disabled people do not receive benefits.

claim: "Under Operation Warp Speed, we’ve pioneered groundbreaking therapies, reducing the fatality rate 85% since April."
rationale: The assertion that Operation Warp Speed alone pioneered therapies that reduced the fatality rate by 85% since April is not supported by available evidence. OWS primarily accelerated vaccine development (and supported some therapeutics), but COVID fatality declines reflect many factors (expanded testing, changing case demographics, improved clinical care, vaccines), and no credible authoritative source attributes an 85% reduction solely to OWS over an unspecified time window.

claim: "Obama-Nelson economic record: Job creation ... at slowest post-recession rate since Great Depression."
rationale: The post‑2009 jobs recovery was notably slow and took longer to regain pre‑recession employment levels than any recovery since World War II, but authoritative analyses and data sources characterize it as the slowest recovery since WWII rather than since the Great Depression. Comparisons to the 1930s are uncommon and problematic because labor‑market data and the structure of the economy differ markedly across that span. Thus the claim overstates the standard historical comparison.

claim: Utah was "the No. 1 job creator in this country during my years of service" as governor, with a 5.9 percent increase in jobs.
rationale: The claim is misleading: while Utah did experience solid job growth during recent gubernatorial terms, whether it was definitively “No. 1” depends on the exact years and whether one measures total jobs, private-sector jobs, or percentage vs. raw gains. The 5.9% figure appears to be a narrowly defined measure for a particular interval (and can be true for one metric), but multiple standard comparisons do not unambiguously support the blanket statement that Utah was the nation’s top job creator during those years.

claim: "Money raised to help (Beto) O’Rourke get elected is being used to fund migrants. This is clearly breaking campaign finance laws."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that funds raised specifically to elect Beto O’Rourke have been used to ‘fund migrants,’ and public campaign filings and reputable reporting do not substantiate that claim. Moreover, whether a particular payment would violate campaign finance laws depends on the specific account making the payment and its purpose; donations to charities or separate nonprofits are not categorically illegal campaign activity.

claim: Video footage from Georgia shows suitcases filled with ballots pulled from under a table and illegally counted after election observers were told to leave.
rationale: False. Multiple contemporaneous investigations and reporting showed the footage was mischaracterized: the items seen were official ballot containers or trays, not suitcases of fraudulent ballots, and counting procedures followed permitted processes with observers not illegally excluded. Georgia election officials, bipartisan audits, and fact-checkers found no evidence that ballots were secretly pulled from under tables and illicitly counted after observers were told to leave.

claim: Before the coronavirus pandemic, the United States had "the greatest economy in the history of our country."
rationale: The phrase is a subjective superlative that cannot be established as an objective fact. While U.S. indicators immediately before the COVID-19 shutdowns (about 2019–early 2020) — low unemployment, high stock market levels and record nominal GDP — were strong, whether that constitutes "the greatest economy in the history of our country" depends on which metrics (real GDP per capita, median income, inequality, labor-force participation, inflation-adjusted output) and time periods are used, so the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: Robert Mueller’s investigative team has "13 hardened Democrats, some big Crooked Hillary supporters, and Zero Republicans."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: while many members of Mueller’s team had donated to Democrats (and some to Hillary Clinton), the characterization that all 13 were "hardened Democrats" and that there were "zero Republicans" is false. Public contribution records and reporting show a mix of past donations and affiliations, and Mueller himself is a registered Republican. Independent fact-checkers reached the same conclusion that the claim overstates partisan uniformity.

claim: California’s Prop 60, which would require condom use in adult films, would put "workers in the adult film industry at risk for lawsuits and harassment."
rationale: Opponents and legal analyses of California's Prop 60 noted the measure did more than mandate condoms: it created new reporting and enforcement mechanisms, allowed civil penalties and private suits against producers, and required disclosure to local public health officials and posting of certain notices. Those provisions plausibly would increase exposure to civil litigation and make performers' workplaces and possibly personal information more visible, raising risks of lawsuits and harassment.

claim: "In Harrisburg, I passed more bills than all the Democrats combined, in terms of legislation affecting the city."
rationale: The claim is implausible and unsupported as stated because passing legislation requires votes of a legislative body and usually involves multiple members; a single official in Harrisburg would not typically 'pass more bills than all the Democrats combined' without a very specific office and timeframe. Public legislative records (city council or state legislature) would be needed to substantiate such a sweeping comparative claim, and no clear evidence was provided.

claim: Says Democratic Senate candidate "Bruce Braley voted to cut $700 billion from Medicare to support Obamacare."
rationale: This is misleading. Bruce Braley did vote for the Affordable Care Act, and that law contained roughly $700–716 billion in net Medicare savings over a decade, but those were largely payment reductions to providers and Medicare Advantage plans and efficiency/fraud measures, not direct cuts to seniors’ guaranteed Medicare benefits as the claim implies.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Nancy Pelosi said, "Employers cutting hours is a good thing. It then gives that person time to pursue their dreams and passions."
rationale: There is no credible record of Rep. Nancy Pelosi saying that employers cutting hours is "a good thing" and gives workers time to pursue dreams; this phrasing circulated as a viral misattributed quote and was debunked by multiple fact-checkers. Pelosi’s public statements around employer cutbacks and health-care policy have criticized hour-cutting as a problem, not praise for it, and no reputable news source or video supports the quoted line.

claim: Says "in this next biennium, the cost of primary and secondary education is going to increase by more that $1000 per student. Half of that $1000 – $500 per student – is accounted for by the increased cost of PERS alone."
rationale: The claim ties specific per‑student dollar amounts to an unspecified jurisdiction and biennium, which makes it unverifiable as stated. State education and retirement cost projections vary widely; while PERS (public employee retirement) increases have raised K–12 costs in some places, I find no authoritative basis to assert a >$1,000 per‑student increase with exactly $500 attributable solely to PERS without citing the jurisdiction, biennium, and budget sources. Given the missing context and variability in official budget projections, the precise numeric claim is unlikely to be reliably true as presented.

claim: 110 people a day move to Austin.
rationale: The statement is too broad and lacks necessary context (timeframe and whether it means Austin city or the metro area). Official population estimates and media reports show Austin’s net gains have varied year to year and by definition (city vs. metro), so a blanket "110 people a day" claim is not reliably true without specifying period and geography. Depending on the year and measure, daily net gains have been both below and above that figure.

claim: In 2007, Ed Gillespie "was paid $300,000 to be the frontman for a coalition that made the individual mandate the centerpiece of its health reform plan."
rationale: There is no credible public evidence that Ed Gillespie was paid $300,000 in 2007 to serve as a ‘frontman’ for a coalition that made an individual mandate its centerpiece. Contemporary reporting and later fact-checking found the specific payment and characterization unsubstantiated and appear to conflate his consulting/lobbying work with broader health‑care advocacy efforts.

claim: "Seventy percent of the people living in abject poverty are women."
rationale: The 70% figure is not supported by the most reliable global poverty data. Women are disproportionately affected by poverty, but authoritative sources and analyses do not substantiate a universal claim that 70% of people in extreme or ‘abject’ poverty are women; moreover poverty is often measured at the household level which complicates attributing poverty to individuals by sex.

claim: "The caliphate has crumbled and ISIS has been defeated."
rationale: The statement mixes a correct point and an incorrect one: ISIS’s self-declared territorial “caliphate” effectively collapsed with the fall of its last stronghold in Syria in 2019, but the organization was not fully defeated. ISIS remains active as an insurgency and through regional affiliates that continue to carry out attacks and recruit. Consequently, saying the caliphate has crumbled is accurate, but claiming ISIS has been defeated is false.

claim: "Joe Biden wants to end school choice."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. Biden has opposed federal funding for private-school voucher programs and emphasized strengthening public schools, but he has not proposed banning charter schools or all forms of parental choice; his positions focus on limiting vouchers and increasing accountability for charters rather than ending school choice outright.

claim: Says there’s "no wait list" for private school vouchers
rationale: The blanket statement that there is “no wait list” for private school vouchers is false in general. Many voucher programs are capped by funding or enrollment and maintain waitlists or use lotteries when applications exceed available slots, so the absence of a waitlist is not universally true.

claim: "America’s hard-working agricultural producers … have taken a disproportionate hit when it comes to illegal retaliatory tariffs."
rationale: The statement overstates and conflates two claims: that U.S. agricultural producers were disproportionately harmed and that the retaliatory tariffs were illegal. While farmers—especially soybean and pork producers—were heavily affected by retaliatory tariffs during the 2018–19 trade disputes (notably with China), other U.S. sectors also sustained large impacts, and the distribution of harm depended on product and market exposure. Moreover, whether particular retaliatory tariffs were "illegal" is contested: many were implemented as lawful countermeasures or authorized by dispute findings, so characterizing them broadly as illegal is inaccurate.
