While the Tampa Bay Rays have frequently been cited as having among the lowest ticket prices in Major League Baseball (and have ranked low on some ‘affordability’ lists in certain years), there is no definitive evidence that their overall prices (tickets, concessions, parking, etc.) have been judged the single most affordable across all professional sports at any sustained point in time.

claim: Obama's budget plan would "take national debt up to about 80 percent of gross national product. ... Historically, it's been about 40 percent."
rationale: The statement is misleading and imprecise. Obama-era budget projections under certain assumptions did show federal debt rising into the ~70–80% of GDP range in future years, but the claim mixes terms (saying GNP rather than the usual GDP) and doesn’t specify gross debt versus debt held by the public; those choices materially change the numbers. The historical “about 40 percent” figure is an oversimplification — debt/GDP has varied widely (WWII exceeded 100%, post‑war decades averaged lower), so the claim as stated is not accurate.

claim: Rubio's "got more experience than Obama had."
rationale: Interpreting “experience” as length of elected/public-office service at the time each ran for president, Rubio had served more years in elected office (state legislature plus multiple years in the U.S. Senate by 2015–16) than Obama had when he launched his 2008 bid (Obama had about two years in the U.S. Senate, though earlier Illinois state senate service). Thus the claim is accurate in the common comparison of years of elected experience.

claim: "A year ago we had the lowest unemployment in history without using taxpayers money."
rationale: The claim is not supported. It is ambiguous about who “we” are and when exactly, but historically (for example in the U.S.) unemployment has reached similar or lower lows (around 3.5% in early 2020), and recent declines in unemployment have been influenced by government fiscal and monetary measures. Saying it happened “without using taxpayers money” is misleading because stimulus, benefits, tax policy and other public actions typically play a material role alongside private hiring.

claim: In Texas, "the No. 1 name for new male babies — many of whom will vote one day — is Jose."
rationale: Recent data on baby names by state show that Jose is not the top male baby name in Texas in recent years; nationally and in Texas the top names have been Liam, Noah, or Mateo rather than Jose. While Jose is a common Hispanic name, it has not ranked No.1 for newborn boys in Texas in the recent SSA/state name lists.

claim: While in Congress, Nathan Deal was a leader when it came to protecting our borders.
rationale: The claim is subjective and overstates Deal's role. While Nathan Deal generally supported tougher immigration enforcement and voted for measures such as border fencing and increased enforcement, he was not widely recognized as a national leader on border security nor did he hold prominent immigration or homeland security committee leadership positions that would substantiate the label “a leader” on the issue. The available record shows a supporter of enforcement rather than a leading architect or national spokesman for border policy.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "voted to deport" young people known as Dreamers.
rationale: There is no record of Marco Rubio having cast a single, explicit roll-call vote that was titled or solely to "deport" DACA recipients. Rubio has a mixed immigration record—supporting some bills that tightened enforcement or opposed certain DACA protections and earlier co-sponsoring comprehensive reform—but that is not the same as a direct vote to deport Dreamers. Claims that he "voted to deport" conflate votes on broader bills or proposals with a specific deportation vote.

claim:
Says U.S. Sen Sherrod Brown "promised that the first stimulus bill would fund the
Brent Spence Bridge."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Sen. Sherrod Brown explicitly promised the first stimulus bill (the March 2020 CARES Act) would fund the Brent Spence Bridge. The first stimulus package was targeted at pandemic relief and did not include major project-specific bridge funding; Brown later advocated for infrastructure funding but did not guarantee that the initial stimulus would pay for that bridge.

claim: The U.S. government spends less on energy innovation "than the pet food industry invests in its own products."
rationale: The claim is misleading: U.S. federal funding for energy innovation (including DOE energy R&D, ARPA‑E and related programs) runs into multiple billions of dollars annually, whereas the pet food industry’s spending specifically on product R&D and development is substantially smaller. Past independent fact‑checks have found similar comparisons false or based on apples‑to‑oranges accounting. The headline conflates different categories (public R&D vs. private product spending) and omits time/frame context.

claim: "NFL attendance and ratings are WAY DOWN. Boring games yes, but many stay away because they love our country."
rationale: The claim overstates both parts: NFL attendance and ratings have fluctuated year-to-year but were not uniformly or dramatically “WAY DOWN” across the league in recent years; declines in some seasons were modest and influenced by many factors. There is no solid evidence that a large share of people are avoiding NFL games/TV primarily out of "love of country" (patriotism); attribution is speculative and unsupported by polling or viewership studies.

claim: Says John F. Kennedy "smoked cannabis in the White House, while president, because he suffered from severe back pain and Addison's disease."
rationale: While John F. Kennedy did suffer severe chronic back pain and received many prescription treatments, there is no credible evidence in his medical records or major biographies that he smoked cannabis in the White House while president. Claims that he had Addison’s disease and used marijuana to treat it are not substantiated by primary medical documentation; historians have documented extensive use of prescription drugs and injections but not verified marijuana use. The assertion appears to be rumor rather than fact.

claim: Banks paid Hillary Clinton "over $1 million and are contributing millions more to elect her."
rationale: This is broadly accurate: Hillary Clinton received more than $1 million in paid speaking fees from Wall Street firms (including Goldman Sachs and other financial institutions) and the financial industry — through corporate PACs, employees and allied outside groups — donated millions of dollars to her 2016 campaign and supportive committees. Multiple news reports and campaign finance disclosures document both the paid speeches and sizable contributions from banks and finance-sector donors.

claim: Speaking of an HIV outbreak in Indiana during his time as governor, says "we immediately deployed health resources."
rationale: The claim that he said “we immediately deployed health resources” is misleading. During the 2015 Scott County HIV outbreak in Indiana the state did eventually deploy treatment resources and accepted CDC help, but officials (including Governor Pence) initially resisted syringe-exchange programs and did not authorize an emergency exchange until weeks later, so “immediately” misstates the timeline. Without a sourced direct quote, the statement overstates the speed of the response.

claim: President Barack Obama’s policies "have resulted in gas prices being reduced from $3.07 per gallon when he was sworn in in 2009 to $2.30 today."
rationale: The claim is both numerically and causally inaccurate. U.S. national average regular gasoline prices were roughly $1.80–$1.90 per gallon around Obama’s Jan 20, 2009 inauguration (not $3.07), and while prices later fell to about $2.30 at times, those movements reflect global oil market supply and demand and other factors rather than being directly caused solely by Obama’s policies.

claim: Says the Ohio Consumers’ Council office employs 74 lawyers and that the funding them is wasteful duplication.
rationale: The Ohio Consumers’ Counsel is a relatively small state office that historically staffs far fewer than 74 full‑time attorneys; publicly available descriptions and staffing summaries show a compact legal team rather than dozens of in‑house lawyers. The added assertion that funding them is “wasteful duplication” is a normative judgment, not an objective fact about staffing. Thus the specific factual claim about employing 74 lawyers is incorrect and the wastefulness claim is opinion-based.

claim: One Wisconsin school district "is so worried about losing state funding that it has stopped giving milk to elementary school kids during snack time."
rationale: There is no verifiable, independently reported evidence that a Wisconsin school district halted milk at elementary snack time specifically because it feared losing state funding. While school districts do make budget-driven changes to food programs, this precise claim names no district and lacks corroboration in public reporting. Given the specificity and absence of sourcing, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Lauren Boebert received a PPP loan for her restaurant."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and public Small Business Administration loan disclosures show that the Boebert family business (Shooters Grill in Rifle, Colorado) received a Paycheck Protection Program loan during the COVID-19 relief round in 2020. Multiple news outlets and aggregated SBA data identified the restaurant as a PPP recipient (reported amount commonly cited around $180,000).

claim: "Some of the wealthiest Americans are African-American now."
rationale: True. Multiple African Americans appear on contemporary lists of the richest Americans — for example, known billionaires and very high-net-worth individuals such as Robert F. Smith, David Steward, Oprah Winfrey, and Michael Jordan have been listed among the wealthiest Americans. Although they are a relatively small share of the top ranks, their presence on wealth lists validates the claim.

claim: "Politicians and their corporate lobbyists are trying to take away my right to spend my paycheck how I want."
rationale: The claim is a broad, unsubstantiated generalization. While some politicians and corporate lobbyists support specific taxes, bans, or regulations that restrict certain purchases, that does not justify the sweeping assertion that they are collectively trying to remove a universal right to spend wages as one pleases. Rights to spend income are not absolute and are routinely limited by law for public-policy reasons, but the claim as stated lacks specific evidence of a coordinated effort to 'take away' that right.

claim: "Since I took office, Michigan has added more than 25,000 auto jobs."
rationale: The claim is not reliably supported by standard labor data. Using the typical BLS/NAICS category for motor vehicles and parts manufacturing and the period beginning when the governor took office (January 2019), public employment series do not show a sustained net gain of more than 25,000 ‘auto’ jobs; employment in the sector rose and fell (notably during the 2020 pandemic) and any larger headline gains usually rely on broader or nonstandard definitions (e.g., including supplier, construction, or temporary jobs). Because the result depends heavily on the precise definition and timeframe, the simple claim is not verifiable as stated.

claim: Hepatitis outbreak in kids may be related to Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the pediatric hepatitis outbreak is caused by the Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine. Public-health investigations have pointed to adenovirus 41 and other factors, and many affected children were too young or not vaccinated against COVID-19; epidemiological data do not show a link to the J&J vaccine.

claim: In the past three years, state legislatures have "enacted more of these restrictions (on abortion) than in the previous 10 years combined."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and cannot be verified as written: whether the last three years saw more abortion restrictions than the previous ten depends on the exact three‑year and ten‑year windows and which measures (bans, waiting‑period laws, clinic regulations) are counted. Major trackers (e.g., Guttmacher, news fact‑checks) documented a sharp increase in state restrictions after 2020–2022, but they do not universally support the blanket claim without specifying dates and types of laws. Because the claim lacks a defined timeframe and category of restrictions, it is not reliably true as stated.

claim: Undocumented immigrants "pay $12 billion a year into Social Security."
rationale: Estimates from the Social Security Administration’s Office of the Chief Actuary and related analyses found that unauthorized (undocumented) workers have paid on the order of $12 billion per year in payroll taxes into Social Security (the widely cited estimate refers to around 2010). While the exact number can vary by year and methodology, the claim reflects a credible, commonly cited estimate rather than being fabricated.

claim: Due to U.S. Senate rules, Democrats need "more than a majority ... to codify Roe vs. Wade."
rationale: Under current Senate rules most legislation can be blocked by a filibuster, and cloture to end debate normally requires 60 votes. Because a broad statute codifying Roe v. Wade would be ordinary legislation, Democrats with only a simple 51-vote majority would generally need more than a bare majority to overcome the filibuster and enact such a law. There are limited exceptions (e.g., reconciliation) or a majority could change the rules, but those are not the standard path for a sweeping abortion-rights law.

claim: "National Guard doctors find hospitals empty of COVID patients."
rationale: The claim is a broad, unspecified generalization that National Guard doctors found hospitals empty of COVID patients. While there were isolated instances where Guard teams arrived at facilities with few COVID cases, extensive reporting from the pandemic documents many hospitals that were overwhelmed during surge periods across different regions, so the blanket statement is inaccurate. The truth depends on specific time and place, not a universal finding.

claim: "I got a letter from 20 people who said they wanted their money back, 14 never gave me a penny."
rationale: There is no verifiable public evidence provided to confirm the speaker received a letter from exactly 20 people or that 14 of those never paid. This is a specific, private claim about correspondence and transactions that cannot be corroborated from available information. Without the original letters and payment records the claim remains unverified and thus treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "In the 18th Congressional District, 100% of electric generation comes from coal."
rationale: The claim is almost certainly false: no U.S. congressional district reliably produces 100% of its electricity from coal. EIA/EPA data and utility records show that generation within districts is typically a mix of fuels (coal, natural gas, renewables, nuclear) and electricity consumption is supplied from regional grids, not exclusively local coal plants. Even coal‑heavy districts have at least some non‑coal generation or imports.

claim: "In South Dakota, I’m putting prayer back in our schools."
rationale: The claim is misleading: U.S. Supreme Court rulings (e.g., Engel v. Vitale and Santa Fe v. Doe) bar school‑sponsored or school‑led prayer, so a state cannot legitimately "put prayer back" as an official school practice. While states can and have protected voluntary, student‑initiated prayer, that is not the same as reinstating government‑sponsored prayer in public schools.

claim: In the United States, we’ve had "12 years in a row of wages declining."
rationale: No widely used U.S. wage measure shows wages falling for 12 consecutive years. Major series such as BLS real average hourly earnings and Census median household income have years of decline and years of increase (for example recovery years after the Great Recession), so there is not a continuous 12-year downward run. The claim also fails to specify which wage metric or time period, and fact-checks of similar assertions have found them inaccurate.

claim: Paul Ryan’s budget "keeps the Obamacare taxes and spending cuts that paid for Obamacare, but then cuts all of the benefits."
rationale: The claim oversimplifies and misstates Paul Ryan’s budget proposals. Ryan repeatedly sought to repeal large portions of the ACA (including many of its tax provisions) while also proposing major changes to Medicare and Medicaid, but he did not merely "keep the Obamacare taxes and spending cuts that paid for Obamacare" wholesale and then simply cut all benefits; his proposals mixed repeal of some ACA taxes, retention of some payment reductions, and broader entitlement restructurings. The statement conflates distinct elements of multiple budgets and presents them as a single, precise policy choice that Ryan did not make.

claim: "In the last two years, super PACs raised more than $180 million -- with roughly half of it coming from fewer than 200 super-rich people and roughly 20 percent from corporations."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no specific two‑year period and the precise breakdowns are not consistently supported by public campaign‑finance analyses. While it is true that a small number of very wealthy donors have supplied a large share of super PAC funding and corporations can and do give, reported totals and percentage shares vary by election cycle and data source, so the exact figures in the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Now, 50% of all of America, more than any other country, is fully vaccinated."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. The phrase “50% of all of America” is ambiguous, but no reliable global snapshot supports that the U.S. (or the Americas collectively) was uniquely highest at 50% fully vaccinated — many countries (for example Portugal, the United Arab Emirates, Spain, Chile and others at various times) have had higher fully vaccinated shares. Without a clear date or definition of “America,” the superlative “more than any other country” is not supported.

claim: Florida students take "an array of standardized high stakes tests which eat up as much as 45 school days per year."
rationale: Florida does administer multiple statewide, end‑of‑course, and industry certification exams, but official testing windows and typical administration schedules occupy only a small number of instructional days rather than 45 full school days. While adding district benchmark tests and preparatory activities increases testing‑related time, reputable counts and state testing schedules do not support the claim that standardized high‑stakes testing consumes as much as 45 full school days per year for typical Florida students.

claim: "We know mask mandates work. There’s enough evidence out there between counties that have done it and counties that haven’t."
rationale: Multiple observational and quasi-experimental studies comparing counties, states, and other jurisdictions with and without mask mandates have found associations between mandates and reduced COVID-19 transmission, hospitalizations, and deaths. Although effect sizes vary with compliance, timing, and concurrent policies, mechanistic laboratory evidence that masks block respiratory droplets plus converging epidemiological results support the claim that mask mandates work to reduce spread.

claim: The Orlando shooter used "a weapon of war."
rationale: The Pulse nightclub shooter (Omar Mateen) used civilian semi-automatic firearms—reported as a SIG Sauer MCX rifle (AR-platform, semi‑automatic) and a Glock 17 handgun—not fully automatic or military select‑fire weapons. Calling those civilian semi‑automatic guns a “weapon of war” is a political characterization; it is not literally accurate by the usual definition of military automatic arms.

claim: California Republican gubernatorial hopeful Meg Whitman "contributed to, and campaigned, for" Democratic Sen. Barbara Boxer.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Meg Whitman both donated to and actively campaigned for Senator Barbara Boxer. While Whitman has made political donations to candidates from both parties at various times, contemporary fact-checking and campaign records do not support the claim that she campaigned on Boxer's behalf.

claim: "Over the past 10 years, the number of people living in Lower Manhattan has nearly doubled. In fact, Lower Manhattan has added more people over the last 10 years than Atlanta, Dallas and Philadelphia combined."
rationale: The blanket claim is false. While parts of Lower Manhattan (depending on exact boundaries) have seen large percentage increases from a small base and may have roughly doubled over certain decadal windows, the absolute number of residents added in Lower Manhattan is on the order of tens of thousands, far smaller than the combined population gains of Atlanta, Dallas, and Philadelphia over the same recent decade. The comparison overstates Lower Manhattan’s absolute growth by conflating high percentage growth from a small base with the much larger numeric gains of major U.S. cities.

claim: "A family of four can make up to $88,000 a year and still get a subsidy for health insurance" under the new federal health care law.
rationale: This specific dollar figure is misleading. Under the Affordable Care Act subsidies are tied to a household's percent of the Federal Poverty Level (generally up to 400% FPL), and the dollar cutoff for a family of four is higher than $88,000 in most recent years (roughly $90–96k depending on the year), so stating a flat $88,000 is inaccurate and omits year and location variation.

claim: Says swabbing a tick with a soap-soaked cotton ball is a "safe, easy way" to remove them from skin.
rationale: Major public-health authorities recommend using fine-tipped tweezers or a dedicated tick removal tool and do not endorse smothering or improvised methods. Swabbing with a soap-soaked cotton ball is not an endorsed “safe” technique and could lead to incomplete removal or cause the tick to regurgitate, raising the risk of pathogen transmission.

claim: Says no elections protest was filed, McCready conceded and "every" county board certified its results from the Mark Harris, Dan McCready race.
rationale: The claim is misleading. McCready did issue a public concession on election night but his campaign later pursued investigations and challenged the results after evidence of absentee-ballot irregularities emerged; the State Board of Elections ultimately ordered a new election. Further, the situation involved state-board hearings and contested certifications tied to alleged fraud, so it is not accurate to say no protest was filed and that every county’s certification settled the matter.

claim: Says George Patton said, "Politicians are the lowest form of life on earth. Liberal Democrats are the lower form of politicians."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Gen. George S. Patton said this. The specific phrase ‘‘Liberal Democrats’’ is anachronistic for Patton (he died in 1945) and the two-part insult appears to be a modern internet misattribution rather than a documented Patton quotation. Given the lack of primary-source support and frequent online circulation as a meme, the attribution is unlikely to be authentic.

claim: The debt ceiling deal will result in "the lowest level of annual domestic spending since Dwight Eisenhower was president."
rationale: The debt‑ceiling agreement includes relatively modest caps on discretionary spending and does not cut overall federal domestic outlays to levels seen in the 1950s. Historical tables and CBO projections show total domestic spending (whether measured in inflation‑adjusted dollars or as a share of GDP) remains well above Eisenhower‑era levels; the claim only becomes plausible under a very narrow and atypical definition of “domestic spending.”

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We’ll never have to worry about China attacking us! They are 12 hours ahead, so we’ll have plenty of time to shoot down their missiles!"
rationale: This is a fabricated and misattributed quote. There is no record in Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's public statements or credible news reporting of her saying this, and the claim also reflects a basic misunderstanding—time zones do not prevent or delay missile attacks.

claim: The EPA "wants to hire 230,000 new government regulators that will cost the taxpayer $21 billion."
rationale: This claim is not supported by available evidence: the EPA’s entire workforce is on the order of roughly 14,000–15,000 employees, and there has been no credible plan or budget request to hire 230,000 new federal 'regulators.' The $21 billion figure does not match EPA direct-hire budget requests and appears to stem from misinterpretation or aggregation of unrelated program funds, grants, or contractor/partner counts rather than planned new federal hires.

claim: "Thousands of Westerners and Americans" are fighting with extremists in eastern Syria and Iraq.
rationale: While several thousand foreign fighters from Western countries (notably from parts of Europe) traveled to Syria and Iraq at the height of the conflict, the number of U.S. citizens who did so was far smaller — generally estimated in the low hundreds. Therefore the blanket claim that "thousands of Americans" are fighting there is incorrect, even if 'thousands of Westerners' (broadly defined) participated historically.

claim: Says "every school will be negatively impacted" if Education Stability Fund is not tapped.
rationale: The claim is an absolute universal statement that is unlikely to be true: whether schools are harmed by not tapping an Education Stabilization/State fund depends on each district’s existing budgets, reserves, state/local aid, and alternative federal programs. While many schools could face negative effects from losing that funding, it is incorrect to assert every single school would be negatively impacted without additional context or evidence.

claim: Social Security is a "Ponzi scheme."
rationale: Calling Social Security a 'Ponzi scheme' is misleading: a Ponzi scheme is a fraudulent investment racket that pays earlier investors with money from later investors while promising high returns and hiding losses. Social Security is a government-run, statutory social insurance program financed by payroll taxes with transparent rules, benefits tied to earnings and legal obligations to pay benefits, not deception or criminal fraud. While its pay‑as‑you‑go elements mean current workers fund current beneficiaries, that structural similarity does not make it a Ponzi scheme.

claim: "CDC Director Robert Redfield says healthy people should NOT wear masks."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Early in the COVID-19 pandemic CDC guidance (which Robert Redfield headed) emphasized masks for sick people and healthcare workers, but on April 3, 2020 the CDC — and Redfield — endorsed cloth face coverings for the general public. Redfield has since supported public mask use, so the blanket statement that he says healthy people should not wear masks is inaccurate without a specific timeframe.

claim: "After California taxes, Trey Lance's $34.1M rookie deal becomes just $16M."
rationale: The statement is misleading: California state tax alone would not reduce a $34.1M rookie deal to $16M. To reach roughly $16M net you must subtract federal top marginal tax (~37%), California top rate (~13.3%) where applicable, Medicare/FICA, agent fees and other deductions, and even then the exact net depends on bonus structure and income apportionment. The claim attributes the entire drop to California taxes and ignores those other major factors and tax apportionment rules.

claim: "While (Chris Christie) talks about job creation, we don't see jobs being created in this state."
rationale: The claim is a broad, absolute statement that cannot be sustained: during Chris Christie’s tenure as New Jersey governor the state recorded net job gains and a falling unemployment rate overall, so it is inaccurate to say no jobs were being created. There were uneven sectoral and regional results and legitimate debate over the pace and quality of growth, but blanket denial of job creation is contradicted by labor statistics for the period.

claim: The climate-change agreement between the United States and China "requires the Chinese to do nothing at all for 16 years."
rationale: The claim is false. The 2014 U.S.–China climate announcement did not "require the Chinese to do nothing for 16 years"; it committed China to peak its CO2 emissions around 2030 and to raise the share of non‑fossil energy to about 20% by 2030, along with domestic policies and actions to achieve those goals. Thus the agreement set targets and commitments rather than allowing total inaction.

claim: "When Rachel Zenzinger was on the Arvada City Council, she voted to spend taxpayer funds for a junket to China."
rationale: I find no reliable, corroborated evidence that Rachel Zenzinger specifically voted as an Arvada City Council member to spend general taxpayer funds for a personal "junket" to China. While she did serve on the Arvada council and there have been disputes about sister-city visits and travel approvals by local councils, available summaries do not document a clear vote authorizing a taxpayer-funded junket by Zenzinger. Because reporting on municipal travel can conflate funded cultural exchanges, reimbursed delegations, or private travel, the claim as phrased is not supported.

claim: Says Keanu Reeves gave a speech that began, "I cannot be part of a world where men dress their wives as prostitutes by showing everything that should be cherished ..."
rationale: There is no credible record of Keanu Reeves delivering a speech containing that line, and the wording appears in widely shared social-media posts that fact-checkers have flagged as misattributed. Public transcripts, interviews, press coverage and reputable quote databases do not support Reeves as the source, indicating the attribution is false.

claim: Says "former Democrat Kelli Ward attacked President Trump's plans to crack down on illegal immigration, saying Trump was making a mistake."
rationale: This claim is inconsistent with the public record: Kelli Ward is a long-time Republican (former Arizona state senator and GOP candidate/party chair) and has generally supported tougher immigration enforcement and President Trump, not publicly attacking his crackdown as a mistake. There is no well-known instance where she, identified as a 'former Democrat,' criticized Trump’s immigration plan in that way.

claim: Says Donald Trump warned outgoing Ghana President against last-minute job appointments.
rationale: I could not find credible evidence that Donald Trump publicly warned an outgoing Ghanaian president about last-minute job appointments; no major news outlets or official statements report such a warning. The claim appears to be an unverified social-media-style assertion or misattribution rather than a documented public comment by Trump.

claim: "We are within the margin of error."
rationale: The claim is too vague to be verified: “within the margin of error” is a statistical statement that requires a specific estimate, its reported margin of error, and the comparator value. Without the poll or measurement, sample size, and confidence level, one cannot determine whether two figures differ by no more than the stated margin of error. Because the necessary context is missing, the claim cannot be validated as true.

claim: Says Kurt Schrader voted to cut $500 billion from Medicare, threatening "thousands of Oregon seniors and their access to their current coverage."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate as stated. Kurt Schrader, a Democratic member of Congress, is not recorded as having voted for a measure that explicitly ‘‘cut $500 billion from Medicare’’; the roughly $500 billion figure is associated with Republican budget/repeal proposals, which Democrats (including Schrader) opposed in key health-care votes. Without a specific bill and date, the assertion that Schrader cast a vote enacting a $500 billion Medicare cut is not supported by the known voting record.

claim: An all-female construction company built the Florida bridge that collapsed.
rationale: This is false. The widely reported Florida pedestrian bridge collapse (FIU, March 2018) involved Munilla Construction Management (MCM) as contractor and FIGG as the designer, and official investigations and contemporaneous news coverage identify those firms and multiple subcontractors rather than an “all-female” construction company. There is no credible evidence that an all-female firm built the collapsed bridge.

claim: Says Jill McCabe "supports late term abortions. Larger baby parts are more profitable."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable reporting that Jill McCabe made the quoted statement endorsing late-term abortions and saying larger baby parts are more profitable. This inflammatory quote matches patterns of fabricated social-media claims about public figures and would have been widely reported if true. Without a verifiable primary source, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "Withheld union dues fund half of Dem (Democratic) campaigns in Florida."
rationale: There is no evidence that “withheld union dues” bankroll half of Democratic campaigns in Florida. Campaign finance records show Democratic candidates receive funding from many sources (individual donors, party committees, PACs, out‑of‑state donors, and unions), and unions’ political spending is typically from voluntary PAC contributions or disclosed political accounts rather than a single pool of mandatory withheld dues. The claim conflates different funding streams and overstates the union share without supporting data.

claim: The IRS is going to be "in charge" of "a huge national database" on health care that will include Americans’ "personal, intimate, most close-to-the-vest-secrets."
rationale: This claim is false. The IRS is not building or 'in charge' of a nationwide health-care database of Americans' intimate medical records — its role under the Affordable Care Act is limited to receiving tax-related health coverage information (e.g., Forms 1095-A) to administer tax credits and penalties. Creation and management of health enrollment systems and medical records are handled by HHS/CMS and private providers, and medical data are generally protected by HIPAA and other privacy rules.

claim: "All of the records, as far as I know, about what we did with health care, those are already available."
rationale: The blanket statement that “all of the records…are already available” is not verifiable and is unlikely to be true. In practice, records about policy actions often include withheld, redacted, or not-yet-released documents (deliberative communications, legal exemptions, private emails), so claiming completeness without specific scope is misleading. The speaker’s hedge (“as far as I know”) further undermines the definitive claim.

claim: "At John Lewis funeral Obama told a room full of people that rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Barack Obama spoke at John Lewis's funeral telling attendees that 'rooms full of people' are too dangerous and urging mail-in voting. Major news accounts of John Lewis's memorial services list other speakers and do not record Obama making such remarks; Obama did not deliver a public funeral address with that message. The claim appears to be a misattribution or fabrication.

claim: Democratic U.S. House candidate Julie Lassa pushed for a "Canadian-style government takeover of health care."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Julie Lassa explicitly advocated a “Canadian-style government takeover of health care.” Public records and campaign materials indicate she supported expanded access/insurance reforms (and endorsed parts of the Affordable Care Act), but not an explicit single‑payer Canadian model; opponents’ ads appear to have conflated or exaggerated her position. Without a direct quote endorsing Canadian single‑payer, the claim is misleading.

claim: "We need to also recognize that we just had two of the coldest years, biggest drop in global temperatures that we have had since the 1980s, the biggest in the last 100 years. We don't talk about that."
rationale: The claim that we just had "two of the coldest years" and the "biggest drop in global temperatures" since the 1980s (or in the last 100 years) contradicts global temperature records. Multiple independent datasets (NASA, NOAA, HadCRUT) show recent years have been among the warmest on record and only small year-to-year variability occurs (often tied to El Niño/La Niña), not a large century-scale drop. There is no evidence of the dramatic global cooling described in the claim.

claim: "70 percent of the income tax that the state collects happens to come from Westchester, Nassau, Suffolk and New York City"
rationale: The precise claim that 70% of the state’s income tax comes from Westchester, Nassau, Suffolk and New York City is not supported by authoritative, year‑to‑year tax reports. New York City and the downstate suburbs do contribute a large share of state personal income tax receipts, but published county‑level PIT data and state revenue reports show the exact share varies and do not consistently equal 70%. Without a specific tax year or definition (resident vs. source income) the 70% figure is not verifiable.

claim: "For the first time in over a decade, business leaders around the world have declared that China is no longer the world’s No. 1 place to invest; America is."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization and factually misleading. While some investor surveys in recent years have shown improving sentiment toward the United States and waning enthusiasm for China amid geopolitical tensions, there is no single, global declaration by business leaders that for the first time in over a decade China has lost top status to America; results vary by survey, metric (FDI flows, confidence indexes, respondents), and year. Historical FDI and investor-confidence data show shifts back and forth, so the categorical claim is not supported.

claim: "The CBO says if we raise the minimum wage the way Charlie (Crist) wants to do it, it would lose 500,000 jobs."
rationale: The Congressional Budget Office's July 2014 report gave a central estimate that raising the federal minimum wage to $10.10 by 2016 would reduce total employment by about 500,000. If Charlie Crist's proposal called for a comparable increase (similar level and timeline), citing the CBO’s 500,000 figure is accurate; the CBO also emphasized uncertainty and a wide range of possible effects.

claim: A photo shows Joe Namath and Al Woodall kneeling on the sideline of a football field during the national anthem.
rationale: The image has been circulated with the claim that Namath and Woodall were kneeling as a political protest during the national anthem, but contemporary evidence and fact-checking indicate the picture is miscaptioned or taken out of context. Historical reporting and fact-checkers found older photos of players taking a knee for pregame prayer or other non-protest reasons, and organized anthem kneeling as a political protest began decades later. Therefore the claim that the photo shows them kneeling specifically during the national anthem is false or misleading.

claim: Members of Congress "have not reduced their salaries ... since the Great Depression," meaning they've gone "eight decades without a pay cut."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While members often block or refuse scheduled increases and there have been years with pay freezes or reductions in take‑home pay (for example by rescinding planned cost‑of‑living increases or cutting leadership stipends), it is incorrect to present an absolute rule that Congress has never cut pay since the Great Depression. Whether a change counts as a "pay cut" depends on definitions (nominal statute, inflation‑adjusted pay, scheduled raises, or withheld pay).

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Steve Southerland "voted himself health care for life."
rationale: There is no record of a congressional vote that explicitly gave Rep. Steve Southerland (or any member) “health care for life.” Members of Congress participate in the Federal Employees Health Benefits program and can continue coverage under retiree rules only if they meet standard federal retirement eligibility; that is not a one-off vote granting lifetime health care. Political ads have sometimes mischaracterized routine votes or federal benefit rules to claim legislators voted themselves lifetime health care, but the literal claim is inaccurate.

claim: Says law enforcement officials alerted the public to check the caps of bottled water for tampering because someone is injecting poison into them, and that a "few people already died in the Richmond area" as a result.
rationale: This specific claim is false: there is no credible evidence that law enforcement issued a public alert about people injecting poison into bottled-water caps and no verified reports that a few people died in the Richmond area as a result. Multiple fact-checkers and local police/public-health offices have denied any such alert or confirmed deaths, and no hospital or coroner reports support the allegation. The claim matches patterns of viral hoaxes that spread without official verification.

claim: A man was arrested "for wearing a T-shirt that says ‘We The People’ and has a picture of the ‘Statue of Liberty.’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a person was arrested solely for wearing a ‘We The People’ T‑shirt with the Statue of Liberty; viral posts claiming this lack corroborating reporting and typically omit context. In the U.S., wearing political clothing is generally protected speech and arrests almost always stem from a separate alleged offense rather than the expressive message alone.

claim: President Barack Obama "had the legal authority" to strike Syria without a vote from Congress.
rationale: The claim is legally contested, not established fact. The Obama administration itself sought Congressional authorization for strikes on Syria in 2013, and legal scholars were divided: some argued limited executive action was permissible under Article II and existing AUMFs, while others said new congressional authorization was required under the War Powers Resolution and Constitution. There is no definitive judicial ruling granting blanket authority to strike without a vote, so stating he "had the legal authority" as an uncontested fact is incorrect.

claim: Says Ted Strickland admits his record on jobs and taxes is "mixed and spotty."
rationale: I can find no reliable record of Ted Strickland himself saying his record on jobs and taxes was "mixed and spotty." That phrase appears to be a rhetorical characterization likely used by opponents or ad copy rather than an admission by Strickland; public statements and interviews from his tenure show him defending his economic record. Without verifiable primary-source quotes, the claim that he "admits" this is unsupported.

claim: Says 89 members of Congress "hold dual citizenship with Israel."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or authoritative list showing 89 U.S. members of Congress hold Israeli citizenship; similar viral claims have been debunked by fact-checkers. While some lawmakers have Jewish heritage, strong ties to Israel, or eligibility under Israel's Law of Return, actual dual Israeli citizenship among sitting members is not documented at that scale and would be atypical and newsworthy if true.

claim: Says Burisma admitted in a Ukrainian court to paying Joe Biden $900,000.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or Ukrainian court record showing Burisma admitted paying Joe Biden $900,000. Public reporting and multiple fact-checks have found no court admission or judgment that Burisma made payments to Joe Biden; allegations appear to stem from unverified claims and doctored or misinterpreted documents. While Hunter Biden was paid for a board position at Burisma, that is not the same as a court-admitted payment to Joe Biden.

claim: The employer mandate "affects only 5 percent of businesses in this country."
rationale: This claim is misleading. The ACA employer mandate applies to employers with 50 or more full‑time equivalent employees, and while that group is a small fraction of all firms (commonly estimated in the low single digits), the exact share varies by data source and year and those employers account for a large share of employment. Saying it “affects only 5 percent of businesses” ignores differences in how “businesses” are counted (firms vs establishments), aggregation rules, and other ways employers can be subject to the rule.

claim: "I, all the way back in January, warned (President Trump that) this pandemic was coming. I talked about what we needed to do."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific person warned President Trump in January and discussed needed actions; without identifying the speaker and providing corroborating evidence (emails, meeting records, contemporaneous public statements or White House logs) this cannot be verified. Public warnings about COVID-19 were made widely in late January and February by various health officials, but there is no general record that an unnamed individual definitively warned the president privately in January as claimed. Given the ambiguity and lack of documented proof, the claim is judged false as stated.

claim: Under the North American Free Trade Agreement, "we lost millions of jobs."
rationale: Most empirical studies do not support the blanket claim that NAFTA caused the loss of multiple millions of U.S. jobs. Research generally attributes a few hundred thousand U.S. manufacturing job losses to rising imports from Mexico under NAFTA (some estimates approach about 1 million when counting indirect effects), while much larger employment declines in manufacturing were driven by automation, productivity gains, and other factors; overall U.S. employment grew after NAFTA. Therefore saying "we lost millions of jobs" is an overstatement not supported by mainstream evidence.

claim: "New evidence ties COVID-19 creation to research funded by Fauci"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that SARS-CoV-2 was created by research funded by Dr. Anthony Fauci. While the NIH/NIAID provided grants to EcoHealth Alliance, which collaborated on coronavirus surveillance with the Wuhan Institute of Virology, U.S. intelligence assessments, NIH statements, and multiple independent fact-checks have found no proof that those grants produced or engineered the virus.

claim: Under Republican-backed state budget, the state education agency estimates expansion of Wisconsin’s school voucher program "could cost nearly $2 billion annually"
rationale: Wisconsin’s Department of Public Instruction produced a fiscal analysis tied to the Republican-backed budget showing that a broad expansion of the state voucher program could cost on the order of nearly $2 billion per year (commonly reported as roughly $1.8–$1.9 billion annually). Media accounts and budget documents cited that DPI estimate as the projected annual cost under full implementation and assumed participation rates.

claim: Wisconsin's Lincoln Hills youth prison has a "66 percent recidivism rate," while "states like Missouri, that have more of a regional model -- 8 percent."
rationale: The claim conflates incommensurate statistics. While some reports have shown Lincoln Hills cohorts with very high reoffending rates (around 60–70% over some follow-up periods), the “8 percent” figure for Missouri reflects a narrowly defined outcome from particular regional programs or short follow-up windows, not a statewide juvenile recidivism rate directly comparable to Lincoln Hills. Presenting them side-by-side without specifying the populations, time windows, or definitions is misleading.

claim: Says El Chapo testified in court that he paid off Nancy Pelosi to keep the U.S.-Mexico border open for drug cartels.
rationale: This claim is false. There is no record in court transcripts or credible news reporting from Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán’s 2019 trial that he testified he paid Nancy Pelosi, and El Chapo did not implicate Pelosi in court. The allegation appears to originate from social-media misinformation rather than any verified testimony or evidence.

claim: Says China and Singapore impose the death penalty on drug dealers.
rationale: Both China and Singapore have laws that authorize and have been used to impose the death penalty for serious drug offenses. China’s criminal code permits capital punishment for large-scale trafficking or production of narcotics, and Singapore has historically imposed the death penalty (previously mandatory) for trafficking above specified thresholds, though some discretionary reforms have narrowed automatic application.

claim: "Phoenix is already one of the kidnapping capitals of the world."
rationale: No reliable international crime statistics or authoritative rankings place Phoenix among the world’s top cities for kidnappings. Although Phoenix has seen increases in reported abductions recently, global kidnapping hotspots (e.g., regions affected by organized criminal groups in parts of Mexico, Nigeria, Venezuela and others) have much higher rates and more systematic kidnapping-for-ransom. The statement is vague and not supported by comparative data.

claim: "We bailed out" Johnson Controls when "we saved the auto industry" and "now they want to avoid paying taxes."
rationale: The claim mixes two assertions that don't both hold. Johnson Controls was not a direct recipient of the 2008–09 U.S. auto bailout, which primarily rescued automakers GM and Chrysler (suppliers generally benefited indirectly but were not the bailout's main targets). It is true the company later pursued corporate tax strategies—most notably a 2016 merger that involved Irish incorporation and drew criticism as a tax inversion—but that does not make the statement that “we bailed out Johnson Controls” accurate.

claim: "Iceland declares all religions are mental disorders."
rationale: This claim is false. Iceland's laws protect freedom of religion and the state does not classify religions as mental disorders; mental-health diagnoses are medical classifications (e.g., ICD/DSM) not government labels applied to faiths. There is no authoritative Icelandic statute or official policy declaring all religions to be mental disorders.

claim: The Republicans' alternative health care plan "will still let insurers raise premiums four times faster than wages."
rationale: The statement is unverified as a universal fact and is framed too imprecisely to be true as written. No authoritative analysis shows any single “Republicans' alternative” health plan would categorically allow insurers to raise premiums at exactly four times the rate of wages across the board; independent and CBO analyses of past GOP proposals projected higher premiums for some populations and under some scenarios but the ratio varies by plan, market, age cohort and timeframe. Because the claim lacks a specified plan, period, and data source, it cannot be confirmed.

claim: President Obama was "raised Muslim."
rationale: The claim is false. Barack Obama's father was Muslim and he spent part of his childhood in Muslim-majority Indonesia, but Obama has repeatedly said he was not raised in the Muslim faith; his mother was not Muslim and he later became a practicing Christian as an adult. Public biographies and his own memoirs describe a childhood without a single religious upbringing rather than being raised Muslim.

claim: "We are imprisoning or giving jail sentences to young people who are smoking marijuana."
rationale: The claim reads as a universal statement but sentencing and enforcement for youth marijuana use vary widely by jurisdiction and over time. In many places simple smoking by young people is handled with citations, fines, or diversion programs rather than jail, although some jurisdictions still criminalize possession and occasional custodial sentences for repeated or aggravated offenses can occur. Because the assertion implies a general, ongoing practice it is inaccurate without jurisdictional context.

claim: Since 2009, the Ohio Republican Party has made more contacts with voters — nearly 6.6 million — than any other GOP state organization in the nation.
rationale: I could not verify an authoritative source showing the Ohio Republican Party made nearly 6.6 million voter contacts since 2009 and more than any other GOP state party. State parties report contacts differently (calls, doors, mail, digital impressions), and there is no standardized, independently audited nationwide tally that supports the specific comparative claim. Given the lack of corroborating data and the plausible existence of rival claims from other large states, the statement is not verifiable as presented.

claim: Video shows Joe Biden saying "we can only re-elect Donald Trump."
rationale: There is no verified, unedited video showing Joe Biden saying the phrase “we can only re-elect Donald Trump.” Viral clips making that claim have been shown to be manipulated, taken out of context, or miscaptioned; multiple independent checks failed to find an original source in which Biden sincerely utters that line. The available evidence indicates the assertion is a misleading interpretation of edited footage rather than an authentic quote.

claim: "New Jersey taxpayers … will now face the highest tolls in the country."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim but lacks specification and is not supported by available comparisons: toll levels vary by facility (per-trip vs per-mile, peak vs off-peak) and several other states and specific crossings (notably New York-area bridges/tunnels, some California bridges, and other tolled facilities) have equal or higher charges. Even with recent New Jersey toll increases, it is incorrect to assert unambiguously that New Jersey motorists now face the highest tolls in the country without defining the metric.

claim: "750 days since Bill Nelson & the Democrats in the Senate passed a budget. How can this be justified?"
rationale: The statement is false as written. It claims a specific 750‑day interval since “Bill Nelson & the Democrats in the Senate passed a budget,” but Bill Nelson left the Senate in January 2019 and budget/resolution passage is a Congress‑level action with no verifiable record matching that precise claim. The assertion provides no date or source and conflates an individual senator with the collective congressional budget process.

claim: Norway decided "that (the coronavirus) should be treated like other respiratory diseases, such as the flu or cold, because… it is no more dangerous than those mentioned."
rationale: This claim misstates the reasoning and overgeneralizes Norway’s policy change. Norway did relax special COVID-19 rules and in some contexts reclassified its legal handling as less exceptional, but officials justified that shift by citing high vaccine and infection-derived immunity, lower pressure on hospitals, and new treatments — not a categorical statement that SARS‑CoV‑2 is inherently no more dangerous than the flu. Independent epidemiological evidence also shows COVID‑19 has caused higher mortality and risk of long‑term effects than typical seasonal influenza, so the quoted claim is misleading.

claim: "U.S. agricultural & food exports are expected to increase more than $2 billion annually under #USMCA"
rationale: There is no clear, authoritative consensus showing U.S. agricultural and food exports will rise by more than $2 billion per year as a direct and guaranteed result of USMCA. Administration fact sheets touted roughly $2 billion in potential gains for agriculture, but independent economic and USITC analyses estimated much smaller or highly uncertain effects; the figure is therefore an optimistic projection, not an established outcome. Because the number depends on modeling assumptions and timing, the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "People have actually broken down the transcripts for oral arguments and (Antonin Scalia) told more jokes and got more laughs than any of the other justices."
rationale: Multiple media accounts and academic observers who have parsed Supreme Court oral-argument transcripts and recordings have reported that Justice Antonin Scalia consistently generated more joking remarks and laughter than his colleagues. Analyses count annotated instances of “laughter” or catalogue humorous exchanges and typically place Scalia at the top in frequency.

claim: "Since 1999, firearm deaths in Ohio have risen 58 percent."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no end year and the percent change depends on which recent year is used; CDC mortality data for Ohio show fluctuations in firearm deaths over time and do not consistently indicate a 58% rise from 1999 to common recent endpoints. Without a specified end point and clear definition (deaths vs. rate, inclusion of suicides), the 58% figure is not supported as a factual, general statement.

claim: Says "72% of refugees admitted into U.S. (2/3 -2/11) during COURT BREAKDOWN are from 7 countries: SYRIA, IRAQ, SOMALIA, IRAN, SUDAN, LIBYA & YEMEN."
rationale: I could not find evidence that 72% of refugees admitted to the U.S. between Feb 3–Feb 11 (or during the unspecified “court breakdown”) came from those seven countries. Public refugee admission data from the State Department show admissions from a wider range of countries and no readily available report confirming that such a high share in that exact short interval came solely from Syria, Iraq, Somalia, Iran, Sudan, Libya and Yemen. The claim appears to conflate or misstate admissions data and uses an unclear timeframe/term.

claim: "I said two years ago that the Fannie and Freddie thing was a very serious problem and we had to work on it."
rationale: The claim asserts the speaker made a specific statement ‘two years ago’ about Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac being a very serious problem and needing work, but no speaker, date, or source is provided to verify that self-report. Without a concrete attribution and contemporaneous public record (speech, tweet, press release) I cannot confirm the quoted prior statement. Because verification requires specific context and evidence that is not present, the claim is treated as unverified and thus judged false for purposes of this check.

claim: "Pfizer and Moderna could share their design with dozens of other pharma companies who stand ready to produce their vaccines and end the pandemic."
rationale: The claim overstates practicality and immediacy. While Pfizer/BioNTech and Moderna could share sequence information, mRNA vaccines require complex, proprietary manufacturing processes, specialized equipment, raw materials, quality-control procedures and regulatory approvals that many firms do not have in place; meaningful scale-up requires detailed tech transfer and time. Even wide production alone would not instantaneously “end the pandemic,” which also depends on distribution, vaccine uptake, equity, and viral evolution.

claim: The U.S. Justice Department "conservatively estimated that guns are used 1.5 million times per year to save lives."
rationale: The U.S. Justice Department did not produce an official, 'conservative' estimate that guns are used 1.5 million times per year to save lives. That number is commonly misattributed to the DOJ but originates from academic survey-based estimates (notably work by Gary Kleck and colleagues) and other extrapolations rather than a Department of Justice estimate.

claim: "We're the only system of federalism in the world."
rationale: The claim is false because many other countries operate under federal systems besides the United States. Examples include Canada, Germany, Australia, India, Brazil, Mexico, Switzerland and several others that divide sovereignty between central and regional governments. The U.S. is one of several federations rather than the only one.

claim: Says Austin trains are "full" at rush hour and "packed" for special events.
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While Austin's commuter rail and light-rail/bus services can see higher loads during major events and some peak periods, transit ridership in Austin is generally modest and trains are not routinely “full” at rush hour across the system. Special events can produce crowded trains, but describing normal rush-hour service as consistently full is not supported by typical ridership data and reports.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker is making voting more difficult by closing Department of Motor Vehicles offices where "low-income voters" live.
rationale: Under Governor Scott Walker’s administration Wisconsin restructured the DMV and closed or reduced hours at a number of branch offices, including in urban areas such as parts of Milwaukee. Because Wisconsin requires a state photo ID to vote, critics and analysts concluded those closures made it harder for low-income and urban residents to obtain IDs and thus could impede voting access; the administration framed the changes as cost-saving and efficiency measures.

claim: "In North Carolina, they used stimulus money to hire one new state worker. His job, apply for more stimulus funds from the taxpayers by the way of the federal government."
rationale: The claim is vague and presents an unsupported, sensational assertion that North Carolina used stimulus funds to hire a single new state worker whose sole job was to apply for more federal stimulus money. While governments sometimes fund grant‑coordinator or grant‑writer positions with federal or one‑time funds, there is no clear, corroborated evidence that North Carolina created exactly one such position funded by stimulus money with the exclusive purpose described. The statement likely conflates or exaggerates routine grant‑administration staffing with a misleading narrative of circular spending.

claim: "President Biden says he wants to ban handguns."
rationale: This is false. President Biden has repeatedly called for bans on 'assault weapons' and for stricter gun regulations (background checks, magazine limits, age restrictions) but there is no reliable record of him advocating a wholesale ban on handguns. The claim appears to conflate assault-weapon proposals with a general handgun ban.

claim: "If Joe Manchin had his way, Judge Gorsuch never would have been able to get a vote."
rationale: This is false. Senator Joe Manchin did not block Judge Neil Gorsuch from receiving a floor vote; Manchin was one of three Democrats who voted to confirm Gorsuch and supported allowing a confirmation vote. The Senate Republican leadership changed filibuster rules (the “nuclear option”) in 2017 to permit a simple-majority confirmation, but Manchin himself did not prevent Gorsuch from getting a vote.

claim: Obamacare has led to fewer health insurance options for millions of Americans.
rationale: Broadly true: after the ACA’s marketplaces launched, many counties experienced insurer exits and consolidation that left consumers with fewer carrier choices in the individual (marketplace) insurance market, affecting millions of enrollees. However, impacts varied by state, year, and market segment — employer-sponsored coverage was largely unaffected and some consumers gained new options through the marketplaces.

claim: "Suntrust Bank cancels account because company sells guns."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that SunTrust Bank has a general practice of cancelling business accounts solely because a company sells firearms. Banks may close merchant or business accounts for specific legal, compliance, or risk-related reasons (including sale of illegal weapons or products violating their policies), so isolated closures could occur, but the blanket claim is unsupported without a specific incident and documentation.

claim: "This election actually was not unusually close."
rationale: The statement is too vague to be supported: it does not identify which election or what metric (popular vote margin, electoral college, seat counts) is being judged. Historical election closeness varies by measure and case—some elections are clearly unusually close by standard metrics while others are not—so a blanket assertion without context is unsupported. Therefore I judge the claim false as stated.

claim: Quotes actor Will Smith as saying: "I’m not afraid to say that Trump and his supporters are ba…"
rationale: I could not verify a reliable source showing Will Smith publicly saying the quoted phrase, and the quote appears truncated and characteristic of viral misattribution. High-profile actors’ political statements are typically reported widely; no reputable records or major media coverage confirm he said that. Without a clear source or context the claim is not supported.

claim: Says Andrew Gillum is running "from the FBI."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Andrew Gillum is literally fleeing or evading the FBI. Although he has been the subject of past investigations and scrutiny, public records and reputable reporting do not support a claim that he is "running from the FBI."

claim: The Chamber of Commerce says new carbon regulations will kill "244,000 jobs a year" and cost average families "$1,200 a year."
rationale: I could not verify a direct Chamber of Commerce statement that literally said new carbon regulations will kill “244,000 jobs a year” and cost average families “$1,200 a year.” The U.S. Chamber and allied groups have warned of large job impacts and higher household costs and have cited third‑party studies with varying estimates, but the precise quoted figures and wording are not attributable to a single clear Chamber release and appear to conflate or round different analyses. Thus the exact claim as presented is not supported by available public records.

claim: "Alabama’s Crimson Tide was disqualified from national championship."
rationale: The statement is false as stated: the Alabama Crimson Tide (particularly the football program) has not been broadly “disqualified from national championship.” Alabama has competed in and won multiple recognized national championships in recent decades (e.g., 2009, 2011, 2012, 2015, 2017, 2020) and there is no widely reported, program-wide disqualification removing their ability to win a national title. If the claim refers to a specific sport, season, or administrative ruling it needs that context to evaluate properly.

claim: Says the Obama administration plans to ban all weapons for U.S. citizens through international treaties.
rationale: This is false. The Obama administration did support an international Arms Trade Treaty to regulate international transfers of conventional weapons, but it did not propose or have a plan to ban all weapons owned by U.S. citizens via treaty. Treaties that would affect domestic law require congressional action (Senate ratification and implementing legislation), and U.S. negotiators explicitly stated the ATT was not intended to govern lawful domestic civilian possession.

claim: "When Nancy Nusbaum was Brown County executive, spending went up nearly 50 percent."
rationale: I find no basis for the claim that Brown County spending rose nearly 50% during Nancy Nusbaum’s time as county executive (she served roughly 2007–2011). County operating budgets rarely jump by that magnitude over a single four-year term absent large one-time capital projects or major structural changes, and such an unusually large increase would have been widely documented. Given typical year-to-year budget changes are much smaller, the specific 50% figure is implausible without additional context or evidence.

claim: Text from someone "connected" to Raleigh police: "antifa may be heading into the wealthy neighborhoods tonight to take what should be theirs."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that an official or reliably connected Raleigh Police source sent a message warning that 'antifa may be heading into the wealthy neighborhoods tonight to take what should be theirs.' Similar warnings circulated on social media during past protests but were not corroborated by Raleigh Police or reputable news outlets, making the specific attribution and claim unverified and likely false.

claim: Says the CEO of Camping World told Trump supporters "Frankly, don’t shop at my business."
rationale: There is no reliable public record or major news reporting that the CEO of Camping World (Marcus Lemonis) explicitly said the quoted line “Frankly, don’t shop at my business.” While Lemonis has made public political comments and criticized certain views, the exact phrase appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase not supported by documented quotes.

claim: Says Texas voters are being asked to act this November on a proposed constitutional amendment affecting property taxes.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and cannot be confirmed as stated because it provides no year or specific amendment. Texas constitutional amendments must be proposed by the state legislature and then placed on a statewide ballot, and timing depends on the legislative calendar; such amendments more commonly appear on even‑year general election ballots. Without a specific referenced amendment and year, the assertion that "Texas voters are being asked to act this November" is not verifiable and is likely incorrect as presented.

claim: The United States paid for a 274-mile wall between Jordan and Syria, "approved by the Dems in the house and senate," in order "to keep ISIS out."
rationale: This claim conflates and exaggerates facts. Jordan built an extensive barrier along its border with Syria and the U.S. has provided broad military and humanitarian assistance to Jordan, but there is no clear evidence the United States directly paid for a specific 274‑mile wall as a discrete project 'approved by the Dems in the house and senate' solely to keep ISIS out. U.S. aid for Jordanian border/security needs was provided as part of wider, bipartisan foreign assistance packages and refugee/security programs, not a single, Democratic‑only approved payment for a 274‑mile wall.

claim: Says the U.S. Department of Justice has "seen in the past" that police department "consent decrees don’t work, that there’s very little change, that oftentimes immediately after a consent decree goes into effect, crime actually goes up."
rationale: This claim overstates and misattributes a generalized finding to the U.S. Department of Justice. The DOJ’s Civil Rights Division has long used consent decrees to reform police practices and has published accounts of institutional improvements under them; while some individual DOJ officials and political critics have argued consent decrees can hinder policing or coincided with crime changes, the Department has not endorsed a blanket conclusion that consent decrees “don’t work” or that crime routinely rises immediately after they take effect. Empirical literature shows mixed results and no consistent, universal immediate crime spike attributable to consent decrees.

claim: Says "47 additional counties used the same software that caused a ‘glitch’ in Antrim County (that switched 6,000 votes from Trump to Biden in that county)" and votes in the state are "potentially fraudulent."
rationale: The claim is false. Although roughly 47 Michigan counties used voting equipment from the same vendor as Antrim, the Antrim misreporting was found to be a configuration/human error that was corrected and audited, not a software ‘glitch’ that flipped 6,000 votes from Trump to Biden. Multiple state and federal reviews (and recounts/audits) found no evidence of systemic or statewide vote switching or fraud tied to that incident.

claim: Sarah Palin was repeating "Abraham Lincoln's words" in discussing the war in Iraq.
rationale: There is no well-documented instance showing Sarah Palin explicitly repeating Abraham Lincoln’s words when discussing the Iraq war. Major public transcripts and contemporaneous fact-checking of her speeches do not record a clear Lincoln quotation used by Palin on that topic, so the claim is unsubstantiated without a specific citation. If a specific speech and quote were provided it could be checked more precisely.

claim: After merging with Tim Hortons of Canada, Burger King is "not moving. … Our headquarters will remain in Miami" and "(we) will continue to pay all of our federal, state and local U.S. taxes."
rationale: After the 2014 merger announcement with Tim Hortons the company publicly stated (via its CEO and press releases) that Burger King operations would remain based in Miami and that it would continue to pay U.S. federal, state and local taxes. Those assurances were widely reported at the time. However, the statements were about the company’s intent and did not eliminate the legal/technical tax consequences of creating a Canadian parent company.

claim: "Human meat found in McDonald’s meat factory"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that human meat was found in a McDonald’s meat factory; such a claim has circulated as an urban legend/hoax. Major food safety authorities, news organizations, and McDonald’s supply-chain audits would have documented and investigated any such event, but nothing substantiates it. The claim aligns with recurring sensational false rumors about fast-food ingredients rather than verified incidents.

claim: "Even today part of Romney’s fortune is invested in China."
rationale: Romney’s wealth has been held in diversified funds and private-equity vehicles that have included holdings with exposure to China, and public disclosures during his political campaigns showed investments with China-linked assets. Because many mutual funds and multinational companies in his portfolios operate or are listed in China, it is accurate to say at least some of his fortune has been invested in China or has China exposure.

claim: "99 percent of all new income today (is) going to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The claim as stated is an overbroad and inaccurate summary of income-share research. Studies using IRS data (e.g., Piketty and Saez) show that in specific post-recession years a very large share of income gains went to the top 1% (commonly cited figure ~95% of gains from 2009–2012), but not a general, ongoing 99% of all new income. Therefore the blanket statement that 99% of all new income today goes to the top 1% is misleading and unsupported.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott is "spending a quarter of a million of our tax dollars to robocall people."
rationale: I could not verify a specific, documented instance in which Governor Rick Scott authorized or spent exactly $250,000 of public funds to place robocalls. Claims like this frequently conflate campaign spending (private funds) with government communications or misstate the amount and purpose of any state-contracted outreach. Without a clear time, agency, contract, or invoice, the precise allegation is unproven.

claim: "Due to the recent downturn in steel production, more than 13,600 Americans have been laid off and the steel industry is facing billions in losses."
rationale: I could not find corroborating evidence that a single recent downturn in U.S. steel production resulted in more than 13,600 American layoffs; public announcements from major U.S. steel producers and government employment data for the sector do not support a sudden, aggregate layoff figure that large. While some firms have announced plant idlings, temporary layoffs, or reduced shifts and the industry has had financial headwinds at times, those actions reported publicly are far smaller and more fragmented than the claim implies.

claim: Says the government has "gotten the TARP money back plus a profit."
rationale: By the mid-2010s the U.S. Treasury reported that TARP repayments, sales proceeds and interest exceeded the amounts originally disbursed, yielding a modest net positive return overall. However this outcome depends on the accounting method and timing — some individual TARP programs (notably certain housing efforts) lost money and independent estimates (e.g., CBO) produce different net-cost figures.

claim: "One of the most troubling aspects of the Rubio-Schumer Gang of Eight bill was that it gave President Obama blanket authority to admit refugees, including Syrian refugees, without mandating any background checks whatsoever."
rationale: The claim is false. The Gang of Eight (S.744) immigration bill did not give President Obama blanket authority to admit refugees nor eliminate background checks; U.S. refugee admissions are governed by separate refugee law and interagency security vetting (State, DHS, FBI) and the bill did not override those statutory screening requirements. The statement likely conflates other executive authorities (like limited parole) or later political rhetoric with the actual text of the immigration reform bill.

claim: "The EPA has tried to define a puddle or a drainage ditch on your farm to be navigable waters and thus subject to massive environmental regulations."
rationale: Federal agencies (the EPA and Army Corps) have in multiple rules and enforcement actions sought to treat small features—such as certain ditches, ephemeral streams, and isolated wet areas—as “waters of the United States” subject to Clean Water Act permitting. The 2015 Clean Water Rule explicitly reached some ditches and intermittent waters, and litigation and agency guidance have repeatedly debated including very small or on‑farm features, though scope has changed with subsequent rules and court decisions.

claim: "The state's unemployment rate is fifth-highest in the country, a full point above the nationwide rate and higher than all of our...neighboring states."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it does not name which state or the time period; state unemployment rankings and the national rate change monthly. Without a specific state and date and checking official BLS/state labor data, one cannot confirm that the state's rate was exactly fifth-highest, one full point above the national rate, and higher than all neighboring states. Therefore the unsupported general claim is judged false given the missing specifics.

claim: "You didn't see Republicans when we had control of the Senate try to rig the game."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. When Republicans controlled the Senate they used several procedural maneuvers that critics described as rigging the rules—for example, Majority Leader Mitch McConnell refused to hold a 2016 hearing for Merrick Garland and Republicans changed Senate rules in 2017 to eliminate the filibuster for Supreme Court nominations and then used majority procedures to confirm nominees. These actions show Republicans did use tactics to shape outcomes while in control of the Senate.

claim: Says Mitt Romney’s investments created zero jobs.
rationale: False. Mitt Romney co‑founded Bain Capital and its investments over decades produced both job growth at some portfolio companies and job losses at others; public records and reporting show many firms expanded and hired under Bain’s ownership.
