rationale: The statement as presented is unverified — there is no widely corroborated public source that definitively states the Georgia Dome would need “up to $350 million” in work over the next five to seven years. Reports and estimates about the Dome’s condition and renovation needs varied during stadium debates, so without a specific source or date this precise figure and timeframe cannot be confirmed.

claim: Annual precipitation "has increased in Rhode Island by over 12 inches in the last century."
rationale: Regional and state climate analyses (NOAA/NCEI, regional Northeast and Rhode Island assessments) show that annual precipitation in Rhode Island has increased over the 20th century, but the magnitude reported is substantially less than 12 inches. Typical published estimates for the Northeast/Rhode Island show increases on the order of a few inches up to around 6–10 inches depending on start/end years and dataset, not an increase exceeding 12 inches.

claim: North Korea’s missiles are "not going to have a capability to reach the United States anytime real soon."
rationale: This claim is false because North Korea has already tested intercontinental-range missiles whose flight profiles indicate ranges sufficient to reach parts or all of the continental United States (notably 2017 Hwasong-14 and Hwasong-15 tests, and later large ICBM tests). U.S. and allied intelligence assessments have judged North Korea can produce ICBMs with the range to reach the U.S., though questions remain about warhead miniaturization and reliable reentry/operational readiness. Thus it is incorrect to say they are not going to have that capability "anytime real soon."

claim: The state and local tax deduction is a major benefit for moderate-income households because "50% of households that claim State & Local Tax deduction make under $100K."
rationale: This claim is incorrect as stated. Analyses by the IRS and tax-policy researchers show SALT deductions and their dollar benefits are concentrated among higher-income taxpayers, and fewer than half of SALT claimants have AGI under $100,000 (especially after the $10,000 SALT cap enacted in 2018). The statement reverses the observed distribution of claimants/benefits.

claim: Says John Cornyn dodged the draft during the Vietnam War.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that John Cornyn actively dodged the Vietnam-era draft. Cornyn, born in 1952, did not serve in the military but benefited from the common student/college deferments and the selective-service lottery system; accusations of intentional draft evasion have not been substantiated by documentary proof.

claim: Quotes Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as saying "I’m speaking with myself, number one, because I have a very good brain and I’ve said lots of things."
rationale: The line "I’m speaking with myself, number one, because I have a very good brain and I’ve said lots of things" is not from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez; it is a well-documented remark made by Donald Trump in public interviews. The claim misattributes Trump's quote to Ocasio-Cortez, so the assertion is false.

claim: "As soon as Chris Christie was governor, he gave tax cuts to millionaires."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Chris Christie campaigned against high-income tax increases and proposed rolling back top rates, but he did not immediately enact a tax cut for millionaires upon taking office in January 2010 — his early years featured budget fights, spending cuts, and proposals that required legislative approval rather than an immediate enacted tax cut for wealthy taxpayers. Any changes affecting top rates were the result of later proposals or legislative negotiations, not an instant giveaway when he became governor.

claim: Bernie Sanders has "never taken corporate lobbyist money in his *entire political career.*"
rationale: Bernie Sanders has for years publicly pledged not to take corporate PAC or lobbyist money in his presidential campaigns, but over his multi‑decade political career he accepted contributions from corporate PACs, corporate executives and donors with lobbying ties earlier in his time in Congress and local office. The absolute claim that he 'never' took corporate lobbyist money for his entire career is contradicted by historical campaign‑finance records showing such contributions before his recent refusal pledge.

claim: Says "85 percent (of immigrants) don’t show up for a scheduled court hearing or call to schedule a court hearing."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Official immigration-court and DHS/EOIR data and independent analyses show non‑appearance (and in‑absentia) rates well below 85% for respondents overall; although rates vary by year, location, and case type, they are not anywhere near 85%. Repeated fact‑checks of similar claims have concluded the 85% figure is a substantial overestimate and lacks credible supporting data.

claim: "Bill Nelson actually voted in favor of higher taxes 272 times."
rationale: The 272 number appears to come from advocacy-group tallies that count a wide range of votes (including procedural votes, amendments, or measures not clearly raising taxes) rather than an authoritative count of distinct votes to increase taxes. Independent fact-checkers have found such claims misleading and there is no official congressional record showing Senator Bill Nelson 'voted in favor of higher taxes 272 times' as an unambiguous fact.

claim: "Under President Obama, U.S. security funding for Israel is at an all-time high."
rationale: The Obama administration negotiated and announced in 2016 a memorandum of understanding committing $38 billion in U.S. military assistance to Israel over 10 years, the largest security assistance package the U.S. has ever pledged to any country. While most of the cash-flow from that agreement was scheduled to begin after Obama left office, the record-level commitment was made under his presidency.

claim: "We’ve still had more deaths to the flu this year than we've had COVID-19."
rationale: This claim is not supported as stated because, based on public health reporting since 2020, COVID-19 has produced substantially more deaths than a typical seasonal flu year in most jurisdictions. Without a clear timeframe or geographic scope the statement is misleading; in the U.S. and globally COVID-19 death tolls since 2020 far exceed annual influenza deaths.

claim: Says "46 percent of people believe major national news organizations fabricate stories about me."
rationale: The claim gives a precise percentage but provides no source, date, population, or named subject ('me'), and I am not aware of a reputable poll that reports exactly 46% of people saying major national news organizations 'fabricate stories about me.' While surveys do show significant distrust in the national media, the specific 46% figure and personalized wording cannot be verified from available public polling. Without a named poll and defined population this specific assertion is unsupported.

claim: "The United States is the No. 1 country in the world for energy resources. … We are the king daddy dogs when it comes to energy."
rationale: The statement is misleading. The U.S. is currently a top producer of oil, natural gas, and total primary energy, but it does not have the largest proven oil or gas reserves (countries like Venezuela, Saudi Arabia and Russia have larger reserves) nor does it unambiguously lead in renewable installed capacity (China is ahead). Calling the U.S. the singular "No. 1 country for energy resources" ignores important distinctions between production, reserves, and types of energy.

claim: Says Rep. Kyrsten Sinema supported a bill that is "essentially encouraging child trafficking."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Kyrsten Sinema voted for or sponsored any bill that ‘essentially encourages child trafficking.’ The claim appears to be rhetorical or hyperbolic political attack language rather than a documented description of legislative text or votes; Sinema’s legislative record does not include support for laws that legalize or promote trafficking of children.

claim: "Same little boy died of COVID-19 in three different countries. Still don’t believe the media is #fakenews?"
rationale: The claim that the same little boy died of COVID-19 in three different countries is false. Individuals cannot die multiple times in different places; such assertions typically arise from reuse or miscaptioning of the same photograph across outlets. Fact-checkers have repeatedly found that images or stories are sometimes recycled or misattributed, not that one child actually died in multiple countries.

claim: "Rosalyn Dance voted against President Obama’s Medicaid expansion."
rationale: This is false. Rosalyn Dance, a Democratic member of the Virginia legislature, supported the Affordable Care Act Medicaid expansion when the General Assembly approved expansion in 2018 (effective 2019); the bill passed with broad Democratic support and she was not recorded as voting against expansion. The claim appears to conflate her with another vote or actor.

claim: Says recent studies indicate that nationally, only 8 percent of white voting-age citizens but 25 percent of African-American voting-age citizens lack government-issued photo IDs.
rationale: The claim gives precise national rates (8% of white voting-age citizens and 25% of African‑American voting‑age citizens lacking government photo ID) but cites no source. While several studies and reports have documented a racial gap in possession of photo IDs, estimates vary substantially by data source, year, and whether the population is citizens, registered voters, or voting‑age adults—no single, recent national study uniformly reports these exact figures. Therefore the statement as presented is misleading without a specific citation and appears unsupported as a definitive national fact.

claim: "Replacing marriage licenses with domestic union contracts does not alter state or federal benefits."
rationale: This is false as a general claim. Federal benefits (tax filing status, Social Security spousal/survivor benefits, immigration sponsorship, veterans' benefits, etc.) are tied to being legally married under federal law or a state-recognized marriage; if a state replaces marriage licenses with a different legal instrument that is not treated as a marriage by federal statutes or agencies, federal benefits can change. State benefits likewise depend on how state law defines and treats the new domestic-union contracts, so outcomes vary and are not guaranteed to be unchanged.

claim: "In my attorney general's office, we've cut the budget 18 percent."
rationale: The statement gives no jurisdiction, officeholder, or time period, so it cannot be independently verified. Government budgets and reported cuts vary by state/office and fiscal year; without specific budget documents or a named attorney general the claim is unsupported and therefore judged false in this context.

claim: "Switzerland (where the government) issues every household a gun . . . has the lowest gun related crime rate of any civilized country in the world!!!"
rationale: The claim is inaccurate in two ways: Switzerland does not ‘issue every household a gun’—it has mandatory military service for men and historically allowed many conscripts to keep service rifles at home, but that is not equivalent to issuing a gun to every household and rules vary. While Switzerland has relatively low gun-homicide rates compared with many countries, several countries (for example Japan, Singapore and others) have equal or lower gun-related homicide rates, so it is incorrect to say Switzerland has the lowest gun-related crime rate of any ‘civilized’ country.

claim: "My plan offers three times as much tax relief to the middle class as Senator McCain's."
rationale: The statement is unverified and likely misleading because it omits which "plan" is meant, the relevant time period, and how "middle class" is defined; comparisons of tax relief require precise, comparable numeric estimates. Without the specific legislative texts or authoritative distributional analyses for both plans, the claim that one plan offers exactly three times as much relief as Senator McCain's cannot be supported.

claim: "We have more coal reserves in the United States than they have oil reserves in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: U.S. proved recoverable coal reserves are on the order of ~250 billion short tons, while Saudi Arabia's proven crude oil reserves are roughly 260–270 billion barrels. Converting coal to barrels-of-oil-equivalent (about 1 short ton coal ≈ 3.5–4 barrels of oil) yields a much larger energy quantity in U.S. coal than in Saudi oil, so the claim is correct in energy-equivalent terms. The conclusion depends on using energy-equivalent comparison rather than raw mass/volume units or different reserve definitions.

claim: Josh Mandel doctored an image in a campaign ad but "forgot to Photoshop the hands that clearly show he put his face on the body of a Black soldier."
rationale: I cannot find credible contemporary reporting or vetted fact-checks showing Josh Mandel doctored a campaign image by pasting his face onto the body of a Black soldier while leaving the hands intact. Major fact‑checking outlets and news coverage do not document such a confirmed incident, and the claim appears to be a specific allegation without corroborating evidence. Given the lack of verifiable sources, the assertion is judged false pending reliable documentation.

claim: Says photos show the Trump-Ukraine whistleblower with Chuck Schumer, Elizabeth Warren, Nancy Pelosi and Hillary Clinton.
rationale: The claim is false: the identity of the 2019 Trump–Ukraine whistleblower was legally protected and not publicly verified, and multiple independent fact-checks found that the photos circulated on social media were misattributed or showed other people at unrelated events, with no credible evidence linking them to the whistleblower. Thus the photos do not reliably show the whistleblower with Schumer, Warren, Pelosi, or Clinton.

claim: A recent on-air protest can’t be real because "there are no live on air television broadcasts in Russia. None. Ever."
rationale: The claim is false — Russian television does include live on-air broadcasts. Major Russian channels and regional stations routinely transmit live news bulletins, breaking-event coverage, talk shows and live special events. While state editorial control can limit or delay live coverage of protests, that does not mean live broadcasts do not exist at all.

claim: House Republican plan would increase costs for Oregon seniors by $6,000 with health care vouchers instead of Medicare
rationale: The claim presents a precise statewide dollar increase without specifying which House Republican plan or timeframe is meant. Analyses of various Republican Medicare-replacement or premium-support proposals (by the CBO and independent groups) show outcomes vary by proposal and state; some scenarios project seniors could face higher costs over time, but there is no universally corroborated figure of a $6,000 increase for Oregon seniors tied to a specific House plan. Without a cited plan and period, the statement is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: Says Dan Feehan "would vote with Pelosi for open borders and amnesty, putting Minnesota families at risk."
rationale: The statement is a partisan characterization that combines speculation about future votes with charged labels (“open borders” and “amnesty”). Public records and typical Democratic positions show support for comprehensive immigration reform, not an unconditional open-borders policy, and there is no clear evidence Feehan has pledged to vote for an ‘open borders’ or blanket amnesty bill with Pelosi. Thus the claim overstates and mischaracterizes his likely positions.

claim: "Eight in 10 people this year can find plans for $75 a month or less."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it lacks crucial context (which population, which marketplace and what year) and is not universally true. Whether 80% of people can find plans at $75/month depends on income, eligibility for premium tax credits, and local premiums; those factors vary widely so the blanket claim is unsupported. Without specifying the eligible subgroup (for example, people eligible for ACA subsidies in specific counties), the assertion overstates what can be proven.

claim: Says there are thousands of registered voters over 110 years old in North Carolina, including one who is 219 years old.
rationale: The claim is not credible: no verified human has lived to 219 (the maximum documented human lifespan is 122), so a registered voter aged 219 is impossible. Having "thousands" of registered voters over 110 is also inconsistent with demographic reality and verified longevity limits; such assertions almost always arise from database errors, misread birth-year fields, or outdated/deceased entries on voter rolls. Thus the specific numbers alleged are false.

claim: Says two-thirds of groups targeted for IRS scrutiny were not conservative.
rationale: Official reviews and contemporaneous reporting found that a large share of the applications singled out by the IRS keyword searches were Tea Party or other conservative groups. The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) and subsequent analyses show a plurality/majority of flagged cases were conservative, so the specific claim that two‑thirds were not conservative is not supported by the available investigations.

claim: Says "Snoop Dogg arrested for conspiracy after talking about his ‘murder Trump’ video."
rationale: There are no credible reports that Snoop Dogg was arrested on conspiracy charges over a video depicting a clown resembling Donald Trump. He did face public criticism for a controversial music/video depiction, but no arrest or conspiracy indictment was reported by major news outlets or law enforcement.

claim: The Senate GOP plan does not raise taxes for Americans earning less than $70,000.
rationale: The statement is false as an absolute claim. Multiple Senate Republican tax proposals that made similar promises were analyzed by independent nonpartisan groups and found to result in tax increases for some households earning under $70,000 once changes to deductions, credits, state-and-local tax caps, and sunset provisions were accounted for. Because the claim names no specific bill or time frame, it cannot be verified and is contradicted by past analytic outcomes.

claim: "Space X’s Starlink internet constellation has angered Russia as it was reported that the Starlink satellite constellation was used to guide the fire" on the Russian ship Moskva.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that SpaceX’s Starlink satellites were used to guide the strike or 'fire' on the Russian cruiser Moskva. Public reporting and expert analysis attributed the damage to Ukrainian Neptune anti-ship missiles (which use their own guidance), and Elon Musk/SpaceX and U.S. officials denied Starlink was used for missile guidance. While Russia publicly objected to Starlink service to Ukraine, the specific claim that Starlink guided the Moskva is unverified and unsupported.

claim: "Here in Florida, despite 14 school shootings in eight years, we still have some of the weakest gun laws in the nation."
rationale: The claim mixes an unverified numeric tally with a subjective policy ranking. The statement that Florida had “14 school shootings in eight years” is ambiguous without a specified timeframe or definition of “school shooting” (counts vary widely). Also, Florida enacted significant gun-law changes after the 2018 Parkland shooting (e.g., raising the age for some gun purchases, waiting periods, and other measures) and most national policy indices do not consistently place Florida among the very weakest states, so the broad assertion that it still has “some of the weakest gun laws in the nation” is misleading.

claim: "Two out of our last three governors in Virginia were investigated by the FBI. One went to jail and one is running for office again in this election."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate. While former Gov. Bob McDonnell faced a federal corruption prosecution, his convictions were later vacated by the U.S. Supreme Court and he did not end up serving time in prison; Ralph Northam was not the subject of an FBI probe; Terry McAuliffe has been the subject of media scrutiny but was not federally charged. Thus it is incorrect to say two of the last three were investigated by the FBI with one jailed and one currently running in the referenced election.

claim: Australia is microchipping its public.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Australian government is implanting microchips in the general public or running a compulsory national microchipping program. Reports that mention implants refer to voluntary RFID/NFC implants by individuals or private entities, pet microchipping requirements, or misinformation, not a government-wide mandatory program.

claim: "Given the results of the primary, the vote of one New Hampshire superdelegate is equal to the votes of about 10,000 grassroots activists."
rationale: The statement is misleading because the voting-weight equivalence of one New Hampshire superdelegate depends on the specific year, turnout, and how you count "grassroots activists." Superdelegates each cast one convention vote, but the number of primary voters per superdelegate is not a fixed ~10,000 — it changes with total votes cast and how many superdelegates exist. Without specifying the election and calculation method, the numeric claim is unsupported.

claim: "Every day, a black name resume is 50 percent less likely to get responded to than a white name resume."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. Field experiments (e.g., Bertrand & Mullainathan 2004) found that resumes with Black-sounding names received roughly 50% fewer callbacks in specific U.S. cities and time periods, but later studies and replications show the effect varies by location, occupation, methodology and time—so it is not true that every day a Black‑named resume is 50% less likely to get a response everywhere.

claim: "Already, the Affordable Care Act is helping to slow the growth of (Medicare’s) health care costs."
rationale: Multiple authoritative analyses (CBO, CMS actuary, Medicare Trustees) concluded that the ACA included provisions that reduce Medicare spending growth — for example lower updates to provider payments, reductions in Medicare Advantage overpayments, and penalties/value-based programs — and projected net reductions in Medicare outlays. Empirical evidence shows per‑beneficiary Medicare spending growth slowed in the early 2010s consistent with those measures, though some of the slowdown also reflected broader economic and health‑care trends.

claim: When the United States "first created the federal income tax, frankly, nobody below a million dollars a year paid anything."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. When the federal income tax was first established under the 16th Amendment in 1913, there was a 1% normal tax on net income above a few thousand dollars (about $3,000 for individuals) and a graduated surtax beginning at much lower levels (around $20,000), so many people with far less than $1 million paid federal income tax. Earlier Civil War–era income taxes also applied to far lower income thresholds.

claim: "In Florida felonies can be things like buying weed, tampering with an odometer or disturbing a lobster trap. So basically spring break."
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes. Tampering with an odometer and certain interference with lobster traps can be third‑degree felonies under Florida law, but buying weed is not categorically a felony — possession or purchase can be a misdemeanor for small amounts and becomes a felony only at higher quantities or when sale/trafficking is involved. The "so basically spring break" remark is a rhetorical exaggeration not supported by the nuances of the statutes.

claim: "In 2011, texting surpassed alcohol as the leading contributing factor in teen driving deaths."
rationale: Official crash data and safety analyses from the early 2010s indicate that distracted driving (a category that can include texting) rose as a leading factor in teen driver fatalities, but there is not reliable evidence that texting alone overtook alcohol as the top contributing factor in 2011. Police crash reports typically underreport cellphone use and media accounts frequently conflated 'texting' with the broader 'distracted driving' category, so the specific claim about texting surpassing alcohol in 2011 is not supported.

claim: Says series of 11 photos are "from the 1918 flu pandemic."
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to confirm that a particular series of 11 photos are from the 1918 influenza pandemic. Many images circulated online are misattributed to 1918, and authenticating historical photographs requires provenance, original captions, or metadata. Without that verification the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "When Abraham Lincoln made the Gettysburg Address speech, the great speech, do you know he was ridiculed? He was ridiculed."
rationale: Contemporary reaction to the Gettysburg Address was mixed and included ridicule: several newspapers and some attendees criticized Lincoln’s brief, plain remarks as inadequate or undignified compared with Edward Everett’s lengthy oration. While many later historians and some contemporaries praised the speech, it is accurate to say he was ridiculed by parts of the press and public at the time.

claim: Claims that Obama said, "For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away."
rationale: There is no reliable record or credible news/fact-check reporting that President Obama ever said the line "For those who oppose our policies, you should just shut up and go away." The phrasing is inconsistent with his public rhetoric and appears to be a fabricated or misattributed quote rather than a documented statement he made.

claim: Say Portland Public Schools' central administration makes up less than 4 percent of the staff.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim that Portland Public Schools' central administration comprises under 4% of staff from authoritative public data. District staffing categorizations and counts are reported variably (by year, job categories, and FTE vs. headcount), so the precise percentage is uncertain and the unsupported blanket statement is not demonstrably true. Without a cited source, the claim should not be accepted as fact.

claim: "Workers have begun removing spires of Cinderella Castle at Magic Kingdom ahead of Hurricane Dorian."
rationale: Contemporary news and eyewitness photos from early September 2019 show Disney cast members removing some of the decorative spires/pinnacles from Cinderella Castle at Magic Kingdom as part of storm preparations for Hurricane Dorian. The castle's small ornamental spires are known to be non-structural and are routinely removed or secured ahead of severe weather, which matches multiple independent reports and images from the park.

claim: Says the United States is "the Saudi Arabia of coal."
rationale: Calling the United States “the Saudi Arabia of coal” is inaccurate. While the U.S. has very large coal reserves and has been a major producer historically, it is not the dominant global producer or exporter and does not exercise the kind of market price-setting influence that Saudi Arabia has in oil markets.

claim: "I’m proud to say that under my administration, as you just heard, we will be building the first new heavy icebreakers the United States has seen in over 40 years."
rationale: The United States last built heavy polar icebreakers (the Polar-class ships like Polar Star and Polar Sea) in the 1970s, so commissioning new heavy icebreakers now would indeed be the first in over 40 years. Recent Polar Security Cutter program contracts and steel-cutting for new heavy icebreakers in the early 2020s confirm that construction is underway or planned under the current administration. Thus the core claim that the administration will be building the first new heavy icebreakers in over four decades is accurate.

claim: "Registered Republican not allowed to vote."
rationale: As stated, the claim is false: being registered as a Republican does not by itself prevent someone from voting. Party registration records affiliation and determines eligibility for some primary types, but general elections are open to eligible voters regardless of party; disenfranchisement occurs for reasons like felony conviction or court-ordered incapacity, not party membership. Some states have closed primaries that limit participation in a party's primary to its members, which might be the source of confusion.

claim: Says Texas GOP platform calls for end to teaching "critical thinking" in public schools.
rationale: This is a misleading characterization. The Texas GOP platform has language opposing Critical Race Theory and certain curricula it views as promoting social-justice ideology, but it does not explicitly call for ending the teaching of 'critical thinking' skills in public schools. The claim appears to conflate or misstate opposition to specific curricular approaches (e.g., CRT) with a blanket ban on teaching critical thinking.

claim: The Obama administration "spent more money on the Cash for Clunkers program than the space program."
rationale: This is false. The Cash for Clunkers (CARS) program was funded at roughly $3 billion in 2009, whereas the U.S. civilian space program (NASA) received roughly $17–19 billion per year during the Obama years and thus far more in total across the administration. Even comparing a single year, NASA's annual budget exceeded the CARS outlay.

claim: "I certainly supported Barack Obama and Joe Biden. ... I was there both times for them."
rationale: This claim is not verifiable as presented because the speaker is not identified and no supporting evidence (public endorsement, campaign appearance records, or contemporaneous reporting) is provided. Without such corroboration the assertion that they “supported Barack Obama and Joe Biden” and “was there both times for them” cannot be confirmed. It could be true for some individuals, but as a standalone claim it is unproven.

claim: A photo shows Democratic U.S. Rep. Maxine Waters and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi posing and smiling in front of a Trump 2020 sign.
rationale: This claim is false — no credible, verifiable photograph shows Rep. Maxine Waters and Speaker Nancy Pelosi posing together in front of a genuine 'Trump 2020' sign. Images with that composition circulated were manipulated or miscaptioned; original event photos and news archives do not contain such signage behind the two Democrats.

claim: "No state generates as much solar power as California, or has as many people whose jobs depend on it."
rationale: Contemporary U.S. energy and industry data consistently show California produces more solar electricity than any other state and also hosts the largest solar workforce. Federal generation statistics (utility-scale plus significant distributed rooftop contributions) and national solar-job censuses list California atop both metrics. While exact numbers shift year-to-year, the dual-claim matches recent authoritative reporting.

claim: Says Daniel Radcliffe has the coronavirus.
rationale: Daniel Radcliffe publicly announced in March 2020 that he had tested positive for COVID-19 and reported mild symptoms while self-isolating; major news outlets covered his statement. He later said he recovered, so the statement is true as a past diagnosis rather than an ongoing infection.

claim: Says Florida Agriculture Commissioner Nikki Fried "spent millions of dollars to put her face on every gas pump across this state."
rationale: This claim is an exaggeration. News reporting and public records show the Agriculture Commissioner’s office authorized inspection/consumer‑information decals and some branded outreach on pumps, but there is no credible evidence she personally spent millions to put her face on every gas pump statewide — critics’ language was hyperbolic and the costs reported were modest and part of routine outreach/inspection activities. The phrase “every gas pump” is rhetorical rather than a documented, statewide million‑dollar purchase order.

claim: "You had (4,925) out-of-state voters… in Georgia."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it lacks critical context (which election/year and who 'you' refers to) and no source is provided for the specific figure 4,925. Official verification requires consulting Georgia Secretary of State voter rolls or certified audit reports, and without that citation the numeric claim cannot be confirmed. Because of this missing context and evidence, I rate the claim as false/unsubstantiated.

claim: Says a Congressional Budget Office report found low-income seniors in Florida will face "800 percent premium increases" under the American Health Care Act.
rationale: This specific claim misattributes and overstates the CBO's findings. The CBO/JCT report projected large premium increases for older people who receive little or no financial assistance in some states, but it did not state that ‘low-income seniors in Florida’ would face an 800% premium increase as a categorical finding. The 800% figure circulated in media analyses and state-level extrapolations, not as a direct statewide CBO conclusion about low-income seniors in Florida.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "voted against the bipartisan Violence Against Women Act."
rationale: The bipartisan Senate reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act in 2013 passed 78–22, and Marco Rubio was one of the senators who voted against that bill. He publicly explained his opposition citing objections to provisions related to undocumented immigrants and expanded protections for same-sex couples/tribal jurisdiction. This matches the claim that he voted against the bipartisan VAWA reauthorization.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "the Germans bombed Pearl Harbor."
rationale: The claim is false. The attack on Pearl Harbor (Dec 7, 1941) was carried out by Imperial Japan, and there is no credible transcript or reputable reporting showing President Joe Biden saying “the Germans bombed Pearl Harbor.” Viral clips that assert he said this have been debunked or shown to be misheard/misattributed or edited.

claim: Says that except for foreign policy, Ron Paul’s voting record and his voting record are virtually identical.
rationale: The claim as written compares Ron Paul’s voting record to Ron Paul’s voting record, which is tautological and therefore identical; saying they are "virtually identical except for foreign policy" is logically inconsistent. If the speaker intended a comparison to a different person, the statement as written is ambiguous and unsupported.

claim: In the United Kingdom, "81% of COVID-19 deaths are among the vaccinated."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it gives a single percentage with no timeframe, age group, or definition of “vaccinated.” While at certain periods in the UK a majority of recorded COVID-19 deaths were among people who had received one or more vaccine doses (largely because most vulnerable people were vaccinated), the exact proportion varied over time, by age group, and by whether boosters or time since vaccination were counted. Vaccination substantially reduces the individual risk of death, so headline percentages without context can be deceptive.

claim: "Tonight in Ohio, more people came out to vote for Barack Obama in an unopposed race than voted for (Mitt) Romney and (Rick) Santorum combined."
rationale: The claim is unlikely: when an incumbent (Barack Obama) ran essentially unopposed in a Democratic primary, turnout on the Democratic side was typically much lower than turnout in the competitive Republican primary between Romney and Santorum. In the relevant Ohio primary season, the combined Republican votes exceeded votes cast for the uncontested Democrat. The statement as written lacks a date and appears to misstate typical primary turnout patterns in that contest.

claim: "Last week Senator Obama's running mate said, get this, 'Raising taxes is patriotic.' "
rationale: There is no credible record that Senator Obama’s 2008 running mate, Joe Biden, said the exact phrase “Raising taxes is patriotic” last week. Public transcripts and contemporary news coverage do not document that quotation, and it appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase of broader comments about taxing high earners. Without a verifiable source for the precise quote, the claim is not supported.

claim: U.S. Rep. Connie Mack "voted to raise his own pay several times."
rationale: I could not find clear, specific evidence that Rep. Connie Mack repeatedly cast standalone votes to directly raise his own salary several times. Congressional pay adjustments are often embedded in broader bills or automatic adjustments, and public fact-checks typically require naming specific roll-call votes and dates—none unambiguously tie multiple deliberate pay-raise votes to a Congressman named Connie Mack. Given the ambiguity (which Connie Mack and which votes) the blanket claim is not supported by clear documentation.

claim: The Redskins Training Camp deal "generated $40 million in new private investment in the city."
rationale: There is no independent evidence that the Redskins training-camp deal directly produced $40 million in new private investment; the $40M figure was reported in promotional materials and economic-impact projections, which typically mix projected visitor spending and public incentives rather than documented private capital commitments. Independent reporting and municipal audits do not corroborate a verifiable $40M of new private investment attributable solely to the deal.

claim: Anthony Fauci was on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years and "currently serves on Gates Foundation."
rationale: This is incorrect. Anthony Fauci is a long‑time federal public health official (NIAID director) and is not listed as having served on the Clinton Foundation board for 20 years; public records and the Clinton Foundation's published board lists do not include him. He also is not a trustee or board member of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation—though he has collaborated with Gates‑funded projects and served on scientific/advisory panels, which may have caused confusion.

claim: Says "56 percent of (the U.S.-Mexico) border is not under our control."
rationale: The claim that 56% of the U.S.-Mexico border is “not under our control” is not supported by authoritative data. U.S. Customs and Border Protection and other federal authorities have legal jurisdiction and operational presence across the entire border even where terrain, fencing, or enforcement levels vary; independent fact-checkers and government statistics do not substantiate a 56% uncontrolled figure. The statement conflates different concepts (physical barrier, enforcement density, criminal activity) and presents an unsupported numeric percentage as fact.

claim: Keystone Pipeline was blocked by Obama on Warren Buffett’s behalf.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Obama blocked the Keystone XL pipeline as a favor to Warren Buffett. The Obama administration publicly cited environmental, climate and regulatory review reasons for denying the permit, and although Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway owned BNSF (which would benefit from oil-by-rail), that business link is correlation and not documented proof of a quid pro quo or that Obama acted on Buffett’s behalf.

claim: Says New Jersey Rep. Leonard Lance voted repeatedly "to let insurance companies charge more to people aged 50 and over."
rationale: I cannot verify that Rep. Leonard Lance "voted repeatedly" to specifically let insurers charge more to people aged 50 and over. While some Republican-sponsored health bills and amendments sought to relax ACA age-rating limits (allowing wider age bands or state waivers), I do not have clear, corroborated roll-call evidence that Lance repeatedly cast votes with that explicit effect. The statement is imprecise about which votes and when, so it is not confirmed as stated.

claim: Says that under the law, New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio "can’t open" the city’s schools.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as a blanket statement. The New York City mayor has substantial authority over the city’s Department of Education and school operations, so he can decide to open or close schools in ordinary circumstances, although those decisions are constrained by state education law and by the governor’s emergency powers and state guidance (as occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic). Thus it is wrong to say he legally "can’t open" the schools without additional context about specific state orders or emergencies.

claim: Says Joe Biden repeatedly told Americans he's going to raise their taxes.
rationale: This is misleading: President Biden frequently said he would not raise taxes on households earning under $400,000 and instead proposed tax increases targeted at corporations and high-income households. He did repeatedly propose or support tax hikes on the wealthy and corporations, but did not repeatedly tell the general public that everyone's taxes would be raised.

claim: Says Texas is "last in mental health expenditures."
rationale: The claim is too broad and unsupported as stated: rankings of “mental health expenditures” depend on the metric (total dollars, per‑capita spending, percent of state budget, Medicaid mental‑health outlays) and the year, and Texas is not consistently the lowest across those measures. Public data show rankings vary by dataset and year, and other states or territories sometimes rank lower on per‑capita or percent‑of‑budget measures. Without a specific metric and timeframe, asserting Texas is “last” is misleading and likely false.

claim: Graduation rates of players at major football colleges "are still twenty points below their male campus peers and worsened in the past three years."
rationale: The claim is a broad, quantitative assertion that is not supported by national NCAA data: gaps between male football players and their male campus peers vary by school and metric and are generally smaller than a uniform 20-percentage-point deficit across 'major football colleges.' Nationwide graduation-rate metrics (GSR and federal rates) have trended upward over decades and do not show a consistent, across-the-board worsening over the past three years. Without a clear definition of “major football colleges,” the specific 20-point figure and the claimed recent decline are not reliably accurate.

claim: "We [the city of Atlanta] are overbuilt on housing."
rationale: The claim is too broad and not supported as a citywide fact: while Atlanta has seen substantial multifamily construction, the region has also experienced sustained population and job growth, relatively low vacancy rates, and rising rents—indicators inconsistent with being broadly "overbuilt." Some specific submarkets or building types (e.g., certain condo segments) may face localized oversupply, but that does not establish a blanket citywide overbuilding.

claim: Says his administration has made "progress" on border enforcement by "putting more boots on the southern border than at any time in our history and reducing illegal crossings to their lowest levels in 40 years."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While staffing for border agencies has been high in recent years, claims of "more boots on the southern border than at any time in our history" depend on how personnel are counted (Border Patrol vs full CBP vs temporary deployments) and are not clearly supported as an uncontested historical maximum. Likewise, crossings were unusually low in 2020 because of pandemic-era restrictions, but migration and apprehension figures have fluctuated and do not clearly establish a sustained "lowest levels in 40 years."

claim: "Crime has been getting worse since Jerry Brown was elected governor."
rationale: Jerry Brown was elected governor in 2010 (taking office 2011) and statewide crime did not uniformly get worse over his tenure; many major categories (especially property crime and overall crime rates) declined for several years, though some categories such as homicides saw increases in certain years. Because the claim is a blanket statement with no timeframe or crime type specified, it is misleading to say crime simply 'has been getting worse' since his election.

claim: Ché Guevara "wrote extensively about the superiority of white Europeans over people of African descent."
rationale: This is false. Che Guevara's published corpus and public political writings focus on Marxist internationalism, anti‑imperialism and revolutionary strategy, not a sustained argument that white Europeans are superior to people of African descent. While some private diary entries and youthful remarks have been criticized as racist or derogatory, they are isolated passages and not an extensive written doctrine of white supremacy.

claim: "Our debt to GDP ratios, our deficit to GDP ratios are quickly approaching the countries we have been reading about for the last year and a half. We are not far behind Ireland, Greece, Portugal and Spain and all these countries we have been reading about."
rationale: Although U.S. deficits rose sharply during the global financial crisis, U.S. debt-to-GDP and deficit-to-GDP were not rapidly converging on the extreme levels seen in Greece and Portugal. Greece's sovereign debt exceeded 100% of GDP and Portugal's debt and fiscal problems were materially worse than the U.S.; while Ireland and Spain had serious banking-related issues, the claim overstates how close U.S. ratios were to those countries. The statement also mixes different measures and lacks a clear timeframe, producing a misleading comparison.

claim: "Principal bans candy canes."
rationale: The claim is presented without any identifying details (which principal, which school, or when) and there is no verifiable evidence provided here to confirm a universal or specific ban. Because school policies vary and the statement is too vague to substantiate, it cannot be confirmed as fact and is classified as false pending specific supporting information.

claim: Shirley Sherrod "was forced to resign before anybody on Fox said a word about this."
rationale: Sherley Sherrod resigned on July 19, 2010 after an edited clip posted by Andrew Breitbart and circulated on conservative blogs prompted the USDA to accept her resignation the same day. Coverage of the episode appeared essentially contemporaneously across conservative outlets, and Fox-affiliated programs and platforms discussed the story very soon after it began circulating, so it is inaccurate to claim she was forced out before anyone at Fox 'said a word.'

claim: On Sandra Day O'Connor: "I think one reason she was a good judge is she had no judicial experience" before she joined the Supreme Court.
rationale: The claim that she had "no judicial experience" before joining the Supreme Court is incorrect. Sandra Day O'Connor served on the Arizona Court of Appeals from 1979 until her 1981 nomination to the U.S. Supreme Court, so she did have state judicial experience prior to the High Court.

claim: Regarding the surgery that saved Jimmy Kimmel's son, "Medicaid has stopped providing this kind of service."
rationale: There is no evidence that Medicaid has broadly stopped covering the type of lifesaving congenital heart surgery Jimmy Kimmel’s infant son received. Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program routinely cover medically necessary pediatric and neonatal surgeries for eligible children, and no federal policy has eliminated such coverage nationwide. Claims that Medicaid “stopped providing this kind of service” misrepresent ongoing coverage or confuse national policy with proposals to cut or restrict Medicaid funding.

claim: "Drone technology now allows an individual to be recorded in their homes by drones as small as birds and immediately uploaded to the internet."
rationale: Modern drone technology includes bird-sized and smaller vehicles that can carry cameras and be flown indoors; many models and payloads are capable of capturing video of individuals in private spaces. These drones and companion systems can stream or upload footage in real time via Wi‑Fi, cellular links, or through a paired controller that relays content to the internet, though practical limits (battery life, navigation, image quality) and legal constraints apply.

claim: "There's nothing in the voting instructions that we've been getting in the last several elections that lets you know" about the limitations of the master lever.
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that no recent voting instructions have informed voters about master-lever limitations. That is unlikely to be true universally: many jurisdictions publish sample ballots, instructions, and poll-worker guidance that describe straight‑ticket/master‑lever behavior and its limits. Because practices vary by state and locality, the blanket "nothing" assertion is inaccurate.

claim: "Big pharmaceuticals pay off — they literally pay off — generics to keep the prices and the competition off the market."
rationale: There is a well-documented practice known as “pay‑for‑delay” or “reverse‑payment” settlements in which brand pharmaceutical companies have paid generic manufacturers to delay market entry, preserving higher prices. Regulatory authorities (e.g., the U.S. FTC) and courts have investigated and litigated numerous such cases, and studies estimate substantial consumer harm from delayed generic competition.

claim: "Drug overdose deaths decreased in 2018 for the first time in 30 years."
rationale: CDC mortality data show drug overdose deaths fell from about 70,237 in 2017 to about 67,367 in 2018, a modest decline and the first year-over-year drop since 1990. Many reports described 2018 as the first decrease in nearly three decades, so saying ‘first time in 30 years’ is a reasonable summary of the statistic.

claim: The U.S. "only ranks 25th worldwide on defense spending as a percentage of GDP."
rationale: The statement gives a specific global rank without citing a year or data source; rankings of U.S. defense spending as a share of GDP vary by dataset and year and are not consistently 25th. Using standard sources (SIPRI/World Bank) the U.S. share is typically around 3–4% of GDP and its rank has ranged roughly from the mid‑teens to mid‑20s depending on the year — so the categorical claim that it “only ranks 25th” is misleading and not reliably true.

claim: Says that Olive Garden is "funding" President Trump's 2020 re-election campaign.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Olive Garden as a corporation funded President Trump’s 2020 re-election campaign. Federal law prohibits direct corporate contributions to federal candidates; any political giving would come through a company PAC or individual employees/owners, and Darden/Olive Garden did not publicly report direct corporate donations to Trump’s campaign. Claims that the chain itself was ‘funding’ Trump misrepresent the legal and factual reality.

claim: Says Kelly Loeffler supports "raising taxes on Georgia's middle class."
rationale: There is no credible record that Kelly Loeffler advocated for raising taxes on Georgia’s middle class; as a Republican senator and 2020 Senate candidate she publicly supported tax cuts and opposed tax increases. Claims that she supports “raising taxes on the middle class” were made in opposition advertising but are not supported by her stated policy positions or legislative record.

claim: Louisiana gets "not one single penny" from Gulf Coast offshore oil revenues.
rationale: This claim is false. Louisiana receives substantial revenue tied to Gulf of Mexico offshore oil and gas through federal revenue-sharing (e.g., GOMESA), state severance taxes, leases and royalties on state-owned submerged lands, and local impact payments used for coastal restoration and budgets. While the precise distribution rules and timing can be complex, it is incorrect to say Louisiana gets "not one single penny."

claim: Says William Taylor and George Kent, the public witnesses in the House impeachment inquiry, are "Never Trumpers."
rationale: William B. Taylor and George P. Kent are career U.S. Foreign Service officers who served in the State Department and testified as professional, nonpartisan witnesses in the House inquiry; there is no credible evidence they are members of the partisan 'Never Trumper' movement. Labeling them as 'Never Trumpers' appears to be a partisan characterization rather than a factual description of their careers or stated political affiliation.

claim: "I'm the only candidate in the Democratic primary, or actually on either side, who Wall Street financiers and hedge fund managers are actually running ads against."
rationale: The claim is an exclusive assertion that no other candidate—Democrat or Republican—is being targeted by Wall Street or hedge-fund-funded ads. Historical advertising and reporting show that finance-industry groups and wealthy fund managers have financed attack ads against multiple candidates across parties (notably progressive Democrats like Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders and various Republicans), so it is extremely unlikely one person would be the only target.

claim: Says when New Jersey adopted guaranteed coverage and cost provisions without a mandate individual health insurance market rates "doubled or tripled" and enrollment dropped from 180,000 people to 80,000 people.
rationale: New Jersey did adopt guaranteed-issue/community-rating rules in the early 1990s, but independent analyses do not support the specific claim that individual-market premiums universally "doubled or tripled" or that enrollment fell exactly from 180,000 to 80,000 as a direct result. Studies and contemporaneous reporting show mixed premium effects and enrollment declines influenced by multiple factors, so the precise magnitudes in the claim are exaggerated or unsupported.

claim: "A majority of the men and women on this stage have previously and publicly embraced amnesty. I am the only candidate on this stage who has never supported amnesty."
rationale: The claim asserts both that a majority on the stage publicly embraced “amnesty” and that the speaker is uniquely never to have supported it. Public records and past debate histories show multiple other candidates have either publicly supported policies critics label as amnesty (e.g., pathways to legal status) or consistently opposed them, so the absolute claim of being the only one is incorrect. Without a precise definition of “amnesty” or identification of the debate stage the sweeping exclusivity is not supported.

claim: Says Florida Gov. Rick Scott "just signed a bill that could make most of Florida’s beaches private."
rationale: This is false. While Gov. Rick Scott signed legislation affecting coastal property rights, shoreline management, and beach restoration funding, he did not sign a law that would convert most of Florida’s beaches into private property. Florida’s public trust doctrine and existing state law maintain public rights to wet-sand beaches and limit wholesale privatization, and the bills in question adjusted procedures or compensation rather than transferring broad public ownership to private owners.

claim: "We had 2 percent of the global market (for advanced batteries) when he (Obama) started. We now have 16 percent, headed to 40 percent by 2015."
rationale: The numbers in the claim are inconsistent with industry data and timelines. While U.S. share of global lithium‑ion cell manufacturing was very small around 2009 (a figure near 2% is plausible), U.S. capacity did not jump to 16% nor was it on track to reach 40% by 2015 — major expansions (e.g., Tesla’s Gigafactory) began after 2014 and significant production capacity only ramped later. Industry reports show Asia (Japan, Korea, China) continued to supply the large majority of advanced batteries through 2015.

claim: "There are precious few religions that actually say you cannot" get vaccinated.
rationale: Major world religions (mainstream Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, Buddhism, etc.) generally do not prohibit vaccination and many religious authorities have explicitly supported or encouraged vaccination. Only a small number of specific sects or groups (for example some adherents of Christian Science or a few very conservative local communities) object on doctrinal grounds, so outright bans by religions are uncommon.

claim: Georgia ranks 49th for women serving in elected state and federal offices.
rationale: This claim is not supported by widely used measures of women’s representation. National trackers (e.g., Rutgers/CAWP datasets) rank states differently depending on year and the exact metric, but Georgia has not consistently placed 49th for combined state and federal elected offices in recent comprehensive rankings — it has generally ranked higher (i.e., better) than 49th. Without a specific year and metric the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "(GM and Chrysler) repaid their loans."
rationale: This is false as stated. While the government recovered most or all of the Chrysler bailout when it sold its stake, General Motors did not fully repay the government—the Treasury recovered substantially less than it lent to GM and recorded a multibillion‑dollar loss after GM’s 2009 restructuring and stock sales. Thus it is incorrect to say both companies repaid their loans in full.

claim: If public employees don’t pay more for benefits starting April 1, 2011, "the equivalent" is 1,500 state employee layoffs by June 30, 2011 and 10,000 to 12,000 state and local government employee layoffs in the next two years.
rationale: The claim states precise layoff counts tied to a single policy change but provides no verifiable source and appears to be a speculative projection rather than an established fact. Layoff numbers of 1,500 by June 30, 2011 and 10,000–12,000 over two years would depend on the specific state, enacted budget choices, and alternative cost-saving measures; independent budget analyses from that period do not uniformly corroborate these exact figures. Because such projections vary widely by assumptions, presenting them as an equivalence is misleading.

claim: Says Pete Gallego "went and lobbied after you fired him from Congress."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Pete Gallego was defeated in his 2014 re-election bid (members of Congress are not 'fired'), and there is no clear evidence that he became a registered federal lobbyist immediately afterward; his post-congressional activity has been in law, campaigning, and local politics rather than documented federal lobbying. Calling it 'went and lobbied after you fired him from Congress' conflates losing an election with being fired and asserts lobbying activity that is not substantiated.

claim: "I unsealed my records" at Marquette University.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as presented because it lacks who “I” refers to, what records were sealed, and when the alleged unsealing occurred. Universities like Marquette protect student records under FERPA and typically do not ‘‘unseal’’ or release records without consent or a court order; without supporting evidence or a named individual and date, the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Under Republicans, recessions happen four times as frequently as under Democrats."
rationale: This claim is a clear exaggeration. Historical recession dating (e.g., by NBER) shows recessions have begun during both Democratic and Republican presidencies and while more post‑World‑War II recessions began under Republican presidents, the difference is far smaller than a 4:1 ratio and depends heavily on the chosen time period and counting method. Economic cycles are driven by many factors beyond which party occupies the White House, so a blanket 4× claim is misleading.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Michael McCaul is "the sixth-richest person in Congress."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as presented because it gives no date or source and cannot be verified against public compilations of congressional wealth. Compilations from organizations that track members' financial disclosures (e.g., OpenSecrets, Roll Call) show Michael McCaul is among the wealthier members of Congress but he is not consistently ranked exactly sixth; rankings change by year and valuation method.

claim: Marijuana today is "genetically modified," with THC levels that "far surpass the marijuana" of the 1970s.
rationale: This statement mixes a true element — average THC concentrations in commonly used cannabis flower have risen substantially since the 1970s — with a false implication that modern cannabis has been widely produced by genetic engineering. Most increases in THC come from selective breeding, cross‑breeding and cloning of high‑THC plants, not from transgenic or laboratory genetic modification. As stated, the claim is therefore misleading and incorrect.

claim: The Convention Center "was sold as a building that would never cost taxpayers a dime."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no context (which convention center, when, or who made the promise) and is an absolute statement that is unlikely to be literally true. Public facility sales or deals are commonly promoted with marketing promises, but actual financing, subsidies, tax exemptions, or later public costs frequently arise, so the blanket assertion that it "would never cost taxpayers a dime" cannot be confirmed without specific evidence.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We need to repeal Daylight Savings Time as a primary measure to decrease the rate of climate change. Less hours of sun shine equal less heat hitting Earth’s surface."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable reporting that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made this statement, and the claim mistakes the effect of daylight saving time: shifting clocks does not change the amount of sunlight or the total solar energy the Earth receives. The quote appears to be a misattribution or fabricated social-media claim rather than a verifiable AOC quote.

claim: Under the Arizona immigration law, police are required to check immigration status if someone's "lawn is overgrown" or if a dog is "barking too loudly."
rationale: Arizona’s 2010 immigration law (SB 1070) did not compel police to check immigration status for trivial complaints like an overgrown lawn or a barking dog. It required officers to make a reasonable attempt to determine immigration status only when the officer had a lawful stop, detention, or arrest and reasonable suspicion the person was unlawfully present; it did not list everyday nuisances as automatic triggers. Court rulings and DOJ guidance also limited broad, automatic checks.

claim: "A Cornell University research study concludes that ethanol generates a 29 percent energy loss, meaning it takes more than a gallon of gasoline to produce a gallon of ethanol."
rationale: A Cornell study by David Pimentel and Tad Patzek (published mid-2000s) concluded that corn ethanol has a roughly −29% net energy balance, i.e., producing a gallon of ethanol requires more fossil-fuel energy input than the energy contained in the ethanol produced. That finding is accurately summarized by saying it represents about a 29% energy loss and implies more than one gallon-equivalent of fossil fuel energy is used per gallon-equivalent of ethanol output.

claim: "In two terms in the Missouri General Assembly, Jason Kander passed ZERO bills that were signed into law."
rationale: This claim is not accurate. Contemporary fact-checks and Missouri legislative records show Kander was associated with at least one measure that became law during his two terms (and he also co-sponsored legislation that passed), so it is false to say he passed zero bills. Disputes often arise over counting only bills where he was the primary sponsor versus co-sponsorship or counting resolutions rather than statutes.

claim: Says Barbara Buono "voted to raise her own pay 40 percent."
rationale: There is no record of Barbara Buono casting a single floor vote that directly increased her own legislative salary by 40%. Fact-checkers and legislative records show pay changes were smaller, occurred over time or as part of broader measures, and the 40% figure is a misleading aggregation or mischaracterization. The ad conflates separate adjustments and timing to create the impression of a single self-authored 40% raise.

claim: Al Sharpton went to Ferguson, Mo., and is "declaring as a matter of fact that ... Michael Brown didn't use any deadly force or posed no deadly threat to the officer."
rationale: It is true Al Sharpton traveled to Ferguson and publicly argued Michael Brown was unarmed and that the killing was unjust, but the claim that he "declared as a matter of fact" that Brown did not use deadly force overstates what he did. Sharpton was acting as an advocate and repeating witness/accounts at protests rather than presenting independently established forensic conclusions; official investigations and competing accounts meant the matter was disputed.

claim: Says the U.S. gives Israel "$3 billion annually" in aid and zero to Detroit.
rationale: The U.S. does provide roughly $3–4 billion a year to Israel under a multi-year military aid agreement, so the ‘‘$3 billion’’ figure is roughly in the right range historically. However the claim that the U.S. gives "zero to Detroit" is incorrect — Detroit receives federal funding through various programs (e.g., HUD block grants, federal transportation and infrastructure grants, FEMA, and pandemic relief). Because the statement mixes a partially-accurate number with a false absolute about Detroit, the overall claim is false.

claim: "The average age of first marijuana use is 12."
rationale: Major national surveys and epidemiological studies show the typical age of first marijuana use is in the mid-to-late teens (commonly around 16–18), not 12. Age 12 may describe the youngest initiators or certain subgroups, but it is not the population average.

claim: "Within the three miles surrounding the University Circle area, infant mortality exceeds some Third World countries."
rationale: The claim is not supported by clear, time‑specific data and appears to conflate localized neighborhood rates with national rates. While parts of Cleveland (including neighborhoods east of University Circle) have had historically high infant mortality for certain demographic groups, there is no well‑documented, current statistic showing that the infant mortality rate within exactly three miles of University Circle exceeds that of named developing countries. The statement is therefore misleading without precise geography, timeframe, and country comparisons.

claim: "We understand that this heroin is primarily coming from Mexico, over the border."
rationale: U.S. drug enforcement reporting and trafficking analyses indicate that most heroin consumed in the United States is supplied by Mexican criminal organizations and crosses the U.S.–Mexico border. While Afghanistan is the largest global source of opium/heroin, Mexican-sourced heroin — including black tar and powder varieties — has been the predominant source for the U.S. market in recent years.

claim: "Walmart rewards everyone with $75 coupon to celebrate its 125th Anniversary"
rationale: This claim is false. Walmart was founded in 1962, so a 125th anniversary would be many decades in the future; there are no credible announcements that Walmart is giving every person a $75 coupon. Similar messages are common scam/phishing tactics promising universal payouts or coupons to get users to click links or provide personal information.

claim: "The pace of missile development between (Kim Jong Il and Kim Jong Un) has increased the testing about twenty-fold."
rationale: While there has been a substantial rise in North Korean missile testing under Kim Jong Un compared with Kim Jong Il, available counts and time windows do not reliably support the precise claim of a ~20-fold increase. Estimates vary depending on which years are compared and what is counted as a "test" (ballistic vs. satellite or cruise launches), so the specific twenty-fold figure is not well established.

claim: Says most of Austin’s biggest parks have recycling though as "many as 293 out of 300" Austin city "parks have no recycling, including almost every neighborhood park."
rationale: The statement is contradictory and unlikely: while many of Austin’s largest, well-maintained parks do have recycling receptacles, the sweeping numeric claim that 'as many as 293 out of 300' city parks have no recycling (including almost every neighborhood park) is unsupported and implausible without a current, comprehensive park inventory. The broad, round-number assertion appears exagerated or taken out of context rather than a verifiable fact.

claim: "After one year, Tennessee’s students made their biggest single-year jump in achievement ever recorded in the state."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false because it is vague about which test, grade, subject, and year are meant; statewide records of achievement use different assessments (state tests vs. NAEP) and do not support a blanket "biggest single-year jump ever recorded" across all measures. Tennessee has reported large gains in particular grades/subjects in some years, but those improvements have been tied to specific assessments or changes in standards and do not constitute a documented largest single-year jump for the state overall.

claim: Says Rick Scott cut education by over a billion dollars, meaning thousands of teachers "lost their jobs" and "class sizes went up."
rationale: The claim oversimplifies and misattributes complex budget and staffing changes. While early in Rick Scott’s term there were reductions and re‑allocations that lowered K–12 dollars in some years (and loss of federal stimulus funding contributed to budget pressure), statewide K–12 funding later increased and there is no clear, direct statewide record that his actions alone caused “thousands” of teachers to be laid off or uniformly larger class sizes across Florida. District-level layoffs and class‑size changes had multiple causes (federal stimulus expiration, local budget choices, changes in categorical funding), so the blanket causal statement is unsupported.

claim: "Both Cruz and Rubio are missing the vast majority of their votes."
rationale: This is false as stated. Public Senate voting records show both Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio have participated in the majority of roll-call votes in their terms and have not missed the "vast majority" (i.e., over half) of votes; typical missed-vote rates for senators are usually a minority percentage. The claim lacks a timeframe or definition of "vast majority," which makes it unsupported as presented.

claim: Says proposed teacher contract "would layer on more restrictive rules."
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify that the quoted assertion was actually made or that the proposed contract would indeed “layer on more restrictive rules.” No speaker, date, jurisdiction, or text of the proposed contract is provided, so the claim cannot be independently confirmed. Without sourcing, the statement should be treated as unverified and therefore labeled false for the purposes of this check.

claim: "If we had been on 'Obamacare' and a bureaucrat was trying to tell me when I could get that CAT scan, that would have delayed my treatment."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) did not create a centralized government bureaucracy that schedules individual CAT scans. The law preserved private insurance markets and expanded Medicaid; decisions about test approvals or scheduling are typically made by insurers, providers, or through prior-authorization processes (which can exist in private plans and government programs) rather than a single government official automatically delaying care.

claim: "For every $1 spent on mitigation, $4 in post-storm cleanup and rebuilding is saved."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad universal claim. While some government and academic studies have reported roughly $4 saved for every $1 spent on certain mitigation programs, benefit–cost ratios vary widely by hazard type, mitigation measure, geography and time horizon, and other studies report different savings (higher or lower). Without specifying the study, program, hazard and methodology, the blanket "for every $1 ... $4 saved" is misleading.

claim: "We work longer hours than any people in the industrialized world, including the Japanese."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. International labor statistics (e.g., OECD data on average annual hours worked) show the United States does not have the longest working hours in the industrialized world — several countries such as Mexico, Costa Rica, Turkey and historically South Korea record higher average hours — and Japan’s average hours are typically lower than or similar to the U.S. depending on the metric. Therefore the blanket statement that “we work longer hours than any people in the industrialized world, including the Japanese” is false.

claim: "I've always known this is a real, this is a pandemic. I've felt it was a pandemic long before it was called a pandemic."
rationale: The statement asserts the speaker personally believed an outbreak was a pandemic before it was officially declared. That is an unverifiable claim about internal belief unless supported by dated, public statements or other contemporaneous evidence. Without identification of the speaker and corroborating records, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false/unverified here.

claim: Says the California congressional district he represents "has a higher GDP than Russia."
rationale: This is not correct. Russia's nominal GDP in recent years has been in the multi‑trillion dollar range (roughly $1.7–2.5 trillion depending on year and source), while even the most economically productive California metro areas, counties or congressional districts have GDPs measured in the hundreds of billions, not trillions. No single U.S. congressional district in California has a larger economy than Russia.

claim: An episode of "The Simpsons" showed Donald Trump in a coffin.
rationale: There is no verified Simpsons TV episode that depicts Donald Trump in a coffin. The Simpsons have referenced Trump (notably the 2000 episode "Bart to the Future" joking about a future Trump presidency) and many doctored images and fan-art have circulated online, but no canonical episode shows Trump in a coffin. Given available episode summaries and widely reported Simpsons moments, the coffin scene appears to be misattributed or fabricated.

claim: If you know someone's name and date of birth you can change their votes on Oregon’s voting website.
rationale: This is false. Oregon does not provide online voting or a web interface that lets someone change another person’s cast ballot; ballots are sent and returned by mail (or dropped off) and are subject to signature verification and chain-of-custody procedures. While a name and date of birth can allow someone to look up registration status or request a replacement ballot in limited circumstances, that is not the same as being able to change another person’s submitted vote via Oregon’s website.

claim: Says he "earned the highest possible credit ratings as state treasurer."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it names no person, state, rating agency, or timeframe; credit ratings are assigned to states by independent agencies, not personally ‘earned’ by a treasurer alone. Without documentary evidence that during a specific treasurer’s tenure a state held the highest possible ratings from major agencies, the assertion cannot be confirmed and thus should be treated as false.

claim: Hillary Clinton "has already said she's going to wipe out the Second Amendment. She doesn't believe in the First Amendment. And, she also believes in big government, which flies in the face of the 10th Amendment"
rationale: The claim is false. Hillary Clinton has advocated for gun-control measures (e.g., assault-weapons bans, universal background checks) but has not said she would 'wipe out the Second Amendment.' She has defended free-speech rights while criticizing rulings like Citizens United and has not stated she "doesn't believe in the First Amendment;" and although she supports an active federal role on many issues, that policy preference is not the same as an explicit rejection of the Tenth Amendment or an admission to acting unconstitutionally.

claim: "Hair stylists are required to undergo more government scrutiny than foreclosure consultants."
rationale: The claim is a broad comparative statement that cannot be supported universally. While cosmetologists/hair stylists are commonly subject to state licensing, training hours, exams and board oversight, regulation of foreclosure consultants varies widely—some jurisdictions require registration, bonding or prohibitions while others impose little formal licensing. Which group faces "more" government scrutiny depends on the jurisdiction and the specific regulatory metrics, so the blanket claim is false.

claim: "A lot of people are talking about" the removal of a "very fair prosecutor" in Ukraine.
rationale: The claim is vague and unsubstantiated: it names no specific prosecutor or timeframe, so there is no verifiable evidence that ‘‘a lot of people’’ are currently discussing the removal of a ‘‘very fair prosecutor’’ in Ukraine. While removals of Ukrainian prosecutors (for example Viktor Shokin in 2016) were widely reported, the broad, quoted assertion here cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: "There's been a 1,700 percent increase in asylum claims over the last 10 years."
rationale: The claim is presented without a location or data source and is not supported by major asylum datasets. Global and major-country asylum application figures have risen in recent years but not by 1,700% over a ten-year span; such an extreme jump would be evident in UNHCR and national statistics. While very large percentage increases can occur from a tiny baseline in a specific country or short time window, the blanket claim as stated is misleading.

claim: "This past (legislative) session, we passed out of the Legislature a resolution requiring Congress to pass a balanced-budget amendment to the (U.S.) Constitution."
rationale: The claim is misleading: a state legislature cannot legally “require” Congress to pass a constitutional amendment. At most a legislature can pass a resolution urging Congress to propose an amendment or submit an Article V application calling for a convention; it cannot compel Congress to act. Without a specific jurisdiction and text, the assertion that the Legislature imposed a binding requirement on Congress is incorrect.

claim: Says "Donald Trump himself contributed $100,000" to the Clinton Foundation.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Donald Trump personally wrote a $100,000 check to the Clinton Foundation. Public donor records and contemporary reporting do not show a personal donation of that amount; at times donations associated with Trump were made by his foundation or businesses and have been conflated with a personal gift.
