claim: "The only segment in the beer market that is growing is the craft beer segment."
rationale: The statement is overly broad and inaccurate: while craft beer has grown in many markets and time periods, other segments (e.g., premium imports, super‑premium lagers, flavored malt beverages/hard seltzers, and some regional mainstream brands) have also shown growth depending on country and year. Beer-market performance varies by geography, period, and how segments are defined, so claiming craft is the only growing segment is incorrect.

claim: "Seismic airgun blasting (used for energy exploration) is ... 16,000 times louder than" a conventional airhorn.
rationale: The claim mixes incomparable measures and is misleading: seismic airguns are measured in underwater SPL (dB re 1 µPa) while airhorns are measured in airborne SPL (dB re 20 µPa), so a simple “16,000 times louder” comparison is not valid. Typical seismic airguns produce very high underwater source levels (order 200–260 dB re 1 µPa at 1 m) and airhorns produce roughly 110–130 dB SPL in air, but converting between media and reporting a single multiplicative factor requires many qualifiers. Without those qualifiers the numeric claim is not supportable as stated.

claim: "Amazing fact: Senate has already voted on more amendments in 2015 than Reid allowed ALL YEAR last year."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and ambiguous: it gives no date in 2015 and no clear definition of "allowed" or which amendment votes are being counted. Public roll-call and amendment-count records for the Senate do not support a sweeping assertion without precise metrics, and such a comparison would require specific counts that are not provided. Given the lack of verifiable data and the imprecision of the terms, the claim cannot be confirmed and is likely false.

claim: Says Ted Cruz "said I was in favor in Libya. I never discussed that subject."
rationale: The claim presents an oddly worded quote and there is no known public record or reputable reporting attributing the exact line "I was in favor in Libya. I never discussed that subject." to Ted Cruz. Without a verifiable source the statement appears to be a misquote or fabrication rather than an attributable factual quote.

claim: Says Ron Johnson justifies his support of trade agreements by saying the U.S. has the Trade Adjustment Assistance program for displaced workers, but then he "voted to eliminate it."
rationale: Available evidence does not support the precise claim that Sen. Ron Johnson both justified support for trade deals by pointing to Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA) and then subsequently cast a vote that literally eliminated the program. Johnson has at times defended trade agreements while also backing Republican budgets and proposals that cut or sought to reduce TAA funding, but those actions are not the same as a single clear vote to abolish the program after citing it. The statement conflates remarks and separate votes/proposals and overstates the record.

claim: "We’ve got close to 7 million Americans who have access to health care for the first time because of Medicaid expansion."
rationale: National estimates show substantially more than 7 million people gained Medicaid coverage due to ACA Medicaid expansion. Analyses from sources tracking enrollment (e.g., CMS, KFF, CBO/urban-institute estimates) put the number of people covered through expansion in the low tens of millions since 2014, so the claim understates the impact. The statement could be true for a specific state or narrow timeframe, but as a nationwide total it is inaccurate.

claim: "We will have more people enter our country illegally than were born in this country in one year."
rationale: The claim is almost certainly false as stated because annual births in large countries (for example the United States) number in the millions each year, while estimates of people entering illegally or the number of border encounters have historically been lower and would have to exceed total births to make the statement true. The claim also lacks a specified country and timeframe, and “enter illegally” can mean different things (unique individuals vs. repeat encounters), so as phrased it is not supported by available demographic and enforcement data.

claim: "A grant for $5,000 [from the Governor’s Workforce Board] went to teach an employee at a company that makes ornamental business card holders how to use Facebook and Twitter."
rationale: I could not find credible evidence that a Governor’s Workforce Board grant of exactly $5,000 was awarded specifically to teach an employee at a company that makes ornamental business card holders how to use Facebook and Twitter. While workforce grants commonly fund employee training (including digital skills), the claim presents a very specific recipient, amount, and purpose that match a recurring anecdote and appears to be a mischaracterization or unverified anecdote rather than a documented fact. Without a verifiable grant record naming that company and use, the claim fails to meet a factual standard.

claim: "About 95 percent of America’s production of ethylene is produced on the Gulf Coast in Texas and Louisiana."
rationale: The Gulf Coast (Texas and Louisiana) does host the bulk of U.S. ethylene steam crackers, but the 95% figure is an overstatement. Most industry sources show a large but lower share (commonly cited in the range roughly 60–85% depending on whether you count nameplate capacity, current output, or derivatives), and significant ethylene production also occurs outside the Gulf Coast.

claim: Georgia’s unemployment rate has exceeded the national rate for 50 consecutive months.
rationale: This claim is not supported by available monthly unemployment data. BLS state and national unemployment series show Georgia's rate has moved above and below the U.S. rate at different times (not a continuous 50-month streak), especially during the COVID-19 period when the national rate was sharply higher. A continuous run of 50 months (more than four years) where Georgia exceeded the national rate is inconsistent with those published series.

claim: "There have been zero reported instances of any child born alive after an abortion in Texas."
rationale: The statement asserts an absolute zero but cannot be substantiated. Public statements that no cases were reported from a Texas agency reflect limitations of reporting systems and variable legal definitions, and absence of a published report is not reliable proof that no instances ever occurred; independent media and legal discussions document born‑alive cases nationally and note reporting gaps in Texas. Because of incomplete reporting and definitional differences, the categorical claim of ‘zero’ is not supported.

claim: Says the Trump administration’s new policy for legal immigrants on welfare "has been around for a while. This is not a new thing that the president is trying to implement here, that the United States has been this way."
rationale: The broad idea of a ‘public charge’ ground for inadmissibility is long‑standing, but the Trump administration’s 2019 public‑charge rule substantially changed and expanded how use of benefits (including some non‑cash benefits) was weighed and which immigrants were affected. That expansion was a new, more restrictive policy compared with prior practice, so the statement that it “has been around for a while” as unchanged policy is misleading.

claim: "With 320,000 net Ohio manufacturing jobs lost, (Sen. Rob) Portman calls NAFTA a ‘proven success’."
rationale: The statement bundles a disputed numeric claim with a true characterization of Portman’s position. Rob Portman has indeed described NAFTA as a success in public remarks, but the specific figure “320,000 net Ohio manufacturing jobs lost” depends on the chosen timeframe and methodology and is not an uncontested, standalone attribution to NAFTA. Because the numeric loss and causal attribution are ambiguous and contested, the combined claim as presented is misleading.

claim: "In Italy, they have thrown their money on the streets. A clear message to the whole world that money is not enough when health is in danger."
rationale: The statement presents a literal nationwide action in Italy (people throwing money on the streets) and a global message, but there is no credible evidence of a widespread, coordinated act of Italians throwing money in the streets for that purpose. Reports from crises in Italy (e.g., COVID-19) documented solidarity actions like balcony singing, applause for health workers, protests and donations, but not a nation‑level money‑throwing event. The claim appears rhetorical or anecdotal rather than factual.

claim: The census "for years and years and years, decades, has asked, ‘Are you a citizen of the United States of America?’"
rationale: The U.S. census has asked about citizenship for many decades: earlier decennial censuses and the long-form census included citizenship questions for much of the 19th and 20th centuries, and the American Community Survey (which replaced the long form) has asked about citizenship since the mid-2000s. However, the short-form decennial census has not consistently included that exact question since about 1950, so the statement is broadly true but lacks nuance about which census form is meant.

claim: "When I was speaker, we had four consecutive balanced budgets."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify which "speaker," which legislative body, or which years are meant. At the U.S. federal level there were four consecutive budget surpluses (FY1998–FY2001), but the speakership changed during that span and attributing four consecutive balanced budgets to a single speaker without specifying context is misleading; moreover, "balanced budgets" and "surpluses" are different fiscal concepts. Given the missing context and potential factual mismatches, the claim as stated is judged false.

claim: "Donald Trump is the first president in modern history (who) did not start a new war."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate because several post‑World War II presidents did not initiate a new large‑scale war before Trump. Examples include Gerald Ford and Jimmy Carter, who avoided starting new major wars, while others (e.g., George H. W. Bush, Clinton, George W. Bush, Obama) did initiate or heavily expand military conflicts. Although Trump did not launch a new major war, he is not the first modern president to avoid doing so.

claim: "Remember that developers are forced to use the ‘195 land union’ contractors, so tap an extra $10 million into any construction project."
rationale: The statement asserts a universal rule that developers are forced to use a specific "195 land union" and that this necessarily adds $10 million to any construction project. There is no known, general rule like this; union/contractor requirements and their cost impacts are specific to particular jurisdictions, redevelopment authorities, or project contracts, and a fixed $10M surcharge is unsupported and implausible without context.

claim: Says "we are overcharging students . . . to help pay for the health care law."
rationale: The statement as a general factual claim is unsupported: the Affordable Care Act did not mandate colleges or universities to ‘overcharge’ students to pay for the law, and there is no broad evidence that students were systematically overcharged for that purpose. While some institutions adjusted student health-plan fees or tuition for various budgetary reasons (including higher healthcare costs), that is not the same as a wide, federal-level policy of overcharging students to fund the health-care law.

claim: "Coolmath Games is being taken down cause it was run by the Mexican drug cartel?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Coolmath Games is operated by a Mexican drug cartel or that any takedown was due to cartel involvement. Coolmath Games is a well-known educational/gaming website run by a private company, and claims linking it to organized crime appear to be misinformation. Reported takedowns or blocks of gaming sites are typically due to school network policies, licensing, domain/hosting issues, or routine business matters, not cartel control.

claim: The United States has experienced "40 straight months of unemployment at 8 percent or higher."
rationale: Official monthly U.S. unemployment (U-3) data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics do not support a continuous 40-month spell at 8% or higher. The rate peaked near 10% in late 2009 during the Great Recession, but the consecutive period at or above 8% was substantially shorter than 40 months according to historical BLS series.

claim: "West Linn has one of the highest per capita rates of home-based businesses in the United States."
rationale: There is no credible national data showing West Linn ranks among the highest U.S. cities by per‑capita home‑based businesses. National sources (Census American Community Survey, SBA) do not list West Linn as a top city for home‑based business rates; claims appear to be local promotional statements rather than verified national comparisons. West Linn may have a relatively high number of home businesses for a city its size, but the stronger claim of being “one of the highest in the United States” is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Gov. Scott Walker (is) more than halfway to (his) 250,000 jobs goal."
rationale: The claim lacks a timeframe and metric, and by commonly reported measures Walker had not clearly achieved more than half of a 250,000‑job target. Walker pledged 250,000 jobs by 2015, but independent employment series (private‑sector and payroll measures) and contested state tallies did not consistently show over 125,000 net jobs attributable to his policies at mid‑term. Because numbers vary by baseline and counting method, the straightforward assertion that he was “more than halfway” is unsupported without qualification.

claim: "Our jobless rate, our unemployment rate, is the lowest of all of the big cities in New Jersey."
rationale: The statement is untestable as phrased because it does not identify which city or what time period is meant; unemployment rates for New Jersey's large cities (e.g., Newark, Jersey City, Paterson, Elizabeth, Camden) fluctuate and no single city consistently records the lowest rate. Without a specific city and date, the claim cannot be verified and is likely false for many plausible timeframes.

claim: Says Jimmy Carter was the last "U.S. president to say flat out those (Israeli) settlements are illegal."
rationale: This is false as stated. While Jimmy Carter has explicitly called Israeli settlements illegal, subsequent U.S. presidents have criticized settlements (calling them "illegitimate," "an obstacle to peace," or a violation of international law via diplomatic actions) but generally avoided publicly saying the settlements were plainly "illegal" while serving as president. The Obama administration allowed a UN Security Council resolution calling settlements a violation of international law, but Obama himself did not "flat out" use the word "illegal."

claim: "After Texas defunded Planned Parenthood, both the unintended pregnancy and abortion rates dropped."
rationale: This is false. Multiple evaluations of Texas’s decision to exclude Planned Parenthood from state family-planning programs found declines in contraceptive services and clients and increases in births (including Medicaid-paid births) among low-income women—consistent with increased unintended pregnancy risk—while any declines in overall abortion counts during the period reflect broader trends and other policy changes, not a clear causal drop due to the defunding. In short, unintended pregnancies did not fall for the affected populations, and the claim that both unintended pregnancy and abortion rates dropped is not supported.

claim: Twenty million Americans are "out of work."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it lacks a timeframe and definition of "out of work." While more than 20 million people were unemployed or filing initial unemployment claims at the peak of the COVID-19 shutdowns in spring 2020, in most other periods (including recent years) the number of unemployed Americans is substantially lower. Without specifying when or what measure is used, the statement cannot be treated as a current factual claim.

claim: After Fahrenheit 9/11 came out, "Bush's approval rating never was better, it only got worse."
rationale: The claim is false because George W. Bush's approval rating did not only decline after Fahrenheit 9/11's June 2004 release; several poll series show his approval rising later in 2004 (notably around and after the November 2004 election) to levels higher than in late June. While his peak approval was much higher immediately after 9/11 in 2001–2002, the absolute statement that it "never was better" after the film is contradicted by polling trends later that year.

claim: "Throughout his time in elected office, Barack Obama has taken multiple positions on banning handguns and the D.C. handgun ban."
rationale: This is true: over his years in elected office Obama made different public statements and policy positions regarding handgun bans and the D.C. handgun law. At various times he voiced support for strict local gun regulations and background checks, while later as a presidential candidate and after the Supreme Court’s Heller decision he acknowledged the Court’s ruling and framed his views differently, showing an evolution and multiple positions. The claim is a broad summary of that change rather than a single specific factual assertion about one vote or quote.

claim: If sea levels rise six feet due to climate change, Waterplace Park in Providence and Wickford village would be swamped
rationale: Both Waterplace Park (a riverside park in downtown Providence at very low elevation near mean sea level) and Wickford village (a historic coastal harbor village) contain large areas only a few feet above current sea level, so a roughly six‑foot rise would inundate or heavily flood those areas. Local topography and built features mean some parcels might remain dry but overall the claim that they would be swamped is consistent with standard sea‑level rise inundation analyses.

claim: "We are now, for the first time ever, energy independent."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. If referring to the United States, it conflates terms and ignores historical data: the U.S. has been a net energy exporter only in recent years by some measures, but it was not the first time ever that the nation produced enough energy for itself (earlier eras were effectively self-sufficient), and “energy independent” is different from temporary net-exporter status. The statement lacks qualifiers (which fuel, which time period) that make it false as an absolute claim.

claim: No one "with a concealed carry permit ever committed a mass shooting."
rationale: The claim is demonstrably false: multiple documented mass shooters in the U.S. were licensed to carry a concealed firearm at the time they committed their crimes. Public records and news investigations have identified specific perpetrators who held state concealed-carry permits, so the absolute statement that no permit-holder ever committed a mass shooting is incorrect.

claim: It "is estimated that as many as 300,000 auto workers may be out of a job before the end of the year."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated and likely false: there is no widely reported, credible estimate that as many as 300,000 auto workers would be out of a job before the end of a given year. Most contemporary industry reports and union notices around major layoff rounds referenced far smaller figures (typically in the thousands to tens of thousands) or gradual reductions over years rather than a single year-end loss of 300,000. Without a cited source, the claim appears to exaggerate the scale and immediacy of job losses.

claim: Says county parties representing more than half the state’s Republican voters approved resolutions "demanding changes" in Texas House leadership.
rationale: Contemporary reporting from Texas news outlets and wire services documented that a broad number of county Republican parties — including several large counties — passed resolutions calling for changes in Texas House GOP leadership, and when tallied those counties account for more than half of the state’s Republican primary voters. The claim matches aggregated counts cited in those reports, though exact totals can shift as more county meetings occur.

claim: More private-sector jobs were created in the second year of the Obama administration than in the eight years of the Bush administration.
rationale: This is false. Bureau of Labor Statistics payroll data show that the total private‑sector job change over George W. Bush’s two terms (the full eight years) exceeded the net private‑sector payroll gains recorded in President Obama’s second year. The claim conflates specific year measurement conventions and omits that comparisons depend on exact start/end months (calendar year vs. presidential year).

claim: "Senator Robert Hurt voted for a bill that’s raised your electric rates seven times."
rationale: This claim is unsupported and misleading. Robert Hurt is better known as a Virginia state legislator and U.S. Representative (not a current U.S. Senator), and there is no documented single vote by him that directly 'raised your electric rates seven times.' Electricity rates are typically adjusted by utilities and public utility commissions, and attributing seven separate rate increases to one legislator's vote lacks evidence and necessary context.

claim: "Governor (Perry), you were a Democrat, having worked for Al Gore as his campaign manager..."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. Rick Perry has been a Republican for his statewide political career and did not serve as Al Gore's campaign manager; Gore's campaign leadership were Democratic operatives, not Perry. Perry's biography shows service as Texas Agriculture Commissioner, Lieutenant Governor and Governor as a Republican, with no role on Gore's campaigns.

claim: "The median income in America has dropped by 10 percent in the last four years."
rationale: This overstates observed changes: available U.S. income series (Census/BLS) do not show a roughly 10% decline in median income across recent four‑year windows through mid‑2024. Year‑to‑year movements have been much smaller and results differ substantially depending on whether the measure is household vs. individual and nominal vs. inflation‑adjusted.

claim: Orrin Hatch co-sponsored a 1993 health care bill that had an individual mandate.
rationale: There is no clear evidence in congressional sponsorship records that Orrin Hatch co‑sponsored a 1993 federal health‑care bill that included a statutory individual mandate. The individual‑mandate idea circulated in various proposals in the late 1980s and 1990s, but attribution of a 1993 co‑sponsorship to Hatch appears to be a mischaracterization or conflation with other bills or later positions.

claim: "Voting in the wrong precinct led to over 14,000 registered voters statewide to lose their vote in 2008."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that voting in the wrong precinct caused over 14,000 registered voters statewide to “lose their vote” in 2008. Election audits and news coverage from that year do not document such a large, single-state impact from wrong-precinct voting; such incidents typically generate far smaller provisional-ballot adjustments. Without a named state or source the claim appears unsubstantiated and unlikely.

claim: "About halfway through fiscal year 2009, Washington has run out of money."
rationale: The claim is not supported as written. If “Washington” means the U.S. federal government, it did not "run out of money" halfway through federal FY2009 (Oct 2008–Sep 2009) — the Treasury continued to meet obligations through borrowing and cash management. If it means the State of Washington, the state experienced budget shortfalls in 2009 but there is no clear evidence it completely exhausted all funds halfway through its FY2009; states typically tap reserves and take budget actions to avoid total insolvency.

claim: "Forty-seven percent of Americans pay no income tax."
rationale: This statement is misleading. The oft-cited “47%” referred to the share of households that paid no federal individual income tax in a specific year (around 2009/2010), not to all Americans or to all types of taxes; many in that group still pay payroll and state/local taxes and the share varies by year. Without specifying year, tax type, and whether it means individuals or households, the claim is inaccurate.

claim: "1 in 4 Rhode Islanders under the age of 65 does not have health insurance."
rationale: This claim is false. Recent U.S. Census American Community Survey and Rhode Island health data show that uninsured rates for Rhode Islanders under 65 have been in the single digits (roughly 4–8% in recent years), not 25%. Rhode Island's Medicaid expansion and ACA-related coverage gains make a 1-in-4 uninsured rate inconsistent with those data.

claim: "59 percent of Americans today believe that Barack Obama is still a Muslim."
rationale: This is false. Multiple reputable national polls over the past decade show far fewer Americans believing Barack Obama is Muslim — typically in the high-teens to low-twenties percent at peak and often lower in later surveys — not 59%. The 59% number does not match established, representative polling and likely arises from a misread, non-representative poll, or deliberate misinformation.

claim: Photo shows Ice Cube and 50 Cent wearing Donald Trump hats.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a genuine photo shows both Ice Cube and 50 Cent wearing Donald Trump hats; images of this kind have circulated as doctored memes and have been debunked in similar cases. The claim likely stems from a manipulated or misattributed image rather than an authentic photograph of the two artists wearing Trump merchandise together.

claim: "You said you went to Delaware State but you forgot the name of your college."
rationale: The claim attributes a specific contradictory statement to an unspecified person but provides no source or evidence. Without an audio/video/transcript or reliable reporting showing the person both said they went to Delaware State and simultaneously forgot the name of their college, the assertion is unverifiable and thus judged false pending corroboration.

claim: "Kim Martin Morrow the CEO of Netflix has just been charged with 15 charges for child pornography"
rationale: This claim is false. Netflix's leadership is publicly known (Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters as co-CEOs, Reed Hastings as former CEO/co-founder), and there is no credible reporting that anyone named Kim Martin Morrow is Netflix's CEO or has been charged with child pornography. A criminal charge of that magnitude against a public company CEO would be widely reported by major news outlets but no such reports exist.

claim: Common Core is "education through Washington D.C."
rationale: The Common Core State Standards were developed and promoted by a state-led initiative (National Governors Association and Council of Chief State School Officers) and were adopted voluntarily by individual states, not imposed by the federal government. The U.S. Department of Education did provide incentives (Race to the Top grants and waiver conditions) that encouraged adoption, but it did not create or directly mandate nationwide implementation, so calling it ‘education through Washington D.C.’ is inaccurate.

claim: Says "I never billed a single hour of my time to the City of Portland in the last 10 years -- so, no revolving door."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented and the conclusion is logically flawed. Without clear attribution, supporting billing/payroll records, or an authoritative audit covering the claimed 10-year period, one cannot confirm that no hours were billed; furthermore, asserting "no revolving door" from a lack of billed hours ignores other forms of compensation or employment that constitute revolving-door activity. Given the ambiguity and lack of evidence, the claim is treated as false/unsupported.

claim: The "3 red stripes" in Joe Biden’s campaign logo refer to a Chinese socialist slogan.
rationale: False. The three red stripes in Biden’s campaign logo form a stylized letter 'E' and have been described as flag-inspired and meant to suggest upward progress; campaign designers and news coverage treat them as American-flag symbolism, not a reference to a Chinese socialist slogan. There is no credible evidence linking the stripes to any Chinese slogan; the claim appears to be a social-media misinterpretation.

claim: The impeachment inquiry hearings "going on behind closed doors over which Congressman Schiff is presiding—they are consistent with the rules" of the U.S. House of Representatives.
rationale: House committees have longstanding authority under House rules to conduct investigations and hold closed-door depositions, and past practice (including the 1974 Nixon inquiry) and legal opinions support that an impeachment inquiry can begin without an initial full House floor vote. Although Republicans disputed the practice and political opponents argued a formal floor authorization was required, the committee-led closed-door proceedings chaired by Rep. Schiff were consistent with House investigatory rules and precedent; the full House later adopted a resolution formalizing procedures.

claim: Says Dennis Miller said that if he didn’t see women protesting the Ghislaine Maxwell trial verdict "you're all frauds. This isn't justice for those women, this is a joke."
rationale: I find no credible reporting, primary source (tweet, clip, interview), or archival record showing Dennis Miller publicly saying that quotation about women protesting the Ghislaine Maxwell verdict. The phrasing does not match known Miller commentary and appears to be uncorroborated or misattributed. Given lack of evidence, the specific quote should be treated as false until a reliable source is produced.

claim: "We know dangerous criminals can slip through immigration at airports just like ours. Yet Joe Donnelly stood right here with the radical left against all efforts to secure our most vulnerable entry points."
rationale: The claim pairs a vague true point (criminals sometimes enter via airports) with a broad, unsupported accusation that Joe Donnelly "stood... with the radical left against all efforts" to secure entry points. Donnelly is a moderate Democrat who has supported some border-security and enforcement measures and there is no evidence he opposed every security effort; the language is partisan hyperbole rather than a factual summary of his record. Therefore the overall claim is false as stated.

claim: "U.S. military at the White House arresting Congress."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the U.S. military is at the White House arresting members of Congress; such an action would be extraordinary and would have been widely reported by major news outlets and official channels. U.S. law and constitutional norms separate military and civilian law enforcement functions, and arrests of federal lawmakers would normally involve civilian authorities and legal processes. The claim conflicts with known reporting and legal constraints, so it is false as stated.

claim: "Jim Justice is the first West Virginia governor to fight for pay raises for educators."
rationale: Jim Justice was a prominent governor who pushed for teacher pay raises during the 2018 statewide strike, but he was not the first West Virginia governor to fight for educator pay increases. Governors before him have proposed, negotiated, and signed teacher pay raises as part of state budgets and education reforms. The claim overstates Justice’s uniqueness in the long history of state-level efforts on teacher compensation.

claim: Says a video shows a "gay party in Italy few weeks before COVID-19."
rationale: The assertion cannot be verified and is likely incorrect: many viral clips have been miscaptioned as showing Italy or a pre‑COVID period, and without video metadata or geolocation there is no evidence this particular clip shows a gay party in Italy a few weeks before COVID‑19. Italy's major outbreak dates to Feb–Mar 2020, and similar footage has been traced to other countries and earlier years, so the specific claim is unsupported.

claim: "But for immigrants, we would have a contracting population..."
rationale: The claim is overly general: whether a population would be contracting without immigrants depends on the specific country and timeframe. Many high-income nations with below-replacement fertility would decline without immigration, but others (or the same countries in different periods) may still have natural increase or demographic momentum that prevents immediate contraction. As stated, the assertion is not universally true.

claim: "CBO reports that delaying the Obamacare individual mandate will reduce the deficit by $35 billion over ten years."
rationale: This is false. The Congressional Budget Office did not report that delaying the Obamacare individual mandate would cut the deficit by $35 billion over ten years; CBO analyses have instead indicated that weakening or repealing the individual mandate increases federal deficits (by large amounts over a decade) and raises the uninsured. The $35 billion figure appears to conflate or misstate other estimates (for different mandates, timing, or scores) rather than reflect a CBO finding about the individual mandate.

claim: Says Tim Tebow wrote, "The government might be preparing us for a cashless society, but it was predicted by the Bible."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Tim Tebow wrote or posted the quoted line; the phrase appears on memes and social posts that have been widely misattributed. While Tebow frequently shares Christian views, searches of his verified accounts and fact-checking reports do not show this exact statement originating from him.

claim: "Smartmatic and Dominion systems ... were built to do this very thing, for changing the results of elections."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Smartmatic or Dominion voting systems were intentionally built to change election results. Multiple independent audits, hand recounts, bipartisan election officials, cybersecurity experts, and court findings in related defamation cases have found no proof of deliberate manipulation by those vendors. Claims of intentional design are conspiracy assertions unsupported by the available investigations.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "knows full well I voted for his amendment to increase military spending to $697 billion."
rationale: There is no clear public record that Senator Marco Rubio offered an amendment specifically to increase military spending to exactly $697 billion or that a named lawmaker publicly acknowledged voting for such an amendment. Defense spending totals and floor amendments are widely reported and the precise $697 billion figure and vote attribution do not match known amendments or roll-call records. Given the lack of supporting evidence, the claim is likely false.

claim: "There's no court session between now and the end of this election."
rationale: The claim is unverified and implausible as stated because it provides no jurisdiction or specific election timeline; courts at different levels and locations set their own calendars and many continue to sit during election periods. Without specifying which court and which election, the blanket statement cannot be supported and is likely false in most contexts.

claim: "More Texans have jobs today than ever before in the history of our state."
rationale: State and federal labor data through 2023–mid‑2024 show Texas payroll employment reached and exceeded prior historical highs, so the statement that more Texans have jobs now than ever before matches those records. The claim is commonly based on Texas Workforce Commission and BLS nonfarm payroll totals, which hit all‑time highs in that period.

claim: Says that singer Dolly Parton said, "Trump in one year is already better than 16 years of Bush, Obama put together."
rationale: There is no record in reputable news media, interviews, or transcripts of Dolly Parton making this statement; the quote circulated as an unattributed social‑media meme and has been debunked by fact‑checkers. Parton has generally avoided partisan endorsements, and major fact‑checking outlets found no evidence she said Trump was "better than 16 years of Bush, Obama put together."

claim: "A portion of everything you pay A.A.R.P goes directly to the Democratic Party."
rationale: AARP does not automatically divert a portion of every member payment to the Democratic Party. AARP is a nonprofit advocacy organization that engages in lobbying and issue advocacy; it also operates a separate political action committee that makes candidate contributions funded by voluntary political donations, not by mandatory dues. While AARP’s political spending and PAC contributions have tended to favor Democrats in recent cycles, that is not the same as taking a portion of every payment and sending it directly to the Democratic Party.

claim: "More than 20 million people are at risk of dying from starvation within 6 months in 4 nations."
rationale: This matches repeated warnings from the UN and major humanitarian agencies (WFP/OCHA) in 2022 stating that more than 20 million people in four countries — commonly listed as Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and Ethiopia — were at risk of starvation and could die within months without urgent aid. The core numeric claim and the 'four nations' framing reflect those official statements, though exact timelines and caseloads can change with new aid or worsening conditions.

claim: "In March 2020 the United States deployed 30,000 troops to Europe to ... free child-trafficked children and arrest deep state cabal members."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or Department of Defense record that the United States deployed 30,000 troops to Europe in March 2020 for operations to free trafficked children or to arrest a so‑called "deep state" cabal. Major news organizations and official military communications from that period document troop movements related to routine NATO rotations, posture changes (e.g., prior drawdowns in Germany), and COVID‑19 responses, not a large law‑enforcement or rescue mission of that type. The claim matches QAnon-style conspiracy narratives and is contradicted by the absence of any verifiable official reporting or corroborating evidence.

claim: Says more Austinites voted in the city’s 1973 election featuring a mayor’s race than in the city’s most recent mayoral election.
rationale: This is unlikely to be true. Austin's population and registered voter rolls have grown substantially since 1973, and contemporary mayoral elections in Austin have produced higher raw vote totals than would have been typical in the early 1970s, so more people voted in the most recent mayoral election than in 1973.

claim: Says David Jolly’s former firm lobbied "for hundreds of millions (of dollars) for a dictator in Pakistan."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that David Jolly’s former employer lobbied on behalf of a Pakistani dictator to obtain "hundreds of millions" of dollars. Reporting on Jolly’s pre-congressional work shows roles at communications and lobbying firms but does not document representation of a Pakistani dictator or securing funds at that scale. The statement appears to conflate or exaggerate unrelated lobbying activity.

claim: Mitt Romney "said it was 'tragic' to end the war in Iraq."
rationale: This is a mischaracterization. Romney criticized a premature U.S. withdrawal from Iraq and warned that leaving too soon would be damaging or "tragic," but he did not assert that ending the war itself was "tragic." The phrase has been taken out of context from remarks opposing a hurried pullout rather than condemning the end of the war outright.

claim: "We have more hospitals that are children’s hospitals than any other state in the union." 
rationale: The claim is presented without specifying which state or timeframe and there is no widely known evidence that any single state unambiguously has more children’s hospitals than all others. Counts of pediatric or children’s hospitals vary by definition (freestanding vs. hospital units) and by data source, so the statement is unverified and likely incorrect as a blanket assertion. Without a precise state and a clear, sourced tally the claim cannot be accepted as true.

claim: The U.S. spends "57 cents on the dollar on defense."
rationale: The claim is misleading as stated. Defense spending is roughly 50–60% of discretionary spending in some recent years (so one could say about 57 cents of each discretionary dollar), but it is only about 10–20% of total federal spending overall — far less than 57 cents on every federal dollar. Without specifying “discretionary” the statement is inaccurate.

claim: Photos show "diesel generators" at the COP26 climate change conference.
rationale: Verified images circulating during COP26 did show diesel-powered generators on or near the Glasgow conference site. Fact-checks and news reports confirmed the units were present (largely serving broadcasters and temporary facilities), though that does not mean the entire summit was powered by them.

claim: "A law enforcement officer is more likely to commit a crime than a CWP (concealed weapons permit) holder."
rationale: There is no robust evidence showing law enforcement officers as a group commit crimes at higher rates than concealed carry permit (CWP) holders. Empirical studies and background-check requirements indicate CWP holders generally have lower arrest and conviction rates than the general population, and law enforcement employment screens and professional sanctions also tend to keep officer criminality relatively low. A direct nationwide comparison showing officers are more likely to commit crimes than permit holders is lacking.

claim: Wall Street megabanks that received bailouts in 2009 now get taxpayer-funded advantages not available to community banks in Ohio.
rationale: Large Wall Street banks that were rescued in 2008–09 continue to enjoy advantages tied to government backstops that community banks typically do not: implicit 'too big to fail' subsidies that lower their funding costs, access to Federal Reserve liquidity facilities and primary-dealer or large-counterparty privileges, and regulatory backstops sized to systemically important firms. Community banks in Ohio generally do not receive those same implicit guarantees or market privileges, even though they have the same deposit-insurance coverage.

claim: "Less mass shootings under Trump!"
rationale: The claim is false as stated. Publicly available compilations (e.g., major gun-violence trackers) show that incidents meeting common definitions of "mass shooting" (often 4+ people shot) rose during the Trump presidency (2017–2020) compared with many prior years, and several of those years were among the highest on record. The statement also omits a clear timeframe and definition, and under alternative, narrower definitions (e.g., 4+ killed) counts differ but do not support the broad claim without qualification.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said: "While there may have been an age difference, Josh Duggar’s transgressions are far less an affront to God than what gays do to each other."
rationale: There is no reliable record or contemporaneous reporting attributing that specific quote to Ted Cruz. Major news outlets and fact-checkers covering reactions to the Josh Duggar revelations did not report Cruz saying words like that; the phrasing appears to be a misattribution or fabricated quote. Given Cruz’s public statements on homosexuality, a paraphrase might be plausible, but the exact sentence has not been substantiated.

claim: Terry McAuliffe favors "taking the Pledge of Allegiance and the 4th of July out of the (school) curriculum."
rationale: There is no public record, policy proposal, or verified quote showing Terry McAuliffe advocated removing the Pledge of Allegiance or the 4th of July from school curriculum. Major fact-checking organizations and news reports that examined similar circulating claims found them to be distortions or mischaracterizations of other remarks about curriculum and instruction. The claim appears to be a misrepresentation rather than a documented position.

claim: "There has never been an alderman who has defeated an incumbent mayor in the history of this great city."
rationale: The statement is an absolute historical claim but gives no city or timeframe, making it effectively unverifiable as written. More importantly, in municipal politics it is common for sitting city council members or aldermen to challenge and sometimes defeat incumbent mayors, so a blanket assertion that this has "never" happened is very unlikely to be true without specific evidence. The burden of proof is on the claimant to name the city and provide comprehensive historical records to support such a universal negative.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott's approval ratings are up.
rationale: The claim provides no timeframe, source, or poll data to verify that Gov. Rick Scott’s approval ratings are currently higher. Approval ratings are measured by specific polls and can vary over time and by pollster; without a cited survey it cannot be confirmed. Because the statement is unsourced and ambiguous, it is treated as not verifiable and therefore labeled false.

claim: "Like every budget passed by the Senate since I have been lieutenant governor, Senate Bill 1 is within the spending limit set by the Texas Constitution."
rationale: The statement overclaims certainty. Whether a Senate budget 'is within the spending limit' depends on the accounting basis used (the Texas constitutional limit applies to general revenue‑related funds and is tied to the comptroller's certified estimate), and independent analyses and disputes have shown Senate proposals can appear compliant under one methodology but exceed the constitutional limit under the comptroller’s standard. Because the claim asserts consistent compliance for every Senate budget since his tenure and unambiguously asserts SB1 is within the limit, it is misleading without specifying the accounting method and certification status.

claim: "Pre-existing conditions are covered under my (health care) plan."
rationale: The statement as a blanket claim is false because whether pre-existing conditions are covered depends on the specific health plan, policy type, and applicable laws. In many places (for example, most individual and employer plans in the U.S. under the Affordable Care Act) insurers cannot deny coverage or charge more for pre-existing conditions, but some plans (short‑term plans, certain grandfathered or limited benefit plans, or plans in other jurisdictions) may exclude them. Always verify the specific policy language and legal protections that apply to your plan.

claim: Arnold Schwarzenegger slept on the ground in front of a bronze statue of himself because he had been turned away from a hotel.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence or mainstream reporting that Schwarzenegger literally slept on the ground in front of a bronze statue of himself after being turned away from a hotel. While Arnold has recounted various stories about being refused service early in his career and there is a statue in his honor, reputable biographies and news accounts do not corroborate the specific episode described and the statue was erected after he became famous. The claim appears to conflate or exaggerate separate events.

claim: "If Sen. Hillary Clinton could enact all of her campaign proposals, taxpayers would be faced with financing more than $777.6-billion in new spending over one White House term."
rationale: The statement presents a precise $777.6 billion figure without citing which proposals were counted or whether offsets (tax increases, savings) were included. Independent cost estimates for Hillary Clinton’s 2007–2008-era campaign proposals varied widely and many proposals were revenue-offset or phased, so an authoritative single ‘‘taxpayer financing’’ total of $777.6 billion is misleading. Fact-checks at the time flagged such aggregated sums as selective and lacking necessary context.

claim: Actions by Joe Biden left "10,000 - 15,000 American citizens abandoned to terrorists in Afghanistan."
rationale: No credible evidence supports that 10,000–15,000 American citizens were left in Afghanistan. U.S. government statements and multiple independent fact-checks reported the number of U.S. citizens remaining after the evacuation was in the low hundreds or fewer, and claims of thousands conflated Afghan nationals, visa holders, or people unaccounted for with U.S. citizens.

claim: "The pension fund in the city of Providence is only 30 percent funded, about the same level as when he [Taveras] took office."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Public records and news reports show Providence’s pension funded ratio was roughly in the high 20s–low 30s around 2011 when Mayor Ángel Taveras took office, but the reported funded level fluctuated and by later years (mid‑2010s) had moved somewhat above 30% depending on the valuation method; different measurement conventions (market vs. actuarial) produce different percentages. Saying it was “only 30 percent… about the same level” glosses over these variations and timing, so the blanket claim is not accurate.

claim: "We got a million jobs."
rationale: The claim "We got a million jobs." is too vague to verify because it does not identify who "we" refers to or the timeframe. Employment claims must be checked against official payroll or unemployment statistics for a specified period; without that context this statement is unverified and treated as false. If given an actor and dates, it could be checked and potentially shown true or false.

claim: An independent payment advisory board created by the health care reform law "can ration care and deny certain Medicare treatments."
rationale: The ACA-created Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) was barred by statute from making recommendations that would ration care, restrict benefits or change eligibility, and its proposals would take effect only if Congress did not enact alternatives achieving equivalent savings. Thus it did not have direct authority to deny specific Medicare treatments. Critics argued cost-cutting recommendations could indirectly affect access, but that is different from explicit power to ration or deny treatments.

claim: The United States is "the only advanced country on Earth" that doesn’t guarantee "paid maternity leave to our workers."
rationale: At the federal level the United States does not guarantee paid maternity leave; the Family and Medical Leave Act guarantees unpaid leave for eligible workers. By contrast virtually all other high-income/‘advanced’ countries (and OECD members) have national laws providing paid maternity or parental leave. That makes the US unique among advanced economies in lacking a nationwide paid maternity-leave guarantee.

claim: "We have the lowest beer tax in the nation."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement but gives no jurisdiction or time frame, so it cannot be verified as true. U.S. states and localities set different beer excise taxes and several states have very low or zero beer taxes, making an unqualified "lowest in the nation" claim unlikely without specifics.

claim: President Joe Biden withdrew troops from Afghanistan "simply because of Trump Derangement Syndrome and they wanted to reverse any policy that Trump had implemented."
rationale: The claim attributes the withdrawal solely to partisan animus rather than policy or security considerations; this is misleading. The Biden administration implemented and completed a pullout that followed the 2020 U.S.-Taliban agreement negotiated under Trump and publicly justified the withdrawal on ending the "forever war," military assessments, and logistical timelines, not an explicit desire simply to reverse Trump's actions. While partisan politics played a role in public debate, there is no credible evidence the decision was made "simply" out of personal or partisan spite.

claim: "Over 60 percent of the provisional ballots cast in [the 2012] election were disqualified because those folks were not duly registered as voters."
rationale: This claim conflates different measures and overstates the count. Nationwide 2012 data (from election administration surveys) show far fewer provisional ballots were rejected overall, and while a substantial share of rejected provisional ballots were due to voters not being registered, that share refers to rejected ballots—not to over 60% of all provisional ballots cast. The statement as written (that over 60% of provisional ballots cast were disqualified for lack of registration) is not supported by the available national-level data.

claim: Insulin prices have "gone THRU THE ROOF for patients/taxpayers bc of manufacturer, health plan & PBM biz practices."
rationale: U.S. insulin list prices and patient out‑of‑pocket costs have risen sharply over the past decade, and multiple analyses and government reports identify manufacturer price increases plus health‑plan and PBM rebate/contracting practices as major contributors to those higher costs. Those practices (high list prices, opaque rebates, incentives that favor higher list prices) have also increased public spending through Medicare, Medicaid, and other programs, so the claim that prices have “gone through the roof” because of these actors is supported.

claim: Says TriMet spends "$10.3 million in police contracts" a year for 56 transit police who must respond to non-transit calls
rationale: The claim conflates different budget and staffing items and overstates the duty obligations. TriMet has in the past had roughly that order of magnitude of sworn transit officers and also pays for policing/contracted public safety, but the $10.3 million figure and the statement that 56 transit police “must respond to non‑transit calls” is misleading: contract dollars can cover multiple agencies/services and budgets vary by year, and TriMet transit police have primary jurisdiction on transit property and normally coordinate with local police on off‑property/non‑transit incidents rather than being required to respond to all non‑transit calls. Without a specific year and budget line, the precise dollar/staffing/response claim is not supported.

claim: Paul Ryan "is one of only six House Republicans who voted for Teddy Kennedy's bill to force Christian employers to hire LGBT employees."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. Edward (Ted) Kennedy sponsored iterations of the Employment Non-Discrimination Act in the Senate, but Paul Ryan’s congressional voting record does not show him as one of a small handful of House Republicans who voted for such a Kennedy-led bill; Ryan has generally opposed ENDA-style measures. The statement appears to conflate different bills, years, and a partisan framing about “forcing” religious employers.

claim: Romney refused to pardon "a decorated soldier" returning from Iraq who had been charged with a crime involving a BB gun when he was 13.
rationale: I can find no contemporaneous record or trustworthy reporting showing Governor Mitt Romney rejected a pardon request specifically for a ‘decorated soldier’ returning from Iraq over a BB‑gun incident at age 13. Gubernatorial pardon records and media coverage of high‑profile veteran pardon requests during Romney’s term do not document such a denial, and a refusal of that nature would likely have generated news attention. The claim appears to be unsupported or conflated with a different case.

claim: "Military tribunals start Jan. 20, 2021."
rationale: There is no evidence that U.S. military tribunals began on January 20, 2021; major news organizations, official government records, and court dockets do not show a mass or new start of military trials on that date. The claim appears to echo conspiracy narratives that predicted tribunals tied to the 2021 inauguration, which did not occur.

claim: The United States "is the only major country that taxes its own exports."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. The U.S. federal government is constitutionally prohibited from imposing export taxes, and several other countries have at times imposed export duties or taxes on particular commodities, so the U.S. is not uniquely taxing exports. The statement likely confuses different tax topics or misstates U.S. policy.

claim: We live in "a time of historically low violent crime rates and historically high gun ownership rates nationally."
rationale: The claim mixes two different trends and is misleading. While violent crime is far below its peaks in the late 20th century, violent crime (and homicides) rose notably in 2020–2021 and remain above the mid-2010s troughs, so describing the present as unambiguously a time of "historically low" violent crime is inaccurate. Likewise, there are record-high counts of guns and surges in purchases/background checks recently, but survey measures of household gun ownership have not consistently reached historical peaks, so the broad phrase "historically high gun ownership rates" is ambiguous and overstated.

claim: "Welders make more money than philosophers."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. Earnings vary by country, experience, and job type: many welders earn mid-range wages, but many philosophers (typically postsecondary philosophy professors) often earn as much or more, while some philosophy-related roles (adjuncts, graduate students) earn less. Because outcomes overlap and depend on definitions and context, the categorical claim is not generally true.

claim: Says Donald Trump "himself has a financial stake in the French company that makes the brand-name version of hydroxychloroquine."
rationale: Sanofi, a French firm, makes the brand Plaquenil (hydroxychloroquine), but Donald Trump’s public financial disclosures and contemporaneous fact-checks found no evidence he personally owned Sanofi stock. While mutual funds or ETFs in which he had indirect interests might hold shares of many companies, that is not the same as Trump himself having a direct financial stake in Sanofi. The claim therefore misstates the nature of any indirect exposure.

claim: "While Exxon Mobil has 40 pages on its media response strategy, its plan for resource protection is only five pages long and its plan for oil removal is just nine pages long."
rationale: There is no readily verifiable, authoritative source showing a single Exxon Mobil plan with exactly 40 pages for media response, five pages for resource protection, and nine pages for oil removal. Response-plan lengths vary by document, jurisdiction, and version, and the claim provides no citation or timeframe, so it is unverified and likely misleading without the original document.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s polling numbers show that he’s "the highest with Hispanics that any Republican has ever been."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that Trump’s Hispanic support is higher than that of any Republican in history; available polling and historical exit-poll data do not conclusively support that. Different polls produce varying Hispanic shares for Trump (and for past Republicans), and historical Republicans such as Richard Nixon and Ronald Reagan recorded comparable or higher Hispanic shares in some surveys, so the assertion that Trump is the highest ever is not supported as a definitive fact.

claim: "Only five Texas counties account for almost 90 percent of the (state’s) cattle industry."
rationale: The claim is not supported by available information—Texas has millions of cattle spread across hundreds of counties, and USDA/NASS county-level data show the largest counties hold only modest shares of the total. It is implausible that five counties would account for nearly 90% of the state's cattle inventory or production; no credible data source reports such an extreme concentration.

claim: "In campaigns in the past with Sen. McCain and President George W. Bush and others, they have tended to release tax records in April."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. While some candidates sometimes release tax returns near the April tax‑filing season, there is no consistent pattern that Sen. McCain, President George W. Bush and other named politicians routinely released tax records in April across their campaigns. Release dates have varied by campaign year and candidate, so saying they 'tended' to do so is not supported.

claim: Most of Kathy Manning’s donors are from out-of-state.
rationale: I cannot confirm that a majority of Kathy Manning’s donors are from out-of-state without checking FEC/OpenSecrets records. Most public claims about donor geography require specifying whether they mean the number of individual donors or the share of dollars and over what time period; such evidence is not presented here. Given that House members commonly receive substantial in-state support, the broad claim is unproven and thus judged false absent data.

claim: "There's not a major bill I know with Hillary's name on it."
rationale: There is no widely known, landmark federal law commonly referred to by Hillary Clinton’s name. While Clinton sponsored and co-sponsored bills as senator, none became major statutes eponymously named for her, and major 21st-century laws are known by other names. Thus the claim that there isn’t a major bill with her name on it is accurate in ordinary usage.

claim: The Obama administration "raised discretionary spending by 24 percent from President George W. Bush's last full-year budget and will run up more debt by October than Bush did in eight years."
rationale: The statement mixes incompatible measures and overstates the case. The “24 percent” figure depends on a selective comparison of budget authority measures and is not supported by standard outlay or consistent-year comparisons of discretionary spending; using commonly reported outlays the increase is substantially smaller. Likewise, President Bush’s eight-year increase in federal debt was on the order of several trillion dollars, and Obama’s accumulated debt by the following October did not exceed Bush’s eight‑year total — the claim conflates timeframes and accounting definitions.

claim: A Fox News affiliate reported on a shooting before it happened.
rationale: The claim is too vague and no verifiable, widely reported instance was found of a Fox News affiliate reliably publishing a report of a shooting that happened after the report (i.e., reporting it before it occurred). News organizations sometimes issue erroneous or premature alerts and later correct them, but that is different from a verified case of predicting or reporting an event before it happened. Without a specific time, place, or citation, the assertion cannot be substantiated and is likely false or a misunderstanding.

claim: Says BLM activist Sasha Johnson tweeted, "The white man will not be our equal but our slave."
rationale: This claim is false. Independent fact-checkers reviewed the alleged tweet and found no record of Sasha Johnson posting it; the circulating screenshot was determined to be fabricated and there is no evidence from her verified accounts or reputable news reports that she tweeted that phrase. The attribution has been repeatedly debunked and Johnson has not been shown to have authored the quote.

claim: "The claim ... that we plan to set up panels of bureaucrats with the power to  kill off senior citizens ... is a lie, plain and simple."
rationale: Claims that the government planned to create panels of bureaucrats with the authority to kill off senior citizens have been repeatedly debunked. Relevant legislation (notably the Affordable Care Act) contained provisions for voluntary advance-care planning and advisory bodies but no statutory authority to authorize killing, and reputable fact-checkers found no evidence of such a plan.

claim: Says only about 250 Texans have been killed in action since 9/11.
rationale: This strongly understates the number. Department of Defense casualty totals for post‑9/11 conflicts number in the multiple thousands, and state-level breakdowns and news compilations show that the number of service members identified as from Texas killed in action is well above 250 (hundreds, commonly reported in the high hundreds to over a thousand depending on definition and timeframe). Therefore the claim that only about 250 Texans have been killed is incorrect.

claim: Before COVID-19, "Iowa had one of the lowest unemployment rates in the country, and many employers were scrambling to find qualified employees to fill their job openings."
rationale: BLS state unemployment data from 2019 and early 2020 show Iowa’s unemployment rate among the lowest in the nation, and contemporaneous news reports and employer surveys documented widespread difficulty filling open positions. Together these sources support the two-part claim that Iowa had low unemployment pre-COVID-19 and that many employers were scrambling to find qualified workers.

claim: "In (Sen. Marco) Rubio's state of Florida alone, Social Security lifts more than -- count it -- a million people out of poverty."
rationale: Official analyses of Social Security’s effect on poverty indicate the program keeps on the order of a million people in Florida out of poverty; state-level tabulations in the mid‑2010s show roughly 1.0–1.2 million Floridians are lifted above the poverty line by Social Security. While exact totals vary by year and methodology, the claim that Social Security lifts “more than a million” people in Florida is supported by government and policy‑research data.

claim: "The Parole Board operates with Mark Herring’s advice and consent."
rationale: The phrase “advice and consent” refers to a legislative confirmation role, not to a state attorney general. Parole board members are appointed by the governor (and in many states confirmed by the legislature), whereas Mark Herring, as attorney general, does not have statutory authority to give advice-and-consent for Parole Board appointments. The AG can provide legal opinions but does not perform confirmations.

claim: Property taxes "are now 18% higher than when (Mark Sharpe) first took office."
rationale: I cannot confirm the claim that property taxes are 18% higher since Mark Sharpe first took office because no specific jurisdiction, baseline year, or metric (tax rate vs. tax bill vs. assessed value vs. total revenue) is provided and I have no corroborating data. Absent clear, cited local tax records showing an 18% increase over the exact period, the assertion is unsupported and therefore treated as false.

claim: "We have laws on the books where people can walk right up to our ports of entry, say ‘I have a credible fear of persecution,’ and we bring them in. We don’t send them back."
rationale: This statement mischaracterizes U.S. asylum law. Federal law requires a "credible fear" screening for people encountered at ports of entry or after interdiction and bars immediate summary return if a credible fear is found, but it does not automatically "bring them in" as permanent residents or prevent later removal; individuals are referred to immigration court and can be detained, released on bond/parole, or removed if their claim fails. Saying "we don’t send them back" is therefore misleading.

claim: Florida drivers who have their cell phones "in hand" can be ticketed $250 and sent to "driving school."
rationale: This claim is not accurate as a blanket statement: Florida law does not automatically impose a $250 fine and mandatory attendance at a driving school merely for having a cell phone “in hand.” Penalties for handheld cellphone or texting violations in Florida vary by statute, offense history, and local enforcement, and mandatory driving-school enrollment is not a universal, fixed consequence for a single handheld-phone violation.

claim: "George Bush never suggested that we eliminate funding for Planned Parenthood."
rationale: The absolute claim that “George Bush never suggested” cutting Planned Parenthood funding is incorrect. The George W. Bush administration reinstated the Mexico City Policy (which limits U.S. funding to organizations that provide or promote abortion) and Bush repeatedly supported restricting federal funding for organizations that perform abortions, positions that were interpreted as targeting Planned Parenthood; Republican legislative efforts during his presidency also sought to curb Planned Parenthood funding. Therefore it is not accurate to say he never suggested eliminating such funding.

claim: Iowa has "the highest high-school graduation rate in the country."
rationale: The claim as stated is misleading because it gives no timeframe or metric and is not consistently true. National graduation-rate data (NCES adjusted cohort graduation rates) fluctuate year-to-year and several states (e.g., New Jersey, Wisconsin, Massachusetts and others) have held or tied for the top rate in different recent years; Iowa is often near the top but is not reliably the single highest state. Without a specific year or definition, asserting Iowa has the highest rate is inaccurate.

claim: "In 2010, everybody said you can't dare let guns go into the national parks, and of course the rapes, murders, robberies and assaults are down about 85 percent since we did that."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a 2010 nationwide policy allowing guns in national parks occurred and no reliable data showing rapes, murders, robberies and assaults in national parks fell about 85% after such a change. National Park Service and FBI statistics show low and variable numbers of violent incidents in parks and no abrupt, uniform 85% decline tied to a 2010 policy; the claim conflates policy, geography, and dramatic crime-change numbers that are not supported by available data.

claim: "The average Republican voter thinks there should be some revenue as part of this deal."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it lacks definition of “this deal” and provides no citation to a poll or study showing a majority or average Republican view. Public opinion among Republicans varies by issue and by how questions are worded, so a blanket claim about the "average Republican voter" cannot be assumed true without specific survey evidence. Therefore the claim is not supported as presented.

claim: Says Jeb Bush "said he would take his pants off and moon everybody ... Nobody reports that."
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or major news reporting that Jeb Bush ever said he would 'take his pants off and moon everybody.' The claim appears to be an unverified or misattributed quotation rather than a documented statement by Bush, so it should be treated as false unless a reliable source is produced.

claim: Four million women have fallen into poverty in the last six years.
rationale: The claim gives no country or baseline and I am unaware of any reputable dataset that reports exactly “four million women” falling into poverty over the last six years as a standalone global or national fact. Poverty statistics are reported by country, measure (income, consumption, or poverty line), and time period; aggregated figures that precise would require specific context and citation. Without that context or supporting authoritative source, the claim cannot be verified and is likely false.

claim: If COVID-19 was real, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge wouldn’t have been "allowed to join 50,000 other football fans inside a stadium."
rationale: The claim asserts a universal rule that large stadium gatherings could not occur if COVID‑19 were real; that is false. Throughout the pandemic public-health rules changed over time and many countries permitted large crowds again once transmission fell, vaccinations rose, or mitigations (testing, masks, distancing) were in place, and members of the royal family did attend high‑attendance events during those periods. Whether a particular appearance was ‘‘allowed’’ depended on timing and local policy, not on the virus’s reality.

claim: Hillary Clinton wants to "wave the white flag of surrender and set a date for withdrawal."
rationale: This characterization is incorrect. Hillary Clinton has generally opposed unconditional withdrawal timetables and instead promoted conditions‑based drawdowns and continued engagement (for example supporting the Afghanistan surge and criticizing fixed withdrawal dates). She has not publicly advocated ‘waving a white flag’ or simply setting a withdrawal date as a policy prescription.

claim: Water rates in Manila, Philippines, "were raised up to 845 percent" when a subsidiary of the World Bank became a partial owner.
rationale: The claim is misleading. While water tariffs in Metro Manila rose substantially after the 1997 privatization (and some activist sources cite very large cumulative percentage increases over many years), the jump was the result of concession contract terms, regulatory adjustments and macro factors (e.g., peso devaluation), not a single immediate 845% increase tied to a World Bank subsidiary 'becoming a partial owner.' The World Bank Group’s private-sector arm (IFC) has provided financing/advice but was not simply a trigger for an instant 845% rate hike as stated.

claim: Forty percent of union members voted Republican in 2008.
rationale: The claim is not precisely correct. 2008 exit polls and survey summaries reported that union voters/union households leaned decisively toward Obama, with the Republican share typically reported in the low-to-mid 40 percent range depending on the source and definition, not exactly 40 percent. The precise percentage varies by dataset and by whether one counts 'union members' or 'union households.'

claim: Says Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ted Cruz "opposes the DREAM Act, which is supported by 85% of Latinos."
rationale: Ted Cruz has a public record of opposing the DREAM Act and similar legislative amnesty measures. Multiple polls over the past decade have shown very strong Latino support for DREAM Act-style relief, frequently in the 80%-range, so the combined claim is supported though exact percentages vary by poll and year.

claim: "Over the past decade, drug prices have risen at three times the rate of inflation."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it lacks a clear measure and timeframe and is not uniformly true. Consumer-price-index measures show prescription drug prices have often risen faster than overall inflation, but typically by less than three times, and when net prices (after rebates) or different drug categories are used the gap is smaller or reverses. Thus the blanket claim that drug prices rose at three times the rate of inflation over the past decade is not supported without more specific definitions and dates.

claim: "Already this calendar year, since January 1, we have had more than 20,000 people come across the border, apprehended, unauthorized."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverified and ambiguous: it gives no date of utterance or which border/jurisdiction is meant. U.S. Customs and Border Protection publishes monthly encounter totals, and many recent months have exceeded 20,000 encounters, but without a specific reporting period the statement cannot be confirmed. Therefore the claim as presented is not reliably supported.

claim: "Barron Trump was born in March 2006 and Melania wasn’t a legal citizen until July 2006. So under this executive order, his own son wouldn’t be an American citizen."
rationale: Barron Trump was born in New York City on March 20, 2006, and anyone born on U.S. soil is generally a U.S. citizen under the 14th Amendment regardless of a parent’s immigration or naturalization status. Even if Melania Trump was not yet a naturalized citizen at that time, that does not negate birthright citizenship. An executive order cannot unilaterally nullify constitutional birthright citizenship without being overturned or amended through the courts and Congress.

claim: "The public option is not funded with public money. It's funded with private insurance premiums."
rationale: The statement is too absolute. While many public option proposals envision enrollees paying premiums similar to private plans, some designs include government subsidies, use of federal or state funds for start-up costs or to cover losses, and could rely on taxpayer money for subsidies or risk pools. Therefore it is incorrect to claim categorically that a public option is not funded with any public money.

claim: "Why was there no news coverage of this raid on the Arizona border? … Seizure was just five days ago. Right on the Arizona border!"
rationale: The claim that there was "no news coverage" of a recent raid/seizure on the Arizona border is unsupported and unlikely. Border raids and seizures are commonly reported by local Arizona outlets, regional TV affiliates, and national wire services; without a specific date, location, or identifying details it is not credible to assert there was zero coverage. Saying the seizure occurred "just five days ago" is unverifiable in this form and does not prove widespread silence by the press.

claim: Says Alex Sink "failed Florida homeowners by using predatory lending practices."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Alex Sink personally engaged in or implemented 'predatory lending practices.' Sink served as Florida Chief Financial Officer and was not a lender; accusations of predatory behavior have appeared in partisan ads but are unsupported by documented actions showing she used predatory lending. The claim conflates political rhetoric with proven misconduct.

claim: "The Democrat controlled House never even asked John Bolton to testify."
rationale: House Democrats did seek John Bolton’s evidence and asked him to testify during the 2019 impeachment inquiry; Bolton’s lawyer publicly said he would comply with a subpoena. While Bolton did not end up giving public testimony before the Senate trial (Republicans and the White House resisted), the claim that Democrats “never even asked” him is incorrect.

claim: Says Donald Trump said, "Make no mistake: They’re not after me. They are after you; your guns, your Christian values, your freedom. I’m just in their way."
rationale: There is no verifiable record of Donald Trump saying that exact sentence verbatim. While Trump has repeatedly used rhetoric claiming opponents are targeting voters’ guns, religious/Christian values, and freedoms, the quoted line appears to be a paraphrase or synthesis rather than an attributable, word-for-word quote from a recorded speech or transcript. Without a primary-source citation (video/transcript) the claim that he said those exact words is unsupported.

claim: "I investigated Abramoff and people ended up in jail."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because it credits an unspecified “I” with conducting investigations that led to jail sentences. Public records show Jack Abramoff and several associates were convicted after investigations by prosecutors, the FBI, congressional committees and journalists, but there is no evidence that an unnamed individual personally conducted those investigations and directly caused the convictions.
